law-of-torts-u1-t6.subtitle: How a tort differs from a crime and from a breach of contract, and when one act is more than one wrong

en.inOneMinute: A tort, a crime and a breach of contract are three different wrongs. A tort breaks a duty fixed by law and is remedied by damages. A crime is a public wrong that the State punishes. A breach of contract breaks a duty the parties created by agreement. One act can be more than one wrong. A reckless driver can face a criminal case and a civil suit at once. Examiners ask for the comparison table and for the statement that all torts are civil wrongs but not all civil wrongs are torts.
legalProvision: Section 2(m), Limitation Act, 1963: a tort is a civil wrong that is not exclusively a breach of contract or trust. Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: defines the crimes and their punishments. It replaced the Indian Penal Code from 1 July 2024. Sections 73 and 74, Indian Contract Act, 1872: compensation for breach of contract, and liquidated damages or penalty named in the contract. Section 395, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (earlier section 357, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973): a criminal court may order that fine money be paid as compensation to the victim. Where no fine is imposed, it may order the accused to pay compensation directly (section 395(3)). It does not replace a civil suit.
en.meaning:
A tort is a private civil wrong. A crime is a public wrong made an offence by law. A breach of contract is a failure to perform a promise made by agreement.

All three are wrongs, but the law treats each differently. The difference lies in the source of the duty, in who starts the case, and in what the court does at the end.

Three wrongs and who acts in each How to read this: each box is one kind of wrong. The text says who brings the case and what the court gives. Tort The injured person sues the wrongdoer in a civil court. The court awards damages. Crime The State prosecutes the accused in a criminal court. The court punishes by fine, prison or both. Breach of contract The promisee sues the party who broke the promise. The court awards damages or orders performance. One act can fall in more than one box, for example a drunk driver who injures a pedestrian. A civil suit does not stop a criminal case, and a criminal case does not stop a civil suit.
keyPoints: Tort is a private wrong and its main remedy is compensation. A court can also grant an injunction (Specific Relief Act, 1963, sections 36 and 38). Crime is a public wrong and the State prosecutes and punishes. Tort duty is fixed by law and owed to persons generally. Contract duty is fixed by agreement. Proof: balance of probabilities for tort and contract, beyond reasonable doubt for crime. One act can be a tort and a crime, and a civil suit is independent of the criminal case. The same facts can give rise to tort and contract claims (White v. John Warwick & Co.). All torts are civil wrongs, but not all civil wrongs are torts. Compensation for violation of Article 21 is a public law remedy, independent of a tort suit and a prosecution (Nilabati Behera).

caseLaws.name: White v
caseLaws.facts: John Warrick & Co. Ltd. (1953) Facts. A newsagent hired a delivery cycle. The saddle slipped and he was thrown and injured. The hire agreement had an exemption clause. Principle. The Court of Appeal held that the clause did not clearly cover negligence, so a claim in negligence could go to trial. Why it matters. The same facts gave a contract claim and a tort claim. Donoghue v. Stevenson (1932) Facts. A snail was found in a bottle of ginger beer. The drinker had no contract with the manufacturer. Principle. The House of Lords held by 3 to 2 that the manufacturer owed her a duty of care, though there was no contract. Why it matters. It shows that a tort duty is fixed by law and does not depend on a contract. Bhim Singh v. State of Jammu & Kashmir (1985) Facts. An MLA of Jammu and Kashmir was arrested in the early hours of 10 September 1985. He was not produced before the Magistrate on 11 September or the Sub Judge on 13 September, though remand orders issued. Principle. The Supreme Court found a gross violation of Articles 21 and 22(2). It awarded Rs 50,000 compensation even though he was already free. Why it matters. The same wrong can be a crime, a tort and a violation of fundamental rights, each with its own remedy. Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa (1993) Facts. A 22-year-old man died in police custody. His mother wrote a letter to the Supreme Court, which was treated as a writ petition. Principle. The Court awarded Rs 1,50,000 and Rs 10,000 costs. It held that compensation under Articles 32 and 226 is a public law remedy, independent of a tort suit or a prosecution, and that sovereign immunity does not bar it. Why it matters. It adds a fourth route to the tort, crime and contract comparison.

selfTest.q: 1. What are the standards of proof in tort and in crime?
selfTest.a: A balance of probabilities in tort, and proof beyond reasonable doubt in crime. 2. Who starts the case in a tort and in a crime? The injured person starts a tort suit. The State prosecutes a crime. 3. Why are not all civil wrongs torts? Breach of contract and breach of trust are civil wrongs that are outside tort. Section 2(m) of the Limitation Act excludes them. 4. In White v. John Warwick & Co., why could the newsagent sue in negligence despite the exemption clause? The clause freed the company from contract liability only. A servant riding the cycle could have sued in negligence, so the company owed a duty of care in tort, and the newsagent need not rely on the contract.

hi.inOneMinute: A tort, a crime and a breach of contract are three different wrongs. A tort breaks a duty fixed by law and is remedied by damages. A crime is a public wrong that the State punishes. A breach of contract breaks a duty the parties created by agreement. One act can be more than one wrong. A reckless driver can face a criminal case and a civil suit at once. Examiners ask for the comparison table and for the statement that all torts are civil wrongs but not all civil wrongs are torts.
legalProvision: Section 2(m), Limitation Act, 1963: a tort is a civil wrong that is not exclusively a breach of contract or trust. Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: defines the crimes and their punishments. It replaced the Indian Penal Code from 1 July 2024. Sections 73 and 74, Indian Contract Act, 1872: compensation for breach of contract, and liquidated damages or penalty named in the contract. Section 395, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (earlier section 357, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973): a criminal court may order that fine money be paid as compensation to the victim. Where no fine is imposed, it may order the accused to pay compensation directly (section 395(3)). It does not replace a civil suit.

law-of-torts-u1-t12.subtitle: Strict, absolute, statutory and vicarious liability: when the law makes a person pay without proof of fault

en.inOneMinute: Most tort liability depends on fault. In some cases the law makes a person pay although he took every care and meant no harm. This is liability without fault, or no-fault liability. It rests on risk. A person who creates a danger and gains from it should bear the loss when the danger hurts others. The main forms are strict liability, absolute liability, statutory no-fault liability and vicarious liability.
legalProvision: Section 164, Motor Vehicles Act, 1988: the owner of the motor vehicle or the insurer must pay Rs 5 lakh on death and Rs 2.5 lakh on grievous hurt . The claimant need not prove any wrongful act, neglect or default. Sections 140 to 144, the older no-fault provisions, were omitted from 1 April 2022. Employees' Compensation Act, 1923: an employer must pay compensation for injury caused by an accident arising out of and in the course of employment, whether or not he was at fault (section 3(1)). The employee gets fixed amounts by formula (section 4). The employer is not liable if the injury disables the employee for three days or less (section 3(1), first proviso). Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991, section 3: the owner must pay relief for death, injury or damage to property from an accident while handling a hazardous substance. The injured person, other than a workman , need not plead or prove any wrongful act, neglect or default (section 3(2)). Accident and hazardous substance (section 2): an accident is a fortuitous , sudden or unintended occurrence while handling a hazardous substance. It does not include an accident by reason only of war or radio-activity. Handling includes manufacture, storage, transport and use. Insurance and fund (sections 4 and 7A): the owner must take out insurance before handling the substance (section 4). The Environmental Relief Fund pays relief under awards of the Collector. It is built from an extra payment with the premium , penalties and interest. Claim procedure (sections 5 to 8): the Collector verifies the accident and invites claims. A claim is made to the Collector within five years of the accident (section 6(3)). The Collector holds a summary inquiry and tries to decide within three months (section 7(7)). The relief is in addition to other compensation, which is reduced by the relief paid (section 8). National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, section 17: for death, injury or damage to property or the environment from an accident or the adverse impact of an activity under an Act in Schedule I, the person responsible must pay relief. The Tribunal fixes it under the heads in Schedule II. A workman is excluded (section 17(1)). No-fault and apportionment: in case of an accident the Tribunal applies the principle of no fault (section 17(3)). If the harm is the combined effect of several activities, it may apportion liability equitably (section 17(2)). Sections 14, 15 and 20: the Tribunal hears civil cases raising a substantial question relating to environment, within six months of the cause of action (section 14). It may order relief, compensation and restitution of property and the environment, within five years, in addition to relief under the 1991 Act (section 15). It applies sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle (section 20). Consumer Protection Act, 2019, sections 82 to 87 (product liability): a complainant may bring a product liability action against a product manufacturer, product service provider or product seller for harm caused by a defective product. Under section 84(2), a manufacturer is liable even if he proves he was not negligent or fraudulent in making the express warranty .
en.meaning:
Liability without fault means that the defendant is liable for harm although he was not negligent and did not intend it. The claimant proves the harm and its link to the defendant's activity, and does not need to prove fault.

It is an exception to the fault theory. The law allows the exception only where the activity is dangerous or the law has a policy reason to protect victims.
keyPoints: Liability without fault means liability without proof of negligence or intention. Reasons: risk, profit, difficulty of proving fault, prevention. Strict liability (Rylands v. Fletcher) has defences. Absolute liability (M.C. Mehta) has none. Section 164 of the Motor Vehicles Act: Rs 5 lakh on death and Rs 2.5 lakh on grievous hurt, no proof of fault. Sections 140 to 144 of the Motor Vehicles Act were omitted from 1 April 2022. Vicarious liability is also liability without the employer's fault. Rylands v. Fletcher needs a non-natural use of land and an escape. The House of Lords affirmed it in 1868. M.C. Mehta: compensation matches the size and capacity of the enterprise. Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action held that law binding and applied the polluter pays principle.

caseLaws.name: Rylands v
caseLaws.facts: Fletcher (1868) Facts. A mill owner's reservoir burst through old mine shafts and flooded a neighbouring mine. He knew nothing of the shafts. Principle. A person who keeps a mischievous thing on his land must keep it in at his peril. The use of land must be non-natural. The House of Lords affirmed the Exchequer Chamber and dismissed the appeal with costs. Why it matters. The origin of strict liability. M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak Case) (1987) Facts. Oleum gas escaped on 4 and 6 December 1985 from a unit of the Shriram complex in Delhi, while the writ petition was still before the Court. Principle. The Supreme Court laid down absolute liability for hazardous industry, with no exception and compensation matched to the enterprise's capacity. The Court directed the Delhi Legal Aid and Advice Board to file compensation actions against Shriram. Why it matters. India's own rule, wider than Rylands v. Fletcher. Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India (1996) Facts. Chemical units in Bichhri village, Rajasthan, left toxic sludge that poisoned wells and soil. Principle. The Supreme Court followed the rule of absolute liability and the polluter pays principle, and ordered the Central Government to recover the cost of repair. It held the Oleum gas law binding and not obiter. Why it matters. It applied absolute liability to pollution.

selfTest.q: 1. Why does the law impose liability without fault?
selfTest.a: Because the person who creates a dangerous risk and benefits from it should bear its cost, and victims often cannot prove fault. 2. How does absolute liability differ from strict liability? Absolute liability, from M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, has no exceptions. Strict liability under Rylands v. Fletcher allows defences such as act of God and act of a stranger. 3. What does section 164 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 provide? Fixed compensation of Rs 5 lakh on death and Rs 2.5 lakh on grievous hurt, payable by the owner or insurer without proof of fault. 4. How did Lord Cairns separate natural from non-natural use of land? A neighbour cannot complain of water that gathers and flows by the laws of nature. If the defendant brings water in quantities and in a manner not the result of work on the land, he acts at his own peril. 5. Why did the Supreme Court move away from Rylands v. Fletcher in M.C. Mehta? The rule grew in the 19th century, before modern science and industry. The Court said it need not feel inhibited by it and laid down absolute liability for hazardous industry. 6. What does the polluter pays principle mean? The cost of preventing or repairing pollution falls on the undertaking that causes it, not on the government or the taxpayer.

te.inOneMinute: చాలా టార్ట్ బాధ్యత తప్పుపై ఆధారపడి ఉంటుంది. కొన్ని సందర్భాల్లో చట్టం ఒక వ్యక్తిని చెల్లించేలా చేస్తుంది, అయినప్పటికీ అతను అన్ని జాగ్రత్తలు తీసుకున్నాడు మరియు ఎటువంటి హాని జరగలేదు. ఇది తప్పు లేని బాధ్యత లేదా తప్పు లేని బాధ్యత. ఇది ప్రమాదంపై ఆధారపడి ఉంటుంది. ప్రమాదాన్ని సృష్టించి, దాని నుండి లాభం పొందిన వ్యక్తి ఆ ప్రమాదం ఇతరులను బాధపెట్టినప్పుడు నష్టాన్ని భరించాలి. ప్రధాన రూపాలు strict liability, absolute liability, చట్టబద్ధమైన దోష రహిత బాధ్యత మరియు vicarious liability.

te.meaning: తప్పు లేకుండా బాధ్యత అంటే ప్రతివాది అతను నిర్లక్ష్యం చేయనప్పటికీ మరియు దానిని ఉద్దేశించనప్పటికీ హానికి బాధ్యత వహిస్తాడు. హక్కుదారు హానిని మరియు ప్రతివాది యొక్క కార్యాచరణకు దాని లింక్‌ను రుజువు చేస్తాడు మరియు తప్పును నిరూపించాల్సిన అవసరం లేదు. ఇది తప్పు సిద్ధాంతానికి మినహాయింపు. యాక్టివిటీ ప్రమాదకరమైనది లేదా బాధితులను రక్షించడానికి చట్టం విధానపరమైన కారణం ఉన్న చోట మాత్రమే చట్టం మినహాయింపును అనుమతిస్తుంది.
keyPoints: తప్పు లేకుండా బాధ్యత అంటే నిర్లక్ష్యం లేదా ఉద్దేశ్యం రుజువు లేకుండా బాధ్యత. కారణాలు: ప్రమాదం, లాభం, తప్పు నిరూపించడంలో ఇబ్బంది, నివారణ. Strict liability (రైలాండ్స్ v. ఫ్లెచర్) డిఫెన్స్‌లను కలిగి ఉంది. Absolute liability (M. C. మెహతా) ఏదీ లేరు. Section 164 మోటారు వాహనాల చట్టం: మరణంపై రూ. 5 లక్షలు మరియు తీవ్రమైన గాయం అయితే రూ. 2.5 లక్షలు, తప్పు రుజువు లేదు. మోటారు వాహనాల చట్టంలోని 140 నుండి 144 వరకు ఉన్న సెక్షన్‌లు 1 ఏప్రిల్ 2022 నుండి తొలగించబడ్డాయి. Vicarious liability కూడా యజమాని యొక్క తప్పు లేకుండా బాధ్యత వహిస్తుంది. రైలాండ్స్ v. ఫ్లెచర్‌కు భూమి యొక్క సహజ వినియోగం మరియు తప్పించుకోవడం అవసరం. హౌస్ ఆఫ్ లార్డ్స్ దీనిని 1868లో ధృవీకరించింది. M. C. మెహతా: పరిహారం సంస్థ యొక్క పరిమాణం మరియు సామర్థ్యంతో సరిపోతుంది. ఇండియన్ కౌన్సిల్ ఫర్ ఎన్విరో-లీగల్ యాక్షన్ చట్టాన్ని కట్టుదిట్టం చేసి, పొల్యూటర్ చెల్లింపు సూత్రాన్ని వర్తింపజేస్తుంది.

hi.inOneMinute: Most tort liability depends on fault. In some cases the law makes a person pay although he took every care and meant no harm. This is liability without fault, or no-fault liability. It rests on risk. A person who creates a danger and gains from it should bear the loss when the danger hurts others. The main forms are strict liability, absolute liability, statutory no-fault liability and vicarious liability.
legalProvision: Section 164, Motor Vehicles Act, 1988: the owner of the motor vehicle or the insurer must pay Rs 5 lakh on death and Rs 2.5 lakh on grievous hurt . The claimant need not prove any wrongful act, neglect or default. Sections 140 to 144, the older no-fault provisions, were omitted from 1 April 2022. Employees' Compensation Act, 1923: an employer must pay compensation for injury caused by an accident arising out of and in the course of employment, whether or not he was at fault (section 3(1)). The employee gets fixed amounts by formula (section 4). The employer is not liable if the injury disables the employee for three days or less (section 3(1), first proviso). Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991, section 3: the owner must pay relief for death, injury or damage to property from an accident while handling a hazardous substance. The injured person, other than a workman , need not plead or prove any wrongful act, neglect or default (section 3(2)). Accident and hazardous substance (section 2): an accident is a fortuitous , sudden or unintended occurrence while handling a hazardous substance. It does not include an accident by reason only of war or radio-activity. Handling includes manufacture, storage, transport and use. Insurance and fund (sections 4 and 7A): the owner must take out insurance before handling the substance (section 4). The Environmental Relief Fund pays relief under awards of the Collector. It is built from an extra payment with the premium , penalties and interest. Claim procedure (sections 5 to 8): the Collector verifies the accident and invites claims. A claim is made to the Collector within five years of the accident (section 6(3)). The Collector holds a summary inquiry and tries to decide within three months (section 7(7)). The relief is in addition to other compensation, which is reduced by the relief paid (section 8). National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, section 17: for death, injury or damage to property or the environment from an accident or the adverse impact of an activity under an Act in Schedule I, the person responsible must pay relief. The Tribunal fixes it under the heads in Schedule II. A workman is excluded (section 17(1)). No-fault and apportionment: in case of an accident the Tribunal applies the principle of no fault (section 17(3)). If the harm is the combined effect of several activities, it may apportion liability equitably (section 17(2)). Sections 14, 15 and 20: the Tribunal hears civil cases raising a substantial question relating to environment, within six months of the cause of action (section 14). It may order relief, compensation and restitution of property and the environment, within five years, in addition to relief under the 1991 Act (section 15). It applies sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle (section 20). Consumer Protection Act, 2019, sections 82 to 87 (product liability): a complainant may bring a product liability action against a product manufacturer, product service provider or product seller for harm caused by a defective product. Under section 84(2), a manufacturer is liable even if he proves he was not negligent or fraudulent in making the express warranty .
hi.meaning: Liability without fault means that the defendant is liable for harm although he was not negligent and did not intend it. The claimant proves the harm and its link to the defendant's activity, and does not need to prove fault. It is an exception to the fault theory. The law allows the exception only where the activity is dangerous or the law has a policy reason to protect victims.
keyPoints: Liability without fault means liability without proof of negligence or intention. Reasons: risk, profit, difficulty of proving fault, prevention. Strict liability (Rylands v. Fletcher) has defences. Absolute liability (M.C. Mehta) has none. Section 164 of the Motor Vehicles Act: Rs 5 lakh on death and Rs 2.5 lakh on grievous hurt, no proof of fault. Sections 140 to 144 of the Motor Vehicles Act were omitted from 1 April 2022. Vicarious liability is also liability without the employer's fault. Rylands v. Fletcher needs a non-natural use of land and an escape. The House of Lords affirmed it in 1868. M.C. Mehta: compensation matches the size and capacity of the enterprise. Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action held that law binding and applied the polluter pays principle.

caseLaws.name: Rylands v
caseLaws.facts: Fletcher (1868) Facts. A mill owner's reservoir burst through old mine shafts and flooded a neighbouring mine. He knew nothing of the shafts. Principle. A person who keeps a mischievous thing on his land must keep it in at his peril. The use of land must be non-natural. The House of Lords affirmed the Exchequer Chamber and dismissed the appeal with costs. Why it matters. The origin of strict liability. M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak Case) (1987) Facts. Oleum gas escaped on 4 and 6 December 1985 from a unit of the Shriram complex in Delhi, while the writ petition was still before the Court. Principle. The Supreme Court laid down absolute liability for hazardous industry, with no exception and compensation matched to the enterprise's capacity. The Court directed the Delhi Legal Aid and Advice Board to file compensation actions against Shriram. Why it matters. India's own rule, wider than Rylands v. Fletcher. Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India (1996) Facts. Chemical units in Bichhri village, Rajasthan, left toxic sludge that poisoned wells and soil. Principle. The Supreme Court followed the rule of absolute liability and the polluter pays principle, and ordered the Central Government to recover the cost of repair. It held the Oleum gas law binding and not obiter. Why it matters. It applied absolute liability to pollution.

selfTest.q: 1. Why does the law impose liability without fault?
selfTest.a: Because the person who creates a dangerous risk and benefits from it should bear its cost, and victims often cannot prove fault. 2. How does absolute liability differ from strict liability? Absolute liability, from M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, has no exceptions. Strict liability under Rylands v. Fletcher allows defences such as act of God and act of a stranger. 3. What does section 164 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 provide? Fixed compensation of Rs 5 lakh on death and Rs 2.5 lakh on grievous hurt, payable by the owner or insurer without proof of fault. 4. How did Lord Cairns separate natural from non-natural use of land? A neighbour cannot complain of water that gathers and flows by the laws of nature. If the defendant brings water in quantities and in a manner not the result of work on the land, he acts at his own peril. 5. Why did the Supreme Court move away from Rylands v. Fletcher in M.C. Mehta? The rule grew in the 19th century, before modern science and industry. The Court said it need not feel inhibited by it and laid down absolute liability for hazardous industry. 6. What does the polluter pays principle mean? The cost of preventing or repairing pollution falls on the undertaking that causes it, not on the government or the taxpayer.

law-of-torts-u1-t3.subtitle: Wrongful act or omission, legal damage and legal remedy, with the remedies in tort

en.inOneMinute: A tort has three elements. There must be a wrongful act or omission by the defendant . The act must cause legal damage, which means the violation of a legal right. The law must give a remedy for it. All three must be present for a claim to succeed. Exam questions ask for the elements and for the remedies, both judicial (court orders) and extra-judicial (lawful self-help). Real life tests the same points when a neighbour's act harms you.
legalProvision: Section 2(m), Limitation Act, 1963: a tort is a civil wrong not exclusively a breach of contract or trust. It does not list the elements, which come from decided cases. Specific Relief Act, 1963: sections 5, 7 and 8 allow recovery of specific immovable and movable property. Sections 36 to 42 deal with injunctions , which are the commonest non-money remedy in tort. Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, sections 34 to 44: the right of private defence of body and property, which is the nearest statutory source of the self-help remedies. Cattle Trespass Act, 1871: the Indian statute that regulates the seizure of trespassing cattle.
en.meaning:
The elements of a tort are the facts the plaintiff must prove to win. They are three:

a wrongful act or omission by the defendant; legal damage to the plaintiff; and a legal remedy for the wrong.

The third element rests on the maxim ubi jus ibi remedium : where there is a right, there is a remedy. The first two rest on the idea that a lawful act, or a loss without a violated right, gives no claim.

Is there a tort? The three questions How to read this: start at the top. Each question must be answered "yes" to move down. Red text shows where the claim fails. 1. Did the defendant do a wrongful act, or omit a legal duty? No: no tort. A lawful act is not a tort, even if it causes loss. 2. Did the act violate a legal right of the plaintiff (legal damage)? No: damnum sine injuria (loss without legal injury). No claim. 3. Does the law give a remedy for that wrong? No: a moral wrong only. No claim. 4. Result A tort is made out. The plaintiff may claim damages, an injunction or other relief.
keyPoints: Three elements: wrongful act or omission, legal damage, legal remedy. An omission is wrongful only when the law imposes a duty to act. Legal damage means violation of a legal right. Loss alone is not enough. Ubi jus ibi remedium: where there is a right, there is a remedy. Judicial remedies: damages, injunction, specific restitution of property. Extra-judicial remedies: self-defence, expulsion of trespasser, re-entry, recaption, distress damage feasant, abatement of nuisance. Self-help must be prompt, reasonable and peaceful. Intention is not a general element: Wilkinson v Downton (intention), Donoghue v Stevenson (duty of care), Rylands v Fletcher (no personal fault needed). A bad motive does not make a lawful act a tort: Bradford Corporation v Pickles.

caseLaws.name: Ashby v
caseLaws.facts: White (1703) Facts. The constables of Aylesbury refused the vote of a qualified voter. The jury gave him £5 damages. Principle. A violation of a legal right is actionable. Where there is a right, there must be a remedy. A refused vote is actionable even if the vote might not have changed the result. Why it matters. It supports the second and third elements: legal damage and a legal remedy. Gloucester Grammar School Case (1410) Facts. A schoolmaster set up a rival school and charged lower fees. The old school lost pupils. Principle. Loss caused by lawful competition gives no claim. Why it matters. It is the early example of damnum sine injuria, where the second element is missing. Bradford Corporation v. Pickles (1895) Facts. Pickles dug on his own land and cut the water supply that fed Bradford's springs. The town said he did it to force a sale. Principle. A lawful act is not made unlawful by a bad motive. Why it matters. It shows that the first element needs a legal wrong, not just a bad purpose. Mogul Steamship Co. Ltd. v. McGregor, Gow & Co. (1892) Facts. A group of shipowners cut freight rates to shut out a rival from the tea trade. Principle. Lawful competition causing loss is damnum sine injuria. Why it matters. It shows loss without legal injury again, in a trade setting. Wilkinson v. Downton (1897) Facts. The defendant, as a practical joke, told the plaintiff falsely that her husband had broken both legs in an accident. She suffered a serious shock, and the jury assessed £100. Principle. A person who wilfully does an act calculated to cause physical harm, and thereby causes it, commits a wrong unless there is a justification. Why it matters. It shows that a wrongful act can be words alone, and that an intentional wrong needs no spite. Donoghue v. Stevenson (1932) Facts. A friend bought a bottle of ginger beer for Mrs Donoghue. She alleged that she found the remains of a snail in it and fell ill. The House of Lords decided by three judges to two. Principle. A person must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions that he can reasonably foresee would injure his neighbour. This is the duty of care. Why it matters. It explains the duty that makes an act or omission wrongful in negligence. Rylands v. Fletcher (1868) Facts. Water from the defendants' new reservoir escaped through old shafts and flooded the plaintiff's neighbouring mine. Principle. A person who brings on his land and keeps there something likely to do mischief if it escapes must keep it in at his peril. Why it matters. It shows a tort where the first element is met without proof of fault.

selfTest.q: 1. What are the three elements of a tort?
selfTest.a: A wrongful act or omission, legal damage, and a legal remedy. 2. Why does Suresh have no claim against a rival who opens a cheaper shop next door? He suffers loss but no legal right is violated. This is damnum sine injuria. 3. What three limits apply to every extra-judicial remedy? It must be prompt, the force must be reasonable, and it must not cause a breach of the peace. 4. Does every tort require intention to harm? No. Wilkinson v Downton is an intentional wrong, Donoghue v Stevenson turns on duty of care, and Rylands v Fletcher needs no fault. 5. A landowner digs on his own land only to spite his neighbour and cuts off the neighbour's water. Is the first element met? No. Under Bradford Corporation v Pickles a lawful use of land does not become a wrong because of a bad motive.

It supports the second and third elements: legal damage and a legal remedy. Gloucester Grammar School Case (1410) Facts. A schoolmaster set up a rival school and charged lower fees. The old school lost pupils. Principle. Loss caused by lawful competition gives no claim. Why it matters. It is the early example of damnum sine injuria, where the second element is missing. Bradford Corporation v. Pickles (1895) Facts. Pickles dug on his own land and cut the water supply that fed Bradford's springs. The town said he did it to force a sale. Principle. A lawful act is not made unlawful by a bad motive. Why it matters. It shows that the first element needs a legal wrong, not just a bad purpose. Mogul Steamship Co. Ltd. v. McGregor, Gow & Co. (1892) Facts. A group of shipowners cut freight rates to shut out a rival from the tea trade. Principle. Lawful competition causing loss is damnum sine injuria. Why it matters. It shows loss without legal injury again, in a trade setting. Wilkinson v. Downton (1897) Facts. The defendant, as a practical joke, told the plaintiff falsely that her husband had broken both legs in an accident. She suffered a serious shock, and the jury assessed £100. Principle. A person who wilfully does an act calculated to cause physical harm, and thereby causes it, commits a wrong unless there is a justification. Why it matters. It shows that a wrongful act can be words alone, and that an intentional wrong needs no spite. Donoghue v. Stevenson (1932) Facts. A friend bought a bottle of ginger beer for Mrs Donoghue. She alleged that she found the remains of a snail in it and fell ill. The House of Lords decided by three judges to two. Principle. A person must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions that he can reasonably foresee would injure his neighbour. This is the duty of care. Why it matters. It explains the duty that makes an act or omission wrongful in negligence. Rylands v. Fletcher (1868) Facts. Water from the defendants' new reservoir escaped through old shafts and flooded the plaintiff's neighbouring mine. Principle. A person who brings on his land and keeps there something likely to do mischief if it escapes must keep it in at his peril. Why it matters. It shows a tort where the first element is met without proof of fault.

selfTest.q: 1. What are the three elements of a tort?
selfTest.a: A wrongful act or omission, legal damage, and a legal remedy. 2. Why does Suresh have no claim against a rival who opens a cheaper shop next door? He suffers loss but no legal right is violated. This is damnum sine injuria. 3. What three limits apply to every extra-judicial remedy? It must be prompt, the force must be reasonable, and it must not cause a breach of the peace. 4. Does every tort require intention to harm? No. Wilkinson v Downton is an intentional wrong, Donoghue v Stevenson turns on duty of care, and Rylands v Fletcher needs no fault. 5. A landowner digs on his own land only to spite his neighbour and cuts off the neighbour's water. Is the first element met? No. Under Bradford Corporation v Pickles a lawful use of land does not become a wrong because of a bad motive.

law-of-torts-u1-t8.subtitle: Fault as a basis of liability in tort: its forms, the fault theory, and proof of fault

en.inOneMinute: Fault means blameworthy conduct. In tort, a person is at fault when he acts with intention, with recklessness , or without the care a reasonable person would take. The general rule is that a defendant is liable only if he is at fault. There are exceptions, where the law makes a person liable although he took every care. In exams, expect the fault theory, its contrast with no-fault liability, and how a plaintiff proves fault.
legalProvision: No statute defines fault in tort. The idea comes from decided cases and writers. Section 114, Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (now section 119, Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023): the court may presume facts that are likely, given the common course of natural events, human conduct and business. The word is "may", so the court is not bound to presume. This supports the use of res ipsa loquitur. Statutes with no fault: section 164, Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 and the Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 make some liability independent of fault. Under the 1991 Act the claimant need not plead or prove a wrongful act, neglect or default (section 3(2)). Section 164, Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, in detail: Sub-section (1) makes the owner of the motor vehicle or the authorised insurer liable to pay Rs 5 lakh for death and Rs 2.5 lakh for grievous hurt caused by an accident arising out of the use of a motor vehicle. Sub-section (2) says the claimant need not plead or establish that the death or hurt was due to any wrongful act, neglect or default of the owner, of the vehicle or of any other person. Sub-section (3) reduces the amount by compensation already paid under any other law. Sub-section (4) says ex gratia payments are not deducted. The older Chapter X, headed "Liability without fault in certain cases", included section 140 (compensation on the principle of no fault). The Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 2019 omitted the whole Chapter with effect from 1 April 2022.
en.meaning:
Fault is conduct for which the law blames a person. It has three forms.

Intention. The person aimed at the result, or knew it was almost certain to follow. Recklessness. The person knew of the risk and went ahead without caring whether harm followed. Negligence. The person did not take the care that a reasonable person would take in the same situation.

The fault theory says that liability in tort should depend on fault. The opposite idea is liability without fault, which makes a person pay although he was careful.
keyPoints: Fault is blameworthy conduct: intention, recklessness or negligence. The general rule: liability follows fault. The plaintiff must prove fault. Res ipsa loquitur lets the court infer it. Contributory negligence reduces damages. Exceptions: strict, absolute, vicarious and statutory liability. No-fault liability rests on risk, not blame. Foresight judged by the reasonable person is the test of carelessness (Wagon Mound No. 1). Intention needs no spite (Wilkinson v. Downton). A lawful act is not made wrongful by bad motive (Bradford v. Pickles). Care is no defence to strict liability: a hazardous activity makes the enterprise liable irrespective of negligence (Shail Kumari).

caseLaws.name: The test
caseLaws.facts: In Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Subhagwanti, the thing that failed was exclusively under the defendant's control. Its failure does not ordinarily happen without negligence. That raises a prima facie case of negligence. The facts found in Subhagwanti. The Clock Tower was about 80 years old. The Chief Engineer said the safe life of the top storey was 40 or 45 years. The mortar had decayed to powder. No earthquake, storm or other natural event was pleaded. The High Court found no evidence worth the name of proper inspections. Any inspections were casual and perfunctory . Taken together, the fall itself "tells its own story" and raised an inference of negligence. Who proves what. The normal rule is that the plaintiff proves negligence. The exception applies where the thing causing damage was exclusively under the defendant's control or management and the happening does not occur in the ordinary course without negligence. The Court relied on the Halsbury statement that a presumption of fault is then raised, which the defendant must overcome by contrary evidence. Result. The trial court (9 July 1953) awarded Rs 25,000, Rs 15,000 and Rs 20,000 in three suits. The High Court (27 November 1959) cut the last two to Rs 7,200 and Rs 9,000. On 24 February 1966 the Supreme Court (V. Ramaswami J.) dismissed the appeals with costs. Latent defects. The Court held that the owner of a structure beside a highway must keep it safe for users of the highway. The owner is responsible "irrespective of whether the damage is caused by a patent or a latent defect". Lack of knowledge of a hidden defect is no defence. Hospital cases. In Cassidy v. Ministry of Health, the Court of Appeal held a hospital authority vicariously liable for negligence of the doctors, surgeons and nurses it employs on a permanent basis. No need to name the careless person. The patient's injury was of a kind that does not ordinarily happen without negligence, and only the hospital's own staff treated him. The patient need not identify which staff member was at fault.

selfTest.q: 1. What are the forms of fault?
selfTest.a: Intention, recklessness and negligence. 2. When can the court infer fault under res ipsa loquitur? When the thing causing harm was under the defendant's control and the accident would not ordinarily happen without negligence. 3. Name two kinds of liability without fault. Absolute liability under M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, and statutory liability under section 164 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. 4. According to Shail Kumari, how does strict liability differ from negligence? In negligence, a defendant who took all reasonable precautions is not liable. In strict liability the precautions taken are not relevant. 5. What need a claimant not prove under section 164(2) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988? That the death or grievous hurt was due to a wrongful act, neglect or default of the owner, the vehicle or any other person. 6. By what standard does Wagon Mound (No. 1) judge what a person ought to have foreseen? The standard of the reasonable man.

caseLaws.facts: మునిసిపల్ కార్పొరేషన్ ఆఫ్ ఢిల్లీ v. సుభగవంతిలో, విఫలమైన విషయం ప్రత్యేకంగా ప్రతివాది నియంత్రణలో ఉంది. దాని వైఫల్యం సాధారణంగా నిర్లక్ష్యం లేకుండా జరగదు. ఇది నిర్లక్ష్యానికి సంబంధించిన ప్రాథమిక కేసును లేవనెత్తుతుంది. సుభగవంతిలో దొరికిన వాస్తవాలు. క్లాక్ టవర్ దాదాపు 80 ఏళ్లనాటిది. పై అంతస్తు యొక్క సురక్షితమైన జీవితం 40 లేదా 45 సంవత్సరాలు అని చీఫ్ ఇంజనీర్ తెలిపారు. మోర్టార్ పొడిగా కుళ్ళిపోయింది. భూకంపం, తుఫాను లేదా ఇతర సహజ సంఘటనలు జరగలేదని విజ్ఞప్తి చేశారు. సరైన తనిఖీల పేరుతో ఎలాంటి ఆధారాలు లేవని హైకోర్టు గుర్తించింది. ఏదైనా తనిఖీలు సాధారణం మరియు పనికిరానివి. కలిసి తీసుకుంటే, పతనం స్వయంగా "తన స్వంత కథను చెబుతుంది" మరియు నిర్లక్ష్యం యొక్క అనుమితిని పెంచింది. ఎవరు ఏమి రుజువు చేస్తారు. సాధారణ నియమం ఏమిటంటే, వాది నిర్లక్ష్యాన్ని రుజువు చేయడం. నష్టం కలిగించే విషయం ప్రత్యేకంగా ప్రతివాది నియంత్రణలో లేదా నిర్వహణలో ఉన్న చోట మినహాయింపు వర్తిస్తుంది మరియు నిర్లక్ష్యం లేకుండా సాధారణ కోర్సులో జరగదు. law-of-torts-u1-t13.subtitle: Liability created by an Act: no-fault statutory compensation and the action for breach of statutory duty

en.inOneMinute: Statutory liability is liability that an Act of Parliament or a State legislature creates. It takes two forms. One is a right to compensation that the Act gives without proof of fault. The other arises when an Act imposes a duty and a person is harmed by its breach. In exams, expect section 164 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, product liability under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, and the enforcement of statutory duties in Municipal Council, Ratlam v. Vardhichand.
legalProvision: Section 164, Motor Vehicles Act, 1988: the owner or insurer must pay Rs 5 lakh on death and Rs 2.5 lakh on grievous hurt , without proof of fault (section 164(2)). Consumer Protection Act, 2019: gives a remedy for harm caused by a defective product (product liability, sections 82 to 87 in Chapter VI).
en.meaning:
Statutory liability is liability whose source is an Act. The court looks at the words of the Act to decide who is liable, to whom and for how much.

Statutory compensation. The Act itself gives a right to a stated sum or relief. It does not depend on the common law of torts. Breach of statutory duty. The Act puts a duty on a person or body. Whether a person harmed by its breach can claim depends on what the Act provides.
keyPoints: Statutory liability is liability created by an Act. Two forms: fixed statutory compensation, and the action for breach of statutory duty. Section 164, Motor Vehicles Act: Rs 5 lakh on death, Rs 2.5 lakh on grievous hurt, no proof of fault. Product liability under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (sections 83 to 87) binds the manufacturer, the service provider and the seller. Municipal Council, Ratlam v. Vardhichand: lack of funds is no defence to a statutory duty. Accepting compensation under section 164 ends the claim petition before the Claims Tribunal (section 166(1), second proviso).

caseLaws.name: Municipal Council, Ratlam v
caseLaws.facts: Vardhichand (1980) Facts. Residents of Ward No. 12, Ratlam asked the Sub-Divisional Magistrate under section 133 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to order the municipality to clean open drains and deal with liquid waste from the nearby Alcohol Plant ( effluent ). Principle. The Supreme Court held that lack of funds is no defence to the duty under section 123 of the M.P. Municipalities Act, 1961. It approved Scheme C, costing about Rs 6 lakhs, to be finished in one year. Why it matters. An Indian case on enforcing statutory duties. Chairman, Railway Board v. Mrs. Chandrima Das (2000) Facts. Hanuffa Khatoon, a Bangladeshi national, was gang-raped by many, including railway employees, in a room at Yatri Niwas, Howrah Station. Mrs. Chandrima Das petitioned. Principle. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the Rs 10 lakhs award. It said the Union can be held vicariously liable for its employees' acts, and the sovereign immunity theory is no longer available in a welfare State. No order as to costs. Why it matters. It shows the State's liability for harm done in running the Railways, a commercial undertaking.

selfTest.q: 1. What is statutory liability?
selfTest.a: Liability created by an Act, either as a right to fixed compensation or as a right to sue for breach of a duty the Act imposes. 2. What happens to a claim petition once the claimant accepts section 164 compensation? It lapses, under the second proviso to section 166(1) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. 3. Does the claimant under section 164 of the Motor Vehicles Act need to prove negligence? No. Section 164(2) says the claimant need not plead or prove any wrongful act, neglect or default.

te.inOneMinute: Statutory liability is liability that an Act of Parliament or a State legislature creates. It takes two forms. One is a right to compensation that the Act gives without proof of fault. The other arises when an Act imposes a duty and a person is harmed by its breach. In exams, expect section 164 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, product liability under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, and the enforcement of statutory duties in Municipal Council, Ratlam v. Vardhichand.
legalProvision: Section 164, Motor Vehicles Act, 1988: the owner or insurer must pay Rs 5 lakh on death and Rs 2.5 lakh on grievous hurt, without proof of fault (section 164(2)). Consumer Protection Act, 2019: gives a remedy for harm caused by a defective product (product liability, sections 82 to 87 in Chapter VI).
te.meaning: Statutory liability is liability whose source is an Act. The court looks at the words of the Act to decide who is liable, to whom and for how much. Statutory compensation. The Act itself gives a right to a stated sum or relief. It does not depend on the common law of torts. Breach of statutory duty. The Act puts a duty on a person or body. Whether a person harmed by its breach can claim depends on what the Act provides.
keyPoints: Statutory liability is liability created by an Act. Two forms: fixed statutory compensation, and the action for breach of statutory duty. Section 164, Motor Vehicles Act: Rs 5 lakh on death, Rs 2.5 lakh on grievous hurt, no proof of fault. Product liability under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (sections 83 to 87) binds the manufacturer, the service provider and the seller. Municipal Council, Ratlam v. Vardhichand: lack of funds is no defence to a statutory duty. Accepting compensation under section 164 ends the claim petition before the Claims Tribunal (section 166(1), second proviso).

caseLaws.name: Municipal Council, Ratlam v
caseLaws.facts: Vardhichand (1980) Facts. Residents of Ward No. 12, Ratlam asked the Sub-Divisional Magistrate under section 133 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to order the municipality to clean open drains and deal with liquid waste from the nearby Alcohol Plant (effluent). Principle. The Supreme Court held that lack of funds is no defence to the duty under section 123 of the M. P. Municipalities Act, 1961. It approved Scheme C, costing about Rs 6 lakhs, to be finished in one year. Why it matters. An Indian case on enforcing statutory duties. Chairman, Railway Board v. Mrs. Chandrima Das (2000) Facts. Hanuffa Khatoon, a Bangladeshi national, was gang-raped by many, including railway employees, in a room at Yatri Niwas, Howrah Station. Mrs. Chandrima Das petitioned. Principle. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the Rs 10 lakhs award. It said the Union can be held vicariously liable for its employees' acts, and the sovereign immunity theory is no longer available in a welfare State. No order as to costs. Why it matters. It shows the State's liability for harm done in running the Railways, a commercial undertaking.

selfTest.q: 1. What is statutory liability?
selfTest.a: Liability created by an Act, either as a right to fixed compensation or as a right to sue for breach of a duty the Act imposes. 2. What happens to a claim petition once the claimant accepts section 164 compensation? It lapses, under the second proviso to section 166(1) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. 3. Does the claimant under section 164 of the Motor Vehicles Act need to prove negligence? No. Section 164(2) says the claimant need not plead or prove any wrongful act, neglect or default.

The "fault theory" of tort liability holds that liability generally requires:

Explanation. The fault theory holds that liability generally requires some degree of fault — intention or negligence — on the defendant's part.

Intention in tort law refers to:

Explanation. Intention is the immediate objective of the act itself, distinct from motive, which is the underlying reason behind it.

As a general rule, a bad motive:

Explanation. A bad motive does not make an otherwise lawful act wrongful — as shown in Bradford Corporation v. Pickles.

Explanation. Malice in law (implied malice) means doing a wrongful act intentionally, without just cause or legal excuse — the sense tort law cares about.

law-of-torts-u1-t14.subtitle: Who may sue and who may be sued in tort: minors, the State, firms and foreign nationals

en.inOneMinute: Parties to proceedings are the claimant who sues and the defendant who is sued. Civil courts try all civil suits unless a law bars them. This note covers the parties that the sources deal with. The Union and the States sue and are sued by their own names under Article 300. A suit against the Government needs two months' notice under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure. A minor sues through a next friend. A firm is liable for the wrongful acts of its partners under the Partnership Act.
legalProvision: Section 9, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908: the courts have jurisdiction to try all suits of a civil nature, except suits whose cognizance is expressly or impliedly barred. Article 300, Constitution of India: the Government of India may sue or be sued by the name of the Union of India. The Government of a State may sue or be sued by the name of the State. This is in the like cases as the Dominion of India and the Provinces or Indian States could have sued or been sued before the Constitution, subject to any law made by Parliament or the State Legislature. Section 25, Indian Partnership Act, 1932: every partner is liable, jointly with all the other partners and also severally , for all acts of the firm done while he is a partner. Section 26, Indian Partnership Act: where a partner causes loss or injury to a third party by a wrongful act or omission in the ordinary course of the firm's business or with his partners' authority, the firm is liable to the same extent as the partner. Section 69(2), Indian Partnership Act: no suit to enforce a right arising from a contract can be filed by or for a firm against a third party unless the firm is registered and the persons suing are shown in the Register of Firms as partners. Order XXXII, Code of Civil Procedure: suits by or against minors and persons of unsound mind. A minor sues by a next friend, and a minor defendant has a guardian for the suit. Section 79, Code of Civil Procedure: in a suit by or against the Central Government the party is named "the Union of India". For a State Government it is "the State". Section 80, Code of Civil Procedure: no suit can be filed against the Government, or a public officer for an official act, until two months after written notice. Section 80(2) allows a suit for urgent or immediate relief with the leave of the Court. Sections 83, 84 and 86, Code of Civil Procedure: aliens suing, foreign States suing, and suits against foreign States, Rulers, Ambassadors and Envoys. A foreign State can be sued only with the consent of the Central Government, certified in writing by a Secretary. Section 9, Companies Act, 2013: a registered company is a body corporate that can sue and be sued by its name. Orders XXIX and XXX, Code of Civil Procedure: suits by or against corporations, and by or against firms in the firm's name.
en.meaning:
The parties to a tort proceeding are the plaintiff (the person claiming) and the defendant (the person against whom the claim is made). Capacity is the legal ability to sue or to be sued.

The question has two sides. Who can bring a claim for a tort ? Who can be made to answer it? The answers differ for minors, persons of unsound mind, companies, the State, firms and foreign States.
keyPoints: Section 9 CPC: civil courts try all civil suits unless barred. In Mohori Bibee the infant sued through his mother as next friend. The Union and States sue and are sued by their names (Article 300). A suit against the Government needs two months' notice (section 80 CPC). A minor sues by a next friend and a minor defendant has a guardian for the suit (Order XXXII). A foreign State can be sued only with the Central Government's consent (section 86 CPC). State liable for non-sovereign acts (Vidyawati). Kasturi Lal's sovereign-act defence was later limited (Chandrima Das). A foreign national can claim compensation from the Union as a public-law remedy (Chandrima Das). A firm is liable for a partner's wrongful act in the ordinary course of business (section 26 Partnership Act).

caseLaws.name: State of Rajasthan v
caseLaws.facts: Vidhyawati (1962) Facts. A government jeep, returning from a repair shop, ran down a pedestrian. Principle. The Supreme Court held the State liable for the driver's negligence, as keeping a vehicle is not a sovereign function. Why it matters. The State can be sued like a private employer for non-sovereign acts. Kasturi Lal Ralia Ram Jain v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1965) Facts. Police seized the appellant firm's gold, and the head constable in charge of it misappropriated it and fled to Pakistan. Principle. The Supreme Court held that the State was not liable, because arrest, search and seizure are sovereign powers. Why it matters. It shows the limit of suing the State. Later cases confined the case. Chairman, Railway Board v. Mrs. Chandrima Das (2000) Facts. A Bangladeshi woman was gang-raped by men including Railway employees at Howrah. Principle. The Supreme Court upheld the award of Rs 10 lakhs and held that a foreign national can claim the protection of Article 21. Why it matters. It shows that a foreign national can sue the Union for compensation.

selfTest.q: 1. In whose name is a suit by or against the Union filed?
selfTest.a: In the name of the Union of India, under Article 300(1) of the Constitution. 2. When is a firm liable for a partner's wrongful act? When the partner acts in the ordinary course of the firm's business or with his partners' authority. The firm is liable to the same extent as the partner (section 26, Indian Partnership Act). 3. Was the State held liable in Vidyawati? Yes. The Supreme Court held the State of Rajasthan liable for the negligence of its jeep driver. 4. How does a minor sue, and who defends a minor defendant? A minor sues by a next friend (Order XXXII, rule 1). The Court appoints a guardian for the suit for a minor defendant (rule 3). 5. What must a person do before suing the Government? Give written notice and wait two months (section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure). With the leave of the Court, a suit for urgent relief can be filed without notice. 6. When can a foreign State be sued? Only with the consent of the Central Government, certified in writing by a Secretary (section 86 of the Code of Civil Procedure).

hi.inOneMinute: Parties to proceedings are the claimant who sues and the defendant who is sued. Civil courts try all civil suits unless a law bars them. This note covers the parties that the sources deal with. The Union and the States sue and are sued by their own names under Article 300. A suit against the Government needs two months' notice under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure. A minor sues through a next friend. A firm is liable for the wrongful acts of its partners under the Partnership Act.
legalProvision: Section 9, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908: the courts have jurisdiction to try all suits of a civil nature, except suits whose cognizance is expressly or impliedly barred. Article 300, Constitution of India: the Government of India may sue or be sued by the name of the Union of India. The Government of a State may sue or be sued by the name of the State. This is in the like cases as the Dominion of India and the Provinces or Indian States could have sued or been sued before the Constitution, subject to any law made by Parliament or the State Legislature. Section 25, Indian Partnership Act, 1932: every partner is liable, jointly with all the other partners and also severally , for all acts of the firm done while he is a partner. Section 26, Indian Partnership Act: where a partner causes loss or injury to a third party by a wrongful act or omission in the ordinary course of the firm's business or with his partners' authority, the firm is liable to the same extent as the partner. Section 69(2), Indian Partnership Act: no suit to enforce a right arising from a contract can be filed by or for a firm against a third party unless the firm is registered and the persons suing are shown in the Register of Firms as partners. Order XXXII, Code of Civil Procedure: suits by or against minors and persons of unsound mind. A minor sues by a next friend, and a minor defendant has a guardian for the suit. law-of-torts-u2-t4.subtitle: Joint and several liability, composite negligence, suing the wrongdoers, release and the right of contribution

en.inOneMinute: Sometimes more than one person causes the same harm. Each wrongdoer is then liable for the whole damage. The victim may proceed against all of them or against any one of them. This is joint and several liability. The one who pays may claim a share from the others. Exams ask for this as a short note, or as a problem on two drivers or on an owner and an insurer.
legalProvision: Order I, rules 3, 3A, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10(2) and 13, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908: all persons may be joined as defendants where a right to relief arising out of the same act or transaction is alleged against them, "jointly, severally or in the alternative", and a common question of law or fact would arise (rule 3). The court may order separate trials if joining defendants may embarrass or delay the trial (rule 3A). Judgment may be given against such one or more defendants as are found liable, "according to their respective liabilities" (rule 4). A defendant need not be interested in all the relief claimed (rule 5). A plaintiff may join, at his option, all or any persons severally, or jointly and severally, liable on one contract (rule 6). A plaintiff in doubt about who is liable may join two or more defendants, so that the question of who is liable, and to what extent, is decided between all parties (rule 7). No suit is defeated by misjoinder or non-joinder, but this does not apply to non-joinder of a necessary party (rule 9). The court may strike out an improperly joined party, or add a person who ought to have been joined, at any stage (rule 10(2)). Objections to non-joinder or misjoinder must be taken at the earliest opportunity, or they are treated as waived (rule 13). Sections 42 to 45, Indian Contract Act, 1872: these deal with joint promises. Section 42 says joint promisors must all fulfil the promise unless a contrary intention appears. Under section 43 the promisee may compel any one or more joint promisors to perform the whole promise. Each promisor may compel every other to contribute equally, unless a contrary intention appears. If one makes default in contribution, the rest bear the loss in equal shares. Section 44 says a release of one joint promisor does not discharge the others, and does not free the released promisor from responsibility to the others. Section 45 deals with joint rights. These sections speak of promises, not torts. This note uses them only as an analogy , and no Act in this syllabus sets a share for tortfeasors. Sections 25 and 26, Indian Partnership Act, 1932: every partner is liable, jointly with all the other partners and also severally, for all acts of the firm done while he is a partner (section 25). The firm is liable to the same extent as the partner for loss caused to a third party by the wrongful act of a partner in the ordinary course of the firm's business, or with the authority of his partners (section 26). Section 168(1), Motor Vehicles Act, 1988: the Claims Tribunal must give notice of the claim to the insurer and hear the parties, including the insurer. In its award it "shall specify the amount which shall be paid by the insurer or owner or driver of the vehicle involved in the accident or by all or any of them, as the case may be".
en.meaning:
Joint tortfeasors are two or more persons who share in one wrong. In this note's explanation, the wrong may be done together by agreement, or one person may answer for another, as a firm answers for its partner or an employer for an employee.

In a second kind of case, two or more persons are negligent separately, and their negligence together injures one victim. The Supreme Court calls this composite negligence and says: "Where a person is injured as a result of negligence on the part of two or more wrong doers, it is said that the person was injured on account of the composite negligence of those wrong-doers" (T.O. Anthony v. Karvarnan, 2008, para 6).

For composite negligence the Court says each wrongdoer "is jointly and severally liable to the injured for payment of the entire damages" (T.O. Anthony, para 6). A partner is likewise liable "jointly with all the other partners and also severally" (Partnership Act, section 25). In this note's words, "jointly" means all can be sued together, and "severally" means each can be sued alone.
keyPoints: Each of two or more wrongdoers who injure a third party is jointly and severally liable for the entire damages (T.O. Anthony, para 6). The injured person may proceed against all or any of them, and need not prove each one's share. Composite negligence differs from contributory negligence. If the claimant is partly at fault, composite negligence does not apply. Owner and insurer may be made jointly and severally liable (Minu B. Mehta). The Tribunal specifies who pays what (section 168(1)). Judgment may be given against defendants "according to their respective liabilities" (Order I, rule 4). The 1956 Law Commission report, quoted in Kaushal Kishor, records that in India there is no legal impediment to one tortfeasor recovering compensation from another. The Merryweather rule does not apply. In contract, joint promisors contribute equally (section 43). A release of one does not discharge the others (section 44).

caseLaws.name: T
caseLaws.facts: O. Anthony v. Karvarnan (2008) Facts. A KSRTC bus driver was hurt in a head-on collision with a private bus. The Tribunal assumed equal fault and halved his compensation. Principle. Composite negligence and contributory negligence differ. Where the injured is partly at fault, there is no automatic 50:50 split (paras 5-7). The Court fixed fault at 25% and 75% (para 8) and awarded an extra Rs 39,575 with 9% interest and costs of Rs 2,000 (paras 11-12). Why it matters. It states the Indian rule on composite negligence. Minu B. Mehta v. Balkrishna Ramchandra Nayan (1977) Facts. The appellant's truck hit the respondent's car. The Tribunal and the High Court awarded compensation. Principle. Proof of negligence is needed before owner or insurer is liable. Their liability is joint and several, and the claimant may proceed against either or both. Why it matters. It shows owner and insurer answering together. State of Maharashtra v. Kanchanmala Vijaysing Shirke (1995) Facts. A clerk, with the authorised driver's leave, drove a State jeep and killed a scooter rider near Ratnagiri (31 March 1980). Principle. The Tribunal absolved the State. The High Court held the State, driver and clerk jointly and severally liable, as the jeep served official work. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal: an authorised act was done in an unauthorised manner, so the State could not escape vicarious liability. Why it matters. It shows an employer answering for its employees. Pushpabai Purshottam Udeshi v. Ranjit Ginning & Pressing Co. (P) Ltd. (1977) Facts. A company's manager was driving the company's car when it hit a tree. A passenger died. The claim was against the company and its insurer. Principle. The Supreme Court held the company vicariously liable for its manager's negligence, as he was driving in the course of his employment. It fixed the insurer's liability only up to Rs. 15,000, the limit under the policy. Why it matters. It shows the employer answering for the employee, with a separate limit for the insurer. State of Rajasthan v. Vidhyawati (1962) Facts. A government jeep ran down a pedestrian. The family sued the driver and the State, and the driver took no part in the case. Principle. The State was held liable for its driver's negligence like any other employer. Why it matters. It shows master and servant answering for the same act.

selfTest.q: 1. What is composite negligence?
selfTest.a: Negligence on the part of two or more persons, who together injure a victim. Each is jointly and severally liable for the entire damages (T.O. Anthony, para 6). 2. What does joint and several liability mean for the victim? The victim may proceed against all the wrongdoers or any of them for the entire damages. He need not prove each one's share. 3. How does composite negligence differ from contributory negligence? In composite negligence two or more wrongdoers injure a third party. In contributory negligence the injured person is himself partly at fault, so his damages are reduced in proportion. 4. Does a wrongdoer who has paid in full have any remedy? According to the Law Commission (1956), quoted in Kaushal Kishor, there is no legal impediment to one tortfeasor recovering compensation from another in India, and the Merryweather rule does not apply.

The Court fixed fault at 25% and 75% (para 8) and awarded an extra Rs 39,575 with 9% interest and costs of Rs 2,000 (paras 11-12). Why it matters. It states the Indian rule on composite negligence. Minu B. Mehta v. Balkrishna Ramchandra Nayan (1977) Facts. The appellant's truck hit the respondent's car. The Tribunal and the High Court awarded compensation. Principle. Proof of negligence is needed before owner or insurer is liable. Their liability is joint and several, and the claimant may proceed against either or both. Why it matters. It shows owner and insurer answering together. State of Maharashtra v. Kanchanmala Vijaysing Shirke (1995) Facts. A clerk, with the authorised driver's leave, drove a State jeep and killed a scooter rider near Ratnagiri (31 March 1980). Principle. The Tribunal absolved the State. The High Court held the State, driver and clerk jointly and severally liable, as the jeep served official work. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal: an authorised act was done in an unauthorised manner, so the State could not escape vicarious liability. Why it matters. It shows an employer answering for its employees. Pushpabai Purshottam Udeshi v. Ranjit Ginning & Pressing Co. (P) Ltd. (1977) Facts. A company's manager was driving the company's car when it hit a tree. A passenger died. The claim was against the company and its insurer. Principle. The Supreme Court held the company vicariously liable for its manager's negligence, as he was driving in the course of his employment. It fixed the insurer's liability only up to Rs. 15,000, the limit under the policy. Why it matters. It shows the employer answering for the employee, with a separate limit for the insurer. State of Rajasthan v. Vidhyawati (1962) Facts. A government jeep ran down a pedestrian. The family sued the driver and the State, and the driver took no part in the case. Principle. The State was held liable for its driver's negligence like any other employer. Why it matters. It shows master and servant answering for the same act.

selfTest.q: 1. What is composite negligence?
selfTest.a: Negligence on the part of two or more persons, who together injure a victim. Each is jointly and severally liable for the entire damages (T.O. Anthony, para 6). 2. What does joint and several liability mean for the victim? The victim may proceed against all the wrongdoers or any of them for the entire damages. He need not prove each one's share. 3. How does composite negligence differ from contributory negligence? In composite negligence two or more wrongdoers injure a third party. In contributory negligence the injured person is himself partly at fault, so his damages are reduced in proportion. 4. Does a wrongdoer who has paid in full have any remedy? According to the Law Commission (1956), quoted in Kaushal Kishor, there is no legal impediment to one tortfeasor recovering compensation from another in India, and the Merryweather rule does not apply.

visuals.caption: The victim and two wrongdoers How to read this: the three boxes are the parties. The lines say what each may do. A red line marks what the law denies.
Comparison Table
visuals.html:
PointComposite negligenceContributory negligence
Whose negligenceTwo or more wrongdoers, other than the claimantThe injured person himself, partly
Who claimsA third party, not a driver or owner of the vehicles involvedA driver, his heirs, or an owner for his own vehicle
Liability to the claimantEach wrongdoer jointly and severally liable for the entire damagesDamages reduced in proportion to the claimant's own negligence
Share of eachClaimant need not prove it, and the court need not decide itThe court must find the claimant's share of fault
ExampleA pedestrian hit by two careless drivers whose cars collideA bus driver injured in a head-on collision who did not slow down

law-of-torts-u2-t1.subtitle: Volenti non fit injuria, plaintiff the wrongdoer, inevitable accident, act of God, private defence, necessity and statutory authority

en.inOneMinute: A claimant may prove a wrongful act and legal damage and still lose. The defendant may plead a general defence. These are grounds on which a defendant tries to escape or reduce liability. The main ones are volenti non fit injuria (consent to risk), plaintiff the wrongdoer, inevitable accident, act of God, private defence, necessity and statutory authority. Learn how consent to a risk works and where it fails, and learn the proof rule for inevitable accident.
legalProvision: No Act lists the general defences. They come from decided cases. Sections 25 to 33, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: consent to harm, acts done in good faith for a person's benefit, acts done under threat and trivial harm. They show how the criminal law treats consent. Sections 34 to 44, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: the right of private defence of body and property, with its limits. Sections 3, 6, 22 and 23, Limitation Act, 1963, and Part VII of its Schedule: the time bar on a suit, and the periods for torts. Section 164(2), Motor Vehicles Act, 1988: in a claim for the fixed compensation, the claimant need not plead or prove a wrongful act, neglect or default. Rylands v. Fletcher (1868): Blackburn J named the claimant's default, vis major and act of God as possible excuses.
en.meaning:
A general defence is a ground that the defendant pleads and proves to escape liability, in whole or in part, even though the claimant has proved the elements of a tort .

In Pushpabai Purshottam Udeshi (1977), the Supreme Court put the burden on the party pleading it. The defences fall in three groups.

Those based on the claimant's own act: volenti non fit injuria, plaintiff the wrongdoer, and contributory negligence. Those based on events no one could control: inevitable accident and act of God. Those based on the defendant's justified act: private defence, necessity and statutory authority.

General defences in three groups How to read this: the big box holds all general defences. Each inner box is one group and lists its defences. General defences pleaded and proved by the defendant Based on the claimant's act he accepted or caused the harm Volenti non fit injuria. Plaintiff the wrongdoer. Contributory negligence. Based on events beyond control no fault Inevitable accident. Act of God. Based on the defendant's justified act the act was lawful or excused Private defence. Necessity. Statutory authority.
keyPoints: Inevitable accident must be proved by the party who pleads it (Pushpabai). Volenti: consent to a risk must be real. Fear or a misunderstanding of facts defeats it. Inevitable accident: the cause could not be avoided by ordinary care and caution. The party pleading it must prove it. Act of God: an excuse that the Rylands case left open. It is no defence to absolute liability. Private defence: never more harm than necessary (section 37(2)). Death may be caused only in the cases in sections 38 and 41. Necessity: section 30 of the Sanhita protects good faith acts for another's benefit, as a criminal-law analogy. Limitation ends a claim even if not pleaded (section 3).

caseLaws.name: Rylands v
caseLaws.facts: Fletcher (1868) Facts. A reservoir burst through old mine shafts and flooded a neighbour's mine. Principle. The owner was liable. Blackburn J said he could excuse himself by showing the claimant's default, or perhaps vis major or the act of God. Why it matters. It is the source of the excuses that later courts discuss. M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak Case) (1987) Facts. Oleum gas leaked from the Shriram plant in Delhi. The Court considered the measure of liability of a hazardous industry. Principle. The Court listed the exceptions to the Rylands rule. It held that absolute liability is not subject to those exceptions. Why it matters. It shows that act of God and consent do not defeat absolute liability. Pushpabai Purshottam Udeshi v. Ranjit Ginning & Pressing Co. (P) Ltd. (1977) Facts. A car left the road and hit a tree. No one saw how it happened, and the claimants sued for the death. Principle. The burden of proving inevitable accident is on the party pleading it. The Court used the proved facts to infer negligence. Why it matters. It shows that a plea of inevitable accident needs proof.

selfTest.q: 1. What does section 25 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita protect?
selfTest.a: Harm to a person above eighteen who has consented, expressly or impliedly, to suffer it or to take its risk. The act must not be intended to cause death or grievous hurt, and the doer must not know it is likely to do so. 2. Who must prove inevitable accident? The party who pleads it. He must show that the cause could not have been avoided by ordinary care and caution (Pushpabai). 3. Does the right of private defence ever allow more harm than necessary? No. Section 37(2) says the right never extends to inflicting more harm than is necessary for defence. 4. Is act of God a defence to absolute liability? No. M.C. Mehta (1987) held that absolute liability is not subject to the exceptions to the Rylands rule.

law-of-torts-u2-t5.subtitle: The rule in Rylands v. Fletcher: its elements, its defences, and its place in Indian law

en.inOneMinute: Under the rule in Rylands v. Fletcher, a person who brings and keeps something dangerous on his land for his own purposes must keep it in at his own risk. If it escapes and causes damage, he is liable even if he was not careless. This is strict liability. It has four essentials and several defences. In exams it is a long answer, often with a problem on a reservoir, a gas leak or a fire. The Indian rule of absolute liability was framed in reaction to it.
legalProvision: No statute states the rule. It is a rule of common law, from the House of Lords in 1868. Article 21, Constitution of India: M.C. Mehta (1987) said the Rylands rule cannot give a standard of liability consistent with "the constitutional norms". Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 and National Green Tribunal Act, 2010: statutes that now give no-fault relief for accidents. The 1991 Act covers hazardous substances (section 3). The Tribunal Act covers accidents under the Acts in its Schedule I (section 17). Section 164, Motor Vehicles Act, 1988: statutory no-fault compensation of fixed amounts. Section 140, the earlier no-fault provision, was omitted from 1 April 2022. This kind of liability is separate from the rule, as Kaushnuma Begum explains. Seven defences: the Supreme Court listed them in Kaushnuma Begum (2001), quoting Winfield.
en.meaning:
The rule was stated by Blackburn J in the Court of Exchequer Chamber in 1866 and affirmed by the House of Lords in 1868 ((1868) LR 3 HL 330). It says that the person who for his own purposes brings on his land and collects and keeps there anything likely to do mischief if it escapes must keep it in at his peril. If he does not, he is prima facie answerable for all the damage which is the natural consequence of its escape.

In the House of Lords, Lord Cairns added a condition: the land must be put to a "non-natural use". The rule is strict liability because the claimant does not have to prove negligence.

The facts of Rylands v. Fletcher

Mill owners built a reservoir on their land through an engineer and contractors. Old, filled-up coal shafts lay under the site, and nobody knew of them. When the reservoir was filled, the water broke through the shafts and flooded the neighbour's mine. The owners were held liable although they took no part in the work and knew nothing of the shafts. The engineer and contractor had not taken reasonable care.

The case went through three courts. The Court of Exchequer held that the claimant had no cause of action . The Court of Exchequer Chamber unanimously reversed this and awarded damages. The House of Lords affirmed that decision and dismissed the appeal with costs (Lord Cairns and Lord Cranworth).
keyPoints: Rule: bring and keep a dangerous thing on your land for your own purposes, and keep it in at your peril. Essentials: dangerous thing, non-natural use, escape, damage. No proof of negligence is needed. Seven defences: consent, common benefit, act of a stranger, statutory authority, act of God, claimant's default, remoteness. The House of Lords requires foreseeability of the harm (Cambridge Water). Kaushnuma Begum applied the rule to motor accidents. India: M.C. Mehta replaced it, for hazardous industry, with absolute liability.

caseLaws.name: Rylands v
caseLaws.facts: Fletcher (1868) Facts. A mill owner's reservoir burst through old mine shafts and flooded a neighbour's mine. Principle. A person who keeps a mischievous thing on his land for his own purposes must keep it in at his peril. The use of land must be non-natural. Why it matters. The origin of strict liability for the escape of dangerous things. M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak Case) (1987) Facts. Oleum gas escaped from one of the units of Shriram Foods & Fertilizers Industries, and compensation claims followed. Principle. The Supreme Court declined to follow Rylands v. Fletcher. It created absolute liability for hazardous industry, with no exceptions. Why it matters. It marks the Indian departure from the English rule. Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India (1996) Facts. Chemical plants in Bichhri village left toxic sludge that polluted wells and soil. Principle. The Supreme Court followed absolute liability and the polluter pays principle. Why it matters. It applies the Indian rule to pollution. M.P. State Electricity Board v. Shail Kumari (2002) Facts.
