law-of-torts-u5-t3.subtitle: The main features of the Act that created consumer rights, Consumer Councils and a three-tier forum

en.inOneMinute: The Consumer Protection Act, 1986 gave Indian consumers a cheap and quick remedy outside the civil courts. Its main features are the Consumer Protection Councils, a three-tier forum of District Forum, State Commission and National Commission, a list of reliefs, and a limitation period of two years. In exams, this topic is asked as "state the salient features of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986". The trap is to mix its features with those of the 2019 Act that replaced it.
legalProvision: Section 1: the Act extends to the whole of India except Jammu and Kashmir. It applies to all goods and services unless the Central Government provides otherwise. Section 2: definitions, including consumer, complainant, defect, deficiency, unfair trade practice and restrictive trade practice. Section 3: the Act is in addition to, and not in derogation of, any other law. Sections 4 to 8B: Central, State and District Consumer Protection Councils. Section 9: establishment of the District Forum, the State Commission and the National Commission. Sections 11, 17 and 21: pecuniary jurisdiction of each agency. Section 14: findings and reliefs of the District Forum. Sections 15, 19 and 23: appeals. Sections 24A, 25, 26 and 27: limitation, enforcement of orders, frivolous complaints and penalties.
en.meaning: The Act was passed in 1986 to provide for better protection of the interests of consumers and for the settling of consumer disputes. It was amended several times, notably in 1991, 1993 and 2002. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 replaced it, and the 2019 Act came into force in July 2020.
keyPoints: Three tiers: District Forum (up to Rs 20 lakh), State Commission (up to Rs 1 crore), National Commission (above Rs 1 crore). Remedy is additional to other laws (section 3). Limitation is two years (section 24A). Appeal period is 30 days at each level, with a pre-deposit. Failure to obey an order: imprisonment of one month to three years, or a fine, or both.

caseLaws.name: Lucknow Development Authority v
caseLaws.facts: M.K. Gupta (1994) Facts. A statutory housing authority argued that building and allotting flats was a sovereign function, so it could not be taken to a consumer forum. Principle. The Supreme Court disagreed and gave "deficiency in service" a purposive reading. Significance. The Act is beneficial legislation and is read widely. Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha (1995) Facts. Conflicting rulings on whether medical work is a service under the Act. Principle. Medical work for a fee is a service, except care that is completely free. Significance. Shows the wide application of the Act.

selfTest.q: 1. Name the three agencies under the 1986 Act. The District Forum, the State Commission and the National Commission. 2. What is the limitation period?
selfTest.a: Two years from the date on which the cause of action arose, extendable for sufficient cause. 3. Which Act replaced the 1986 Act? The Consumer Protection Act, 2019.

Its main features are the Consumer Protection Councils, a three-tier forum of District Forum, State Commission and National Commission, a list of reliefs, and a limitation period of two years. In exams, this topic is asked as "state the salient features of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986". The trap is to mix its features with those of the 2019 Act that replaced it.
legalProvision: Section 1: the Act extends to the whole of India except Jammu and Kashmir. It applies to all goods and services unless the Central Government provides otherwise. Section 2: definitions, including consumer, complainant, defect, deficiency, unfair trade practice and restrictive trade practice. Section 3: the Act is in addition to, and not in derogation of, any other law. Sections 4 to 8B: Central, State and District Consumer Protection Councils. Section 9: establishment of the District Forum, the State Commission and the National Commission. Sections 11, 17 and 21: pecuniary jurisdiction of each agency. Section 14: findings and reliefs of the District Forum. Sections 15, 19 and 23: appeals. Sections 24A, 25, 26 and 27: limitation, enforcement of orders, frivolous complaints and penalties.
hi.meaning: The Act was passed in 1986 to provide for better protection of the interests of consumers and for the settling of consumer disputes. It was amended several times, notably in 1991, 1993 and 2002. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 replaced it, and the 2019 Act came into force in July 2020.
keyPoints: Three tiers: District Forum (up to Rs 20 lakh), State Commission (up to Rs 1 crore), National Commission (above Rs 1 crore). Remedy is additional to other laws (section 3). Limitation is two years (section 24A). Appeal period is 30 days at each level, with a pre-deposit. Failure to obey an order: imprisonment of one month to three years, or a fine, or both.

caseLaws.name: Lucknow Development Authority v
caseLaws.facts: M.K. Gupta (1994) Facts. A statutory housing authority argued that building and allotting flats was a sovereign function, so it could not be taken to a consumer forum. Principle. The Supreme Court disagreed and gave "deficiency in service" a purposive reading. Significance. The Act is beneficial legislation and is read widely. Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha (1995) Facts. Conflicting rulings on whether medical work is a service under the Act. Principle. Medical work for a fee is a service, except care that is completely free. Significance. Shows the wide application of the Act.

selfTest.q: 1. Name the three agencies under the 1986 Act. The District Forum, the State Commission and the National Commission. 2. What is the limitation period?
selfTest.a: Two years from the date on which the cause of action arose, extendable for sufficient cause. 3. Which Act replaced the 1986 Act? The Consumer Protection Act, 2019.

law-of-torts-u5-t6.subtitle: The six consumer rights in section 2(9) of the 2019 Act and how each is protected

en.inOneMinute: Section 2(9) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 lists six consumer rights. They are the right to safety, to information, to access at competitive prices, to be heard, to seek redressal, and to consumer awareness. The list says "includes", so it is not closed. In exams, this topic is asked as "explain the rights of consumers", and as a problem matching facts to a right. The usual trap is to give the older list of 1986 or the American four rights as if they were the current law.
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, section 2(9): defines consumer rights. Sections 5, 7 and 9: the Central, State and District Councils render advice on promotion and protection of consumer rights. Section 18: the Central Authority protects, promotes and enforces the rights of consumers as a class. Consumer Protection Act, 1986, section 6: the earlier list of six rights, with the right to consumer education in place of consumer awareness.
en.meaning:
"Consumer rights" in section 2(9) includes the six rights set out below. The word "includes" means that other rights can also be recognised.

What a consumer right is, and why the law gives it

A consumer right is a protection the law gives to a buyer, because a buyer is usually the weaker party in the market. The seller knows the product, controls the price and writes the terms. The buyer often cannot test the goods, cannot follow the technical details and cannot bargain over a printed contract. Three weaknesses explain the six rights. The buyer is exposed to unsafe goods. The buyer lacks information. The buyer has little bargaining power .

The six rights answer these weaknesses in order. Safety, information, and choice at fair prices protect the buyer before and during the purchase. If something still goes wrong, the buyer needs a voice, a remedy, and enough knowledge to use them. Those are the rights to be heard, to seek redressal and to consumer awareness.

Rights and remedies are different things

A right says what the consumer is entitled to expect. A remedy is what the consumer can get when the right is violated. Section 2(9) only defines the rights. To enforce one, the consumer files a complaint under section 35 on one of the grounds in section 2(6), and the Commission can give relief under section 39(1). Because section 2(9) says consumer rights "includes" the six, the list is open.
keyPoints: Six rights in section 2(9): safety, information, choice at competitive prices, to be heard, redressal, awareness. The list uses "includes", so it is open. The 1986 list had consumer education in place of awareness. The Authority protects rights as a class (section 18). Councils advise on promotion of rights.

caseLaws.name: Lucknow Development Authority v
caseLaws.facts: M.K. Gupta (1994) Facts. A statutory housing authority argued that it could not be sued before a consumer forum. Principle. The Supreme Court read deficiency in service in a purposive way to protect consumers. Significance. The right to redressal is not cut down by technical objections. L.I.C. of India v. Consumer Education & Research Centre (1995) Facts. A consumer organisation challenged a term of a policy that shut out the self-employed. Principle. The term was arbitrary under Article 14 and was struck down. Significance. Shows consumer rights and the role of consumer organisations. SpiceJet Ltd. v. Ranju Aery (2017) Facts. An airline cancelled a connecting flight, refused a refund and offered no alternative. Principle. The consumer fora held it a deficiency in service and gave relief. Significance. The right to redressal in action.

selfTest.q: 1. How many rights does section 2(9) list?
selfTest.a: Six. 2. Which right did the 1986 Act call consumer education? The right to consumer awareness in the 2019 Act. 3. Who protects consumer rights as a class? The Central Consumer Protection Authority.

law-of-torts-u5-t5.subtitle: Who is a consumer under section 2(7) of the 2019 Act: buyers, users, beneficiaries, and who is left out

en.inOneMinute: A consumer is a person who buys goods or hires services for a consideration. A user of the goods or a beneficiary of the services, with the buyer's approval, is also a consumer. A person who buys goods for resale, or any goods or services for a commercial purpose, is not. In exams, this topic is asked as "define consumer and discuss who is excluded", and as a problem on a business buyer, a free service or a family member. The usual trap is the commercial purpose test and the livelihood exception.
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, section 2(7): defines consumer. Section 2(5): defines complainant. Section 2(42): defines service. It does not include the rendering of any service free of charge or under a contract of personal service. Section 2(16): defines e-commerce. Section 35: who may file a complaint.
en.meaning:
Section 2(7) says that a consumer is any person who does either of two things.

Buys goods. He buys any goods for a consideration which has been paid or promised, or partly paid and partly promised, or under a system of deferred payment. The definition includes any user of the goods, other than the buyer, when the use is with the approval of the buyer. It does not include a person who obtains the goods for resale or for any commercial purpose. Hires or avails of services. He hires or avails of any service for a consideration which has been paid or promised, or partly paid and partly promised, or under a system of deferred payment. The definition includes any beneficiary of the service, other than the hirer, when the service is availed with the approval of the hirer. It does not include a person who avails of a service for any commercial purpose.
keyPoints: A consumer buys goods or hires services for a consideration, paid, promised or in instalments. A user or beneficiary with approval is a consumer. Resale and commercial purpose are excluded, except exclusive use for livelihood by self-employment. Free services and personal service contracts are outside the Act. Online and offline buying are covered.

caseLaws.name: Indian Medical Association v
caseLaws.facts: V.P. Shantha (1995) Facts. Conflicting rulings on whether a doctor's or hospital's work is a service under the Act. Principle. Medical service for a fee is a service. Free care is excluded only if free to every patient. Contracts of personal service are excluded. Significance. Patients are consumers. Lucknow Development Authority v. M.K. Gupta (1994) Facts. A statutory housing authority argued that building and allotting flats was a sovereign function. Principle. It gave a service, and the flat buyer was a consumer. Significance. Public bodies can be opposite parties. Spring Meadows Hospital v. Harjot Ahluwalia (1998) Facts. A nurse injected a minor patient without a sensitivity test, leaving him in a vegetative state. Principle. The child, as beneficiary, and the parents, as the persons who hired the service, are both consumers. Significance. Beneficiaries and hirers can each claim. Bar of Indian Lawyers v. D.K. Gandhi (2024) Facts. A client sued his advocate before a consumer forum for deficiency in service. Principle. An advocate's service is a contract of personal service, so the complaint is not maintainable. Significance. Advocates are outside the Act.

selfTest.q: 1. Is a person who buys goods for resale a consumer?
selfTest.a: No. Goods bought for resale or any commercial purpose are excluded. 2. Is a user of the goods a consumer? Yes, if the use is with the approval of the buyer. 3. Is a client a consumer of his advocate's service? No. The Supreme Court held it a contract of personal service.

law-of-torts-u5-t7.subtitle: What counts as a defect in goods or a deficiency in service under the 2019 Act, how it is proved and the leading cases

en.inOneMinute: A defect is a fault in goods. A deficiency is a fault in a service. Both are grounds for a consumer complaint. Deficiency includes negligence and the deliberate withholding of relevant information. In exams, this topic is asked as "distinguish defect from deficiency and explain the remedies", and as a problem on a faulty product or a bad service. The trap is to forget that goods are tested in a laboratory and services are judged on the evidence.
legalProvision: Section 2(10): defines "defect". Section 2(11): defines "deficiency". Section 2(42): defines "service". It excludes services rendered free of charge or under a contract of personal service. Section 2(6): a complaint may allege that goods suffer from defects, that services suffer from deficiency, that a price above the fixed or displayed price was charged, or that hazardous goods or services are offered. Section 38(2): procedure when goods are alleged to be defective, including laboratory testing. Section 39: findings and reliefs of the District Commission.
en.meaning:
A defect is any fault, imperfection or shortcoming in the quality, quantity, potency , purity or standard in relation to the goods. The standard is one required to be maintained by or under any law or under any contract, express or implied . It also covers a standard claimed by the trader in any manner.

A deficiency is any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature and manner of performance of a service. The performance is one required to be maintained by or under any law, or one that a person has undertaken to perform under a contract or otherwise. It includes any act of negligence or omission or commission by that person that causes loss or injury to the consumer, and deliberate withholding of relevant information from the consumer.
keyPoints: Defect: goods. Deficiency: services. Standard comes from law, contract or the trader's own claim. Deficiency includes negligence and withholding of relevant information. Laboratory report within 45 days. Free services and personal service contracts are outside the Act.

caseLaws.name: Lucknow Development Authority v
caseLaws.facts: M.K. Gupta (1994) Facts. A housing authority argued that building and allotting flats was a sovereign function. Principle. Housing construction is a service, and a failure to deliver is a deficiency. Significance. Wide reading of deficiency in service. Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha (1995) Facts. Conflicting rulings on medical service under the Act. Principle. Medical service for a fee is a service. Significance. Medical negligence is a deficiency. Spring Meadows Hospital v. Harjot Ahluwalia (1998) Facts. A nurse injected a minor without a sensitivity test, leaving him in a vegetative state. Principle. Child and parents are consumers; each can be compensated on a different head. Significance. Compensation for medical deficiency. SpiceJet Ltd. v. Ranju Aery (2017) Facts. An airline cancelled a connecting flight and refused a refund. Principle. Deficiency in service by an airline. Significance. Transport services are covered. Om Prakash v. Reliance General Insurance Co. Ltd. (2017) Facts. An insurer rejected a genuine theft claim for notice given eight days late. Principle. An explained delay is not a ground to reject a genuine claim. Significance. Insurance is a service; unfair rejection is a deficiency. Bharathi Knitting Co. v. DHL Worldwide Express Courier (1996) 4 SCC 704 Facts. An exporter sent export documents by courier, and the cover did not reach its destination. The air bill, which the exporter had signed, limited DHL's liability to US $100 and excluded consequential loss. law-of-torts-u5-t11.subtitle: The regulator created by sections 10 to 27 to protect consumers as a class: its structure, functions and powers

en.inOneMinute: The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) is a regulator created by section 10 of the 2019 Act. It protects, promotes and enforces consumer rights as a class. It can investigate, recall goods, order refunds, impose penalties on false advertisements, and search and seize. In exams, this topic is asked as "explain the establishment, composition and powers of the CCPA". The usual trap is to confuse it with the Commissions, which decide individual complaints.
legalProvision: Section 10: establishment, objects and composition. Section 11: rules on qualifications and service conditions of the Chief Commissioner and Commissioners. Sections 12 to 14: vacancies, officers and procedure. Section 15: the Investigation Wing. Section 16: power of the District Collector. Section 17: complaints to the authorities. Section 18: powers and functions. Section 19: preliminary inquiry and investigation. Section 20: power to recall goods. Section 21: directions and penalties for false or misleading advertisements. Section 22: search and seizure. Section 23: designation of another body to function as the Authority. Section 24: appeal to the National Commission. Sections 88 and 89: penalties for non-compliance and for false advertisements. Section 2(4): the Central Authority means the Central Consumer Protection Authority established under section 10. Section 92: a court takes cognizance of an offence under section 88 or 89 only on a complaint by the Central Authority or an officer it authorises. Section 93: an officer who searches or seizes under section 22 knowing there are no reasonable grounds is punishable with imprisonment up to one year, or fine up to Rs 10,000, or both.
en.meaning: The Central Authority is defined in section 2(4) as the Central Consumer Protection Authority established under section 10. Its purpose is to regulate matters relating to violation of rights of consumers, unfair trade practices and false or misleading advertisements which are prejudicial to the interests of the public and consumers. It also promotes, protects and enforces the rights of consumers as a class.
keyPoints: Established under section 10; a Chief Commissioner and other Commissioners. Acts for consumers as a class. Powers: inquire, file complaints, intervene, recall goods, search and seize. Penalty on a false advertisement: up to Rs 10 lakh, and up to Rs 50 lakh for each subsequent contravention. Appeal to the National Commission within 30 days.

caseLaws.name: Indian Medical Association v
caseLaws.facts: V.P. Shantha (1995) Facts. Conflicting rulings on whether medical work is a service under the consumer law. Principle. Medical work for a fee is a service. Significance. Class-wide complaints on such services can also be taken up by the Authority.

selfTest.q: 1. Which section establishes the Authority?
selfTest.a: Section 10 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. 2. Who heads the Investigation Wing? A Director-General. 3. Where is an appeal against the Authority's order filed? In the National Commission, within 30 days of receipt of the order.

law-of-torts-u5-t9.subtitle: The agencies that settle consumer disputes: three Commissions, mediation cells and the regulator

en.inOneMinute: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 sets up a three-tier machinery for consumer disputes: the District Commission in each district, the State Commission in each State and the National Commission. It adds mediation cells and a regulator, the Central Consumer Protection Authority. In exams, this topic is asked as "explain the redressal machinery under the Act", and as a problem on where to file and how to appeal. The usual trap is to mix the composition, the value limits and the appeal periods of the three tiers.
legalProvision: Section 28: a District Commission in each district, with a President and not less than two members. Section 42: a State Commission in each State, with a President and not less than four members. Section 53 and 54: the National Commission, with a President and not less than four members. Sections 34, 47 and 58: jurisdiction of the three Commissions. Section 38: procedure and powers of a Commission, including interim orders and the powers of a civil court. Sections 40, 50 and 60: review of orders. Sections 41, 51 and 67: appeals. Sections 71 and 72: enforcement of orders and penalty for non-compliance. Sections 74 to 81: mediation. Sections 34(2) and 47(4): where a complaint is filed with the District and State Commissions (territorial jurisdiction). Section 35: who may file a complaint, and the fee. Section 36: admission of a complaint within 21 days, and how the bench sits. Section 39: the reliefs a Commission may order. Sections 52 and 73: time to decide an appeal, and appeals against orders under section 72.
en.meaning: The redressal machinery means the set of agencies that the Act creates to hear and decide consumer disputes. A "consumer dispute" is a dispute in which the person against whom a complaint is made denies or disputes the allegations (section 2(8)).
keyPoints: Three tiers: District (sections 28, 34), State (sections 42, 47), National (sections 53, 58). Members: President and at least two (District), at least four (State and National). Appeals: 45 days to the State Commission, then 30 days each, with 50 per cent deposit. Commissions have civil court powers and can pass interim orders. Mediation cells and the Authority add to the machinery. Time limits: complaint two years (section 69); appeals 45, 30 and 30 days; review 30 days; late filing allowed for sufficient cause.

caseLaws.name: Lucknow Development Authority v
caseLaws.facts: M.K. Gupta (1994) Facts. A statutory housing authority argued that it was exercising a sovereign function and could not be taken to a consumer forum. Principle. The Supreme Court disagreed and held that the Act applies to its services. Significance. The machinery reaches public bodies as well. SpiceJet Ltd. v. Ranju Aery (2017) Facts. An airline cancelled a connecting flight, refused a refund and offered no alternative. The consumer fora, in turn, found for the family. Principle. Three fora up to the National Commission held that this was a deficiency in service. Significance. The tiers work as a ladder of review.

selfTest.q: 1. Who establishes the National Commission?
selfTest.a: The Central Government. 2. How many members does a State Commission have? A President and not less than four members. 3. Where is an appeal from the National Commission filed? In the Supreme Court within 30 days.

law-of-torts-u5-t8.subtitle: Restrictive trade practices, unfair trade practices and unfair contracts under the 2019 Act, with the full list of unfair practices

en.inOneMinute: A restrictive trade practice manipulates prices or the flow of supplies and imposes unjustified costs on consumers. An unfair trade practice uses an unfair or deceptive method to promote sale, use or supply of goods or services. An unfair contract has terms that cause a significant change in the consumer's rights. In exams, this topic is asked as "define unfair trade practice and list its forms", and as a problem on a false claim, a bargain price or a lucky draw. The trap is to mix the three terms and to forget that a bill must be issued.
legalProvision: Section 2(41): restrictive trade practice. Section 2(46): unfair contract. Section 2(47): unfair trade practice. Section 2(6)(i): a complaint may allege that an unfair contract or unfair trade practice or restrictive trade practice has been adopted by a trader or service provider. Section 39(1)(g): the Commission may order the opposite party to discontinue the unfair or restrictive trade practice and not to repeat it. Sections 18, 21 and 22: the Central Authority prevents unfair trade practices, and can issue directions, impose penalties and conduct search and seizure. Section 94: measures to prevent unfair trade practices in e-commerce and direct selling.
en.meaning:
A restrictive trade practice is a trade practice that tends to manipulate price or its conditions of delivery, or to affect the flow of supplies in the market relating to goods or services. It does so in a way that imposes unjustified costs or restrictions on consumers.

An unfair trade practice is a trade practice which, to promote the sale, use or supply of goods or the provision of a service, adopts any unfair method or unfair or deceptive practice.

An unfair contract is a contract between a manufacturer, trader or service provider on one side and a consumer on the other, with terms that cause a significant change in the rights of the consumer.
keyPoints: Restrictive: manipulating price or supply (section 2(41)). Tie-in sale is an example. Unfair: unfair or deceptive method to promote sales (section 2(47)). Unfair contract: significant change in consumer's rights (section 2(46)). Not issuing a bill and refusing to take back defective goods are unfair trade practices. Remedy: order to discontinue and not repeat, with compensation.

Significance. The Act now gives consumers a remedy against practices that manipulate price or supply to their cost.

selfTest.a: Yes. Requiring a consumer to buy other goods or services as a condition is listed in section 2(41). 2. How long must a seller take back defective goods if the bill is silent? Within 30 days. 3. Which Commissions hear complaints against unfair contracts? The State Commission (up to Rs 10 crore) and the National Commission (above Rs 10 crore).

law-of-torts-u5-t12.subtitle: Chapter VI of the 2019 Act: when a manufacturer, a service provider or a seller must pay for harm from a defective product

en.inOneMinute: Product liability is the responsibility of a product manufacturer, a product service provider or a product seller to compensate a consumer for harm caused by a defective product or a deficient service. Chapter VI of the 2019 Act (sections 82 to 87) states who is liable and when. In exams, this topic is asked as "explain product liability under the 2019 Act", and as a problem on a defective product that causes injury. The usual traps are the five grounds against a manufacturer and the point that a manufacturer is liable even without negligence for a breach of express warranty.
legalProvision: Section 2(34): "product liability" means the responsibility of a product manufacturer or product seller, of any product or service, to compensate for any harm caused to a consumer by a defective product manufactured or sold, or by deficiency in services relating to it. Section 2(35): "product liability action" is a complaint filed before a District, State or National Commission to claim compensation for the harm. Sections 2(36), 2(37) and 2(38): definitions of product manufacturer, product seller and product service provider. Section 82: the Chapter applies to every claim for compensation under a product liability action for harm caused by a defective product. Section 83: the action lies against a manufacturer, a product service provider or a product seller. Section 84: liability of the product manufacturer. Section 85: liability of the product service provider. Section 86: liability of product sellers. Section 87: exceptions. Section 39(1)(e): the Commission may order compensation in a product liability action.
en.meaning: Product liability is the responsibility to compensate for harm caused by a defective product, or by faulty service in relation to it. It is a form of liability that rests on the defect and on the part the person played in producing, servicing or selling the product, and not only on carelessness.
keyPoints: Chapter VI, sections 82 to 87. Three defendants: manufacturer (section 84), service provider (section 85), seller (section 86). Manufacturer grounds: manufacturing defect, design defect, deviation, breach of express warranty, no adequate instructions or warnings. Manufacturer is liable for the express warranty even without negligence. Exceptions in section 87: misuse, alteration, obvious danger and others.

caseLaws.name: Donoghue v
caseLaws.facts: Stevenson (1932) Facts. A decomposed snail was found in a bottle of ginger beer bought for the claimant by a friend. Principle. A manufacturer owes a duty of care to the ultimate consumer, without a contract. Significance. The common law root of product liability. M.P. State Electricity Board v. Shail Kumari (2002) Facts. A cyclist died after touching a live wire lying on a road. The Board said that a stranger had stolen electricity from its line. Principle. The Board was liable under strict liability, and the act of a stranger was not a defence. Significance. Shows liability without proof of negligence for those who supply a dangerous product or service.

selfTest.q: 1. Which section lists the grounds of liability of a manufacturer?
selfTest.a: Section 84. 2. When is a seller liable if the manufacturer is not known? Under section 86(d), he is liable for the product he sold. 3. Is a manufacturer liable for an express warranty without negligence? Yes. Section 84(2) says so.

law-of-torts-u5-t10.subtitle: The advisory Councils at Central, State and District level that promote and protect consumer rights

en.inOneMinute: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 creates three advisory bodies: the Central Council, a State Council in each State and a District Council in each district. They advise on promotion and protection of consumer rights. They do not decide disputes. In exams, this topic is asked as "explain the composition and objects of the Consumer Protection Councils". The usual trap is to confuse the Councils, which advise, with the Commissions, which decide.
legalProvision: Sections 3 to 5: the Central Consumer Protection Council, its meetings and objects. Sections 6 and 7: State Consumer Protection Councils and their objects. Sections 8 and 9: District Consumer Protection Councils and their objects. Section 2(9): the consumer rights that the Councils are to promote and protect. Corresponding sections of the 1986 Act: sections 4 to 8B.
en.meaning: A Consumer Protection Council is an advisory body. Its purpose is to render advice on the promotion and protection of consumer rights under the Act. It has no power to hear complaints or pass orders.
keyPoints: Councils are advisory and do not decide disputes. Chairs: Union Minister (Central), State Minister (State), Collector (District). Meetings: at least one a year (Central), at least two a year (State, District). Object: advice on promotion and protection of consumer rights. Sections 3 to 9 of the 2019 Act.

caseLaws.name: L
caseLaws.facts: I.C. of India v. Consumer Education & Research Centre (1995) Facts. A consumer organisation challenged a policy term that shut out the self-employed. Principle. The term was arbitrary under Article 14 and was struck down. Significance. Shows how consumer bodies carry the consumer voice that the Councils are meant to promote.

selfTest.q: 1. Who chairs the District Council?
selfTest.a: The Collector of the district. 2. How often must the State Council meet? At least twice a year. 3. Can a Council order compensation? No. It is advisory only.

law-of-torts-u5-t13.subtitle: The reliefs a Consumer Commission can give under section 39, with interest, compensation, punitive damages and enforcement

en.inOneMinute: If a complaint is proved, the Commission can order the opposite party to remove the defect, replace the goods, refund the price with interest, pay compensation, stop an unfair practice, withdraw hazardous goods, issue a corrective advertisement and pay costs. Section 39 lists these reliefs. In exams, this topic is asked as "what reliefs can a Consumer Commission grant", and as a problem on a defective product with a claim for money. The usual trap is to forget compensation for mental agony and the power to award punitive damages.
legalProvision: Section 39(1): findings and reliefs of the District Commission. Sections 49 and 59 apply the same procedure and reliefs to the State and National Commissions. Section 38(8): interim orders. Section 39(2): sums obtained under section 39(1) are credited to a prescribed fund. Sections 40, 50 and 60: review. Sections 41, 51 and 67: appeals, with a deposit of 50 per cent. Sections 71 and 72: enforcement as a decree and the penalty for non-compliance. Sections 74 to 81: settlement through mediation. Sections 20 and 21: reliefs by the Central Authority: recall of goods, refund and discontinuation.
en.meaning: A remedy is the relief that the law gives to a person whose right has been violated. Under the Consumer Protection Act, the remedy is the order that a Commission makes when it is satisfied that the goods suffer from a defect, or that the allegations about services, unfair trade practices or product liability are proved.
keyPoints: Section 39(1) lists the reliefs: repair, replace, refund with interest, compensation, and more. Compensation includes harassment and mental agony. Punitive damages can be granted in a fit case. Class relief: at least 25 per cent of the value of the goods or services. Non-compliance: imprisonment of one month to three years, or a fine of Rs 25,000 to Rs 1 lakh.

caseLaws.name: Lucknow Development Authority v
caseLaws.facts: M.K. Gupta (1994) Facts. An allottee deposited money for a flat and did not get possession on time. Principle. Compensation extends to harassment and mental agony. Interest, possession or refund and Rs 10,000 were ordered. Significance. Purposive reading of compensation. SpiceJet Ltd. v. Ranju Aery (2017) Facts. An airline cancelled a connecting flight and refused a refund. The family bought a costlier replacement. Principle. The family was entitled to a refund, reimbursement of the extra cost and compensation. Significance. Reliefs in an air travel dispute. Spring Meadows Hospital v. Harjot Ahluwalia (1998) Facts. A minor patient was left in a vegetative state after an injection given without a sensitivity test. Principle. The child and the parents may each be awarded compensation on a different head. Significance. Separate heads of compensation.

selfTest.q: 1. Can the Commission award punitive damages?
selfTest.a: Yes. The proviso to section 39(1)(d) gives it that power in a fit case. 2. Does compensation cover mental agony? Yes, as held in Lucknow Development Authority v. M.K. Gupta. 3. What is the minimum sum where many consumers cannot be identified? At least 25 per cent of the value of the defective goods or services sold.

caseLaws.facts: M. K. Gupta (1994) Facts. An allottee deposited money for a flat and did not get possession on time. Principle. Compensation extends to harassment and mental agony. law-of-torts-u5-t4.subtitle: The Act that replaced the 1986 law: a regulator, product liability, mediation, e-commerce rules and e-filing

en.inOneMinute: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 replaced the 1986 Act. It adds a regulator (the Central Consumer Protection Authority), a chapter on product liability, mediation, e-commerce rules, e-filing, and heavier penalties for false advertisements. In exams, this topic is asked as "explain the scheme and new features of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019". The usual trap is to forget the new features and to mix up the appeal periods and the penalties.
legalProvision: Section 1: the Act extends to the whole of India. A notification of 30 October 2019 made it applicable to the Union territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh. It applies to all goods and services unless the Central Government provides otherwise. Section 2: definitions, including consumer (2(7)), consumer rights (2(9)), defect (2(10)), deficiency (2(11)), e-commerce (2(16)), product liability (2(34)), restrictive trade practice (2(41)), unfair contract (2(46)) and unfair trade practice (2(47)). Chapter II (sections 3 to 9): Consumer Protection Councils. Chapter III (sections 10 to 27): Central Consumer Protection Authority. Chapter IV (sections 28 to 73): Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions. Chapter V (sections 74 to 81): mediation. Chapter VI (sections 82 to 87): product liability. Chapter VII (sections 88 to 93): offences and penalties. Chapter VIII (sections 94 to 107): miscellaneous, including section 94 on e-commerce and direct selling, section 100 (the Act is in addition to other laws) and section 107 (repeal of the 1986 Act).
en.meaning: The 2019 Act is the present law that protects consumers in India. It does more than settle disputes. It also prevents unfair practices through a regulator, and it covers modern markets such as e-commerce and direct selling.
keyPoints: 2019 Act replaced the 1986 Act (section 107). New: Central Authority, product liability, mediation, e-commerce and e-filing. Jurisdiction by consideration paid: Rs 50 lakh, Rs 2 crore under the 2021 Rules. Appeals: 45 days to the State Commission, then 30 days each, with a 50 per cent deposit. Limitation: two years. False advertisement: up to two years and Rs 10 lakh.

caseLaws.name: Lucknow Development Authority v
caseLaws.facts: M.K. Gupta (1994) Facts. A statutory housing authority claimed to act in a sovereign function when it built and allotted flats. Principle. The Supreme Court read "deficiency in service" in a wide, purposive way. Significance. The consumer Acts are beneficial laws. SpiceJet Ltd. v. Ranju Aery (2017) Facts. An airline cancelled a connecting flight, refused a refund and offered no alternative. Principle. The consumer fora, up to the National Commission, held it a deficiency in service. Significance. Shows the Act applied to transport services.

selfTest.q: 1. What is the limitation period for a complaint?
selfTest.a: Two years from the date on which the cause of action arose, extendable for sufficient cause. 2. On what does the jurisdiction of a Commission depend? The consideration paid for the goods or services. 3. Which chapter deals with product liability? Chapter VI, sections 82 to 87.

law-of-torts-u5-t16.subtitle: Electronic filing of consumer complaints and the other places where the 2019 Act allows electronic means

en.inOneMinute: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 allows a consumer complaint to be filed electronically, the fee to be paid electronically, the hearing to be held by video conferencing, and notices to be served by electronic means. This saves travel and cost, and it helps a consumer file where he lives. In exams, this topic is asked as a short note on e-filing and other electronic features of the 2019 Act. The usual trap is to confuse e-filing, which is a procedure, with e-commerce, which is the market that the Act also regulates.
legalProvision: Section 35(1), proviso: a complaint may be filed electronically in the manner prescribed . Section 35(2): the fee is payable in the manner prescribed, including in electronic form. Section 38(6): a party may be heard in person or through video conferencing , with leave of the Commission. Section 38(4): the Commission may require an electronic service provider to give information, documents or records . Section 65: notices may be served by registered post, speed post, an approved courier, or any other mode including electronic means. A notice may also be served on an electronic service provider at the address on its platform. Section 17: a complaint of violation of consumer rights as a class may be sent in writing or in electronic mode to the District Collector, a regional Commissioner or the Central Authority. Section 2(16) and 2(17): definitions of e-commerce and of electronic service provider. Section 94: the Central Government may take measures to prevent unfair trade practices in e-commerce and direct selling.
en.meaning: E-filing means making a complaint and other filings through an electronic system, instead of on paper at the registry. The Act does not itself describe the portal or the format. It leaves the manner to be prescribed by rules, and a government online system for consumer complaints has been provided for this purpose.
keyPoints: Complaint may be filed electronically (section 35(1) proviso). Fee may be paid in electronic form (section 35(2)). Video conferencing hearing with leave (section 38(6)). Notices by electronic means (section 65). Limitation of two years still applies.

caseLaws.name: This topic rests on the text of the Act and the rules made under it
caseLaws.facts: No judgment in this collection is relied on for it.

selfTest.q: 1. Which section allows electronic filing?
selfTest.a: The proviso to section 35(1). 2. Can the fee be paid electronically? Yes, under section 35(2). 3. Does e-filing change the limitation period? No. The two years in section 69 apply.

en.meaning:
What best describes 'consumerism'?

Explanation. Consumerism is a collective, organised movement — through associations, advocacy, and legislative lobbying — not merely individual shopping caution.

Why couldn't ordinary tort remedies alone correct market-wide consumer harms such as adulteration or false advertising?

Explanation. Tort remedies compensate one injured consumer at a time, long after harm occurs, and only if that consumer can afford to litigate — inadequate for correcting market-wide problems.

The doctrine of caveat emptor means

Explanation. Caveat emptor, 'let the buyer beware', historically placed the responsibility of examining goods before purchase on the buyer, with limited seller disclosure duties.

Consumerism pushed the law towards a philosophy closer to which principle?

law-of-torts-u5-t15.subtitle: Step by step: who may complain, where, within what time, how the Commission admits and decides the complaint

en.inOneMinute: A consumer files a written complaint, with the prescribed fee, before the right Commission within two years. The Commission decides admission within 21 days. The opposite party gets 30 days to reply. The Commission hears the case on affidavits and documents and tries to decide within three months, or five months if goods must be tested. In exams, this topic is asked as "describe the procedure for filing and disposal of a consumer complaint". The usual traps are the deemed admission after 21 days, the time for the reply and the time for the laboratory report.
legalProvision: Section 2(6): defines "complaint": an allegation in writing, made by a complainant for obtaining relief under the Act. Section 35: manner in which a complaint is made, and who may make it. Section 34(2): the place where the complaint is filed. Section 36: proceedings before the District Commission, including admission. Section 37: reference to mediation . Section 38: procedure on admission of a complaint. Section 39: findings and reliefs. Section 69: limitation period of two years. Section 65: service of notices.
en.meaning: A consumer dispute is a dispute where the person against whom a complaint is made denies or disputes the allegations (section 2(8)). The procedure is the series of steps from the filing of the complaint to the order. It is meant to be quick, simple and cheap, and it is not bound by the technical rules of a civil suit.
keyPoints: Written complaint with the prescribed fee. E-filing allowed. Admission ordinarily within 21 days. Deemed admitted if not decided. Reply in 30 days, extendable by up to 15 days. Laboratory report in 45 days. Decision in three or five months. Limitation: two years from the cause of action. Late complaint: sufficient cause and recorded reasons (section 69(2)). A continuing wrong gives a fresh period (Limitation Act, section 22).

caseLaws.name: Spring Meadows Hospital v
caseLaws.facts: Harjot Ahluwalia (1998) Facts. A minor patient was left in a vegetative state. The parents and the child each claimed compensation. Principle. Both the child as beneficiary and the parents as hirers are consumers who can complain. Significance. Who may complain. Om Prakash v. Reliance General Insurance Co. Ltd. (2017) Facts. An insurer rejected a genuine theft claim because notice was eight days late. Principle. A satisfactorily explained delay is not a ground to reject a genuine claim. Significance. A consumer complaint can succeed against an unfair rejection. SpiceJet Ltd. v. Ranju Aery (2017) Facts. A passenger filed a complaint for a refund, extra costs, compensation and litigation costs. Principle. The complaint succeeded before the District Forum, the State Commission and the National Commission. Significance. Shows a complaint travelling through the tiers.

selfTest.q: 1. When is a complaint deemed admitted?
selfTest.a: When the District Commission does not decide the question of admission within 21 days of filing. 2. How long does the opposite party have to reply? 30 days, extendable by up to 15 days. 3. How long to decide a complaint that needs testing of goods? The Commission endeavours to decide within five months.

law-of-torts-u5-t19.subtitle: Settling consumer disputes by agreement: mediation under the 2019 Act and the place of other alternative dispute resolution

en.inOneMinute: Alternative dispute resolution (ADR) means settling a dispute without a full trial. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 builds one ADR method into the Commissions: mediation. A Commission can send the parties to mediation if a settlement looks possible, and the parties must agree in writing. In exams, this topic is asked as a short note on ADR and consumer disputes, or on mediation under the Act. The usual trap is to think that mediation is compulsory. It needs the written consent of both parties.
legalProvision: Section 37: at the first hearing or later, if elements of a settlement acceptable to the parties appear, the District Commission may ask the parties to give written consent within five days to mediation under Chapter V. On consent, it refers the matter within five days. prescribed cases are excluded. Section 74: a consumer mediation cell is set up with each District and State Commission by the State Government, and with the National Commission and its regional Benches by the Central Government. Section 75: each Commission prepares a panel of mediators on the recommendation of a selection committee of its President and a member. The panel is valid for five years. Section 79: mediation is held in the cell, and the mediator is guided by the principles of natural justice. Section 80: a settlement is written down and signed by the parties, and the mediator sends it with a report to the Commission. Section 81: the Commission passes an order recording the settlement within seven days. Section 100: the Act is in addition to, and not in derogation of, any other law in force. Section 2(25): mediation means the process by which a mediator mediates the consumer disputes. Section 41 (third proviso ):
en.meaning: ADR covers methods such as negotiation, mediation, conciliation, arbitration and Lok Adalats. In these methods, the parties, with the help of a neutral person or body, reach a result outside the ordinary court process. In the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the method given a place inside the Act is mediation. A mediator helps the parties reach their own agreement and does not decide the dispute.
keyPoints: Mediation needs written consent of the parties within five days (section 37). A consumer mediation cell is attached to each Commission (section 74). The panel of mediators is valid for five years (section 75). The Commission records a settlement within seven days (section 81). If mediation fails, the Commission hears all issues. Mediation ends in three months from the first appearance unless extended (Regulation 11(2)).

caseLaws.name: This topic rests on the text of the Act
caseLaws.facts: No judgment in this collection is relied on for it.

selfTest.q: 1. Is mediation compulsory under the 2019 Act?
selfTest.a: No. The parties must consent in writing. 2. Within how many days must the Commission record a settlement? Seven days from receiving the settlement report (section 81). 3. What happens if mediation fails? The Commission continues to hear all the issues.

law-of-torts-u5-t14.subtitle: Pecuniary, territorial, appellate and revisional jurisdiction of the three Commissions, and the powers they exercise

en.inOneMinute: Each Commission has original jurisdiction over complaints of a certain value, appellate jurisdiction over the tier below, and a revisional power to correct jurisdictional errors. Territorial jurisdiction decides in which place the complaint is filed. The Commissions have the powers of a civil court for certain purposes. In exams, this topic is asked as "discuss the jurisdiction and powers of the Consumer Commissions", and as a problem on where a complaint must be filed. The usual traps are the pecuniary limits and the consideration-paid test.
legalProvision: Section 34: jurisdiction of the District Commission, pecuniary and territorial. Section 47: jurisdiction of the State Commission, including appeals and revision. Section 58: jurisdiction of the National Commission, including appeals and revision. Section 36 and 38: proceedings, admission, procedure and powers. Sections 40, 50 and 60: review. Sections 48 and 62: transfer of cases. Section 61: power of the National Commission to set aside ex parte orders. Section 65: service of notice by registered post, speed post, courier or electronic means. Section 66: experts to assist the State or National Commission. Section 69: limitation of two years.
en.meaning: Jurisdiction is the authority of a Commission to hear and decide a matter. It has several parts. Pecuniary jurisdiction depends on the value of the consideration paid. Territorial jurisdiction depends on the place. Appellate jurisdiction is the power to hear appeals. Under revisional jurisdiction, a Commission can call for the record and correct a jurisdictional error.
keyPoints: Pecuniary jurisdiction is by consideration paid. Territorial jurisdiction includes the complainant's residence or place of work. State and National Commissions also have appellate and revisional jurisdiction. Commissions have civil court powers and can pass interim orders. Limitation is two years. District and State Commission President and members are appointed by the State Government on a Selection Committee's recommendation, serve four years or to age 65, and can be reappointed once. State Commission President: a High Court Judge, serving or former. District Commission President: a District Judge, serving, former or qualified.

caseLaws.name: SpiceJet Ltd
caseLaws.facts: v. Ranju Aery (2017) Facts. The District Forum and the State Commission found SpiceJet liable for cancelling a flight with no refund. SpiceJet filed a revision petition before the National Commission. Principle. The National Commission, in its revisional jurisdiction, will not disturb concurrent findings of fact unless there is jurisdictional error or material illegality. Significance. Limits of revisional jurisdiction. Lucknow Development Authority v. M.K. Gupta (1994) Facts. A statutory authority said that the forum had no jurisdiction because it acted in a sovereign function. Principle. The Supreme Court held that the Act applies to the housing service. Significance. Jurisdiction extends to public bodies that give services for consideration. Bar of Indian Lawyers v. D.K. Gandhi (2024) Facts. A client sued his advocate before a consumer forum. Principle. An advocate's service is a contract of personal service, so the complaint is not maintainable. Significance. Limits on what the Commissions can hear.

selfTest.q: 1. On what does the Commission's pecuniary jurisdiction depend?
selfTest.a: On the consideration paid for the goods or services. 2. Where can a complaint be filed? Where the opposite party resides or does business, where the cause of action arises, or where the complainant resides or works for gain. 3. Which Commission transfers cases between States? The National Commission, under section 62. 4. What is the term of a District or State Commission member? Four years or up to age 65, whichever is earlier, with reappointment for one more term (rule 10 of the 2020 Rules). 5. Who recommends appointments to the District and State Commissions? A Selection Committee headed by the Chief Justice of the High Court or a nominated High Court Judge (rule 6).

hi.inOneMinute: Each Commission has original jurisdiction over complaints of a certain value, appellate jurisdiction over the tier below, and a revisional power to correct jurisdictional errors. Territorial jurisdiction decides in which place the complaint is filed. The Commissions have the powers of a civil court for certain purposes. In exams, this topic is asked as "discuss the jurisdiction and powers of the Consumer Commissions", and as a problem on where a complaint must be filed. The usual traps are the pecuniary limits and the consideration-paid test.
legalProvision: Section 34: jurisdiction of the District Commission, pecuniary and territorial. Section 47: jurisdiction of the State Commission, including appeals and revision. Section 58: jurisdiction of the National Commission, including appeals and revision. Section 36 and 38: proceedings, admission, procedure and powers. Sections 40, 50 and 60: review. Sections 48 and 62: transfer of cases. Section 61: power of the National Commission to set aside ex parte orders. Section 65: service of notice by registered post, speed post, courier or electronic means. Section 66: experts to assist the State or National Commission. Section 69: limitation of two years.
hi.meaning: Jurisdiction is the authority of a Commission to hear and decide a matter. It has several parts. Pecuniary jurisdiction depends on the value of the consideration paid. Territorial jurisdiction depends on the place. Appellate jurisdiction is the power to hear appeals. Under revisional jurisdiction, a Commission can call for the record and correct a jurisdictional error.
keyPoints: Pecuniary jurisdiction is by consideration paid. Territorial jurisdiction includes the complainant's residence or place of work. State and National Commissions also have appellate and revisional jurisdiction. Commissions have civil court powers and can pass interim orders. Limitation is two years. District and State Commission President and members are appointed by the State Government on a Selection Committee's recommendation, serve four years or to age 65, and can be reappointed once. State Commission President: a High Court Judge, serving or former. District Commission President: a District Judge, serving, former or qualified.

caseLaws.name: SpiceJet Ltd
caseLaws.facts: v. Ranju Aery (2017) Facts. The District Forum and the State Commission found SpiceJet liable for cancelling a flight with no refund. SpiceJet filed a revision petition before the National Commission. Principle. The National Commission, in its revisional jurisdiction, will not disturb concurrent findings of fact unless there is jurisdictional error or material illegality. Significance. Limits of revisional jurisdiction. Lucknow Development Authority v. M.K. Gupta (1994) Facts. A statutory authority said that the forum had no jurisdiction because it acted in a sovereign function. Principle. The Supreme Court held that the Act applies to the housing service. Significance. Jurisdiction extends to public bodies that give services for consideration. Bar of Indian Lawyers v. D.K. Gandhi (2024) Facts. A client sued his advocate before a consumer forum. Principle. An advocate's service is a contract of personal service, so the complaint is not maintainable. Significance. Limits on what the Commissions can hear.

selfTest.q: 1. On what does the Commission's pecuniary jurisdiction depend?
selfTest.a: On the consideration paid for the goods or services. 2. Where can a complaint be filed? Where the opposite party resides or does business, where the cause of action arises, or where the complainant resides or works for gain. 3. Which Commission transfers cases between States? The National Commission, under section 62. 4. What is the term of a District or State Commission member? Four years or up to age 65, whichever is earlier, with reappointment for one more term (rule 10 of the 2020 Rules). 5. Who recommends appointments to the District and State Commissions? A Selection Committee headed by the Chief Justice of the High Court or a nominated High Court Judge (rule 6).

en.meaning:
Under Section 2(7) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a 'consumer' is a person who buys goods or avails a service for consideration, but excludes a person acting for a

Explanation. A person who buys goods or avails a service for a 'commercial purpose' is excluded from the definition of 'consumer' under Section 2(7).

Which of the following buyers is NOT excluded from being a 'consumer', despite the commercial-purpose exclusion?

Explanation. The Act expressly carves out goods bought and used exclusively for earning one's livelihood through self-employment from the commercial-purpose exclusion.

Besides the person who actually pays for goods or a service, who else does the definition of 'consumer' include?

Explanation. The definition extends to a user of goods with the buyer's approval and a beneficiary of a service with the hirer's approval, even if they did not personally pay.

How many consumer rights does the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 expressly recognise?

en.inOneMinute: Read the full set here, or use the practice card above to test yourself one question at a time.
en.meaning:
Before any consumer-specific statute existed, which tort was the primary remedy available to a consumer injured by a defective product or careless service?

Explanation. Before consumer-specific legislation, an injured consumer's only real remedy was the tort of negligence — proving a duty of care, breach, and resulting damage.

What barrier did the doctrine of privity of contract traditionally create for an injured consumer?

Explanation. Privity of contract meant a buyer generally had no claim against a manufacturer or other party they had no direct contract with, even if that party's carelessness caused the harm.

In Donoghue v. Stevenson, what did the House of Lords hold about a manufacturer's duty of care?

Explanation. The House of Lords held that a manufacturer's duty of care to the ultimate consumer exists independently of contract, removing privity as a bar to a negligence claim.

In Cassidy v. Ministry of Health, the Ministry relied on an older, narrower view of hospital liability. Which test did the Court of Appeal move away from?

law-of-torts-u5-t17.subtitle: When a consumer wrong goes on day after day, and how the two-year limitation of section 69 applies

en.inOneMinute: A consumer complaint must be filed within two years from the date on which the cause of action arose. If the wrong goes on, as when a builder keeps failing to hand over a flat, the cause of action continues, and a fresh period of limitation begins every day that the wrong continues. In exams, this topic is asked as a short note on continuous cause of action and limitation, and as a problem on a long delay in a housing or insurance claim. The usual trap is to count two years from the first default alone.
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, section 69(1): a Commission shall not admit a complaint unless it is filed within two years from the date on which the cause of action has arisen. Section 69(2): a complaint may be entertained after that period if the complainant shows sufficient cause, and the Commission records its reasons for condoning the delay. Consumer Protection Act, 1986, section 24A: the same two-year rule in the earlier Act. Limitation Act, 1963, section 22: in the case of a continuing breach of contract or a continuing tort, a fresh period of limitation begins to run at every moment of the time during which the breach or the tort continues. Section 34(2)(c): a complaint may be filed in the District Commission within whose limits the cause of action arises wholly or in part. Section 47(4) uses the same test for the State Commission. Section 58 has no place-of-filing test for the National Commission. Section 107 (repeal and savings): anything done under the 1986 Act is deemed done under the corresponding provision of the 2019 Act, so far as it is not inconsistent.
en.meaning: A cause of action is the set of facts that gives a person the right to sue. A continuous cause of action arises when the wrong is not complete in one act but goes on, so that the right to sue renews as long as the wrong continues.
keyPoints: Limitation is two years from the cause of action (section 69). Late complaints can be admitted with reasons recorded. A continuing wrong gives a fresh period every day. Non-delivery of possession and non-refund are common continuing wrongs. File promptly even when the wrong continues. Section 5 of the Limitation Act covers appeals and applications. Section 69(2) has its own sufficient-cause clause for complaints. For civil suits on torts, libel, slander, false imprisonment and malicious prosecution have one year (Schedule, Articles 73 to 76).

caseLaws.name: Samruddhi Co-operative Housing Society v
caseLaws.facts: Mumbai Mahalaxmi Construction (2022) Facts. Flat owners took possession in 1997, but the builder never obtained the occupancy certificate. The National Commission dismissed the society's complaint as time-barred (decided 11 January 2022). Principle. The builder's duty under the Maharashtra Ownership Flats Act, 1963 and its contract continued. The failure is a continuing wrong, so the complaint was not barred by limitation. The failure is also a deficiency in service. Significance. Leading case on continuing cause of action in housing disputes. Lucknow Development Authority v. M.K. Gupta (1994) Facts. An allottee deposited money for a flat and did not get possession on time. Principle. Delay in possession is a deficiency in service, with interest, possession or refund and compensation. Significance. Delay in housing is the usual source of continuing default. Om Prakash v. Reliance General Insurance Co. Ltd. (2017) Facts. An insurer rejected a genuine theft claim because notice was eight days late. Principle. An explained delay is not a ground to reject a genuine claim. Significance. The cause of action arose on the repudiation.

selfTest.q: 1. From when does the two-year period run?
selfTest.a: From the date on which the cause of action arose. 2. What does a continuing wrong do to limitation? It gives a fresh period of limitation each day that the wrong continues. 3. Can a late complaint be heard? Yes, if the complainant shows sufficient cause and the Commission records its reasons. 4. Does section 5 of the Limitation Act apply to a complaint under section 69? Section 5 covers appeals and applications. Section 69(2) of the 2019 Act gives its own power to condone delay for sufficient cause.

law-of-torts-u5-t20.subtitle: What counts as a misleading advertisement, and the penalties the Central Authority and the courts can impose

en.inOneMinute: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 deals with misleading advertisements on two levels. The Central Consumer Protection Authority can order the advertisement to stop and can impose a money penalty on the maker and the endorser. A court can also punish the manufacturer or service provider with imprisonment and fine. In exams, this topic is asked as a short note on misleading advertisements and their penalties. The usual trap is to mix the Authority's penalty under section 21 with the court's punishment under section 89.
legalProvision: Section 2(28): a misleading advertisement is one that falsely describes a product or service or gives a false guarantee. It is also one that is likely to mislead consumers about nature, substance, quantity or quality, or that conveys a representation that would be an unfair trade practice. An advertisement that deliberately conceals important information is misleading too. Section 2(18): an endorsement is a message, statement, demonstration, or depiction of a name, likeness or seal that makes the consumer believe it reflects the opinion, finding or experience of the person endorsing. Section 21: the Central Authority may direct discontinuance or modification of the advertisement, impose a penalty, and bar an endorser. Section 89: a manufacturer or service provider who causes a false or misleading advertisement prejudicial to consumers is punishable with imprisonment up to two years and fine up to Rs 10 lakh. For each later offence, imprisonment up to five years and fine up to Rs 50 lakh. Section 92: a court takes cognizance of an offence under section 88 or section 89 only on a complaint by the Central Authority or an officer it authorises. Section 88: failing to comply with a direction of the Central Authority under section 20 or 21 is punishable with imprisonment up to six months, or fine up to Rs 20 lakh, or both. Section 24: a person aggrieved by an order of the Central Authority under section 20 or 21 may appeal to the National Commission within 30 days of receiving the order. Section 39(1)(l) and (n): a Commission deciding a complaint may order a corrective advertisement, at the cost of the opposite party, to neutralise a misleading advertisement. It may also order the party to stop issuing misleading advertisements. Section 93: an officer who searches or seizes under section 22 knowing there are no reasonable grounds is punishable with imprisonment up to one year, or fine up to Rs 10,000, or both.
en.meaning: A misleading advertisement is not limited to a plain lie. It includes an advertisement that is likely to mislead, one that makes a promise that would be an unfair trade practice, and one that hides important information on purpose. An endorser is the person whose name, face, message or seal is used to lend credit to the advertisement.
keyPoints: Misleading advertisement is defined in section 2(28). Authority penalty: up to Rs 10 lakh; later up to Rs 50 lakh (section 21). Endorser bar: up to one year; later up to three years. Endorser's defence: due diligence (section 21(5)). Court punishment: up to two years and Rs 10 lakh; later up to five years and Rs 50 lakh (section 89).

law-of-torts-u5-t18.subtitle: How the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 gives civil remedies for consumers and creates criminal offences for serious wrongs

en.inOneMinute: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 works on two tracks. The civil track gives the consumer relief such as replacement, refund and compensation. The criminal track punishes the wrongdoer with imprisonment or fine for serious wrongs, such as ignoring a Commission's order, a false advertisement, or selling adulterated or spurious goods. In exams, this topic is asked as a short note or an essay comparing civil and criminal liability under the Act. The usual trap is to say that a consumer complaint can send a trader to jail. It cannot, except through section 72 for disobeying an order.
legalProvision: Section 39: the District Commission, after finding a defect, deficiency or unfair trade practice proved, orders removal of the defect, replacement, refund, compensation, or other relief. Sections 82 to 87: product liability. A manufacturer , product service provider or product seller is liable for harm caused by a defective product. Section 72: failure to comply with a Commission's order is punishable with imprisonment of one month to three years, or fine of Rs 25,000 to Rs 1 lakh, or both. Section 88: failure to comply with a direction of the Central Authority under section 20 or 21 is punishable with imprisonment up to six months, or fine up to Rs 20 lakh, or both. Section 89: a false or misleading advertisement is punishable with imprisonment up to two years and fine up to Rs 10 lakh, and for each later offence imprisonment up to five years and fine up to Rs 50 lakh. Section 90: selling products containing an adulterant is punishable, with heavier punishment as the injury grows. Section 91: the same for spurious goods. Section 92: a court may take cognizance offences under sections 88 and 89 only on a complaint by the Central Authority or an officer it authorises. Section 93: an officer who makes a vexatious search or seizure is punishable with imprisonment up to one year, or fine up to Rs 10,000, or both.
en.meaning: Civil liability is a duty to repair the consumer's loss by giving relief or money. Criminal liability is a duty to answer to the State for an offence and to suffer the punishment the law lays down. One act, such as selling unsafe food, can lead to both.
keyPoints: Civil track: section 39 relief and product liability (sections 82 to 87). Section 72: one month to three years, fine Rs 25,000 to Rs 1 lakh. Section 89: up to two years and Rs 10 lakh; later offence up to five years and Rs 50 lakh. Sections 90 and 91: punishment grows with the injury; death carries at least seven years. Section 92: cognizance of sections 88 and 89 only on the Central Authority's complaint.

caseLaws.name: Indian Medical Association v
caseLaws.facts: V.P. Shantha (1995) Facts. Conflicting rulings on whether a doctor's or hospital's work is service under the 1986 Act. Principle. Medical work for a fee is service. The patient can seek civil relief before the consumer forum. Significance. Civil liability of professionals under the Act. Spring Meadows Hospital v. Harjot Ahluwalia (1998) Facts. A nurse injected a minor patient without a sensitivity test, leaving him in a vegetative state. Principle. Both the child and the parents are consumers who can each be compensated on their own head of loss. Significance. Compensation as civil liability.

law-of-torts-u5-t21.subtitle: Chapter V of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019: the mediation cell, the panel of mediators, their duties and how a settlement becomes an order

en.inOneMinute: Chapter V of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (sections 74 to 81) sets up mediation inside the consumer forums. Each Commission has a consumer mediation cell with a panel of mediators valid for five years. A mediator must disclose any interest, and the Commission records the settlement within seven days. In exams, this topic is asked as a long answer on the empanelment, appointment and duties of mediators and the settlement of disputes. The usual trap is to confuse empanelment, which creates the panel, with nomination, which picks one mediator for one dispute.
legalProvision: Section 37: reference to mediation by the District Commission, with written consent of the parties within five days. Section 74: establishment of the consumer mediation cell. Section 75: empanelment of mediators. Section 76: nomination of mediators from the panel. Section 77: duty of the mediator to disclose certain facts. Section 78: replacement of a mediator. Section 79: procedure for mediation. Section 80: settlement through mediation. Section 81: recording of the settlement and passing of the order. Consumer Protection (Mediation) Rules, 2020: made by the Central Government (G.S.R. 450(E), 15 July 2020, in force from 20 July 2020). They cover the cell, the selection committee, excluded matters, refund of fee and the effect of a settlement. Consumer Protection (Mediation) Regulations, 2020: made by the National Commission (24 July 2020). They cover empanelment, fee, training, code of conduct, procedure, confidentiality and reports.
en.meaning: Mediation is a way of settling a dispute in which a neutral mediator helps the parties reach an agreement. Empanelment means putting a person on the approved panel of mediators. Nomination means choosing a mediator from that panel for a particular dispute.
keyPoints: A mediation cell is attached to every Commission (section 74). The panel is valid for five years, on the recommendation of a selection committee (section 75). The mediator must disclose any interest or doubt about independence (section 77). The mediator is guided by natural justice (section 79). The Commission records the settlement within seven days (section 81). Mediation ends in three months from the first appearance unless extended (Regulation 11(2)). The mediator cannot impose a settlement, and the proceedings are confidential (Regulations 12 and 13). The complainant gets the full application fee back if a settlement is reached (Rule 5).

en.meaning:
Under which section of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 is the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) established?

Explanation. Section 10 empowers the Central Government to establish the CCPA by notification.

What is the key difference between the CCPA and the District/State/National Commissions?

Explanation. The CCPA's mandate is regulatory/preventive protection of consumers as a class, distinct from the Commissions' role of adjudicating individual complaints.

On what basis can the CCPA initiate an inquiry or investigation?

Explanation. The CCPA can act suo motu (on its own initiative), on a complaint, or on the direction of the Central Government.

Who heads the CCPA's Investigation Wing?

en.meaning:
Under section 34(1) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the District Commission hears complaints where the consideration paid does not exceed:

Explanation. Section 34(1) fixes the limit at Rs 1 crore and lets the Central Government prescribe another value. The 2021 Rules prescribed Rs 50 lakh. Section 107 repealed the Consumer Protection Act, 1986.

What is the single most significant structural innovation of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019?

Explanation. The CCPA is a dedicated regulatory body that can investigate and act on its own initiative, without waiting for an individual consumer complaint — something the 1986 Act had no equivalent of.

How does the 2019 Act treat product liability differently from the position under the 1986 Act?

Explanation. The 2019 Act, for the first time, gives product liability its own dedicated statutory chapter with defined standards, instead of requiring reliance purely on common-law negligence.

Which of the following transactions did the 2019 Act expressly bring within the definition of 'consumer', closing a gap under the 1986 Act?

Which chapter of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 introduces the formal mediation mechanism?

Explanation. Chapter V, Sections 74 to 81, introduces the formal statutory mediation mechanism under the 2019 Act.

Under Section 74, where are consumer mediation cells attached?

How are mediators selected under Sections 75-76?

Explanation. The Act establishes a three-tier structure of Consumer Protection Councils — Central, State, and District.

en.meaning:
What is the fundamental character of civil liability under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019?

Explanation. Civil liability under the Act is compensatory — refund, replacement, compensation, and discontinuation orders — not punitive.

Can civil liability and criminal liability under the Act arise from the same underlying conduct?

Explanation. Civil liability (before a Commission) and criminal liability (before a criminal court) can both arise from the same conduct, serving different purposes through different processes.

Under Section 89, the punishment for a first offence of causing a false or misleading advertisement prejudicial to consumers is

Explanation. Section 89 prescribes imprisonment up to two years and a fine up to ten lakh rupees for a first offence.

Under Section 89, what is the punishment for a subsequent (repeat) offence?
