environmental-law-u3-t11.subtitle: The authorities that prevent and control pollution, and how they work together

en.inOneMinute: Pollution control in India rests on several authorities. Pollution Control Boards grant consent and give directions. The Central Government makes rules and gives directions under the Environment (Protection) Act. Biodiversity bodies regulate access to biological resources. The National Green Tribunal hears disputes and appeals against their orders. Each authority has its own Act and tools.
legalProvision: Water Act, 1974: sections 3 and 4 (Boards), 16 and 17 (functions), 25 (consent), 33A (directions). Air Act, 1981: sections 3 and 4 (the same Boards), 21 (consent), 31A (directions). Environment (Protection) Act, 1986: section 3 (measures and authorities), section 5 (directions). Biological Diversity Act, 2002: section 8 (Authority), section 22 (State Boards), section 41 (Committees). National Green Tribunal Act, 2010: sections 14 and 16 (jurisdiction), section 22 (appeal).
en.meaning:
The "pollution control mechanism" is the set of bodies and powers that prevent, control and reduce pollution. Some bodies regulate in advance, by consent and rules. Others act after a breach , by directions, penalties or a decision.

Who controls pollution How to read this: start at the top box and follow the lines down to each authority and its main tool. Pollution control mechanism Pollution Control Boards Consent and directions under the Water Act and Air Act. Central Government Measures, rules and directions under the 1986 Act. Biodiversity bodies Approval, intimation and benefit sharing. National Green Tribunal Disputes, relief and appeals.
keyPoints: Boards: Water Act and Air Act; consent and directions. Central Government: 1986 Act, sections 3 and 5. Biodiversity bodies: Authority, State Boards, Committees. Tribunal: sections 14 and 16; appeal to the Supreme Court. The Wild Life (Protection) Act is outside Schedule I.

caseLaws.name: M
caseLaws.facts: C. Mehta v. Union of India (Ganga Pollution Case) Facts. Untreated sewage from Kanpur flowed into the Ganga, and the Mahapalika had sent no treatment proposal to the State Board. Principle. The Court enforced the duties of the municipal body and the Boards and held the Mahapalika mainly responsible. Significance. It shows the Court pushing the Boards and local bodies to act. Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India Facts. Tanneries in Tamil Nadu discharged untreated effluent into the Palar area. Principle. The Central Government had to constitute an authority under section 3(3) of the 1986 Act with power to give directions under section 5. Significance. It shows the Central Government's authorities in use. A.P. Pollution Control Board v. Prof. M.V. Nayudu (Retd.) Facts. A Board refused consent for a factory near two lakes. The appellate authority and the High Court ruled for the company. Principle. The Court referred technical questions to an expert statutory body. Significance. It led to calls for expert environmental tribunals.

selfTest.q: 1. Which body grants consent for effluent discharge?
selfTest.a: The State Pollution Control Board. 2. Which section lets the Central Government give directions? Section 5 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. 3. Where does an appeal from the Tribunal go? To the Supreme Court.

environmental-law-u3-t8.subtitle: The umbrella Act: general power to protect the environment, directions, standards and penalties

en.inOneMinute: The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 is the umbrella Act. Section 3 gives the Central Government a wide power to take all measures needed to protect and improve the environment. Section 5 lets it give written directions, including closure. Many rules and notifications flow from it, such as rules on hazardous waste. It acts on any pollutant, not on water or air alone. It was made to carry out the Stockholm decisions of 1972.
legalProvision: The main sections, read from the Act as stored on this site, are these.

Preamble: the Act implements decisions of the Stockholm Conference of June 1972 on protecting and improving the human environment. Section 2(a): "environment" includes water, air and land, and the interrelationship between them and human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organism and property. Section 2(b) and (c): an " environmental pollutant " is a substance in a concentration that is or tends to be injurious to the environment. "Environmental pollution" is its presence in the environment. Section 2(d): "handling" means manufacture, processing, treatment, package, storage, transportation, use, collection, destruction, conversion, offering for sale, transfer or the like of a substance. Section 2(f): an "occupier" is the person who has control over the affairs of the factory or premises. For a substance, it includes the person in possession of it. Section 2(e): a "hazardous substance" is a substance or preparation that can cause harm to human beings, other creatures, plants, property or the environment, by its properties or its handling. Section 3: power of the Central Government to take all measures it considers necessary or expedient. Section 5: power to give written directions, including closure, prohibition or regulation of an industry and stopping of electricity, water or other service. Section 6: power to make rules on the matters in section 3. Section 7: no discharge or emission above the prescribed standards. Section 8: hazardous substances may be handled only by the prescribed procedure and safeguards. Sections 14A, 14B and 15: penalties.
en.meaning:
The Act is called an umbrella Act because it gives the Central Government one general power that covers all types of pollution and all steps to prevent it. The Water Act and the Air Act deal with one medium each. This Act reaches soil, hazardous substances, accidents and anything else that harms the environment.

The definition of "environment" joins water, air and land with people and other living things. A harm to any link in that chain is a harm to the environment.

Powers that flow from the Act How to read this: start at the top box and follow the lines down. Each box is a power or duty in the Act. Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 Section 3: measures All steps the Central Government thinks necessary, including standards and restrictions on areas. Section 5: directions Written orders, including closure and stopping electricity or water. Section 6: rules Standards, limits, safeguards for hazardous substances. Sections 7 and 8: duties Stay within standards. Handle hazardous substances safely. Sections 14A, 14B, 15: penalties Money penalties, with a daily penalty for continuing breach.
keyPoints: Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 carries out the Stockholm decisions. Section 3: all measures. Section 5: directions. Section 6: rules. Section 7: standards. Section 8: hazardous substances. Section 14A: Rs 1 lakh to Rs 15 lakh for breach of section 7 or 8. Section 15: Rs 10,000 to Rs 15 lakh for other breaches. caseLaws.name: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v
caseLaws.facts: Union of India Facts. Tanneries in five Tamil Nadu districts discharged untreated effluent. Principle. The Court directed the Central Government to constitute an authority under section 3(3) with power to give directions under section 5. It held that the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle are part of Indian law. Significance. It shows how sections 3(3) and 5 are used. Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India Facts. Chemical plants in Bichhri left about 2,440 tonnes of toxic sludge. Principle. Section 3 lets the Central Government take necessary measures, and section 5 lets it direct. With the wide definition in section 2(a), these cover removal of sludge and recovery of the cost from the industry. Significance. It shows the breadth of sections 3 and 5. Alembic Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. Rohit Prajapati Facts. Three industries at Ankleshwar began production without environmental clearance . A circular offered clearance after the event. Principle. The circular was unsustainable in law because the EIA notification of 27 January 1994, made under section 3, needs prior clearance. Closure was set aside as disproportionate, and each industry had to deposit Rs 10 crores. Significance. It shows limits on delegated rules made under section 3.

selfTest.a: Section 3. 2. Which section allows closure of an industry? Section 5. 3. Which section covers hazardous substances? Section 8.

environmental-law-u3-t12.subtitle: The two earlier bodies, the Acts behind them and why the National Green Tribunal replaced them

en.inOneMinute: Before the National Green Tribunal, two Acts set up specialised bodies. The National Environment Tribunal Act, 1995 gave strict, no-fault liability for accidents with hazardous substances. The National Environment Appellate Authority Act, 1997 created an Authority to hear appeals on environmental clearance. The National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 repealed both Acts and took over their work.
legalProvision: National Environment Tribunal Act, 1995 (Act 27 of 1995): strict liability for damage from any accident while handling a hazardous substance, and a Tribunal for quick disposal of such cases. National Environment Appellate Authority Act, 1997: an Authority to hear appeals on environmental clearance. Section 38, National Green Tribunal Act, 2010: repeal and savings. It repeals both Acts, dissolves the Authority when the Tribunal is established and moves its pending cases to the Tribunal. Section 15, National Green Tribunal Act, 2010: relief and compensation, including for accidents with hazardous substances, in addition to relief under the Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991.
en.meaning:
A tribunal is a body outside the ordinary courts that decides disputes in a special field. An appellate authority hears appeals against decisions of other bodies. The two Acts set up one of each, for environmental matters .

From two bodies to one How to read this: read the boxes from left to right on a wide screen, or from top to bottom on a phone. 1995 The National Environment Tribunal Act provides for no-fault liability for hazardous substance accidents. 1997 The National Environment Appellate Authority Act creates the Authority. Later The Supreme Court in Nayudu refers technical questions to the Authority. 2010 The National Green Tribunal Act repeals both Acts.
keyPoints: National Environment Tribunal Act, 1995: no-fault liability for hazardous substance accidents. National Environment Appellate Authority Act, 1997: clearance appeals. Nayudu: technical questions referred to the Authority. Both Acts repealed by section 38 of the NGT Act, 2010. 1995 Act: five-year limit to claim (section 4); appeal to the Supreme Court in 90 days (section 24); penalty up to 3 years or Rs 10 lakh (section 25). 1997 Act: appeal in 30 days (condonable up to 90) against clearance; disposal in 90 days (section 11); penalty up to 7 years or Rs 1 lakh (section 19).

caseLaws.name: A
caseLaws.facts: P. Pollution Control Board v. Prof. M.V. Nayudu (Retd.) Facts. A company sought consent to build a factory within 10 km of the Himayat Sagar and Osman Sagar lakes. The Board refused. The appellate authority and the High Court ruled for the company. Principle. The Court explained the precautionary principle and the reversed burden of proof. It referred two technical issues to the National Environmental Appellate Authority for its opinion within three months. Significance. It shows the Authority at work and the need for expert bodies.

selfTest.q: 1. What did the 1995 Act deal with?
selfTest.a: No-fault liability for accidents with hazardous substances. 2. What did the Appellate Authority hear? Appeals on environmental clearance. 3. Which Act repealed both? The National Green Tribunal Act, 2010.

environmental-law-u3-t13.subtitle: The National Green Tribunal Act, 2010: composition, original and appellate jurisdiction, relief and appeal

en.inOneMinute: The National Green Tribunal (NGT) is a special forum for environmental disputes. Its bench mixes judicial members and expert members. It hears civil cases with a substantial environmental question under seven listed Acts. It can order relief, compensation and restoration. It also hears appeals against orders such as environmental clearance. It must apply sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle. An appeal from the NGT goes to the Supreme Court.
legalProvision: The main sections of the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 (Act No. 19 of 2010) are these.

Section 3: the Central Government establishes the Tribunal by notification. Section 4: a full-time Chairperson, ten to twenty full-time Judicial Members and ten to twenty full-time Expert Members, as notified. Section 14: jurisdiction over all civil cases where a substantial question relating to environment arises from the implementation of the enactments in Schedule I. Section 15: relief, compensation and restitution . Section 16: appellate jurisdiction. Section 20: the Tribunal must apply the principles of sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle. Section 22: appeal to the Supreme Court. Section 29: civil courts cannot hear matters the Tribunal decides.
en.meaning:
The National Green Tribunal is a statutory body for quick and expert decisions in environmental cases. The Supreme Court had urged expert environmental bodies earlier, in A.P. Pollution Control Board v. Prof. M.V. Nayudu, where it referred technical questions to an expert authority. The Tribunal combines law and science on one bench.

Its work has three parts. It decides civil disputes (original jurisdiction), it hears appeals against certain orders, and it awards relief and restoration.

What the Tribunal can do How to read this: start at the top box and follow the lines to the three kinds of work. Each box names the section. National Green Tribunal Civil disputes (section 14) Substantial environmental question under a Schedule I Act. Relief and restoration (section 15) Compensation, restitution of property and of the environment. Appeals (section 16) Against orders and directions under listed Acts, including environmental clearance.
keyPoints: NGT Act, 2010 (Act No. 19 of 2010). Expert Members equal Judicial Members on a bench. Section 14: civil cases under seven Schedule I Acts, six months. The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 is not in Schedule I. Section 15: relief, compensation, restitution, five years. Section 16: appeals within thirty days. Section 20: three binding principles. Section 22: appeal to the Supreme Court within ninety days.

caseLaws.name: Hanuman Laxman Aroskar v
caseLaws.facts: Union of India Facts. The NGT upheld the environmental clearance for an airport at Mopa in Goa with added conditions. Two appeals reached the Supreme Court. Principle. The Tribunal has a duty of merits review under section 16(h) and must apply section 20. Failing to consider vital issues raises a substantial question of law under section 22. The Court suspended the clearance. Significance. It defines the Tribunal's duty when it hears an appeal on clearance. Alembic Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. Rohit Prajapati Facts. The Tribunal struck down a circular offering clearance after the event, revoked the clearances and ordered closure of three industries. Principle. The Supreme Court held the circular unsustainable. It set aside closure as disproportionate and required each industry to deposit Rs 10 crores. Significance. It shows proportionality in an appeal from the Tribunal. A.P. Pollution Control Board v. Prof. M.V. Nayudu (Retd.) Facts. A factory near two lakes was refused consent. The Court referred the technical questions to the National Environmental Appellate Authority. Principle. Technical environmental questions should go to expert bodies. Significance. It shows why a mixed expert and judicial tribunal was needed.

selfTest.q: 1. How many Acts are in Schedule I?
selfTest.a: Seven. 2. Where does an appeal from the NGT go? To the Supreme Court, within ninety days, under section 22. 3. Which section requires the three environmental principles? Section 20.

hi.inOneMinute: The National Green Tribunal (NGT) is a special forum for environmental disputes. Its bench mixes judicial members and expert members. It hears civil cases with a substantial environmental question under seven listed Acts. It can order relief, compensation and restoration. It also hears appeals against orders such as environmental clearance. It must apply sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle. An appeal from the NGT goes to the Supreme Court.

Section 3: the Central Government establishes the Tribunal by notification. Section 15: relief, compensation and restitution . Section 16: appellate jurisdiction. Section 20: the Tribunal must apply the principles of sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle. Section 22: appeal to the Supreme Court. Section 29: civil courts cannot hear matters the Tribunal decides.

environmental-law-u3-t10.subtitle: The Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016

en.inOneMinute: India controls hazardous waste by rules, not by a separate Act. The Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016 were made under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. Anyone who handles such waste needs authorisation from the State Pollution Control Board. Every movement within India needs a manifest. Import for disposal is not allowed.
legalProvision: The rules below are read from the Gazette notification G.S.R. 395(E) of 4 April 2016.

Making of the Rules: they were made under sections 6, 8 and 25 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, in supersession of the Hazardous Wastes (Management, Handling and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2008. They came into force on the date of publication. Rule 3: definitions, including "hazardous waste", "other wastes" and "manifest". Rule 4: responsibilities of the occupier. Rule 6: authorisation. Rule 7: suspension or cancellation. Rules 11 to 15: import and export, and illegal traffic. Rule 16: treatment, storage and disposal facilities. Rule 19: manifest. Rule 22: accident reporting. Rule 23: liability. Rule 24: appeal.
en.meaning:
Rule 3(1)(17) defines hazardous waste as waste that is physical, chemical, biological, reactive, toxic, flammable, explosive or corrosive in a way that causes or is likely to cause danger to health or environment. It includes waste listed in Schedule I and waste above the limits in Schedule II.

"Other wastes" are the wastes in Parts B and D of Schedule III for import or export, and they include such waste generated in India. A manifest is the transporting document prepared and signed by the sender.

Life of hazardous waste under the Rules How to read this: follow the boxes from top to bottom. Each step must be completed before the next. 1. The occupier obtains authorisation from the State Board (rule 6). 2. The waste is packed and labelled, and moved by an authorised transporter (rules 17 and 18). 3. The sender prepares a manifest for the movement (rule 19). 4. Result The waste reaches a treatment, storage and disposal facility or an authorised recycler (rule 16).
keyPoints: Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules, 2016: G.S.R. 395(E), 4 April 2016, under sections 6, 8 and 25 of the 1986 Act. Authorisation from the State Board: rule 6, Form 1. Manifest: seven copies in Form 10 (rule 19). No import for disposal; import for recycling needs permission (rule 12). Liability for damage: rule 23. Appeal in thirty days: rule 24.

The Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 has been officially renamed by the 2023 Amendment as:

Explanation. The Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act, 2023 renamed the parent Act as the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam. The Amendment received the President's assent on 4 August 2023.

en.meaning:
According to its Preamble, the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 implements the decisions of which conference?

Explanation. The Preamble says the Act implements the decisions of the Stockholm Conference of June 1972 on protecting and improving the human environment. It is an umbrella Act, because it reaches every kind of pollution and not one medium alone.

Section 3 of the EPA, 1986 is significant because it:

Explanation. Section 3's broad, general power is the legal basis for the EIA Notification, CRZ Notifications, Hazardous Waste Rules, Plastic/Solid Waste Rules, and most other Indian environmental subordinate legislation.

How does the Central Government's Section 5 direction power differ from the State Board's powers under the Water/Air Acts?

Explanation. Section 5 is exercised directly by the Central Government (not a State Board) and is broader, not confined to a single pollution medium.

Section 8 of the EPA, 1986 is the statutory foundation for which set of rules?

environmental-law-u4-t1.subtitle: The State's directive and the citizen's fundamental duty to protect the environment

en.inOneMinute: Two short provisions put the environment into the Constitution. Article 48A tells the State to protect and improve the environment. Article 51A(g) makes the same task a fundamental duty of every citizen. Both were inserted in 1976 and took effect on 3 January 1977. Neither gives a court power to order anything on its own. Courts use them to give content to Article 21, which can be enforced.
legalProvision: Article 48A (Part IV): "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) (Part IVA): it is the duty of every citizen of India "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". Article 37: the provisions of Part IV are not enforceable by any court. They are still fundamental in governing the country, and the State must apply them in making laws. Source of both: the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, sections 10 and 11, in force from 3 January 1977.
en.meaning:
Article 48A is a Directive Principle of State Policy . It is an instruction to the State, meaning the governments and legislatures, to make the environment a goal of policy. Article 51A(g) is one of the Fundamental Duties . It is an instruction to each citizen.

The two provisions cover different ground. Article 48A adds forests and wild life to the State's task. Article 51A(g) adds lakes, rivers and a duty of kindness to animals.

Two provisions, one aim How to read this: start at the top box. Each leaf names the part of the Constitution, the person bound and the work required. Environment in the Constitution Article 48A (Part IV) Binds the State. Protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wild life. Article 51A(g) (Part IVA) Binds every citizen. Protect and improve the natural environment and show compassion.
keyPoints: Article 48A: Part IV, binds the State, not enforceable (Article 37). Article 51A(g): Part IVA, binds the citizen, names no penalty. Both inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976, in force from 3 January 1977. Courts read both with Article 21. Article 51A(g) includes compassion for living creatures.

caseLaws.name: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v
caseLaws.facts: Union of India Facts. Tanneries in five Tamil Nadu districts let untreated waste flow into the land and the Palar river. Principle. The precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle are part of the environmental law of India. The Court drew them from Articles 21, 47, 48A and 51A(g). Significance. It shows both provisions giving content to Article 21. M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Ganga Pollution Case) Facts. Untreated sewage from Kanpur poured into the Ganga. The Court gave directions to the Kanpur Nagar Mahapalika and others. Principle. The Court cited Article 51A(g) as the ground for directing the Central Government to have environment lessons taught in schools. Significance. It shows a Fundamental Duty producing a court direction. M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Vehicular Pollution Case) Facts. M.C. Mehta asked for directions on vehicle pollution in Delhi. Principle. The Directive Principles make protection of the environment a State obligation. Article 51A makes it a citizen's duty. The Court set up an expert committee and kept the petition pending for monitoring. Significance. It states both duties side by side.

selfTest.q: 1. Which Article tells the State to safeguard forests and wild life?
selfTest.a: Article 48A. 2. In which Part is Article 51A(g)? Part IVA, Fundamental Duties. 3. Why can a court not enforce Article 48A alone? Article 37 says Part IV is not enforceable by any court.

environmental-law-u4-t6.subtitle: Which legislature can make an environmental law: Article 246, the Seventh Schedule and Articles 252 to 254

en.inOneMinute: "Environment" is not a subject in any of the three Lists of the Seventh Schedule. Environmental topics are spread across them. Forests and wild animals are on the Concurrent List. Water is on the State List. Parliament can still legislate on water by State consent (Article 252) or to carry out an international decision (Article 253). If a State law and a Central law clash on a Concurrent List subject, the Central law prevails unless the State law was reserved for the President and received assent (Article 254).
legalProvision: Article 246: Parliament has exclusive power over the Union List (List I). A State Legislature has exclusive power over the State List (List II). Both can legislate on the Concurrent List (List III). Article 248: Parliament has exclusive power over any matter not in the Concurrent or State List. Entry 97 of the Union List says the same. Article 252: if the Legislatures of two or more States pass resolutions asking for it, Parliament may legislate on a State matter. Other States may adopt that Act later. Article 253: Parliament may make any law for implementing a treaty, agreement or convention, or a decision made at an international conference. Article 254: a State law repugnant to a Central law on a Concurrent List subject is void to the extent of the repugnancy. Article 254(2) saves it if it was reserved for the President and he assents . Parliament can still override it later. Relevant entries: List I entries 13, 14, 54 and 56. List II entries 5, 6, 17, 18 and 23. List III entries 17, 17A and 17B.
en.meaning:
Legislative competence is the power of a legislature to make a law on a subject. A law made outside that power is invalid, whatever its aim. This is why the first question about any environmental statute is which legislature could make it.

The three Lists work as follows. The Union List is for Parliament alone. The State List is for States alone. The Concurrent List is for both.

Where environmental subjects sit How to read this: start at the top box and follow the lines to the three Lists. Each leaf names an environmental subject and its entry. Seventh Schedule Union List Entry 56: inter-State rivers. Entry 54: mines, as Parliament declares. Entries 13 and 14: conferences and treaties. State List Entry 17: water. Entry 6: public health. Entry 18: land. Entry 23: mines. Concurrent List Entry 17: cruelty to animals. Entry 17A: forests. Entry 17B: wild animals and birds.
keyPoints: Environment is not a listed subject; its parts sit in all three Lists. Entries 17A and 17B: Concurrent List, from 3 January 1977. Water: State List entry 17; Water Act through Article 252. Article 253: laws to implement treaties and international decisions. Article 254: Central law prevails over repugnant State law, unless the President assents.

caseLaws.name: Animal Welfare Board of India v
caseLaws.facts: A. Nagaraja Facts. The Animal Welfare Board said Jallikattu and bullock-cart races violate the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act. Tamil Nadu had its own Act on the subject. Principle. Both Acts fall under entry 17 of the Concurrent List. The Tamil Nadu Act was repugnant to the Central Act and void under Article 254(1). Significance. It applies Article 254 to an environmental subject on the Concurrent List.

selfTest.q: 1. In which List are forests?
selfTest.a: The Concurrent List, entry 17A. 2. Which Article did the Water Act, 1974 use? Article 252, through State resolutions. 3. What happens to a repugnant State law on a Concurrent subject? It is void to the extent of the repugnancy, unless the President assented (Article 254).

environmental-law-u4-t4.subtitle: Article 19(1)(g) and Article 19(6): when a law can limit a business to protect the environment

en.inOneMinute: Every citizen has a freedom to practise a profession or carry on any trade or business. This is Article 19(1)(g). The freedom is not absolute. Article 19(6) lets the State make laws that put reasonable restrictions on it in the interests of the general public. Environmental laws use this power. They require consent before a factory starts, allow closure of a polluting unit, and set clean-up duties. A restriction must be made by law and must be reasonable.
legalProvision: Article 19(1)(g): all citizens have the right "to practise any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business". Article 19(6): nothing in sub-clause (g) stops the State from making a law that imposes, "in the interests of the general public, reasonable restrictions" on the right. Article 19(6)(i) and (ii): the State may also make laws on professional qualifications. It may also make laws on a trade or service run by the State or a State-owned corporation. Consent: section 25 of the Water Act and section 21 of the Air Act need the previous consent of the State Board. Directions: section 5 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and section 33A of the Water Act can direct the closure, prohibition or regulation of an industry.
en.meaning:
A reasonable restriction is a limit on a freedom that is not excessive or arbitrary compared with the harm it prevents. Protecting the environment serves the general public. A law that controls polluting trades can therefore fall inside Article 19(6).

The public has an interest in clean air and water, which Article 21 protects. Courts weigh trade against that interest.

Is an environmental restriction on business valid? How to read this: start at the top. Each box must be answered "yes" to move down. The text beside a box shows where the restriction fails. 1. Is the restriction made by a law? Article 19(6) No: a mere executive order has no statutory backing. 2. Is it in the interests of the general public? Protection of the environment No: it fails Article 19(6). 3. Is it reasonable and not excessive for the harm it prevents? Proportionality No: the court can set aside or reduce it. 4. Result The restriction is valid.
keyPoints: Article 19(1)(g): freedom of profession, occupation, trade, business. Article 19(6): reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public. Tests: made by law; public interest; reasonable. Section 5 of the 1986 Act allows closure, prohibition or regulation of an industry. Alembic: closure set aside as disproportionate.

caseLaws.name: M
caseLaws.facts: C. Mehta v. Union of India (Ganga Pollution Case) Facts. Untreated sewage from Kanpur and wastes from industries polluted the Ganga. Principle. Applications for licences to set up new industries must be refused unless trade effluents are treated. Immediate action must be taken against existing polluting industries. Significance. It makes treatment a condition of starting a business. Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of U.P. Facts. Limestone quarrying in the Mussoorie hills caused landslides and dried up springs. Principle. The most harmful quarries were closed, despite hardship to owners. Significance. It puts the public's right to a healthy environment above the owners' business loss. Alembic Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. Rohit Prajapati Facts. The Tribunal ordered closure of three industries and revoked their clearances. Principle. The Supreme Court set aside the closure as disproportionate and required each industry to deposit Rs 10 crores. Significance. It shows proportionality as the limit on a restriction.

selfTest.q: 1. Which clause allows reasonable restrictions on trade and business?
selfTest.a: Article 19(6). 2. Name one statute that restricts a business without the Board's consent. The Water Act (section 25) or the Air Act (section 21). 3. Which case set aside a closure as disproportionate? Alembic Pharmaceuticals v. Rohit Prajapati.

environmental-law-u4-t2.subtitle: How the Supreme Court read a right to a clean environment into Article 21

en.inOneMinute: The Constitution does not use the words "right to a wholesome environment". The Supreme Court read the right into Article 21, which protects life and personal liberty. Because Article 21 is a Fundamental Right, a citizen can enforce it directly in the Supreme Court or a High Court. The right covers pollution-free water and air. environmental-law-u4-t5.subtitle: What Article 31C protects, what the 42nd Amendment added and what Minerva Mills struck down

en.inOneMinute: Article 31C protects certain laws from being struck down for breaching Article 14 (equality) or Article 19 (the six freedoms). The law must give effect to the State policy in Article 39(b) or (c). Those clauses deal with sharing the community's material resources and preventing concentration of wealth. The 42nd Amendment tried to extend the shield to every Directive Principle. The Supreme Court struck that extension down in Minerva Mills (1980). Article 31C does not protect a law from a challenge under Article 21.
legalProvision: Article 31C: as printed, a law giving effect to State policy on the principles in Part IV is not void for inconsistent with Article 14 or Article 19. This applies notwithstanding Article 13. Since Minerva Mills, only the principles in Article 39(b) and (c) count. State laws: a State law gets this protection only if it was reserved for the President and received his assent. Article 39(b): the ownership and control of the material resources of the community are so distributed as best to serve the common good. Article 39(c): the economic system must not concentrate wealth and the means of production to the common detriment. History in the footnotes: inserted by the 25th Amendment, 1971 (in force 20 April 1972). The 42nd Amendment, section 4, widened it to Part IV as a whole (in force 3 January 1977). Section 4 was declared invalid in Minerva Mills.
en.meaning:
Article 31C is a shield , not a power. It does not let the State make a law. It protects a law that is already made from a particular kind of attack. The protected laws are those that give effect to the State policy in Article 39(b) or (c).

The shield covers only two attacks: Article 14 and Article 19. A law protected by Article 31C can still be challenged under Article 21.

Does Article 31C shield this law? How to read this: start at the top. Each box must be answered "yes" to move down. The text beside a box shows where the shield fails. 1. Does the law give effect to the policy in Article 39(b) or Article 39(c)? Minerva Mills No: Article 31C does not apply. 2. If it is a State law, was it reserved for the President and did he assent? Proviso to Article 31C No: Article 31C does not apply to it. 3. Is the challenge under Article 14 or Article 19? Article 31C No: a challenge under Article 21 is not shielded. 4. Result The law cannot be struck down on that ground.
keyPoints: Article 31C shields from Articles 14 and 19, not Article 21. Only laws giving effect to Article 39(b) or (c) qualify. 25th Amendment, 1971; widened by the 42nd Amendment, 1976. Minerva Mills (1980): extension struck down, 4:1. A State law needs the President's assent.

caseLaws.name: Minerva Mills Ltd
caseLaws.facts: v. Union of India Facts. A nationalised textile mill challenged the Sick Textile Undertakings (Nationalisation) Act, 1974 and the 42nd Amendment's changes to Article 31C and Article 368. Principle. The extension of Article 31C to all Directive Principles was struck down, 4:1. Article 31C protects only laws on Article 39(b) and (c). Significance. It is the reason the shield is narrow today. I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu Facts. The Gudalur Janmam Estates Act, 1969 (forest lands in the Janmam estates) and a West Bengal land revenue Act were inserted in the Ninth Schedule. The insertions were challenged. Principle. Ninth Schedule laws added after 24 April 1973 must meet the basic structure test, judged by the effect on rights under Articles 21, 14 and 19. Significance. Article 31B is not a blanket shield. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala Facts. A religious head challenged Kerala land reform Acts. The case grew into a challenge to the 24th, 25th and 29th Amendments. Principle. A thirteen-Judge Bench heard the case. The words barring court review of the declaration in Article 31C were struck down. Significance. It removed the bar on judicial review in the original Article 31C.

selfTest.q: 1. From which Articles does Article 31C shield a law?
selfTest.a: Article 14 and Article 19. 2. Which case struck down the 42nd Amendment's extension of Article 31C? Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980). 3. Does Article 31C protect a law from an Article 21 challenge? No.

environmental-law-u4-t3.subtitle: The international claim to development and how Indian courts balance it with the environment

en.inOneMinute: The right to development comes from international documents, not from a Fundamental Right in Part III of the Constitution. The UN Declaration of 1986 calls it an inalienable human right. Indian courts do not treat development and the environment as enemies. They apply sustainable development to allow a project only with safeguards. The precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle are its essential features.
legalProvision: Declaration on the Right to Development, 1986: adopted by UN General Assembly resolution 41/128 on 4 December 1986. Article 1(1) says every person and all peoples may take part in and benefit from development. Rio Declaration, 1992, Principle 3: the right to development must be fulfilled so as to meet equitably the developmental and environmental needs of present and future generations. Constitution: no Article in Part III lists a right to development. Articles 21, 48A and 51A(g) supply the environmental side of the balance. National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, section 20: the Tribunal must apply sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle.
en.meaning:
The right to development is the claim of people to share in economic and social progress. The 1986 Declaration treats it as a human right. It is a claim in international law, not a listed right in Indian constitutional law.

Indian courts handle the claim through sustainable development . In Vellore, the Court described it as a balancing concept between ecology and development. It also quoted the Brundtland definition: development that meets the needs of the present without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

How the claim is handled in India How to read this: start at the top box. The two lower boxes show the source of the claim and the tool the courts use to balance it. Development and environment Right to development (international) 1986 Declaration. Rio Principle 3. Sustainable development (Indian law) Balancing concept. Includes the precautionary and polluter pays principles.
keyPoints: UN Declaration on the Right to Development: 4 December 1986. Rio Principle 3 links development with environmental needs of present and future generations. Not a listed Fundamental Right in Part III. Vellore: sustainable development is a balancing concept. Narmada was decided 2:1.

caseLaws.name: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v
caseLaws.facts: Union of India Facts. Tanneries in five Tamil Nadu districts polluted the Palar river and the land around it. Principle. Sustainable development is a balancing concept between ecology and development. The precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle are its essential features. Significance. It is the standard source for the balance. M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Taj Trapezium Case) Facts. Industrial emissions in the Taj Trapezium Zone were damaging the Taj Mahal. Principle. The old view that development and ecology cannot go together is no longer acceptable. Industries had to switch to natural gas or relocate. Significance. It shows development continuing under limits. Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India Facts. The Sardar Sarovar Dam displaced many people, mostly tribal and rural communities. Principle. By a 2:1 majority, the dam could proceed, with height increases tied to rehabilitation. Significance. It shows the balance at work and the limits on judicial review of policy.

selfTest.q: 1. Which document calls development an inalienable human right?
selfTest.a: The Declaration on the Right to Development, 1986. 2. How do Indian courts balance development and environment? Through sustainable development, with the precautionary and polluter pays principles. 3. Was the Narmada decision unanimous? No. It was decided 2:1.

environmental-law-u4-t7.subtitle: Articles 32 and 226: how environmental disputes reach the Supreme Court and the High Courts

en.inOneMinute: A writ is a formal court order. Article 32 lets a person go straight to the Supreme Court to enforce a Fundamental Right. Article 226 lets a High Court issue writs for a Fundamental Right and also "for any other purpose". Environmental cases mostly arrive through public interest litigation. A public-spirited person or group can sue for people who cannot go to court. The Court can also keep a case open for years and supervise the government, which is called continuing mandamus.
legalProvision: Article 32(1) and (2): the right to move the Supreme Court to enforce the rights in Part III is guaranteed. The Court may issue directions, orders or writs, including habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari. Article 32(4): this right shall not be suspended except as the Constitution provides. Article 226(1): every High Court may issue directions, orders or writs throughout its territories "for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose". Article 226(2): a High Court may also act where the cause of action arises wholly or in part within its territories, even if the authority sits elsewhere. Article 21: the usual Fundamental Right pleaded in environmental petitions.
en.meaning:
Writ jurisdiction is a court's power to issue writs. The five writs are habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari. In environmental cases the most useful is mandamus, a command to a public authority to do its duty.

Habeas corpus : produce a detained person before the court. Mandamus : perform a public duty. Prohibition : stop a lower court or tribunal from acting beyond its power. Quo warranto : show by what authority a public office is held. Certiorari : quash an order of a lower authority.

Where to file an environmental writ How to read this: go down the boxes in order. A "No" answer sends you to the result beside the box. 1. Is a Fundamental Right, such as Article 21, in issue? Article 32 No: only a High Court can hear it, under Article 226, for an ordinary legal right. Yes: the petition can be filed in the Supreme Court under Article 32, or in a High Court under Article 226.
keyPoints: Article 32: Supreme Court, Part III rights only, itself in Part III. Article 226: High Courts, Part III rights and "any other purpose". PIL relaxes locus standi; a petition must still be in genuine public interest. Rural Litigation Kendra (1985): a letter treated as an Article 32 petition. Continuing mandamus: Godavarman and vehicular pollution.

caseLaws.name: Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v
caseLaws.facts: State of U.P. Facts. A Dehradun organisation wrote in July 1983 about illegal limestone quarrying in the Mussoorie hills. Principle. The letter was treated as an Article 32 petition. An expert committee classified the quarries and the Court closed the most harmful. Significance. It shows letters and expert committees in writ jurisdiction. M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Ganga Pollution Case) Facts. Untreated sewage from Kanpur polluted the Ganga. Principle. A public-spirited person who is not a riparian owner can bring a petition to make authorities perform their duties. Significance. It relaxes locus standi. T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India Facts. A petition about illegal felling near the Nilgiris grew into a nationwide inquiry into forests. Principle. The Court may keep a petition open and issue successive orders, using expert bodies. Significance. It is the leading example of continuing mandamus. M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Vehicular Pollution Case) Facts. M.C. Mehta sought directions on vehicle pollution in Delhi. Principle. The Court set up a committee and held the petition pending for monitoring. Significance. It shows supervision without a final order. Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar Facts. The petitioner complained of slurry in the Bokaro river but had earlier sought permission to collect it. Principle. The right to life under Article 21 includes the right to enjoy pollution-free water and air. The petition itself was dismissed as a private grievance. Significance. It marks the limit of PIL.

selfTest.q: 1. Which Article lets a High Court issue writs "for any other purpose"?
selfTest.a: Article 226. 2. Which case treated a letter as an Article 32 petition? Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of U.P. 3. What is continuing mandamus? Keeping a writ petition open and issuing successive orders to supervise compliance.

environmental-law-u4-t9.subtitle: What a green belt is, why it is required and where the law uses it

en.inOneMinute: A green belt is a strip or zone of trees and plants that is planted and kept on purpose. It sits around an industry, between an industrial area and homes, or around a growing city. It traps dust, softens noise and separates land uses. A consent condition, court order or town plan usually requires it. It supports pollution control but does not replace it.
legalProvision: Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, section 5: the Central Government may direct the closure, prohibition or regulation of any industry, operation or process. Water Act, 1974, section 25: previous consent of the State Board for an industry that discharges effluent. Air Act, 1981, section 21: previous consent for an industrial plant in an air pollution control area. Twelfth Schedule (Article 243W): municipal functions include urban planning (item 1), regulation of land-use (item 2) and urban forestry, protection of the environment and promotion of ecological aspects (item 8). Constitution, Articles 48A and 51A(g): the State's directive and the citizen's duty to protect the environment, the broad basis for such measures.
en.meaning: A green belt is a deliberately planted and maintained zone of trees and plants, required as a planning or regulatory condition. It differs from a park or a tree-planting drive because the law or an authority requires it for a stated purpose.
keyPoints: A green belt is a planted zone required for a stated purpose. Advantages: filters dust, softens noise, separates land uses, gives habitat. Required by consent conditions, court orders and town planning. Taj Trapezium: NEERI's Green Belt Development Plan. It supports, but does not replace, control at the source.

caseLaws.name: M
caseLaws.facts: C. Mehta v. Union of India (Taj Trapezium Case) Facts. Industrial emissions were damaging the Taj Mahal. Principle. The green belt recommended by NEERI was set up around the Taj under the Court's monitoring. Significance. A court enforced a green belt. Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India Facts. Toxic waste from chemical plants at Bichhri polluted wells and soil. Principle. NEERI suggested that the contaminated area be developed as a green belt at the polluter's expense. Significance. It links green belts with the polluter pays idea.

environmental-law-u4-t8.subtitle: How the Supreme Court built rights, principles and procedures for environmental protection

en.inOneMinute: Much of Indian environmental law was built by the Supreme Court, case by case. The Court read a right to a clean environment into Article 21. It relaxed who may sue, created new principles, and supervised the government for years. The key doctrines are absolute liability, the precautionary principle, the polluter pays principle, sustainable development and the public trust doctrine. Parliament later put some of them into statute, such as section 20 of the National Green Tribunal Act.
legalProvision: Article 21: protection of life and personal liberty, read to include a healthy environment. Articles 32 and 226: the writ powers of the Supreme Court and the High Courts. Articles 48A and 51A(g): the State's directive and the citizen's duty on the environment, used as support. Article 142: the Supreme Court's power to do complete justice, used for directions in Hanuman Laxman Aroskar. Section 20, NGT Act, 2010: the Tribunal must apply sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle.
en.meaning:
Environmental jurisprudence is the body of rules and principles that courts have developed to protect the environment. In India the courts filled gaps where statutes were silent or weakly enforced. They did so mainly through writ petitions.

What the judiciary built How to read this: start at the top box. Each branch names a kind of contribution, with an example case. Judicial role in environmental law Rights Pollution-free water and air under Article 21 (Subhash Kumar). Procedure Letters, PIL, expert committees, continuing mandamus (Rural Litigation Kendra, Godavarman). Principles Absolute liability, precaution, polluter pays, public trust (Oleum, Vellore, Kamal Nath). Balancing and limits Sustainable development and proportionality (Narmada, Alembic).
keyPoints: Oleum (decided December 1986): absolute liability, no exceptions. Vellore (1996): precautionary and polluter pays principles. Kamal Nath (1996): public trust doctrine. Narmada (2000): 2:1, sustainable development. Section 20, NGT Act: principles now statutory.

caseLaws.name: Municipal Council, Ratlam v
caseLaws.facts: Vardhichand Facts. Ward 12, New Road, Ratlam had open drains, no latrines for the poor and foul liquid from an alcohol plant. Principle. Section 133 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is a mandatory duty on the Magistrate. Lack of funds is no defence for the Municipality. Significance. Courts can force statutory bodies to act on sanitation. M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak Case) Facts. Oleum gas leaked from Shriram's plant at Kirti Nagar, Delhi on 4 and 6 December 1985. Principle. A hazardous enterprise is absolutely liable, with no exceptions. Compensation matches its size and capacity. Significance. It created absolute liability in India. Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India Facts. Tanneries in five Tamil Nadu districts polluted the Palar river and land. Principle. The precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle are part of Indian law. Significance. It is the source of the two principles. M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath Facts. A motel on the Beas river held leased forest land. The Court took notice of a news item. Principle. The public trust doctrine is part of Indian law. The lease was cancelled. Significance. It limits the State's power over fragile resources. T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India Facts. A petition on illegal felling near the Nilgiris became a nationwide inquiry. Principle. "Forest" has its dictionary meaning. The Court supervises through continuing mandamus. Significance. It shows the Court as a long-term supervisor. Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India Facts. The Sardar Sarovar Dam displaced many people. Principle. By 2:1, the dam could continue with resettlement conditions. Bharucha J. dissented. Significance. It shows sustainable development and judicial restraint. Animal Welfare Board of India v. A. Nagaraja Facts. The Animal Welfare Board challenged Jallikattu and bullock-cart races. Principle. They violate the animal cruelty law. The Court said Parliament is expected to elevate the rights of animals. Significance. It widens environmental concern to animal rights. Hanuman Laxman Aroskar v. Union of India Facts. The NGT upheld clearance for an airport at Mopa, Goa. Two appeals reached the Supreme Court. Principle. The process failed at each stage. The Court suspended the clearance and directed the expert appraisal committee to revisit it. Significance. It sets the standard for clearance and for the Tribunal's review.

selfTest.q: 1. Which case created absolute liability in India?
selfTest.a: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (the Oleum gas leak case). 2. Which case made the precautionary and polluter pays principles part of Indian law? Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996). 3. Was Narmada Bachao Andolan unanimous? No. It was decided 2:1.

Articles 48A and 51A(g): the State's directive and the citizen's duty on the environment, used as support. Article 142: the Supreme Court's power to do complete justice, used for directions in Hanuman Laxman Aroskar. Section 20, NGT Act, 2010: the Tribunal must apply sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle.
hi.meaning: Environmental jurisprudence is the body of rules and principles that courts have developed to protect the environment. In India the courts filled gaps where statutes were silent or weakly enforced. They did so mainly through writ petitions. What the judiciary built How to read this: start at the top box. Each branch names a kind of contribution, with an example case. Judicial role in environmental law Rights Pollution-free water and air under Article 21 (Subhash Kumar). Procedure Letters, PIL, expert committees, continuing mandamus (Rural Litigation Kendra, Godavarman). Principles Absolute liability, precaution, polluter pays, public trust (Oleum, Vellore, Kamal Nath). Balancing and limits Sustainable development and proportionality (Narmada, Alembic).
keyPoints: Oleum (decided December 1986): absolute liability, no exceptions. Vellore (1996): precautionary and polluter pays principles. Kamal Nath (1996): public trust doctrine. Narmada (2000): 2:1, sustainable development. Section 20, NGT Act: principles now statutory.

caseLaws.name: Municipal Council, Ratlam v
caseLaws.facts: Vardhichand Facts. Ward 12, New Road, Ratlam had open drains, no latrines for the poor and foul liquid from an alcohol plant. Principle. Section 133 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is a mandatory duty on the Magistrate. Lack of funds is no defence for the Municipality. Significance. Courts can force statutory bodies to act on sanitation. M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak Case) Facts. Oleum gas leaked from Shriram's plant at Kirti Nagar, Delhi on 4 and 6 December 1985. Principle. A hazardous enterprise is absolutely liable, with no exceptions. Compensation matches its size and capacity. Significance. It created absolute liability in India. Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India Facts. Tanneries in five Tamil Nadu districts polluted the Palar river and land. Principle. The precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle are part of Indian law. Significance. It is the source of the two principles. M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath Facts. A motel on the Beas river held leased forest land. The Court took notice of a news item. Principle. The public trust doctrine is part of Indian law. The lease was cancelled. Significance. It limits the State's power over fragile resources. T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India Facts. A petition on illegal felling near the Nilgiris became a nationwide inquiry. Principle. "Forest" has its dictionary meaning. The Court supervises through continuing mandamus. Significance. It shows the Court as a long-term supervisor. Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India Facts. The Sardar Sarovar Dam displaced many people. Principle. By 2:1, the dam could continue with resettlement conditions. Bharucha J. dissented. Significance. It shows sustainable development and judicial restraint. Animal Welfare Board of India v. A. Nagaraja Facts. The Animal Welfare Board challenged Jallikattu and bullock-cart races. Principle. They violate the animal cruelty law. The Court said Parliament is expected to elevate the rights of animals. Significance. It widens environmental concern to animal rights. Hanuman Laxman Aroskar v. Union of India Facts. The NGT upheld clearance for an airport at Mopa, Goa. Two appeals reached the Supreme Court. Principle. The process failed at each stage. The Court suspended the clearance and directed the expert appraisal committee to revisit it. Significance. It sets the standard for clearance and for the Tribunal's review.

selfTest.q: 1. Which case created absolute liability in India?
selfTest.a: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (the Oleum gas leak case). 2. Which case made the precautionary and polluter pays principles part of Indian law? Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996). 3. Was Narmada Bachao Andolan unanimous? No. It was decided 2:1.

environmental-law-u5-t3.subtitle: When a State answers in international law for environmental harm that crosses its border

en.inOneMinute: State liability asks when a State must answer to another State for environmental harm that began on its soil. The answer has two parts: the harm must be traced to the State's own conduct, and that conduct must break an international duty. The test is not automatic. The State is judged by what it did to prevent the harm. If it took reasonable care, it is much harder to blame it. If it knew of a risk and did nothing, it is much easier.
legalProvision: Trail Smelter Arbitration (1938 and 1941): Canada answered for fumes from a privately owned smelter and had to pay compensation for past damage. Stockholm Declaration, 1972, Principle 22: States are to cooperate to develop the law on liability and compensation for victims of pollution.
en.meaning:
State liability here means the international responsibility of a State, described under State responsibility . It arises when two things are present.

The conduct, an act or an omission , can be attributed to the State. That conduct breaches a duty the State owes under international law, such as the no-harm rule.
keyPoints: Two elements: attributable conduct and breach of an international duty. Standard: due diligence, not automatic strict liability. A State can answer for a private polluter's harm. Remedies: stop the wrong, then restitution, compensation or satisfaction. Climate change: causation is hard to prove, but State responsibility rules apply (ICJ advisory opinion, 2025).

caseLaws.name: Trail Smelter Arbitration (United States v
caseLaws.facts: Canada) Facts. A Canadian smelter's fumes damaged land in Washington State. Principle. Canada was responsible for a private smelter's harm. It had to pay compensation and keep the smelter within set limits. Significance. It shows State responsibility for private polluters and the remedy of a regime of controls.

selfTest.q: 1. What standard applies to State liability for environmental harm?
selfTest.a: Due diligence, not strict liability. 2. Name the three forms of reparation. Restitution, compensation and satisfaction. 3. Which decision in this note shows a State answering for a private polluter? The Trail Smelter Arbitration.

environmental-law-u5-t1.subtitle: The rules, treaties and institutions through which States protect the environment together

en.inOneMinute: Pollution, climate change and loss of species do not stop at a border. No single country can solve them. The international environmental regime is the set of principles, treaties and bodies that States have built to deal with them together. It has four layers: customary rules, non-binding declarations, binding treaties and institutions. Exam answers score by keeping these layers apart and placing each instrument in the right one.
legalProvision: Article 51(c) of the Constitution of India: the State shall endeavour to foster respect for international law and treaty obligations. Article 253: Parliament may make any law for India or any part of it to implement a treaty, agreement or convention. The same Article covers any decision of an international conference or body. Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and Air Act, 1981: their preambles refer to the Stockholm conference of June 1972, which shows how an international event led to Indian statutes. Biological Diversity Act, 2002: its preamble refers to the Convention on Biological Diversity signed at Rio de Janeiro on 5 June 1992.
en.meaning:
A regime is a set of principles, rules and decision-making bodies that States accept for one subject. The international environmental regime covers the rules on pollution crossing borders, protection of species and habitats, the ozone layer, the climate and sustainable development.

The four layers of the regime How to read this: start at the top box and follow the lines down. Each green box is one layer, with an example under it. International environmental regime Customary rules No-harm rule; bind all States Soft-law declarations Stockholm 1972, Nairobi 1982, Johannesburg 2002 Binding treaties Ramsar, Bonn, Biodiversity, Climate Convention, Kyoto, Paris Institutions UNEP and the Conferences of the Parties
keyPoints: Four layers: customary rules, soft law, treaties, institutions. Stockholm, Nairobi and Johannesburg are declarations; Ramsar, Bonn, the Climate Convention, Kyoto and Paris are treaties. UNEP was created by General Assembly resolution of 15 December 1972. Article 253 lets Parliament legislate to implement a treaty. Vellore: sustainable development is part of customary international law.

caseLaws.name: Trail Smelter Arbitration (United States v
caseLaws.facts: Canada) Facts. Fumes from a smelter at Trail, British Columbia, damaged land in Washington State. Principle. A State must not allow its territory to be used to cause serious injury to another State. Significance. It is the earliest authority behind the customary layer of the regime. Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India Facts. Tanneries in Tamil Nadu discharged untreated effluent into the Palar river area. Principle. Sustainable development is part of customary international law, and a customary rule not contrary to domestic law is deemed incorporated in it. Significance. It shows how international rules enter Indian courts.

selfTest.q: 1. Which Article lets Parliament legislate to implement a treaty?
selfTest.a: Article 253. 2. Is the Stockholm Declaration binding? No. It is soft law. 3. Which case treated sustainable development as customary international law? Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India.

visuals.caption: The four layers of the regime How to read this: start at the top box and follow the lines down. Each green box is one layer, with an example under it.
Comparison Table
visuals.html:
PrincipleWhat it says
1Human beings are at the centre of concerns for sustainable development and are entitled to a healthy and productive life in harmony with nature.
2States have the sovereign right to exploit their own resources, and the responsibility to ensure their activities do not damage other States or areas beyond national jurisdiction.
3 and 4The right to development must meet the needs of present and future generations equitably (3). Environmental protection is an integral part of development and cannot be considered in isolation (4).
5 and 6All States and people must co-operate to eradicate poverty (5). Developing countries, especially the least developed and most vulnerable, get special priority (6).
7States co-operate in global partnership to conserve and restore the Earth's ecosystem. They have common but differentiated responsibilities. Developed countries acknowledge their responsibility given their pressures on the environment and their technologies and finances.
8 and 9States reduce and eliminate unsustainable production and consumption (8). States co-operate on capacity-building and technology transfer (9).
10Public participation: access to environmental information held by public authorities, a chance to take part in decisions, and effective access to judicial and administrative proceedings, including redress and remedy.
11 and 12States shall enact effective environmental legislation, and standards of some countries may be inappropriate and costly for developing countries (11). A supportive open economic system; trade measures for environmental purposes must not be arbitrary discrimination or a disguised restriction on trade (12).
13States shall develop national law on liability and compensation for victims of pollution and other environmental damage, and co-operate to develop international law on damage to areas beyond their jurisdiction.
14States should discourage or prevent the relocation and transfer to other States of activities and substances that cause severe degradation or harm to health.
15The precautionary approach: where there are threats of serious or irreversible damage, lack of full scientific certainty shall not be used as a reason for postponing cost-effective measures.
16National authorities should promote internalization of environmental costs, bearing in mind that the polluter should, in principle, bear the cost of pollution.
17Environmental impact assessment shall be undertaken for proposed activities likely to have a significant adverse impact and subject to a decision of a competent national authority.
18 and 19Immediate notification of natural disasters and emergencies likely to harm other States (18). Prior and timely notification, information and early good-faith consultation on activities with significant transboundary effects (19).
20 to 22Role of women (20), youth (21), and indigenous and local communities (22) in environmental management and development.
23 to 26Protect the environment of people under oppression, domination and occupation (23). Warfare is inherently destructive of sustainable development, so States respect international law protecting the environment in armed conflict (24). Peace, development and environmental protection are interdependent and indivisible (25). Environmental disputes are resolved peacefully under the UN Charter (26).
27States and people co-operate in good faith and partnership in fulfilling the Principles and developing international law in the field of sustainable development.

environmental-law-u5-t6.subtitle: The first world conference on the environment: its Declaration, Action Plan and the body it created

en.inOneMinute: The United Nations Conference on the Human Environment met at Stockholm from 5 to 16 June 1972. It adopted the Stockholm Declaration with 26 Principles, an Action Plan with 109 recommendations, and led to the creation of UNEP. The Declaration is not a treaty. It is soft law. Yet it is the starting point of modern international environmental law, and it is named in two Indian Acts.
legalProvision: Principle 21: In accordance with the UN Charter and the principles of international law, States have the sovereign right to exploit their own resources under their own environmental policies. They have the responsibility to ensure that activities within their jurisdiction or control do not damage the environment of other States or of areas beyond national jurisdiction. Principle 22: States shall cooperate to develop the international law on liability and compensation for victims of pollution. Principle 1: Man has the fundamental right to freedom, equality and adequate conditions of life in an environment of a quality that permits a life of dignity and well-being. He bears a solemn responsibility to protect and improve the environment for present and future generations. Policies of apartheid, racial segregation, discrimination and colonial or other oppression stand condemned. Principle 2: The natural resources of the earth, including air, water, land, flora and fauna and representative samples of natural ecosystems, must be safeguarded for present and future generations through careful planning or management. environmental-law-u5-t2.subtitle: Pollution that starts in one State and harms another: the no-harm rule and why courts cannot solve it alone

en.inOneMinute: Transboundary pollution is pollution that starts in one State and harms people, land or water in another State, or in areas that belong to no State. Smoke across a border, a poisoned river and a thinning ozone layer are all examples. An Indian court cannot order a factory in another country to stop. So the answer lies in international law. Its oldest rule is the no-harm rule: a State must not let its territory be used to cause serious harm to a neighbour.
legalProvision: Trail Smelter Arbitration (1938 and 1941): no State may use its territory, or let it be used, to cause serious injury by fumes in another State. The injury must be shown by clear and convincing evidence. Stockholm Declaration, 1972, Principle 21: States have the sovereign right to use their own resources. They also have a responsibility to ensure that activities within their control do not damage the environment of other States or of areas beyond national jurisdiction. Rio Declaration, 1992, Principle 2: repeats the same idea of State responsibility. Customary international law: the no-harm rule binds States even without a treaty.
en.meaning:
Transboundary pollution is harm to the environment of one State, or of an area beyond any State, caused by a source in the territory or control of another State. It has two shapes.

Point-to-point harm: the source and the victim can both be named and lie fairly close. Example: smoke from a border factory, or waste dumped into a river that flows into the next country. Global harm: the pollutant mixes into the air or the sea first, and the damage appears everywhere. Examples are ozone depletion and climate change .

How a transboundary pollution claim travels How to read this: follow the boxes from top to bottom. Each step leads to the next. The last box is the usual outcome. 1. A source in State A releases fumes or waste. 2. The pollution crosses into State B. 3. State B shows serious harm with clear evidence. 4. State B claims against State A under the no-harm rule. 5. Result Talks, a treaty or arbitration decide on stopping the harm and on compensation.
keyPoints: Transboundary pollution: harm in one State, or beyond any State, from a source in another State. Two shapes: point-to-point and global. No-harm rule: Trail Smelter (1938 and 1941); Stockholm Principle 21. The State answers for failing to control private polluters; the standard is due diligence. Global harm is handled by treaties, not by claims after the event.

caseLaws.name: Trail Smelter Arbitration (United States v
caseLaws.facts: Canada) Facts. Sulphur dioxide fumes from a Canadian lead-zinc smelter at Trail, British Columbia, damaged crops and forests across the border in Washington State. Principle. No State may use or permit the use of its territory to cause serious injury by fumes in another State, if the injury is proved by clear and convincing evidence. Significance. It is the founding authority for the no-harm rule and for State responsibility for private polluters.

selfTest.q: 1. Which case first stated the no-harm rule between States?
selfTest.a: The Trail Smelter Arbitration (United States v. Canada). 2. Why can an Indian court not stop a foreign polluter? Its orders do not run beyond India's borders. 3. Give one example each of point-to-point and global harm. Point-to-point: smoke from a border factory. Global: ozone depletion or climate change.

environmental-law-u5-t4.subtitle: Rules that bind every State without a treaty, and how they reach Indian courts

en.inOneMinute: A treaty binds only the States that sign it. Customary international law is different. It binds all States, because they follow a practice and believe the law requires it. In environmental law, the no-harm rule is the standard example. Indian courts also treat some environmental principles as customary law, and they can then apply them at home.
legalProvision: Article 38(1)(b) of the Statute of the International Court of Justice: lists international custom as evidence of a general practice accepted as law. Article 51(c) of the Constitution of India: the State shall endeavour to foster respect for international law and treaty obligations. Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum (1996): the Supreme Court held that sustainable development is part of customary international law. It added that a customary rule not contrary to domestic law is deemed incorporated in it.
en.meaning:
A rule of customary international law needs two things.

A general and consistent practice of States. A belief that the practice is required by law, called opinio juris (belief that the practice is legally required).

Practice without that belief is only habit. A belief without practice is only a wish.
keyPoints: Custom = general State practice + opinio juris. It binds all States without a treaty. No-harm rule: customary, from Trail Smelter. Vellore: sustainable development is customary; a customary rule not contrary to domestic law is deemed incorporated.

caseLaws.name: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v
caseLaws.facts: Union of India Facts. Tanneries in Tamil Nadu discharged untreated effluent, polluting land and drinking water around the Palar river. Principle. Sustainable development is part of customary international law. A customary rule not contrary to municipal law is deemed incorporated in domestic law. Significance. It is the leading Indian authority for using customary rules in environmental cases. Trail Smelter Arbitration (United States v. Canada) Facts. Fumes from a Canadian smelter damaged land in Washington State. Principle. No State may use or permit the use of its territory to cause serious injury to another State, shown by clear and convincing evidence. Significance. It states the no-harm rule that is treated as customary law.

selfTest.q: 1. What are the two elements of custom?
selfTest.a: General State practice and opinio juris. 2. Which case held sustainable development to be customary international law? Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India. 3. When does a customary rule apply in India? When it is not contrary to domestic law.

environmental-law-u5-t5.subtitle: Why a parent company is hard to sue for a subsidiary's pollution, and the routes that have opened

en.inOneMinute: International law was built for States, not companies. A victim of a multinational company's pollution cannot sue it before an international tribunal in the way one State can arbitrate against another. The company's own structure adds a second barrier. A parent and its local subsidiary are separate legal persons. The Bhopal gas leak showed this problem.
legalProvision: Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster (Processing of Claims) Act, 1985: authorised the Government of India to act as the exclusive representative of all victims, and so to consolidate their claims. United Nations Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (2011): 31 principles on the State's duty to protect, the company's responsibility to respect and access to remedy. They are soft law.
en.meaning:
A multinational company is a company group that operates in several countries, usually through locally incorporated subsidiaries. The home State is where the parent sits. The host State is where the subsidiary runs its plant.

The question here is when the parent, or the group, answers in law for environmental harm done by the subsidiary in the host State.
keyPoints: International law binds States, not companies. Separate corporate personality shields a parent. Bhopal: Government of India as exclusive representative of victims under the 1985 Act. Guiding Principles, 2011: soft law with 31 principles. Home-court claims against a parent turn on a duty of care shown on the facts.

caseLaws.name: M
caseLaws.facts: C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak Case) Facts. A leak of oleum gas from a Delhi plant harmed people nearby. Principle. Enterprises engaged in hazardous or inherently dangerous activities face absolute liability. Significance. It is the Indian answer to the kind of harm seen at Bhopal.

selfTest.q: 1. What did the Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster (Processing of Claims) Act, 1985 do?
selfTest.a: It authorised the Government of India to act as the exclusive representative of all victims. 2. Are the UN Guiding Principles binding? No. They are soft law. 3. Does owning a subsidiary make a parent automatically liable? No. The parent and subsidiary are separate legal persons.

Enterprises engaged in hazardous or inherently dangerous activities face absolute liability. Significance. It is the Indian answer to the kind of harm seen at Bhopal.

selfTest.q: 1. What did the Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster (Processing of Claims) Act, 1985 do?
selfTest.a: It authorised the Government of India to act as the exclusive representative of all victims. 2. Are the UN Guiding Principles binding? No. They are soft law. 3. Does owning a subsidiary make a parent automatically liable? No. The parent and subsidiary are separate legal persons.

hi.inOneMinute: International law was built for States, not companies. A victim of a multinational company's pollution cannot sue it before an international tribunal in the way one State can arbitrate against another. The company's own structure adds a second barrier. A parent and its local subsidiary are separate legal persons. The Bhopal gas leak showed this problem.
legalProvision: Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster (Processing of Claims) Act, 1985: authorised the Government of India to act as the exclusive representative of all victims, and so to consolidate their claims. United Nations Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (2011): 31 principles on the State's duty to protect, the company's responsibility to respect and access to remedy. They are soft law.
hi.meaning: A multinational company is a company group that operates in several countries, usually through locally incorporated subsidiaries. The home State is where the parent sits. The host State is where the subsidiary runs its plant. The question here is when the parent, or the group, answers in law for environmental harm done by the subsidiary in the host State.
keyPoints: International law binds States, not companies. Separate corporate personality shields a parent. Bhopal: Government of India as exclusive representative of victims under the 1985 Act. Guiding Principles, 2011: soft law with 31 principles. Home-court claims against a parent turn on a duty of care shown on the facts.
