environmental-law-u5-t9.subtitle: The treaty that protects animals which cross borders: Appendix I, Appendix II and range States

en.inOneMinute: The Bonn Convention is the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals. It was adopted at Bonn on 23 June 1979 and came into force on 1 November 1983. It covers all migratory wild animals, not only birds. A species that crosses many countries is safe only if every country on its route protects it. The Convention brings those countries together.
legalProvision: Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals: adopted at Bonn on 23 June 1979, in force from 1 November 1983. Appendix I: migratory species that are endangered. Range States must prohibit taking them, with narrow exceptions such as scientific purposes or traditional subsistence use. Appendix II: migratory species with an unfavourable conservation status, or that would benefit from international cooperation. Range States shall endeavour to conclude agreements (Article II(3)(c)). Constitution of India, Article 253: Parliament may legislate to implement a treaty.
en.meaning:
A migratory species is one that moves across national borders in its life cycle. A range State is a country in which the species lives or which it crosses.

The treaty is often wrongly called a convention on migratory birds. Its correct title speaks of migratory species of wild animals. It reaches whales, dolphins, sea turtles, bats and land mammals as well as birds.
keyPoints: Adopted at Bonn, 23 June 1979; in force 1 November 1983. Covers all migratory wild animals, not only birds. Appendix I: strict protection. Appendix II: cooperation through agreements. India has been a Party since 1 November 1983. Art III(5): four exceptions to the ban on taking, each precise and limited in space and time. Art I: migratory species, Range State, taking, favourable status. Art XII(3): stricter domestic laws allowed.

caseLaws.name: No case page in this subject turns on the Bonn Convention
caseLaws.facts: Questions on it are answered from the Convention's structure.

selfTest.q: 1. What is the full title of the Bonn Convention?
selfTest.a: The Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals. 2. Which Appendix lists endangered species? Appendix I. 3. What is a range State? A country in which a migratory species lives or which it crosses.

visuals.caption: Comparison Table
visuals.html:
ArticleWhat it says
Article I(1)Defines the key words. A migratory species is a population, or a geographically separate part of it, of wild animals a significant proportion of whose members cyclically and predictably cross one or more national jurisdictional boundaries. Conservation status is the sum of influences on its long-term distribution and abundance. Status is favourable when the population sustains itself, the range is not shrinking, habitat is sufficient, and distribution and abundance approach historic levels; if any condition fails, it is unfavourable. Endangered means in danger of extinction throughout all or a significant portion of its range. Range covers all areas the species inhabits, stays in, crosses or overflies on its normal migration route. Taking means hunting, fishing, capturing, harassing, deliberate killing, or attempting any such conduct.
Article I(1)(h)A Range State is any State that exercises jurisdiction over any part of the range of the species. It also includes a State whose flag vessels take the species outside national jurisdictional limits.
Article IIFundamental principles. Parties acknowledge the need to avoid any migratory species becoming endangered (Art II(2)). They should promote and support research. They shall endeavour to give immediate protection to Appendix I species and to conclude Agreements for Appendix II species (Art II(3)).
Article IIIAppendix I lists endangered species, on reliable evidence including the best scientific evidence available (Art III(1)-(2)). A species can be removed only if it is no longer endangered and is not likely to become endangered again through loss of protection (Art III(3)). Range States of Appendix I species shall endeavour to conserve and restore habitat, remove obstacles to migration, and control other endangering factors, including exotic species (Art III(4)). They shall prohibit taking (Art III(5)). They must tell the Secretariat of any exceptions as soon as possible (Art III(7)).
Article III(5)Exceptions to the ban on taking are allowed only if: (a) the taking is for scientific purposes; (b) it enhances the propagation or survival of the species; (c) it accommodates the needs of traditional subsistence users; or (d) extraordinary circumstances so require. Each exception must be precise as to content and limited in space and time, and should not operate to the disadvantage of the species.
Article IVAppendix II lists species with an unfavourable conservation status that need international agreements, and species that would significantly benefit from international cooperation (Art IV(1)). A species may be listed in both Appendices (Art IV(2)).
Article VGuidelines for Agreements. The object is to restore the species to a favourable conservation status or keep it there (Art V(1)). An Agreement should cover the whole range and be open to accession by all Range States, whether or not they are Parties to the Convention (Art V(2)). Each Agreement should, as a minimum, identify the species and its migration route, designate a national authority for each Party, provide for settlement of disputes, and, for cetaceans, prohibit any taking not permitted under another multilateral agreement (Art V(4)).
Article VIThe Secretariat keeps an up-to-date list of Range States. Range States report to the Conference of the Parties, through the Secretariat, at least six months before each ordinary meeting, on measures taken.
Articles VII-IXThe Conference of the Parties is the decision-making organ (Art VII). A Scientific Council gives scientific advice (Art VIII). The Secretariat is provided by the Executive Director of the United Nations Environment Programme (Art IX).
Articles X-XIThe Convention is amended by a two-thirds majority of Parties present and voting (Art X). The Appendices are amended the same way, on proposals backed by the best scientific evidence (Art XI). A Party may enter a reservation to an Appendix amendment within ninety days.
Article XII(3)The Convention does not affect the right of Parties to adopt stricter domestic measures for listed species, or domestic measures for unlisted species.
Articles XIII-XIVDisputes go first to negotiation, then by mutual consent to arbitration, in particular the Permanent Court of Arbitration at The Hague, and the arbitral decision binds (Art XIII). General reservations are not allowed. Specific reservations are allowed (Art XIV).
Articles XV-XIXOpen for signature at Bonn until 22 June 1980, then for accession. It enters into force on the first day of the third month after the fifteenth instrument is deposited (Art XVIII). A Party may denounce it at any time, effective twelve months after notice (Art XIX).

environmental-law-u5-t7.subtitle: The UN body that coordinates global environmental work: how it was created, what it does and what it cannot do

en.inOneMinute: UNEP is the United Nations Environment Programme. The General Assembly set it up on 15 December 1972, after the Stockholm conference. Its home is Nairobi. It is not an environmental police force. Its job is to watch the state of the environment, set the agenda and help States negotiate treaties. It cannot force any State to obey.
legalProvision: General Assembly resolution 2997 (XXVII), 15 December 1972: the resolution on institutional and financial arrangements for international environmental cooperation, which led to UNEP and a 58-member Governing Council. General Assembly resolution 67/251 (March 2013): renamed the Governing Council as the UN Environment Assembly, after the Council moved to universal membership in 2013.
en.meaning: UNEP is the main UN body for environmental matters. It is a programme of the United Nations, not a treaty body. Its work is to coordinate, to advise and to build agreement among States.
keyPoints: UNEP: General Assembly resolution 2997 (XXVII), 15 December 1972; Nairobi. Governing Council of 58 members, replaced by the UN Environment Assembly with universal membership. Role: monitor, set the agenda, support treaty-making. No enforcement power.

caseLaws.name: No Indian court case turns on the role of UNEP
caseLaws.facts: The body appears through the treaties it serves, which are studied in their own notes.

selfTest.q: 1. Which resolution created UNEP?
selfTest.a: General Assembly resolution 2997 (XXVII), 15 December 1972. 2. Where is UNEP based? Nairobi. 3. Can UNEP enforce environmental treaties? No. Its role is to coordinate and support.

environmental-law-u5-t8.subtitle: The treaty on wetlands: the Ramsar List, wise use and the Montreux Record

en.inOneMinute: The Ramsar Convention is the treaty on wetlands. It was signed on 2 February 1971 at Ramsar, Iran. It asks each member country to list wetlands of international importance and to use all its wetlands wisely. It predates the Stockholm conference of 1972. It binds only the States that join, and the Convention entered into force for India on 1 February 1982.
legalProvision: Convention on Wetlands of International Importance especially as Waterfowl Habitat: signed at Ramsar, Iran, on 2 February 1971 and in force from 21 December 1975. Core duties of each Party: to designate at least one wetland for the List of Wetlands of International Importance. The second duty is to promote the wise use of all wetlands in its territory. Constitution of India, Article 253: Parliament may legislate to implement a treaty, so the Convention enters Indian law through Indian statutes and rules.
en.meaning:
A wetland is an area of marsh, fen, peatland or water, whether natural or artificial, permanent or temporary, fresh, brackish or salt. Article 1 also includes marine water not deeper than six metres at low tide. The Convention protects these areas because they control floods, refill groundwater, clean water and give homes to waterbirds that migrate across countries.

The treaty is an early one among the modern global environmental treaties. Its concern is one type of ecosystem.
keyPoints: Signed 2 February 1971 at Ramsar, Iran; in force 21 December 1975. Duties: designate at least one wetland and promote wise use of all. Montreux Record: listed sites whose ecological character is changing. In force for India from 1 February 1982. Art 2(3): listing keeps sovereignty. Art 2(5): deletion only in urgent national interest. Art 4(2): compensate by new reserves. Art 3(2): report changes in ecological character. Art 11: denunciation after five years.

caseLaws.name: No case page in this subject turns on the Ramsar Convention
caseLaws.facts: Questions on it are answered from the treaty's own duties.

selfTest.q: 1. When was the Ramsar Convention signed?
selfTest.a: 2 February 1971. 2. What are the two core duties? Designate at least one wetland for the List, and promote wise use of all wetlands. 3. What is the Montreux Record? A register of listed wetlands whose ecological character is changing or at risk.

visuals.caption: Comparison Table
visuals.html:
ArticleWhat it says
Article 1Defines wetlands (marsh, fen, peatland or water; natural or artificial; permanent or temporary; static or flowing; fresh, brackish or salt; marine water up to six metres deep at low tide) and waterfowl (birds ecologically dependent on wetlands).
Article 2Each Party designates suitable wetlands for the List, with precise boundaries on a map (Art 2(1)). Selection is on international significance in ecology, botany, zoology, limnology or hydrology, and waterfowl wetlands come first (Art 2(2)). Listing does not prejudice the exclusive sovereign rights of the Party (Art 2(3)). At least one wetland must be designated on signing or on depositing the instrument of ratification or accession (Art 2(4)).
Article 2(5)-(6)A Party may add wetlands, extend boundaries, or, because of its urgent national interests, delete or restrict listed wetlands. It must inform the Bureau at the earliest possible time. It must consider its international responsibilities for migratory waterfowl stocks when it designates or changes entries.
Article 3Parties plan to promote conservation of listed wetlands and, as far as possible, wise use of wetlands in their territory (Art 3(1)). Each Party must arrange to be informed at the earliest possible time if a listed wetland's ecological character has changed, is changing or is likely to change through technological developments, pollution or other human interference, and must pass this on without delay to the Bureau (Art 3(2)).

It entered into force four months after seven States became Parties, and for each later Party four months after signature without reservation or deposit of its instrument (Art 10).

environmental-law-u5-t10.subtitle: The ten-year review of Stockholm: what the 1982 Nairobi session said and what followed from it

en.inOneMinute: There is no binding "Nairobi Convention, 1982". What happened was a special session of the UNEP Governing Council, held in Nairobi from 10 to 18 May 1982. It marked ten years since Stockholm. The session adopted the Nairobi Declaration, a soft-law statement. Its importance is historical. It belongs to the chain that led to the Brundtland Commission and the idea of sustainable development.
legalProvision: Special session of the UNEP Governing Council, Nairobi, 10 to 18 May 1982: a session of special character called by the General Assembly. It marked the tenth anniversary of the Stockholm conference. Nairobi Declaration: adopted on 18 May 1982. It expressed satisfaction at progress since 1972 and anxiety about the future. General Assembly resolution 38/161 (19 December 1983): set up the special commission later called the World Commission on Environment and Development.
en.meaning:
The Nairobi Declaration is a political statement of governments, not a treaty. Like the Stockholm Declaration, it is soft law . It creates no duty that a court or tribunal can enforce .

The syllabus title sometimes appears as "Nairobi Convention". That name is wrong for this topic. The correct instrument is the Nairobi Declaration of 1982.
keyPoints: Nairobi session: UNEP Governing Council, 10 to 18 May 1982; Declaration adopted 18 May. It is a declaration, not a convention. Resolution 38/161 (19 December 1983) led to the Brundtland Commission. Our Common Future (1987) gave the main definition of sustainable development.

caseLaws.name: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v
caseLaws.facts: Union of India Facts. Tanneries in Tamil Nadu discharged untreated effluent, polluting land and water around the Palar river. Principle. The Court set out the history of sustainable development, quoted the Brundtland definition, and held the concept part of customary international law. Significance. It carries the Brundtland idea, which grew out of this chain, into Indian law.

selfTest.a: No. The 1982 outcome is the Nairobi Declaration, which is soft law. 2. Which body held the 1982 Nairobi session? The Governing Council of UNEP, in a special session. 3. Which resolution set up the Brundtland Commission? General Assembly resolution 38/161 of 1983.

environmental-law-u5-t11.subtitle: The Convention on Biological Diversity: three objectives, sovereign rights over resources and benefit sharing

en.inOneMinute: The Convention on Biological Diversity is the main treaty on life on Earth in all its variety. Its text was adopted at Nairobi on 22 May 1992 and opened for signature at the Rio Earth Summit on 5 June 1992. It has three aims: conserve biodiversity, use it sustainably, and share its benefits fairly. The third aim answers the problem of biopiracy. India gives effect to the treaty through the Biological Diversity Act, 2002.
legalProvision: Convention on Biological Diversity: adopted at Nairobi on 22 May 1992, opened for signature at Rio de Janeiro on 5 June 1992 and in force from 29 December 1993. Three objectives: conservation of biological diversity, sustainable use of its components, and fair and equitable sharing of the benefits from genetic resources. India and the Convention: India signed on 5 June 1992 and ratified on 18 February 1994. It became a Party on 19 May 1994 (CBD Secretariat list of Parties). Biological Diversity Act, 2002, preamble: records that India is a Party to the Convention, signed at Rio on 5 June 1992 and in force from 29 December 1993. The preamble adds that the Convention reaffirms the sovereign rights of States over their biological resources.
en.meaning:
Biological diversity is the variety of life: the range of species, the genes within them and the ecosystems they form. The Convention covers all of it, not one type of habitat.

It was one of two binding treaties signed at the Rio Earth Summit of June 1992. The other was the Convention on climate change. Together they were signed by 153 nations, according to the Vellore judgment.
keyPoints: Adopted 22 May 1992; opened for signature 5 June 1992; in force 29 December 1993. Three objectives: conservation, sustainable use, fair and equitable benefit sharing. States have sovereign rights over their biological resources. Cartagena (2000, in force 2003) and Nagoya (2010, in force 2014). India: Biological Diversity Act, 2002. Art 15: access needs prior informed consent and mutually agreed terms (15(5), 15(4)); Art 8(j): traditional knowledge; Art 14: impact assessment. Art 8: in-situ; Art 9: ex-situ. Art 19(3): protocol on living modified organisms. Art 37: no reservations.

The Court recorded that the Rio Earth Summit of June 1992 produced two conventions, on biological diversity and climate change, signed by 153 nations. It held sustainable development to be part of customary international law. Significance. It places the Convention in the story of sustainable development.

selfTest.q: 1. What are the three objectives of the Convention?
selfTest.a: Conservation, sustainable use and fair and equitable benefit sharing. 2. Which Protocol deals with living modified organisms? The Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety. 3. Which Indian Act reflects the Convention? The Biological Diversity Act, 2002.

visuals.caption: Comparison Table
visuals.html:
ArticleWhat it says
PreambleConservation of biological diversity is a "common concern of humankind". States have sovereign rights over their own biological resources and are responsible for conserving them. Lack of full scientific certainty should not postpone measures to avoid or minimize a threat of significant reduction or loss of biological diversity. In-situ conservation is the fundamental requirement, and ex-situ measures play an important supporting role. Indigenous and local communities depend on biological resources, and women play a vital role.
Article 1The three objectives: conservation of biological diversity, sustainable use of its components, and fair and equitable sharing of benefits from genetic resources. They are pursued by appropriate access to genetic resources, appropriate transfer of technologies and appropriate funding.
Article 2Defines biological diversity as the variability among living organisms from all sources, including diversity within species, between species and of ecosystems. Also defines biological resources, genetic material, genetic resources, ecosystem, habitat, in-situ and ex-situ conservation, protected area, country of origin, country providing genetic resources, biotechnology and sustainable use (use at a rate that does not lead to long-term decline of biological diversity).
Article 3Principle. States have the sovereign right to exploit their own resources under their environmental policies. They have the responsibility to ensure that activities within their jurisdiction or control do not damage the environment of other States or areas beyond national jurisdiction.
Articles 4-5Jurisdictional scope: the Convention applies to biodiversity components within national jurisdiction, and to processes and activities under a Party's jurisdiction or control wherever their effects occur. Parties cooperate on areas beyond national jurisdiction.
Articles 6-7Each Party develops national strategies, plans or programmes and integrates biodiversity into sectoral policies (Art 6). Each Party identifies and monitors important components of biodiversity and activities with significant adverse impacts (Art 7).
Article 8In-situ conservation, "as far as possible and as appropriate": a system of protected areas; regulation of biological resources; protection of ecosystems and habitats; restoration of degraded ecosystems and recovery of threatened species; control of risks from living modified organisms; prevention or eradication of harmful alien species; legislation to protect threatened species. Art 8(j), subject to national legislation, respects, preserves and maintains the knowledge and practices of indigenous and local communities, with their approval, and encourages equitable sharing of benefits from that knowledge.
Article 9Ex-situ conservation, predominantly to complement in-situ measures, preferably in the country of origin, including facilities, recovery of threatened species and their reintroduction into natural habitats.
Articles 10-13Sustainable use: integrate conservation into national decision-making, protect customary use consistent with conservation (Art 10). Adopt economic and social incentives (Art 11). Research and training, with special needs of developing countries (Art 12). Public education and awareness (Art 13).
Article 14Environmental impact assessment of proposed projects likely to have significant adverse effects on biodiversity, with public participation where appropriate (Art 14(1)(a)). Notification and consultation on activities affecting other States. Immediate notification of imminent or grave danger across borders. The Conference of the Parties will examine liability and redress, including restoration and compensation, for damage to biodiversity (Art 14(2)).
Article 15Access to genetic resources. Authority to determine access rests with national governments and is subject to national legislation (15(1)). Parties facilitate access for environmentally sound uses (15(2)). Access is on mutually agreed terms (15(4)) and subject to prior informed consent of the providing Party unless it determines otherwise (15(5)). Each Party takes measures to share research results and benefits from commercial and other use fairly with the providing Party, on mutually agreed terms (15(7)).
Articles 16-18Access to and transfer of technology, including biotechnology, to developing countries on fair and most favourable terms, while recognizing adequate and effective protection of intellectual property rights (Art 16). Exchange of information (Art 17). Technical and scientific cooperation (Art 18).
Article 19Biotechnology and distribution of its benefits. Parties provide for effective participation in biotechnology research by Parties that provide the genetic resources (19(1)). Parties shall consider the need for a protocol on the safe transfer, handling and use of living modified organisms, including advance informed agreement (19(3)).
Articles 20-21, 39Developed country Parties provide new and additional financial resources to meet the agreed full incremental costs of developing country Parties (Art 20(2)). A financial mechanism on a grant or concessional basis works under the authority of the Conference of the Parties (Art 21). The Global Environment Facility is the interim institutional structure, provided that it has been fully restructured in accordance with Article 21 (Art 39).
Articles 23-25The Conference of the Parties reviews implementation and adopts protocols (Art 23). A Secretariat services meetings (Art 24). A Subsidiary Body on Scientific, Technical and Technological Advice advises the Conference (Art 25).
Articles 26-27Each Party reports on measures taken (Art 26). Disputes go to negotiation, then good offices or mediation. A Party may accept arbitration or the International Court of Justice as compulsory. Otherwise, conciliation applies (Art 27).
Articles 28, 36-38Protocols are adopted at a meeting of the Conference of the Parties (Art 28). The Convention enters into force on the ninetieth day after the thirtieth instrument is deposited (Art 36). No reservations may be made (Art 37). A Party may withdraw two years after entry into force for it, effective one year after notice (Art 38).

Lack of full scientific certainty should not postpone measures to avoid or minimize a threat of significant reduction or loss of biological diversity. In-situ conservation is the fundamental requirement, and ex-situ measures play an important supporting role. Indigenous and local communities depend on biological resources, and women play a vital role.
Article 1The three objectives: conservation of biological diversity, sustainable use of its components, and fair and equitable sharing of benefits from genetic resources. They are pursued by appropriate access to genetic resources, appropriate transfer of technologies and appropriate funding.
Article 2Defines biological diversity as the variability among living organisms from all sources, including diversity within species, between species and of ecosystems. Also defines biological resources, genetic material, genetic resources, ecosystem, habitat, in-situ and ex-situ conservation, protected area, country of origin, country providing genetic resources, biotechnology and sustainable use (use at a rate that does not lead to long-term decline of biological diversity).
Article 3Principle. States have the sovereign right to exploit their own resources under their environmental policies. They have the responsibility to ensure that activities within their jurisdiction or control do not damage the environment of other States or areas beyond national jurisdiction.
Articles 4-5Jurisdictional scope: the Convention applies to biodiversity components within national jurisdiction, and to processes and activities under a Party's jurisdiction or control wherever their effects occur. Parties cooperate on areas beyond national jurisdiction.
Articles 6-7Each Party develops national strategies, plans or programmes and integrates biodiversity into sectoral policies (Art 6). Each Party identifies and monitors important components of biodiversity and activities with significant adverse impacts (Art 7).
Article 8In-situ conservation, "as far as possible and as appropriate": a system of protected areas; regulation of biological resources; protection of ecosystems and habitats; restoration of degraded ecosystems and recovery of threatened species; control of risks from living modified organisms; prevention or eradication of harmful alien species; legislation to protect threatened species. Art 8(j), subject to national legislation, respects, preserves and maintains the knowledge and practices of indigenous and local communities, with their approval, and encourages equitable sharing of benefits from that knowledge.
Article 9Ex-situ conservation, predominantly to complement in-situ measures, preferably in the country of origin, including facilities, recovery of threatened species and their reintroduction into natural habitats.
Articles 10-13Sustainable use: integrate conservation into national decision-making, protect customary use consistent with conservation (Art 10). Adopt economic and social incentives (Art 11). Research and training, with special needs of developing countries (Art 12). Public education and awareness (Art 13).
Article 14Environmental impact assessment of proposed projects likely to have significant adverse effects on biodiversity, with public participation where appropriate (Art 14(1)(a)). Notification and consultation on activities affecting other States. Immediate notification of imminent or grave danger across borders. The Conference of the Parties will examine liability and redress, including restoration and compensation, for damage to biodiversity (Art 14(2)).
Article 15Access to genetic resources. Authority to determine access rests with national governments and is subject to national legislation (15(1)). Parties facilitate access for environmentally sound uses (15(2)). Access is on mutually agreed terms (15(4)) and subject to prior informed consent of the providing Party unless it determines otherwise (15(5)). Each Party takes measures to share research results and benefits from commercial and other use fairly with the providing Party, on mutually agreed terms (15(7)).
Articles 16-18Access to and transfer of technology, including biotechnology, to developing countries on fair and most favourable terms, while recognizing adequate and effective protection of intellectual property rights (Art 16). Exchange of information (Art 17). Technical and scientific cooperation (Art 18).
Article 19Biotechnology and distribution of its benefits. Parties provide for effective participation in biotechnology research by Parties that provide the genetic resources (19(1)). Parties shall consider the need for a protocol on the safe transfer, handling and use of living modified organisms, including advance informed agreement (19(3)).
Articles 20-21, 39Developed country Parties provide new and additional financial resources to meet the agreed full incremental costs of developing country Parties (Art 20(2)). A financial mechanism on a grant or concessional basis works under the authority of the Conference of the Parties (Art 21). The Global Environment Facility is the interim institutional structure, provided that it has been fully restructured in accordance with Article 21 (Art 39).
Articles 23-25The Conference of the Parties reviews implementation and adopts protocols (Art 23). A Secretariat services meetings (Art 24). A Subsidiary Body on Scientific, Technical and Technological Advice advises the Conference (Art 25).
Articles 26-27Each Party reports on measures taken (Art 26). Disputes go to negotiation, then good offices or mediation. A Party may accept arbitration or the International Court of Justice as compulsory. Otherwise, conciliation applies (Art 27).
Articles 28, 36-38Protocols are adopted at a meeting of the Conference of the Parties (Art 28). The Convention enters into force on the ninetieth day after the thirtieth instrument is deposited (Art 36). No reservations may be made (Art 37). A Party may withdraw two years after entry into force for it, effective one year after notice (Art 38).

hi.inOneMinute: The Convention on Biological Diversity is the main treaty on life on Earth in all its variety. Its text was adopted at Nairobi on 22 May 1992 and opened for signature at the Rio Earth Summit on 5 June 1992. It has three aims: conserve biodiversity, use it sustainably, and share its benefits fairly. The third aim answers the problem of biopiracy. India gives effect to the treaty through the Biological Diversity Act, 2002.
legalProvision: Convention on Biological Diversity: adopted at Nairobi on 22 May 1992, opened for signature at Rio de Janeiro on 5 June 1992 and in force from 29 December 1993. Three objectives: conservation of biological diversity, sustainable use of its components, and fair and equitable sharing of the benefits from genetic resources. India and the Convention: India signed on 5 June 1992 and ratified on 18 February 1994. It became a Party on 19 May 1994 (CBD Secretariat list of Parties). Biological Diversity Act, 2002, preamble: records that India is a Party to the Convention, signed at Rio on 5 June 1992 and in force from 29 December 1993. The preamble adds that the Convention reaffirms the sovereign rights of States over their biological resources.
hi.meaning: Biological diversity is the variety of life: the range of species, the genes within them and the ecosystems they form. The Convention covers all of it, not one type of habitat. It was one of two binding treaties signed at the Rio Earth Summit of June 1992. The other was the Convention on climate change. Together they were signed by 153 nations, according to the Vellore judgment.
keyPoints: Adopted 22 May 1992; opened for signature 5 June 1992; in force 29 December 1993. Three objectives: conservation, sustainable use, fair and equitable benefit sharing. States have sovereign rights over their biological resources. Cartagena (2000, in force 2003) and Nagoya (2010, in force 2014). India: Biological Diversity Act, 2002. Art 15: access needs prior informed consent and mutually agreed terms (15(5), 15(4)); Art 8(j): traditional knowledge; Art 14: impact assessment. Art 8: in-situ; Art 9: ex-situ. Art 19(3): protocol on living modified organisms. Art 37: no reservations.

caseLaws.name: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v
caseLaws.facts: Union of India Facts. Tanneries in Tamil Nadu discharged untreated effluent, polluting the Palar river area. Principle. The Court recorded that the Rio Earth Summit of June 1992 produced two conventions, on biological diversity and climate change, signed by 153 nations. It held sustainable development to be part of customary international law. Significance. It places the Convention in the story of sustainable development.

selfTest.q: 1. What are the three objectives of the Convention?
selfTest.a: Conservation, sustainable use and fair and equitable benefit sharing. 2. Which Protocol deals with living modified organisms? The Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety. 3. Which Indian Act reflects the Convention? The Biological Diversity Act, 2002.

What actually took place in Nairobi in 1982?

Explanation. There is no binding 'Nairobi Convention'; the 1982 Nairobi session was a UNEP Governing Council Special Session that adopted the non-binding Nairobi Declaration.

What did the Nairobi Declaration conclude about environmental progress since Stockholm (1972)?

Explanation. Reports of the session say the Declaration was positive about progress since 1972 but anxious about the future, and called for fresh commitment to environmental protection.

environmental-law-u5-t16.subtitle: The 17 Sustainable Development Goals: what they are, their environmental goals and their legal weight

en.inOneMinute: The Sustainable Development Goals, or SDGs, are 17 goals with 169 targets. The UN General Assembly adopted them in September 2015 as part of the 2030 Agenda. They are meant to guide action for 15 years, to 2030. They are not a treaty. They are a political commitment, so they count as soft law. Yet they shape budgets, policy and the way courts discuss sustainable development.
legalProvision: General Assembly resolution 70/1, "Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development": adopted on 25 September 2015 without a vote. The Goals and targets: 17 goals and 169 targets, intended to guide action over the next 15 years. NITI Aayog: the Indian body that publishes the SDG India Index, which monitors the performance of States and Union Territories on the goals.
en.meaning: The Sustainable Development Goals are a set of global goals for ending poverty, protecting the planet and building peaceful societies. They apply to all countries, rich and poor, and are linked so that progress on one helps others.
keyPoints: Adopted 25 September 2015; General Assembly resolution 70/1. 17 goals, 169 targets, to guide action to 2030. Soft law, not a treaty. India: NITI Aayog and the SDG India Index. The 5Ps: People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace, Partnership. In effect from 1 January 2016.

caseLaws.facts: Union of India Facts. Tanneries in Tamil Nadu discharged untreated effluent, polluting land and drinking water around the Palar river. Principle. Sustainable development, with the precautionary and polluter pays principles, is part of the environmental law of India. Significance. It gives Indian legal force to the idea that the SDGs promote.

environmental-law-u5-t13.subtitle: The ten-year review of Rio: the three pillars of sustainable development and the push to implement

en.inOneMinute: There is no binding "Johannesburg Convention". The event was the World Summit on Sustainable Development, held in Johannesburg from 26 August to 4 September 2002. It reviewed ten years of progress since the Rio Earth Summit, so it is called Rio+10. It produced two non-binding documents, the Johannesburg Declaration and a Plan of Implementation. It is best remembered for the three pillars of sustainable development and for voluntary partnerships.
legalProvision: World Summit on Sustainable Development, Johannesburg, 26 August to 4 September 2002: held under General Assembly resolution 55/199 as a ten-year review of the Rio conference. Johannesburg Declaration on Sustainable Development, paragraph 5: the participants assume a collective responsibility to advance and strengthen the interdependent and mutually reinforcing pillars of sustainable development. The text names those pillars: economic development, social development and environmental protection.
en.meaning:
The Johannesburg Declaration is a political statement of the governments at the Summit. It is soft law . The Plan of Implementation is a long action plan that goes with it. Neither is a treaty and neither can be enforced in court.

The syllabus sometimes writes "Johannesburg Convention". That is wrong. The correct name is the Johannesburg Declaration, 2002.
keyPoints: World Summit on Sustainable Development, 26 August to 4 September 2002; Rio+10. Outputs: Johannesburg Declaration and Plan of Implementation, both non-binding. Three pillars: economic development, social development, environmental protection. Type II outcomes: voluntary partnerships.

selfTest.a: No. The outcome is the non-binding Johannesburg Declaration. 2. Name the three pillars of sustainable development. Economic development, social development and environmental protection. 3. What are Type II outcomes? Voluntary partnership initiatives among governments, business and civil society.

environmental-law-u5-t14.subtitle: The parent climate treaty: its objective, principles and the Annex I, Annex II and non-Annex I groups

en.inOneMinute: The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change is the parent treaty of the climate regime. It was adopted on 9 May 1992, opened for signature at Rio and came into force on 21 March 1994. It sets an aim but no binding numbers. Exam answers must keep that straight, and must know the three groups of Parties: Annex I, Annex II and non-Annex I.
legalProvision: Adoption and entry into force: adopted at United Nations Headquarters, New York, on 9 May 1992; opened for signature at the Rio Earth Summit; in force from 21 March 1994. India: signed on 10 June 1992 and ratified on 1 November 1993 (UN Treaty Collection). Article 2, objective: to stabilise greenhouse gas concentrations at a level that prevents dangerous human interference with the climate system. Article 3, principles: including common but differentiated responsibilities, with developed countries taking the lead, and precaution. Article 4, commitments: Annex II Parties are to provide new and additional financial resources, and technology transfer, so that developing countries can meet their commitments.
en.meaning:
A framework convention sets up an aim, principles and institutions, and leaves detailed duties to later protocols. The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change is the framework for the world's response to climate change .

Its Parties meet at the Conference of the Parties , the Convention's supreme body. Kyoto was adopted at the third meeting in 1997 and Paris at the twenty-first in 2015.

The groups of Parties under the Convention How to read this: the outer box holds all Parties. Inner boxes are smaller groups. Annex II sits inside Annex I. All Parties to the Convention Annex I: industrialised countries and economies in transition Kyoto targets applied here Annex II: the OECD members of Annex I Article 4: finance and technology Non-Annex I: developing countries, including India No binding Kyoto target

Art 4(1): all Parties; Art 4(2): Annex I, aim of 1990 levels; Art 4(3)-(5): Annex II finance and technology; Art 4(7): developing countries depend on that support. Art 11: financial mechanism. Comparison Table
visuals.html:
ArticleWhat it says
Article 1Definitions. Climate change is a change of climate attributed directly or indirectly to human activity that alters the composition of the global atmosphere, in addition to natural climate variability. Greenhouse gases are gaseous constituents of the atmosphere, natural and anthropogenic, that absorb and re-emit infrared radiation. A sink removes a greenhouse gas from the atmosphere. A source releases one. A reservoir stores one. Adverse effects are significant deleterious effects on ecosystems, socio-economic systems, and human health and welfare.
Article 2The ultimate objective of the Convention and any related legal instruments is stabilization of greenhouse gas concentrations at a level that would prevent dangerous anthropogenic interference with the climate system. The level should be reached within a time-frame that lets ecosystems adapt naturally, keeps food production safe, and lets economic development proceed in a sustainable manner.
Article 3Principles: (1) equity and common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities, with developed countries taking the lead; (2) full consideration of the special needs of developing countries, especially vulnerable ones; (3) precautionary measures, where lack of full scientific certainty is not a reason for postponing action, and policies should be cost-effective; (4) a right to promote sustainable development; (5) a supportive and open international economic system, and no arbitrary or unjustifiable discrimination or disguised restriction on trade.
Article 4(1)Commitments of all Parties, taking into account common but differentiated responsibilities: national inventories of emissions and removals; national programmes to mitigate climate change and facilitate adaptation; technology transfer; conservation of sinks and reservoirs such as forests and oceans; adaptation planning; research; information exchange; education and public awareness; and reporting under Article 12. Gases controlled by the Montreal Protocol are outside these duties.
Article 4(2)Developed country Parties and other Parties in Annex I commit to adopt national policies and take measures to limit emissions and protect and enhance sinks, showing that they are taking the lead (4(2)(a)). Each must report details, "with the aim of" returning to 1990 levels of emissions (4(2)(b)). The Conference of the Parties reviews the adequacy of these commitments at its first session and again not later than 31 December 1998 (4(2)(d)). A Party outside Annex I may notify that it intends to be bound by (a) and (b) (4(2)(g)).
Articles 4(3)-(5)Annex II Parties provide new and additional financial resources to meet the agreed full costs of developing country Parties' reporting under Article 12(1), and the agreed full incremental costs of implementing measures (4(3)). They assist particularly vulnerable developing countries with adaptation costs (4(4)). They take all practicable steps to promote, facilitate and finance transfer of environmentally sound technology (4(5)).
Articles 4(6)-(8)Flexibility for Annex I Parties in transition to a market economy (4(6)). Developing countries will implement their commitments effectively only as developed countries implement theirs on finance and technology. Economic and social development and poverty eradication are their first and overriding priorities (4(7)). Special attention to small island countries, low-lying coastal areas, arid and semi-arid areas, drought and desertification, fragile ecosystems and countries dependent on fossil fuels (4(8)).
Articles 5-6, 12Research and systematic observation (Art 5). Education, training and public awareness (Art 6). Each Party communicates its national inventory and a description of steps taken. Annex I Parties add details of policies and projected emissions (Art 12).
Articles 7-10The Conference of the Parties is the supreme body and keeps implementation under regular review (Art 7). A Secretariat is established (Art 8). A Subsidiary Body for Scientific and Technological Advice (Art 9) and a Subsidiary Body for Implementation (Art 10) assist it.
Article 11Financial mechanism: a mechanism for resources on a grant or concessional basis, including technology transfer, under the guidance of and accountable to the Conference of the Parties, with equitable and balanced representation of all Parties.
Articles 13-14The Conference considers a multilateral consultative process for questions of implementation (Art 13). Disputes go to negotiation or other peaceful means, and a Party may accept arbitration or the International Court of Justice as compulsory (Art 14).
Articles 15-17Amendments are adopted by consensus, or as a last resort by a three-fourths majority of Parties present and voting (Art 15). The Conference may adopt protocols at an ordinary session. Only Parties to the Convention may be Parties to a protocol (Art 17).
Articles 22-25Entry into force on the ninetieth day after the fiftieth instrument is deposited (Art 23). No reservations may be made (Art 24). A Party may withdraw after three years from entry into force for it, effective one year after notice (Art 25).
Annexes I and IIAnnex I lists the industrialised countries and countries in transition to a market economy. Annex II lists the developed countries of Annex I, without the countries in transition.

en.inOneMinute: Read the full set here, or use the practice card above to test yourself one question at a time.
en.meaning:
Why does classical international law create a structural gap for multinational corporation (MNC) liability?

Explanation. International law in its classical form binds States, not private companies, so a victim usually cannot sue an MNC before an international tribunal the way one State can arbitrate against another.

In the Bhopal Gas Tragedy litigation, why did the US court dismiss the case against Union Carbide Corporation?

Explanation. The US District Court held India was the appropriate forum since the plant, victims, and evidence were all located there, sending the case back to Indian courts.

Which Indian legislation authorised the Government of India to represent all Bhopal victims in a single consolidated claim?

Explanation. The Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster (Processing of Claims) Act, 1985 authorised the Government of India to represent all victims in a consolidated claim, leading to the 1989 settlement.

The doctrine of 'separate corporate personality' creates difficulty in MNC liability cases because:

environmental-law-u5-t15.subtitle: The agreement in which every country sets its own climate plan: NDCs, the temperature goal and the stocktake

en.inOneMinute: The Paris Agreement was adopted at the 21st Conference of the Parties (COP21) on 12 December 2015. It came into force on 4 November 2016. Its goal is to hold warming well below 2 degrees Celsius and to pursue 1.5 degrees. Unlike Kyoto, every country makes its own plan, called a Nationally Determined Contribution. India ratified the Agreement on 2 October 2016.
legalProvision: Adoption: at COP21, Paris, on 12 December 2015, under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change. Entry into force: 4 November 2016, once at least 55 countries representing at least 55 per cent of emissions had ratified. Article 2: hold the rise in global average temperature well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5 degrees. Article 4: each Party prepares, communicates and updates its Nationally Determined Contribution, and each new one should show progression. Article 14: a global stocktake assesses collective progress. The first concluded at COP28 in Dubai in 2023.
en.meaning: The Paris Agreement is a treaty adopted under the Climate Change Convention. A Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) is a Party's own plan to cut or limit its greenhouse gas emissions. COP21 is the name of the conference, the 21st Conference of the Parties, where the Agreement was adopted.
keyPoints: Adopted at COP21 on 12 December 2015; in force 4 November 2016. Goal: well below 2 degrees, pursue 1.5 degrees. Every Party files its own NDC; each new one should show progression. Global stocktake under Article 14; first concluded at COP28, Dubai, 2023. India signed 22 April 2016 and ratified 2 October 2016. Art 2(1)(a)-(c): temperature, adaptation, finance. Art 4(9): NDC every five years. Art 4(4): developed countries lead with absolute targets. Art 6: voluntary cooperation. Art 8: loss and damage. Art 9: finance. Art 15: non-punitive compliance. Art 21: 55 Parties and 55 per cent of emissions.

selfTest.q: 1. When was the Paris Agreement adopted?
selfTest.a: 12 December 2015, at COP21. 2. What is an NDC? A Party's own plan to cut or limit its greenhouse gas emissions. 3. When did India ratify the Agreement? 2 October 2016.

visuals.caption: Comparison Table
visuals.html:
ArticleWhat it says
Article 2The Agreement enhances the implementation of the Convention. It aims at (a) holding the increase in global average temperature to well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels and pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5 degrees, (b) increasing the ability to adapt and foster climate resilience without threatening food production, and (c) making finance flows consistent with a low-emission, climate-resilient pathway (Art 2(1)). It is implemented to reflect equity and common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities, in the light of different national circumstances (Art 2(2)).
Article 3All Parties undertake and communicate ambitious efforts. Their efforts will represent a progression over time, recognizing the need to support developing country Parties.
Article 4Parties aim to reach global peaking of emissions as soon as possible, recognizing it will take longer for developing countries, and to reach a balance between emissions by sources and removals by sinks in the second half of the century (4(1)). Each Party shall prepare, communicate and maintain successive NDCs and pursue domestic mitigation measures (4(2)). Each successive NDC represents a progression and reflects the Party's highest possible ambition (4(3)). Developed countries should continue taking the lead with economy-wide absolute reduction targets. Developing countries should continue enhancing mitigation and are encouraged to move over time to economy-wide targets (4(4)). Least developed countries and small island developing States may prepare special strategies (4(6)). An NDC is communicated every five years (4(9)), may be adjusted upward at any time (4(11)) and is recorded in a public registry (4(12)). Parties account for NDCs with transparency, avoiding double counting (4(13)).
Article 5Parties should conserve and enhance sinks and reservoirs, including forests, and are encouraged to support activities, commonly called REDD+, which reduce emissions from deforestation and forest degradation in developing countries.
Article 6Voluntary cooperative approaches. Internationally transferred mitigation outcomes are voluntary, authorized by participating Parties, and must avoid double counting (6(2)-(3)). A mechanism is established under the authority of the Conference of the Parties serving as the meeting of the Parties, for use on a voluntary basis (6(4)). Non-market approaches are also recognized (6(8)).
Article 7Global goal on adaptation: enhancing adaptive capacity, strengthening resilience and reducing vulnerability to climate change.
Article 8Loss and damage. Parties recognize the importance of averting, minimizing and addressing loss and damage from the adverse effects of climate change, including extreme weather events and slow onset events. The Warsaw International Mechanism is placed under the authority of the Conference of the Parties serving as the meeting of the Parties. Areas of cooperation include early warning systems, emergency preparedness and risk insurance.
Article 9Finance. Developed country Parties shall provide financial resources to assist developing countries with both mitigation and adaptation (9(1)). Other Parties are encouraged to provide support voluntarily (9(2)). environmental-law-u5-t12.subtitle: The first climate treaty with binding emission targets, and why they applied only to developed countries

en.inOneMinute: The Kyoto Protocol was adopted on 11 December 1997. It gave binding numerical targets for cutting greenhouse gases to Annex I countries only, the developed and transition economies. Developing countries such as India had no binding target. It created three flexible market mechanisms, including the Clean Development Mechanism. It came into force on 16 February 2005 and was later extended by the Doha Amendment.
legalProvision: Kyoto Protocol to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change: adopted at the third Conference of the Parties in Kyoto, Japan, on 11 December 1997. Entry into force: 16 February 2005, after ratification by at least 55 Parties covering at least 55 per cent of Annex I carbon dioxide emissions in 1990. Doha Amendment: adopted in December 2012 for a second commitment period from 2013 to 2020 with a target of 18 per cent below 1990 levels. It entered into force on 31 December 2020. India: a Party since accession on 26 August 2002, as a non-Annex I country. India accepted the Doha Amendment on 8 August 2017 (UN Treaty Collection).
en.meaning: The Kyoto Protocol is a treaty adopted under the Climate Change Convention. The Convention only stated a goal . The Protocol added numbers, deadlines and consequences. It applies the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities : all share the duty, but developed countries carry the first and heaviest burden.
keyPoints: Adopted 11 December 1997; in force 16 February 2005. Binding targets only for Annex I countries. Mechanisms: emissions trading, Joint Implementation, Clean Development Mechanism. Doha Amendment: second period 2013 to 2020, in force 31 December 2020. India acceded on 26 August 2002 and had no binding target. It accepted the Doha Amendment on 8 August 2017. Art 3(1): at least 5 per cent below 1990 levels, 2008 to 2012. Art 3(7): Annex B percentage multiplied by five. Art 6: Joint Implementation. Art 12: Clean Development Mechanism. Art 17: emissions trading. Art 10: no new commitments for non-Annex I Parties. Art 25: 55 Parties and 55 per cent of Annex I carbon dioxide emissions for 1990.

selfTest.q: 1. Which countries had binding targets under Kyoto?
selfTest.a: Annex I countries only. 2. Name the three flexible mechanisms. Emissions trading, Joint Implementation and the Clean Development Mechanism. 3. When did the Doha Amendment enter into force? On 31 December 2020.

visuals.caption: Comparison Table
visuals.html:
ArticleWhat it says
Article 2Annex I Parties implement policies and measures, such as better energy efficiency, protection and enhancement of sinks and reservoirs, sustainable forest management and afforestation, sustainable agriculture, renewable energy, phasing out subsidies that run counter to the Convention's objective, limiting transport emissions, and recovering methane from waste and energy.
Article 3(1)Annex I Parties must, individually or jointly, ensure that their aggregate emissions of the greenhouse gases listed in Annex A do not exceed their assigned amounts under Annex B. The aim is to reduce overall emissions "by at least 5 per cent below 1990 levels in the commitment period 2008 to 2012".
Article 3(2)-(3)Each Annex I Party must show demonstrable progress by 2005. Net changes from afforestation, reforestation and deforestation since 1990 count towards the commitment.
Article 3(7), (9)For 2008 to 2012, the assigned amount is the Annex B percentage of 1990 emissions multiplied by five. Commitments for later periods are set by amending Annex B, and consideration must begin at least seven years before the end of the first period.
Article 3(10)-(13)Units acquired under Articles 6, 12 and 17 are added to the buyer's assigned amount, and units transferred are subtracted from the seller's. A Party whose emissions fall below its assigned amount may bank the surplus for later periods.
Article 4Annex I Parties may fulfil their commitments jointly (commonly called a bubble). Their combined emissions must not exceed their assigned amounts. If the group fails, each Party is responsible for its own level set in the agreement.
Articles 5, 7, 8Annex I Parties must have a national system to estimate emissions and removals, report supplementary information in their annual inventories, and undergo expert review.
Article 6Joint Implementation. An Annex I Party may transfer to or acquire from another Annex I Party emission reduction units from projects, if the project has the approval of the Parties, gives a reduction that is additional to what would otherwise occur, and the acquisition is supplemental to domestic action.
Article 10All Parties, taking into account common but differentiated responsibilities, advance existing commitments under Article 4(1) of the Convention, "without introducing any new commitments for Parties not included in Annex I".
Article 11Developed country Parties in Annex II provide new and additional financial resources and technology transfer through the financial mechanism.
Article 12Clean Development Mechanism. Its purpose is to assist non-Annex I Parties in achieving sustainable development and to assist Annex I Parties in complying with their commitments (12(2)). Non-Annex I Parties gain from project activities that produce certified emission reductions, and Annex I Parties may use those reductions towards part of their commitments (12(3)). It is supervised by an executive board (12(4)). Reductions are certified on voluntary participation, real, measurable and long-term benefits, and additionality (12(5)). A share of proceeds covers administrative expenses and helps vulnerable developing countries meet adaptation costs (12(8)). Reductions obtained from 2000 can count in the first period (12(10)).
Article 17Emissions trading. Parties in Annex B may participate in emissions trading to fulfil Article 3 commitments, supplemental to domestic action.
Article 18The Parties approve procedures and mechanisms on non-compliance, including an indicative list of consequences.
Articles 25-27Entry into force on the ninetieth day after not less than 55 Parties to the Convention, including Annex I Parties accounting for at least 55 per cent of Annex I carbon dioxide emissions for 1990, have deposited instruments (Art 25). No reservations (Art 26). A Party may withdraw after three years from entry into force for it, effective one year after notice (Art 27).
Annexes A and BAnnex A lists six gases: carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, hydrofluorocarbons, perfluorocarbons and sulphur hexafluoride. Annex B gives each Party's commitment as a percentage of its base year. Examples: European Community and most European States 92, United States 93, Japan and Canada 94, Russian Federation, Ukraine and New Zealand 100, Norway 101, Australia 108, Iceland 110.

Article 17Emissions trading. Parties in Annex B may participate in emissions trading to fulfil Article 3 commitments, supplemental to domestic action.
Article 18The Parties approve procedures and mechanisms on non-compliance, including an indicative list of consequences.
Articles 25-27Entry into force on the ninetieth day after not less than 55 Parties to the Convention, including Annex I Parties accounting for at least 55 per cent of Annex I carbon dioxide emissions for 1990, have deposited instruments (Art 25). No reservations (Art 26). A Party may withdraw after three years from entry into force for it, effective one year after notice (Art 27).
Annexes A and BAnnex A lists six gases: carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, hydrofluorocarbons, perfluorocarbons and sulphur hexafluoride. Annex B gives each Party's commitment as a percentage of its base year. Examples: European Community and most European States 92, United States 93, Japan and Canada 94, Russian Federation, Ukraine and New Zealand 100, Norway 101, Australia 108, Iceland 110.

en.meaning:
Transboundary pollution is best defined as pollution that:

Explanation. Transboundary pollution originates in one State's territory or control and causes or threatens environmental harm in another State or in areas beyond any State's jurisdiction.

Which of these is an example of 'diffuse or global' transboundary harm rather than 'point-to-point' harm?

Explanation. Greenhouse gases mix into the shared global atmosphere before causing harm, so no single source can be traced to a specific injury in a specific country — this is diffuse/global transboundary harm.

The 'no-harm' principle in international environmental law was first authoritatively established by:

Explanation. The Trail Smelter Arbitration between the United States and Canada first held that a State must not allow its territory to be used to cause serious, provable injury to another State's territory.

Why do ordinary domestic court remedies usually fail for victims of transboundary pollution?

law-of-contract-ii-u1-t1.subtitle: Section 124 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: A contract of indemnity is a contract in which one person promises to make good the loss of another. The person who promises is the promisor . The person who is protected is the promisee . Section 124 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 defines it. The loss may be caused by the promisor's own conduct or by the conduct of any other person. Key points for the answer: the definition word for word, the two sources of loss, and the Act's illustration.
en.meaning:
The meaning of the definition (section 124)

Rule. A contract of indemnity is a contract by which one party promises to save the other from loss. The party who promises is the promisor. The party who is promised protection is the promisee. Section 124 uses these two words.

Take the definition in parts, as you would in the exam.

It is a contract. Section 124 begins "A contract by which...". One party makes a promise. The promise is to save the other party from loss. The loss is caused to the other party by conduct. The section names whose conduct it may be (see below).

Example. Rao owns a shop in Guntur. Sita tells Rao: "If anyone takes proceedings against you over the cheque you accepted from my brother, I will make good your loss." Sita is the promisor and Rao is the promisee. The promise is to save Rao from loss, so it is a contract of indemnity.

First source of loss: the conduct of the promisor himself

Rule. The loss may be caused to the promisee by the conduct of the promisor himself. The promisor then promises to save the promisee from the results of the promisor's own acts.

Example. Kumar sells a cart-load of grain to Latha and promises: "If my earlier sale of this grain to anyone else causes you loss, I will make it good." The loss would come from Kumar's own conduct. The promise fits section 124.

Second source of loss: the conduct of any other person

Rule. The loss may be caused to the promisee by the conduct of any other person. The section says "any other person". In the Act's illustration, C is a third person.

The Act's own illustration is of this kind. A promises B protection against the consequences of proceedings that C may take against B for a sum of 200 rupees. C is a third person. The loss would come from C's conduct in taking proceedings. The Act says this is a contract of indemnity.

Example. Dev agrees to indemnify Esha against any proceedings that Farid may take against Esha for Rs 200. Farid sues Esha. The loss comes from Farid's conduct, not from Dev's. Dev's promise is still a contract of indemnity. This is the Act's own illustration with new names.

Is section 124 the whole law of indemnity?

Rule. No. Sections 124 and 125 are not exhaustive of the law of indemnity. The Contract Act is both an amending and a consolidating Act. It does not contain the whole law of contract applied by Indian courts ( Gajanan Moreshwar , para 3).

What section 124 covers. One kind of indemnity only: a promise to save the other from loss caused by the conduct of the promisor or of any other person. What it does not cover. Indemnity for loss caused by events or accidents that do not or may not depend on the conduct of the promisor or any other person. It also does not cover a liability the indemnified person incurred by doing something at the request of the indemnifier (para 3). What section 125 covers. Only the rights of the indemnity-holder when he is sued. The indemnity-holder has other rights besides those in section 125 (para 4). Application. In Gajanan Moreshwar the plaintiff became liable by doing something at the defendant's request. So the Court held that section 124 did not apply at all (para 4). Result. The Indian courts apply the same equitable principles that the courts in England apply (para 7).

When can the indemnity-holder sue?

Old common-law rule. Under English common law, the indemnity-holder could not sue until he had actually suffered loss. This was hard on him. If he was sued, he had to wait for the judgment and pay it first. If he could not pay, he could not use his indemnity at all ( Gajanan Moreshwar , para 7).

The rule of equity. Equity softened this. Once the holder's liability has become absolute, he can make the indemnifier pay off the claim. He can also make the indemnifier pay enough money into Court to meet the claim when it is made (para 7).

The test used in India. The Court asks two questions. Has the indemnified person incurred a liability? Is that liability absolute? If yes to both, he can call on the indemnifier to save him from the liability and pay it off. He need not wait to suffer actual loss ( Gajanan Moreshwar , paras 5 and 7; approved in Khetarpal Amarnath , quoted in VPS Healthcare , para 19).

Absolute and contingent liability. A liability is absolute when the promisee has no answer to a claim on it, for example where he has personally promised to pay ( Gajanan Moreshwar , para 8). The defendant in Gajanan Moreshwar argued that the liability was only contingent, because a sale of the mortgaged property might leave no deficit. The Court rejected this (para 8).

Absolute obligation and indemnity. A promise to take on an absolute obligation can be enforced without any actual loss. In a true indemnity, the risk of loss stays contingent. A contract of indemnity is one in which a party undertakes to save another party harmless from loss or damage arising from a particular transaction or claim ( VPS Healthcare , para 19). So the wording of the promise decides whether it is an indemnity or an absolute obligation (para 19).

Contrary decisions. Two earlier decisions had said that a suit on an indemnity before actual loss is premature: Shankar Nimbaji v. Laxman Supdu (1939) 42 Bom LR 175 and Chand Bibi v. Santoshkumar Pal (1933) ILR 60 Cal 761. Chagla J. confined the first to its own facts, where no loss could be known until the security was sold. He would not read it to mean that actual loss is always needed (para 5). He did not follow the second. He called it an unconsidered judgment, with no authorities cited, that may turn on the wording of the covenant. He preferred Osman Jamal & Sons v. Gopal Purshattam (1928) ILR 56 Cal 262, a considered decision that allowed the suit before payment (para 6). It was also conceded in Gajanan Moreshwar that such a suit would lie in England (para 7).

What the Court may order. The Court may direct the indemnifier to get the promisee released from the liability within a fixed time. If he fails, he may be directed to pay into Court the amount needed to meet it ( Gajanan Moreshwar , para 10).

How to test a promise against section 124 How to read this: start at the top and answer each box. If you can answer yes to all three, the promise is a contract of indemnity under section 124. 1. Is there a contract? 2. Does one party promise to save the other from loss? That party is the promisor. The other is the promisee. 3. Is the loss caused by the promisor's own conduct, or by the conduct of any other person? If yes, it is a contract of indemnity (section 124).
keyPoints: Section 124 defines a contract of indemnity. One party promises to save the other from loss. The loss may be caused by the conduct of the promisor himself or of any other person. The party who promises is the promisor. The party protected is the promisee. The Act's illustration: A indemnifies B against proceedings C may take against B for 200 rupees. The rights of the promisee when he is sued are in section 125.

caseLaws.name: Gajanan Moreshwar Parelkar v
caseLaws.facts: Moreshwar Madan Mantri , AIR 1942 Bom 302. Sections 124 and 125 are not exhaustive. An indemnity-holder whose liability is absolute can sue without first suffering loss. Khetarpal Amarnath v. Madhukar Pictures (1955 SCC OnLine Bom 73). Agreed with Gajanan Moreshwar and stated the test (quoted in VPS Healthcare , para 19): has the indemnified person incurred a liability, and is it absolute? VPS Healthcare Private Limited v. Prabhat Kumar Srivastava , 2026 INSC 361. Supreme Court. Quoted that test (paras 19 and 24). Held that the promise to "ensure" that no liability is recovered points to an absolute obligation (para 19). It was a case of a liability that had already crystallised, not an indemnity that matures only on final confirmation (para 28). The promoters had to pay or deposit the amount within 30 days (para 29).

selfTest.q: 1. What is a contract of indemnity under section 124?
selfTest.a: It is a contract by which one party promises to save the other from loss caused to him by the conduct of the promisor himself, or by the conduct of any other person. 2. Whose conduct may cause the loss? The conduct of the promisor himself, or the conduct of any other person (section 124). 3. In the Act's illustration, who takes the proceedings and for how much? C may take proceedings against B in respect of a certain sum of 200 rupees. A has contracted to indemnify B against the consequences. This is a contract of indemnity.

law-of-contract-ii-u1-t5.subtitle: Sections 124, 125, 126, 140 and 145 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: In a contract of indemnity, one party promises to save the other from loss (section 124). In a contract of guarantee, a surety promises the creditor to answer for the principal debtor's default (section 126). The two are different contracts with different rules. The differences that follow from the Act are in the persons, in what is promised, in what sets the promise working, and in the rights after payment. Key points for the answer: a table of differences based on sections 124 and 126, with the sections on rights (125, 140 and 145).
en.meaning:
Difference 1: the definitions (sections 124 and 126)

Rule. Section 124 speaks of a promise to save the other party from loss. Section 126 speaks of a contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person in case of his default.

Example. Dev promises Esha: "If Farid takes proceedings against you over Rs 200, I will save you from the loss." That promise is a promise to save from loss. Now Sita promises a bank: "If my brother Ravi does not repay his loan, I will." That promise is to discharge the liability of a third person in case of his default.

Difference 2: the persons

Rule. Section 124 speaks of "one party" promising "the other". These are the promisor and the promisee. Section 126 names three persons: the surety, the principal debtor and the creditor.

Example. In Dev's promise to Esha there are two parties, Dev and Esha. In Sita's promise to the bank there are three persons: Sita (surety), Ravi (principal debtor) and the bank (creditor).

Difference 3: what sets the promise working

Rule. In indemnity the loss is caused by the conduct of the promisor himself or of any other person (section 124). In guarantee the promise operates "in case of his default", meaning the default of the third person (section 126).

Difference 4: rights after payment (sections 125, 140 and 145)

Rule. The indemnity-holder's rights against the promisor are in section 125: damages, costs and compromise sums, on the conditions stated. The surety's rights are in sections 140 and 145. Under section 140 he takes the creditor's rights against the principal debtor once he has paid all he is liable for. Under section 145 the principal debtor impliedly promises to indemnify him.

Example. Esha is sued by Farid and is ordered to pay Rs 200 as damages. She recovers it from Dev under section 125, if the conditions of that section are met. If Sita pays the bank Ravi's loan, she takes the bank's rights against Ravi (section 140) and can recover what she rightfully paid from Ravi (section 145).

Difference 5: form

Rule. Section 126 says a guarantee may be oral or written. Section 124 does not say anything about the form of a contract of indemnity.

Which contract is it? How to read this: start at the top and follow the answer for the promise you are testing. 1. Does one party promise to save the other from loss caused by the promisor's or any other person's conduct? Yes: contract of indemnity (section 124). 2. Does a person promise a creditor to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person if that third person defaults? Yes: contract of guarantee (section 126).
keyPoints: Indemnity: section 124. Guarantee: section 126. Indemnity has a promisor and a promisee. Guarantee has a surety, a principal debtor and a creditor. Indemnity: a promise to save from loss. Guarantee: a contract to discharge a third person's liability in case of his default. The indemnity-holder's rights are in section 125. The surety's rights are in sections 140 and 145. A guarantee may be oral or written. Section 124 is silent on form.

en.inOneMinute: A contract of guarantee is a contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person if he defaults. There are three persons: the surety , the principal debtor and the creditor . Section 126 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 defines all four terms. It also says a guarantee may be oral or written. en.meaning:
The meaning of the definition (section 126)

Rule. A contract of guarantee is a contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person in case of his default. Take the definition in parts.

It is a contract. The contract is to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person. This is to happen in case of that third person's default.

Example. Ravi borrows Rs 1 lakh from a bank in Guntur. His sister Sita tells the bank: "If Ravi does not repay, I will repay." Sita's contract with the bank is a contract to discharge the liability of a third person, Ravi, in case of his default. It is a contract of guarantee.

The three persons: surety, principal debtor and creditor

Rule. Section 126 names the three persons by their roles.

The surety is the person who gives the guarantee. The principal debtor is the person in respect of whose default the guarantee is given. The creditor is the person to whom the guarantee is given.

Example. In the example above, Sita is the surety. Ravi is the principal debtor. The bank is the creditor.

Form: oral or written

Rule. Section 126 says a guarantee may be either oral or written. The Act does not require writing.

Example. Sita could give the bank a signed letter of guarantee. She could also give the guarantee by word of mouth. Section 126 allows both.

The principal debtor owes a promise or liability to the creditor. 2. The surety gives the creditor a guarantee. The guarantee is to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of the principal debtor in case of his default. 3. The principal debtor defaults. The surety's guarantee comes into play (see "Rights and liabilities of Surety").
