law-of-contract-ii-u1-t2.subtitle: Section 125 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: In a contract of indemnity, the person who is protected is the promisee. He is also called the indemnity-holder. Section 125 gives him three rights against the promisor when he is sued. He can recover the damages he is compelled to pay, the costs he is compelled to pay, and the sums he paid under a compromise. The first right has no extra condition. The second and third rights depend on conditions. Key points for the answer: the opening words "acting within the scope of his authority", the three clauses, and the conditions on costs and compromise.
en.meaning:
The opening words: "acting within the scope of his authority"

Rule. Section 125 gives the three rights to a promisee "acting within the scope of his authority". The rights are therefore for a promisee who acts within his authority.

The section does not define "scope of his authority" in other words.

Right 1: damages he is compelled to pay (clause 1)

Rule. The promisee can recover all damages which he may be compelled to pay in any suit. The damages must be in respect of a matter to which the promise to indemnify applies. Clause (1) has no condition about the promisor's orders or about prudence.

Example. Ravi promises Meena: "If anyone sues you over the stock you bought through my broker, I will indemnify you." A supplier sues Meena over that stock. The court orders Meena to pay Rs 50,000 as damages. The suit is about the matter the promise covers. Meena can recover the Rs 50,000 from Ravi under clause (1).

Right 2: costs he is compelled to pay (clause 2)

Rule. The promisee can recover all costs which he may be compelled to pay in the suit. Clause (2) lets him recover costs in two cases.

He did not contravene the orders of the promisor in bringing or defending the suit, and he acted as it would have been prudent for him to act in the absence of any contract of indemnity. The promisor authorized him to bring or defend the suit.

Example. The supplier sues Meena. Ravi had authorized her to defend the suit. She defends it, loses, and is ordered to pay Rs 5,000 as costs. She can recover the Rs 5,000 because the promisor authorized her to defend. Suppose instead that Ravi had told her not to defend, and she defended anyway. She would have contravened his orders, so the first case in clause (2) would not help her.

Right 3: sums paid under a compromise (clause 3)

Rule. The promisee can recover all sums which he may have paid under the terms of any compromise of the suit. Clause (3) lets him recover in two cases.

The compromise was not contrary to the orders of the promisor, and it was one which it would have been prudent for the promisee to make in the absence of any contract of indemnity. The promisor authorized him to compromise the suit.

Example. The supplier's claim against Meena is Rs 50,000. Ravi has not given any orders. Meena settles for Rs 30,000, a figure a careful person would have accepted even without an indemnity. The compromise was not contrary to Ravi's orders. She can recover the Rs 30,000 under clause (3).

What can the promisee recover under section 125? How to read this: start at the top. The promisee has been sued on a matter the promise covers. Then check each kind of sum. 1. The promisee, acting within the scope of his authority, is sued on a matter the promise to indemnify applies to. 2. Damages he is compelled to pay (clause 1). Recoverable. No extra condition in the clause. 3. Costs he is compelled to pay (clause 2). Recoverable if he did not contravene the promisor's orders and acted prudently, or if the promisor authorized the suit. 4. Sums paid under a compromise (clause 3). Recoverable if the compromise was not contrary to the promisor's orders and was prudent, or if the promisor authorized it.
keyPoints: Section 125 gives rights to the promisee "acting within the scope of his authority". Clause (1): all damages he is compelled to pay in the suit, on a matter the promise covers. Clause (2): costs, if he did not contravene the promisor's orders and acted prudently, or if the promisor authorized the suit. Clause (3): compromise sums, if the compromise was not contrary to the promisor's orders and was prudent, or if the promisor authorized it. The test of prudence is what he would do "in the absence of any contract of indemnity". The definition of a contract of indemnity is in section 124.

hi.inOneMinute: In a contract of indemnity, the person who is protected is the promisee. He is also called the indemnity-holder. Section 125 gives him three rights against the promisor when he is sued. He can recover the damages he is compelled to pay, the costs he is compelled to pay, and the sums he paid under a compromise. The first right has no extra condition. The second and third rights depend on conditions. Key points for the answer: the opening words "acting within the scope of his authority", the three clauses, and the conditions on costs and compromise.
hi.meaning: The opening words: "acting within the scope of his authority" Rule. Section 125 gives the three rights to a promisee "acting within the scope of his authority". The rights are therefore for a promisee who acts within his authority. The section does not define "scope of his authority" in other words. Right 1: damages he is compelled to pay (clause 1) Rule. The promisee can recover all damages which he may be compelled to pay in any suit. The damages must be in respect of a matter to which the promise to indemnify applies. Clause (1) has no condition about the promisor's orders or about prudence. Example. Ravi promises Meena: "If anyone sues you over the stock you bought through my broker, I will indemnify you." A supplier sues Meena over that stock. The court orders Meena to pay Rs 50,000 as damages. The suit is about the matter the promise covers. Meena can recover the Rs 50,000 from Ravi under clause (1). Right 2: costs he is compelled to pay (clause 2) Rule. The promisee can recover all costs which he may be compelled to pay in the suit. Clause (2) lets him recover costs in two cases. He did not contravene the orders of the promisor in bringing or defending the suit, and he acted as it would have been prudent for him to act in the absence of any contract of indemnity. The promisor authorized him to bring or defend the suit. Example. The supplier sues Meena. Ravi had authorized her to defend the suit. She defends it, loses, and is ordered to pay Rs 5,000 as costs. She can recover the Rs 5,000 because the promisor authorized her to defend. Suppose instead that Ravi had told her not to defend, and she defended anyway. She would have contravened his orders, so the first case in clause (2) would not help her. Right 3: sums paid under a compromise (clause 3) Rule. The promisee can recover all sums which he may have paid under the terms of any compromise of the suit. Clause (3) lets him recover in two cases. The compromise was not contrary to the orders of the promisor, and it was one which it would have been prudent for the promisee to make in the absence of any contract of indemnity. The promisor authorized him to compromise the suit. Example. The supplier's claim against Meena is Rs 50,000. Ravi has not given any orders. Meena settles for Rs 30,000, a figure a careful person would have accepted even without an indemnity. The compromise was not contrary to Ravi's orders. She can recover the Rs 30,000 under clause (3). What can the promisee recover under section 125? How to read this: start at the top. The promisee has been sued on a matter the promise covers. Then check each kind of sum. 1. The promisee, acting within the scope of his authority, is sued on a matter the promise to indemnify applies to. 2. Damages he is compelled to pay (clause 1). Recoverable. No extra condition in the clause. 3. Costs he is compelled to pay (clause 2). Recoverable if he did not contravene the promisor's orders and acted prudently, or if the promisor authorized the suit. 4. Sums paid under a compromise (clause 3). Recoverable if the compromise was not contrary to the promisor's orders and was prudent, or if the promisor authorized it.
keyPoints: Section 125 gives rights to the promisee "acting within the scope of his authority". Clause (1): all damages he is compelled to pay in the suit, on a matter the promise covers. Clause (2): costs, if he did not contravene the promisor's orders and acted prudently, or if the promisor authorized the suit. Clause (3): compromise sums, if the compromise was not contrary to the promisor's orders and was prudent, or if the promisor authorized it. The test of prudence is what he would do "in the absence of any contract of indemnity". The definition of a contract of indemnity is in section 124.

law-of-contract-ii-u1-t4.subtitle: Sections 126, 127, 142, 143 and 144 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: The Indian Contract Act, 1872 does not list the essentials of a guarantee in one place. They come from several sections. A guarantee is a contract to answer for a third person's default (section 126). It needs consideration (section 127). It is invalid if the creditor obtained it by misrepresentation or by keeping silent about material circumstances (sections 142 and 143). Key points for the answer: the third person's default, the three persons, consideration under section 127 with its illustrations, and the invalidity rules in sections 142 to 144.
en.meaning:
Characteristic 1: a contract about a third person's default (section 126)

Rule. A guarantee is a contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person in case of his default. The third person is the principal debtor.

Example. Ravi borrows Rs 1 lakh from a bank. His sister Sita promises the bank to repay if Ravi does not. This is a contract about a third person's default.

Characteristic 2: three persons and any form (section 126)

Rule. A guarantee has a surety, a principal debtor and a creditor. It may be oral or written.

Example. In the example above, Sita is the surety, Ravi the principal debtor and the bank the creditor. Sita may give the guarantee in a signed letter or by word of mouth.

Characteristic 3: consideration (section 127)

Rule. Anything done, or any promise made, for the benefit of the principal debtor, may be a sufficient consideration to the surety for giving the guarantee. The section speaks of a benefit to the principal debtor.

The Act gives three illustrations.

Illustration (a): B asks A to sell and deliver goods to him on credit. A agrees, provided C will guarantee payment of the price. C promises in consideration of A's promise to deliver the goods. This is sufficient consideration for C's promise. Illustration (b): A sells and delivers goods to B. C afterwards asks A to forbear to sue B for the debt for a year, and promises to pay if B does not. A agrees to forbear. This is sufficient consideration for C's promise. Illustration (c): A sells and delivers goods to B. C afterwards, without consideration, agrees to pay for them if B defaults. The agreement is void.

Example. Hema delivers goods to Gopi on credit because Ibrahim promises to pay if Gopi does not. Hema's delivery is for the benefit of Gopi, the principal debtor. It is sufficient consideration for Ibrahim's guarantee.

Characteristic 4: no misrepresentation by the creditor (section 142)

Rule. A guarantee is invalid if the creditor obtained it by misrepresentation concerning a material part of the transaction. The misrepresentation must have been made by the creditor, or with his knowledge and assent.

Example. A creditor tells Chandu that the principal debtor's shop is free of debt, knowing it is not. Chandu gives a guarantee on that statement. The guarantee is invalid under section 142.

Characteristic 5: no concealment by the creditor (section 143)

Rule. A guarantee is invalid if the creditor obtained it by keeping silence as to material circumstances.

The Act gives two illustrations.

Illustration (a): A engages B as clerk to collect money. B fails to account for some of his receipts, so A asks him to furnish security. C guarantees B's duly accounting. A does not tell C about B's previous conduct. B makes default. The guarantee is invalid. Illustration (b): A guarantees to C payment for iron to be supplied to B, to the amount of 2,000 tons. B and C have privately agreed that B should pay five rupees per ton beyond the market price, the excess to pay off an old debt. This agreement is concealed from A. A is not liable as a surety.

Characteristic 6: a guarantee on a condition about a co-surety (section 144)

Rule. Where a person gives a guarantee on a contract that the creditor shall not act on it until another person has joined as co-surety, the guarantee is not valid if that other person does not join.

Example. Kiran agrees to guarantee a loan to Lata, on the condition that the bank does not act on it until Mohan also joins as co-surety. Mohan never joins. Kiran's guarantee is not valid.

Checking a guarantee How to read this: start at the top and go down. A "no" at any box may make the guarantee invalid or void. 1. Is it a contract to answer for a third person's default (section 126)? 2. Is there consideration for the benefit of the principal debtor (section 127)? Where goods are already delivered and the promise has no consideration, the agreement is void (illustration (c)). 3. Did the creditor obtain it without misrepresentation (section 142) and without concealment (section 143)? Otherwise it is invalid. 4. If it was given on a co-surety condition, did the co-surety join (section 144)? Otherwise it is not valid.
keyPoints: A guarantee is a contract about a third person's default (section 126). Three persons: surety, principal debtor, creditor. It may be oral or written. Consideration: anything done or promised for the principal debtor's benefit is enough (section 127). A guarantee after delivery, with no consideration, is void (illustration (c) to section 127). Misrepresentation by the creditor makes it invalid (section 142). So does keeping silence as to material circumstances (section 143). A co-surety condition that is not met makes it not valid (section 144).

law-of-contract-ii-u1-t6.subtitle: Sections 129, 130 and 131 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: The Indian Contract Act, 1872 names one kind of guarantee: the continuing guarantee. A guarantee which extends to a series of transactions is a continuing guarantee (section 129). The surety may revoke it by notice to the creditor, as to future transactions (section 130). The death of the surety also revokes it, as to future transactions, unless the contract says otherwise (section 131). Key points for the answer: the definition, the Act's illustrations, and the two ways of revocation with their effect.
en.meaning:
What is a continuing guarantee? (section 129)

Rule. A guarantee which extends to a series of transactions is a continuing guarantee. The test is whether the guarantee extends to a series of transactions.

The Act's illustrations show the test at work.

In illustration (a), the guarantee covers the collection and payment of rents. This is a continuing guarantee. In illustration (b), the guarantee covers any tea supplied from time to time. It is a continuing guarantee, so A is liable up to £100 for the later supply of £200. In illustration (c), the guarantee covers the price of five sacks of flour to be delivered by B to C. It is not a continuing guarantee, so A is not liable for the later four sacks.

Example. Anil guarantees payment to Babu, a rice dealer in Guntur, of up to Rs 50,000 for any rice Babu supplies to Chandu from time to time. The guarantee covers a series of supplies. It is a continuing guarantee.

The other side: a guarantee that is not continuing

Rule. A guarantee which does not extend to a series of transactions is not a continuing guarantee. Illustration (c) to section 129 shows one. The 2017 paper calls such a guarantee a "simple guarantee". The Act does not use that label.

Example. Dev guarantees payment of the price of one consignment of cement that Esha will deliver to Farid. This covers one transaction. It is not a continuing guarantee.

Revocation by notice (section 130)

Rule. A continuing guarantee may at any time be revoked by the surety, as to future transactions, by notice to the creditor. The effect is limited to future transactions. Past transactions remain covered.

The Act's illustrations show this.

In illustration (a), A revokes after B has discounted bills for 2,000 rupees. A is discharged from liability for any later discount. A is still liable for the 2,000 rupees if C defaults. In illustration (b), B has already drawn on C and C has accepted the bill before A gives notice of revocation. C dishonours the bill at maturity. A is liable.

Example. In the rice example, Anil gives notice to Babu after Babu has supplied rice worth Rs 20,000. Rice supplied after the notice is no longer covered. Anil remains liable for the Rs 20,000 if Chandu defaults on it.

Revocation by the surety's death (section 131)

Rule. The death of the surety operates as a revocation of a continuing guarantee, as regards future transactions. This is so in the absence of any contract to the contrary. The guarantee may say otherwise.

Example. Anil dies. Babu then supplies rice to Chandu. The guarantee is revoked as to that future supply, unless the guarantee contract says otherwise.

Revoking a continuing guarantee How to read this: start at the top. Check whether the guarantee is continuing. Then check the way of revocation and its effect. 1. Does the guarantee extend to a series of transactions (section 129)? Yes: it is a continuing guarantee. No: it is not. 2. The surety gives notice to the creditor (section 130), or the surety dies (section 131). 3. Effect: the guarantee is revoked as to future transactions. Transactions already made stay covered (section 130, illustrations).
keyPoints: A continuing guarantee extends to a series of transactions (section 129). The surety may revoke it by notice to the creditor, as to future transactions (section 130). The surety's death revokes it as to future transactions, unless the contract says otherwise (section 131). Revocation does not affect transactions already made (illustrations to section 130). The Act names only the continuing guarantee. It does not use the label "simple guarantee".

law-of-contract-ii-u1-t9.subtitle: Sections 148 and 149 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: A bailment is the delivery of goods by one person to another for some purpose, on a contract that the goods will be returned or otherwise disposed of as the person delivering directs. The person who delivers is the bailor . The person who receives is the bailee . Sections 148 and 149 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 define bailment and say how delivery is made. Key points for the answer: the definition word for word, the two names, the explanation to section 148 and the rule on delivery in section 149.
en.meaning:
The meaning of bailment (section 148)

Rule. Bailment is the delivery of goods by one person to another for some purpose, upon a contract that the goods shall, when the purpose is accomplished, be returned or otherwise disposed of according to the directions of the person delivering them.

Goods are delivered by one person to another. The delivery is for some purpose. It is upon a contract that the goods will be returned, or disposed of as the bailor directs, when the purpose is accomplished.

Example. Ravi gives his scooter to a garage in Guntur for repair. The garage will return it when the repair is done. Ravi delivers goods to the garage for a purpose, on a contract that they will be returned. Ravi is the bailor and the garage is the bailee.

Bailor and bailee

Rule. The person delivering the goods is the bailor. The person to whom they are delivered is the bailee.

Example. Sita leaves her sewing machine with Lata for a week. Sita is the bailor. Lata is the bailee.

The explanation: a person already in possession

Rule. If a person already in possession of the goods of another contracts to hold them as a bailee, he thereby becomes the bailee. The owner becomes the bailor, although the goods may not have been delivered by way of bailment.

Example. Kiran already holds Mohan's bicycle. Kiran and Mohan now make a contract that Kiran will hold it as a bailee. By that contract Kiran becomes the bailee and Mohan the bailor, although the bicycle was not delivered by way of bailment.

How delivery is made (section 149)

Rule. Delivery may be made by doing anything which has the effect of putting the goods in the possession of the intended bailee, or of any person authorized to hold them on his behalf.

Example. Dev sends his goods to Esha's warehouse. Esha's authorized warehouse manager takes them in. The goods are in the possession of a person authorized to hold them on Esha's behalf. Delivery to Esha is complete.

Is it a bailment? How to read this: start at the top and answer each box. If you can answer yes to all, the transaction is a bailment under section 148. 1. Are goods delivered by one person to another (section 149 says how)? 2. Is it for some purpose? 3. Is it upon a contract that the goods will be returned or disposed of as the person delivering directs, when the purpose is accomplished? If yes to all three, it is a bailment. The deliverer is the bailor and the receiver is the bailee.
keyPoints: Section 148 defines bailment: delivery of goods by one person to another for some purpose, on a contract that they will be returned or disposed of as the person delivering directs. The person delivering is the bailor. The person receiving is the bailee. If a person already holds another's goods and contracts to hold them as a bailee, he becomes the bailee (explanation to section 148). Delivery means doing anything that puts the goods in the possession of the bailee, or of a person authorized to hold them for him (section 149). Pledge is bailment as security for a debt or a promise (section 172).

Key points for the answer: the definition word for word, the two names, the explanation to section 148 and the rule on delivery in section 149.
te.meaning: The meaning of bailment (section 148) Rule. Bailment is the delivery of goods by one person to another for some purpose, upon a contract that the goods shall, when the purpose is accomplished, be returned or otherwise disposed of according to the directions of the person delivering them. Goods are delivered by one person to another. The delivery is for some purpose. It is upon a contract that the goods will be returned, or disposed of as the bailor directs, when the purpose is accomplished. Example. Ravi gives his scooter to a garage in Guntur for repair. The garage will return it when the repair is done. Ravi delivers goods to the garage for a purpose, on a contract that they will be returned. Ravi is the bailor and the garage is the bailee. Bailor and bailee Rule. The person delivering the goods is the bailor. The person to whom they are delivered is the bailee. Example. Sita leaves her sewing machine with Lata for a week. Sita is the bailor. Lata is the bailee. The explanation: a person already in possession Rule. If a person already in possession of the goods of another contracts to hold them as a bailee, he thereby becomes the bailee. The owner becomes the bailor, although the goods may not have been delivered by way of bailment. Example. Kiran already holds Mohan's bicycle. Kiran and Mohan now make a contract that Kiran will hold it as a bailee. By that contract Kiran becomes the bailee and Mohan the bailor, although the bicycle was not delivered by way of bailment. How delivery is made (section 149) Rule. Delivery may be made by doing anything which has the effect of putting the goods in the possession of the intended bailee, or of any person authorized to hold them on his behalf. Example. Dev sends his goods to Esha's warehouse. Esha's authorized warehouse manager takes them in. The goods are in the possession of a person authorized to hold them on Esha's behalf. Delivery to Esha is complete. Is it a bailment? How to read this: start at the top and answer each box. If you can answer yes to all, the transaction is a bailment under section 148. 1. Are goods delivered by one person to another (section 149 says how)? 2. Is it for some purpose? 3. Is it upon a contract that the goods will be returned or disposed of as the person delivering directs, when the purpose is accomplished? If yes to all three, it is a bailment. The deliverer is the bailor and the receiver is the bailee.
keyPoints: Section 148 defines bailment: delivery of goods by one person to another for some purpose, on a contract that they will be returned or disposed of as the person delivering directs. The person delivering is the bailor. The person receiving is the bailee. If a person already holds another's goods and contracts to hold them as a bailee, he becomes the bailee (explanation to section 148). Delivery means doing anything that puts the goods in the possession of the bailee, or of a person authorized to hold them for him (section 149). Pledge is bailment as security for a debt or a promise (section 172).

law-of-contract-ii-u1-t10.subtitle: Sections 148 and 149 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: The Act does not list the essentials of bailment in a separate section. They come from the words of section 148 and section 149. Every bailment needs a delivery of goods, between two persons, for some purpose, upon a contract, with a duty to return the goods or to dispose of them as the person delivering directs. Key points for the answer: the elements in the order of the definition, with section 149 on delivery and the explanation to section 148 for goods already in the bailee's possession.
en.meaning:
Requisite 1: delivery of goods

Rule. Bailment is the "delivery of goods". Section 149 says delivery may be made by doing anything which puts the goods in the possession of the intended bailee, or of any person authorized to hold them on his behalf. The explanation to section 148 adds the case where the bailee is already in possession of the goods.

Example. Anil's goods are placed in the possession of a clerk whom Babu has authorized to hold goods for him. Delivery to Babu is made. In a separate case, Chandu only promises Dev that he will look after Dev's goods one day, but the goods never reach Chandu or anyone authorized for him. There is no delivery.

Requisite 2: one person delivers to another

Rule. The goods are delivered "by one person to another". The deliverer is the bailor. The receiver is the bailee.

Example. Esha leaves her bicycle with Farid. Esha is the bailor. Farid is the bailee.

Requisite 3: for some purpose

Rule. The goods are delivered "for some purpose". Section 148 says "some purpose" and lists none.

Example. Gopi gives cloth to a tailor to be made into a coat. The purpose is stitching. Hema leaves her car with a friend while she travels. The purpose is safe keeping.

Requisite 4: upon a contract

Rule. The delivery is "upon a contract". Section 148 itself speaks of a contract that the goods will be returned or otherwise disposed of.

Example. Ibrahim delivers goods to Kiran on the agreed terms that Kiran will return them after a month. The delivery is upon a contract.

Requisite 5: return or disposal as directed

Rule. The contract must provide that the goods shall, when the purpose is accomplished, be returned or otherwise disposed of according to the directions of the person delivering them.

Example. Lata gives wheat to a mill to be ground. The mill must return the flour, or deliver it to a person Lata names. This meets the requisite of return or disposal as directed.

The requisites How to read this: all of them must be present for a bailment under section 148. 1. Delivery of goods (section 149). 2. By one person to another. 3. For some purpose. 4. Upon a contract. 5. That the goods will be returned or disposed of as the person delivering directs, when the purpose is accomplished. All present: bailment.
keyPoints: Elements in section 148: delivery of goods, by one person to another, for some purpose, upon a contract, with return or disposal as the person delivering directs. Delivery: anything putting the goods in the possession of the bailee or of a person authorized for him (section 149). A person already holding another's goods may become a bailee by contract (explanation to section 148). If one requisite is missing, the transaction does not fit the definition.

law-of-contract-ii-u1-t7.subtitle: Sections 126, 128, 132, 137, 138 and 140 to 147 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: A surety stands behind a borrower. The lender is the creditor . The borrower is the principal debtor . The surety's duty to pay is as wide as the borrower's. The lender may ask the surety to pay at once. After paying, the surety gets rights against the borrower, the lender's securities and other sureties. Key points for the answer: the section 128 rule, the case Bank of Bihar v. Damodar Prasad and these three rights.
en.meaning:
Liability: as wide as the debtor's (section 128)

Rule. The surety is liable for as much as the principal debtor owes, including interest and charges that fall due. The only limit is what the contract provides. This is what coextensive means in section 128.

The bond may cap the amount, as in Bank of Bihar v. Damodar Prasad (Rs. 12,000 and interest). Section 145 separately limits what the surety can recover from the borrower: no more than the borrower really owed.

Example. Meena guarantees a bank loan of Rs 2 lakh taken by her brother Ravi in Vijayawada. Ravi defaults . Meena is liable for the whole Rs 2 lakh and the interest due. If her bond had capped her at Rs 1 lakh with interest, that cap would govern. The Act's own illustration holds a guarantor of a dishonoured bill of exchange liable for the amount, the interest and the charges.

Liability: immediate, with no need to sue the debtor first

Rule. The creditor does not have to sue the principal debtor first. In Bank of Bihar the bond made demand the only condition. Once the creditor demanded payment and it was not met, the surety was liable at once. A guarantee may set other conditions, so always read its terms. The Supreme Court said the liability was immediate. It was not deferred until the creditor had exhausted his remedies against the principal debtor.

The surety cannot tell the creditor to chase the debtor first. In the absence of some special equity, the surety also cannot restrain execution against him on the ground that the debtor is solvent.

Example. This is what happened in Bank of Bihar v. Damodar Prasad (see the case below). The Supreme Court set aside an order that made the bank exhaust its remedies against the borrower first.

Liability: delay by the creditor does not free the surety (section 137)

Rule. Mere forbearance by the creditor to sue the principal debtor does not discharge the surety. The guarantee may say otherwise, and then it governs.

Example. Kiran owes Mohan a debt guaranteed by Suresh. The debt becomes payable. Mohan does not sue Kiran for a year. Suresh is not discharged. This is the Act's own illustration to section 137.

Liability: two persons liable together, one acting as surety only between themselves (section 132)

Rule. Two persons may take a liability together and agree privately that one of them will pay only if the other fails. The creditor is not a party to that private agreement. Each of the two stays fully liable to the creditor, even if the creditor knows of the arrangement.

Example. Hari and Gita sign one joint loan document for Rs 1 lakh with a cooperative bank. Privately they agree that Gita will pay only if Hari fails. The bank knows this. The bank can still sue Gita directly. This follows the Act's illustration to section 132, where a joint and several promissory note signed by A as surety for B does not stop C from suing A.

Liability: none where the guarantee was obtained by misrepresentation or concealment (sections 142 to 144)

Rule. A guarantee is invalid if the creditor obtained it by a misrepresentation about a material part of the transaction, made by him or with his knowledge and assent. It is also invalid if he obtained it by keeping silent about material circumstances. An invalid guarantee binds no one, so the surety owes nothing.

Section 144 deals with a related case. A person may give a guarantee on the condition that the creditor will not act on it until another person joins as co-surety. If that other person does not join, the guarantee is not valid.

Example. Anand employs Bala as a cashier. Bala has already failed to account for some of the money he collected. Anand asks Chandu to guarantee Bala's accounts and does not tell him about this. Bala later defaults. Chandu's guarantee is invalid. This is the Act's illustration (a) to section 143.

Right against the principal debtor: subrogation and indemnity (sections 140 and 145)

Rule. The surety pays first and recovers afterwards. A surety who pays all he is liable for steps into the creditor's shoes under section 140. This is subrogation . The surety can then proceed against the principal debtor with the creditor's rights.

Section 145 adds a second route. The principal debtor impliedly promises to indemnify the surety. The surety recovers sums he has rightfully paid, and not sums he paid wrongfully.

Example. Suresh is surety for Kiran's debt to Mohan. Mohan sues Suresh. Suresh defends on reasonable grounds but loses and pays the debt with costs. He recovers both the debt and the costs from Kiran. Had he defended with no reasonable ground, he could recover the debt but not the costs. This follows the Act's illustrations to section 145.

Right against the creditor: benefit of securities (section 141)

Rule. The surety is entitled to every security the creditor holds against the principal debtor when the guarantee is given. This is so even if the surety does not know about it. If the creditor loses it, or gives it up without the surety's consent, the surety is discharged to the extent of its value.

Only the security that exists when the guarantee is given counts. A further security that the creditor obtains later is not covered.

Example. Lakshmi lends her tenant Venkat Rs 2,000 on Ramesh's guarantee. She also holds a mortgage of Venkat's furniture for the debt. She cancels the mortgage. Venkat becomes insolvent and Lakshmi sues Ramesh. Ramesh is discharged to the value of the furniture. This is the Act's illustration (a) to section 141.

Right against co-sureties: sharing the loss (sections 138, 146 and 147)

Rule. Where several sureties guarantee the same debt, each must bear an equal share unless they agreed otherwise. If they are bound in different sums, they pay equally within the limits of those sums. So a surety who pays more than his share can claim the excess from the others.

If the creditor releases one co-surety, the others are not discharged (section 138). The released surety is also not freed from his responsibility to the other sureties.

Example. A, B and C are sureties to D for Rs 3,000 lent to E. E defaults. As between themselves they pay Rs 1,000 each. In the Act's illustration to section 147, sureties are bound in sums of Rs 10,000, Rs 20,000 and Rs 40,000, and the debtor defaults by Rs 40,000. A pays Rs 10,000, and B and C pay Rs 15,000 each.

From default to recovery How to read this: start at the top and follow the boxes down. The last box shows who the surety can recover from. 1. The principal debtor defaults and the creditor demands payment. 2. The surety is liable at once (section 128). The creditor need not sue the principal debtor first. 3. The surety pays all he is liable for. 4. The surety takes over the creditor's rights (section 140) and has an implied indemnity (section 145). Sums rightfully paid can be recovered from the principal debtor. 5. Co-sureties share the loss (sections 146 and 147). A surety who paid more than his share recovers the excess from the others.

The creditor need not exhaust remedies against the principal debtor first (Bank of Bihar v. Damodar Prasad). Mere forbearance to sue does not discharge the surety (section 137). The surety's rights against the principal debtor begin on payment: section 140 (creditor's rights) and section 145 (implied indemnity). Section 141: the surety has the benefit of the securities held when the guarantee is given. A later security is not covered. A, B and C are sureties to D for Rs 3,000 lent to E. E defaults. As between themselves they pay Rs 1,000 each. In the Act's illustration to section 147, sureties are bound in sums of Rs 10,000, Rs 20,000 and Rs 40,000, and the debtor defaults by Rs 40,000. A pays Rs 10,000, and B and C pay Rs 15,000 each. From default to recovery How to read this: start at the top and follow the boxes down. The last box shows who the surety can recover from. 1. The principal debtor defaults and the creditor demands payment. 2. The surety is liable at once (section 128). The creditor need not sue the principal debtor first. 3. The surety pays all he is liable for. 4. The surety takes over the creditor's rights (section 140) and has an implied indemnity (section 145). Sums rightfully paid can be recovered from the principal debtor. 5. Co-sureties share the loss (sections 146 and 147). A surety who paid more than his share recovers the excess from the others.

The creditor need not exhaust remedies against the principal debtor first (Bank of Bihar v. Damodar Prasad). Mere forbearance to sue does not discharge the surety (section 137). The surety's rights against the principal debtor begin on payment: section 140 (creditor's rights) and section 145 (implied indemnity). Section 141: the surety has the benefit of the securities held when the guarantee is given. A later security is not covered. Sections 146 and 147: co-sureties contribute equally, within the limits of their sums. Release of one co-surety does not discharge the others (section 138). A private arrangement between two joint promisors does not bind the creditor (section 132). A guarantee obtained by misrepresentation or concealment is invalid (sections 142 and 143).

caseLaws.name: Bank of Bihar v
caseLaws.facts: Damodar Prasad (1968) Facts. A bank lent money to Damodar Prasad on the guarantee of Paras Nath Sinha. The trial court decreed the suit against both but barred execution against the guarantor until the bank had exhausted its remedies against the borrower. Principle. The surety's liability is immediate. Without some special equity, he cannot restrain execution against him until the creditor has exhausted his remedies against the principal. The surety must pay and then recover from the principal under section 140. Why it matters. It is the Supreme Court authority for the point that a creditor may proceed against the surety without first proceeding against the debtor.

selfTest.q: 1. What does it mean to say that the surety's liability is coextensive?
selfTest.a: It means the surety is liable for as much as the principal debtor owes, unless the contract provides otherwise (section 128). 2. Can a surety insist that the creditor sue the principal debtor first? No. The liability is immediate. In the absence of some special equity, the surety cannot restrain execution until the creditor has exhausted his remedies against the principal (Bank of Bihar v. Damodar Prasad). 3. What does a surety get on paying the creditor? All the rights the creditor had against the principal debtor (section 140), and an implied indemnity for sums rightfully paid (section 145).

law-of-contract-ii-u1-t12.subtitle: Sections 150 to 161, 163 to 167, 170, 171, 180 and 181 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: The Act gives the bailor and the bailee duties and rights. The bailor must disclose known faults (section 150), repay necessary expenses where the bailee is unpaid (section 158) and answer for his title (section 164). The bailee must take proper care (section 151), use the goods only as the bailment allows (sections 153 and 154), bear the consequences of mixing goods (sections 155 to 157), and return them with any increase (sections 160, 161 and 163). The bailee has a lien for his service (section 170). Bankers, factors and certain others have a general lien (section 171). Key points for the answer: the duties of each party, the liens and the Act's illustrations.
en.meaning:
Duties of the bailor

Rule. The bailor has these duties under the Act.

Disclose faults (section 150). He must disclose faults he is aware of that materially interfere with the use of the goods or expose the bailee to extraordinary risks. If goods are bailed for hire, he is responsible for damage from faults whether aware or not. Illustration (a): A lends B a horse he knows to be vicious without saying so. The horse runs away and B is injured. A is responsible. Illustration (b): A hires a carriage from B. It is unsafe, though B is not aware, and A is injured. B is responsible. Repay necessary expenses (section 158) where the bailee receives no remuneration. Indemnify for early return of a gratuitous loan (section 159) , to the extent the borrower's loss exceeds the benefit he derived. Answer for his title (section 164). He is responsible to the bailee for loss the bailee sustains because the bailor was not entitled to make the bailment, to receive back the goods or to give directions.

Example. Ravi lends his scooter to Sita knowing that its brakes are faulty and does not tell her. The brakes fail and Sita is hurt. Ravi is responsible for the damage arising directly from the fault (section 150).

Duties of the bailee: care, and no unauthorised use

Rule. The bailee must take the care of section 151. If he has taken that care, and there is no special contract, he is not responsible for loss, destruction or deterioration (section 152).

If the bailee does an act inconsistent with the conditions, the bailor may avoid the bailment (section 153). If he uses the goods otherwise than as the bailment allows, he must compensate the bailor for damage arising from or during that use (section 154).

Section 153, illustration: A lets a horse to B for hire for his own riding. B drives it in his carriage. At A's option, this terminates the bailment. Section 154, illustration (a): A lends a horse to B for his own riding only. B allows C, a member of his family, to ride it. C rides with care, but the horse accidentally falls and is injured. B must compensate A. Section 154, illustration (b): A hires a horse in Calcutta from B expressly to march to Benares. A marches to Cuttack instead. The horse accidentally falls and is injured. A must compensate B.

Example. Kiran borrows Lata's sewing machine for his own use at home. He lets his neighbour use it, and it is damaged during that use. Kiran must compensate Lata for the damage arising during the use (section 154).

Mixing the goods: consequences for the bailee (sections 155 to 157)

Rule. The effect of mixing depends on consent and on whether the goods can be separated.

With the bailor's consent: both have an interest in the mixture in proportion to their shares (section 155). Without consent, goods can be separated: the property remains with the parties. The bailee bears the expense of separation and any damage from the mixture (section 156). Illustration: A bails 100 marked bales of cotton to B, who mixes them with his own differently marked bales. A may have his 100 bales back and B bears all the expense of separation. Without consent, goods cannot be separated: the bailee must compensate the bailor for the loss of the goods (section 157). Illustration: A bails a barrel of Cape flour worth Rs 45 to B, who mixes it with country flour worth Rs 25 a barrel. B must compensate A.

Duties of the bailee: return, and increase or profit

Rule. The bailee must return the goods, or deliver them as the bailor directs, without demand, as soon as the time has expired or the purpose is accomplished (section 160). If by his default they are not returned at the proper time, he is responsible for loss, destruction or deterioration from that time (section 161). In the absence of a contract to the contrary, he must deliver any increase or profit from the goods (section 163). Illustration: A leaves a cow with B to be taken care of. The cow has a calf. B must deliver the calf as well as the cow.

Example. Dev leaves his goat with Esha for a month. The goat has a kid. At the end of the month Esha must return the goat and the kid (section 163).

Joint owners, a bailor without title, and rival claimants (sections 165 to 167)

Rule. If joint owners bail goods, the bailee may deliver them back to one of them without the consent of all, unless they agreed otherwise (section 165). If the bailor has no title and the bailee in good faith delivers them back to the bailor, the bailee is not responsible to the owner (section 166). A person other than the bailor who claims the goods may apply to the Court to stop delivery to the bailor and to decide the title (section 167).

Rights of the bailee: liens (sections 170 and 171)

Rule. A bailee who has rendered service involving labour or skill on the goods, in accordance with the purpose of the bailment, may retain them until he receives due remuneration, unless the contract says otherwise (section 170). This is the particular lien.

Illustration (a): A delivers a rough diamond to B, a jeweller, to be cut and polished. B may retain the stone until he is paid. Illustration (b): A gives cloth to B, a tailor, to make a coat. B promises to deliver the coat as soon as it is finished and to give three months' credit for the price. B is not entitled to retain the coat until he is paid.

Bankers, factors, wharfingers, attorneys of a High Court and policy-brokers may retain goods bailed to them as security for a general balance of account, in the absence of a contract to the contrary. No other persons may do so unless there is an express contract (section 171). This is the general lien.

Rights against third persons (sections 180 and 181)

Rule. If a third person wrongfully deprives the bailee of the use or possession of the goods, or injures them, the bailee may use the remedies the owner could have used. Either the bailor or the bailee may sue the third person (section 180). What is obtained is dealt with between them according to their respective interests (section 181).

Rights of the bailor

Rule. The bailor may avoid the bailment where the bailee does an act inconsistent with its conditions (section 153). He is entitled to compensation for damage from unauthorised use (section 154), for goods lost by mixing (section 157), and for loss after default in returning (section 161). He may require return of a gratuitous loan at any time (section 159). He is entitled to any increase or profit (section 163).

Can the bailee keep the goods until he is paid? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Did the bailee render a service involving labour or skill on the goods, in accordance with the purpose of the bailment? Yes: particular lien (section 170), unless the contract says otherwise. 2. Is he a banker, factor, wharfinger, attorney of a High Court or policy-broker? Yes: general lien for a general balance of account (section 171), unless the contract says otherwise. 3. Neither? No right to retain for a general balance, unless there is an express contract (section 171).
keyPoints: Bailor: disclose known faults (section 150), and for hire he is responsible whether aware or not. Repay necessary expenses where the bailee is unpaid (section 158). Bailee: ordinary prudence (section 151). Not responsible if he took that care and there is no special contract (section 152). Unauthorised use: bailor may avoid (section 153). Bailee compensates for damage from or during such use (section 154). Mixing: with consent, shared in proportion (section 155). Without consent, separable: bailee bears the cost (section 156). Not separable: compensation (section 157). Return without demand (section 160). Increase or profit goes to the bailor (section 163). Particular lien: service involving labour or skill (section 170). General lien: bankers, factors, wharfingers, attorneys of a High Court, policy-brokers (section 171).

selfTest.q: 1. What standard of care must a bailee take under section 151?
selfTest.a: As much care as a man of ordinary prudence would, under similar circumstances, take of his own goods of the same bulk, quality and value. 2. Who has a general lien under section 171? Ravi lends his scooter to Sita knowing that its brakes are faulty and does not tell her. The brakes fail and Sita is hurt. Ravi is responsible for the damage arising directly from the fault (section 150). Duties of the bailee: care, and no unauthorised use Rule. The bailee must take the care of section 151. If he has taken that care, and there is no special contract, he is not responsible for loss, destruction or deterioration (section 152). If the bailee does an act inconsistent with the conditions, the bailor may avoid the bailment (section 153). If he uses the goods otherwise than as the bailment allows, he must compensate the bailor for damage arising from or during that use (section 154). Section 153, illustration: A lets a horse to B for hire for his own riding. B drives it in his carriage. At A's option, this terminates the bailment. Section 154, illustration (a): A lends a horse to B for his own riding only. B allows C, a member of his family, to ride it. C rides with care, but the horse accidentally falls and is injured. B must compensate A. Section 154, illustration (b): A hires a horse in Calcutta from B expressly to march to Benares. A marches to Cuttack instead. The horse accidentally falls and is injured. A must compensate B. Example. Kiran borrows Lata's sewing machine for his own use at home. He lets his neighbour use it, and it is damaged during that use. Kiran must compensate Lata for the damage arising during the use (section 154). Mixing the goods: consequences for the bailee (sections 155 to 157) Rule. The effect of mixing depends on consent and on whether the goods can be separated. With the bailor's consent: both have an interest in the mixture in proportion to their shares (section 155). Without consent, goods can be separated: the property remains with the parties. The bailee bears the expense of separation and any damage from the mixture (section 156). Illustration: A bails 100 marked bales of cotton to B, who mixes them with his own differently marked bales. A may have his 100 bales back and B bears all the expense of separation. Without consent, goods cannot be separated: the bailee must compensate the bailor for the loss of the goods (section 157). Illustration: A bails a barrel of Cape flour worth Rs 45 to B, who mixes it with country flour worth Rs 25 a barrel. B must compensate A. Duties of the bailee: return, and increase or profit Rule. The bailee must return the goods, or deliver them as the bailor directs, without demand, as soon as the time has expired or the purpose is accomplished (section 160). If by his default they are not returned at the proper time, he is responsible for loss, destruction or deterioration from that time (section 161). In the absence of a contract to the contrary, he must deliver any increase or profit from the goods (section 163). Illustration: A leaves a cow with B to be taken care of. The cow has a calf. B must deliver the calf as well as the cow. Example. Dev leaves his goat with Esha for a month. The goat has a kid. At the end of the month Esha must return the goat and the kid (section 163). Joint owners, a bailor without title, and rival claimants (sections 165 to 167) Rule. If joint owners bail goods, the bailee may deliver them back to one of them without the consent of all, unless they agreed otherwise (section 165). If the bailor has no title and the bailee in good faith delivers them back to the bailor, the bailee is not responsible to the owner (section 166). A person other than the bailor who claims the goods may apply to the Court to stop delivery to the bailor and to decide the title (section 167). Rights of the bailee: liens (sections 170 and 171) Rule. A bailee who has rendered service involving labour or skill on the goods, in accordance with the purpose of the bailment, may retain them until he receives due remuneration, unless the contract says otherwise (section 170). This is the particular lien. Illustration (a): A delivers a rough diamond to B, a jeweller, to be cut and polished. B may retain the stone until he is paid. Illustration (b): A gives cloth to B, a tailor, to make a coat. B promises to deliver the coat as soon as it is finished and to give three months' credit for the price. B is not entitled to retain the coat until he is paid. Bankers, factors, wharfingers, attorneys of a High Court and policy-brokers may retain goods bailed to them as security for a general balance of account, in the absence of a contract to the contrary. No other persons may do so unless there is an express contract (section 171). This is the general lien. Rights against third persons (sections 180 and 181) Rule. If a third person wrongfully deprives the bailee of the use or possession of the goods, or injures them, the bailee may use the remedies the owner could have used. Either the bailor or the bailee may sue the third person (section 180). What is obtained is dealt with between them according to their respective interests (section 181). Rights of the bailor Rule. The bailor may avoid the bailment where the bailee does an act inconsistent with its conditions (section 153). He is entitled to compensation for damage from unauthorised use (section 154), for goods lost by mixing (section 157), and for loss after default in returning (section 161). He may require return of a gratuitous loan at any time (section 159). He is entitled to any increase or profit (section 163). Can the bailee keep the goods until he is paid? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Did the bailee render a service involving labour or skill on the goods, in accordance with the purpose of the bailment? Yes: particular lien (section 170), unless the contract says otherwise. 2. Is he a banker, factor, wharfinger, attorney of a High Court or policy-broker? Yes: general lien for a general balance of account (section 171), unless the contract says otherwise. 3. Neither? No right to retain for a general balance, unless there is an express contract (section 171).
keyPoints: Bailor: disclose known faults (section 150), and for hire he is responsible whether aware or not. Repay necessary expenses where the bailee is unpaid (section 158). Bailee: ordinary prudence (section 151). Not responsible if he took that care and there is no special contract (section 152). Unauthorised use: bailor may avoid (section 153). Bailee compensates for damage from or during such use (section 154). Mixing: with consent, shared in proportion (section 155). Without consent, separable: bailee bears the cost (section 156). Not separable: compensation (section 157). Return without demand (section 160). Increase or profit goes to the bailor (section 163). Particular lien: service involving labour or skill (section 170). General lien: bankers, factors, wharfingers, attorneys of a High Court, policy-brokers (section 171).

selfTest.q: 1. What standard of care must a bailee take under section 151?

What must a bailee do with the calf of a cow left with him? Deliver the calf as well as the cow to the bailor (section 163, illustration).

law-of-contract-ii-u1-t11.subtitle: Sections 150, 158, 159, 162 and 172 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: The Act has no section that lists the kinds of bailment. Its words refer to a bailment for hire (section 150) and a gratuitous bailment (sections 158, 159 and 162). A bailment of goods as security for a debt or a promise is a pledge (section 172). Key points for the answer: the two kinds, the rules the Act gives for each, and the link to pledge.
en.meaning:
Kind 1: bailment for hire

Rule. Section 150 speaks of goods "bailed for hire". There the bailor is responsible for damage arising directly from faults in the goods whether he was or was not aware of them.

Example. Anil hires a carriage from Babu. The carriage is unsafe, though Babu is not aware of it, and Anil is injured. Babu is responsible to Anil for the injury. This is the Act's own illustration (b) to section 150.

Kind 2: gratuitous bailment

Rule. The Act uses the word "gratuitous" in sections 159 and 162. Section 158 speaks of a bailee who is to receive no remuneration. The Act gives these rules.

The bailor must repay the bailee the necessary expenses incurred for the purpose of the bailment, where the goods are to be kept, carried or have work done on them and the bailee gets no remuneration (section 158). The lender may at any time require the return of the thing, even though he lent it for a specified time or purpose. If the borrower acted on the faith of the loan so that early return would cause him loss exceeding the benefit he derived, the lender who compels return must indemnify him for the excess (section 159). The bailment is terminated by the death of the bailor or of the bailee (section 162). The first part of section 150, the bailor's duty to disclose faults of which he is aware, applies to every bailment. The second part adds the rule for goods bailed for hire.

Example. Chandu lends his bicycle to Dev for a month without charge. After a week Chandu asks for it back. Under section 159 he may require its return at any time. If Dev had, on the faith of the month-long loan, made arrangements so that early return would cost him more than the benefit he got, Chandu would have to indemnify him for the excess. If Chandu dies during the month, the gratuitous bailment ends (section 162).

Pledge: bailment as security (section 172)

Rule. A bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt or performance of a promise is called a pledge. The Act gives pledge its own sections (172 to 179).

Example. Esha borrows Rs 50,000 and hands her gold chain to the lender as security until she repays. This is a bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt. It is a pledge.

Which kind of bailment? How to read this: start at the top and follow the answer. 1. Are the goods bailed as security for a debt or a promise? Yes: pledge (section 172). 2. If not, are the goods bailed for hire? Yes: bailment for hire (section 150). 3. Otherwise, where the Act's words speak of a gratuitous loan or a bailee who is to receive no remuneration: Gratuitous bailment (sections 158, 159, 162).
keyPoints: The Act does not list kinds. Its words show bailment for hire and gratuitous bailment, and pledge is bailment as security. For hire: the bailor is responsible for damage from faults whether aware or not (section 150). Gratuitous: the bailor repays necessary expenses (section 158). The lender may require return at any time (section 159). Death of either party ends it (section 162). Pledge: bailment as security for a debt or promise (section 172).

law-of-contract-ii-u1-t8.subtitle: Sections 130, 131, 133 to 139 and 141 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: A surety is discharged when the Act says so. The Act gives several ways. A continuing guarantee may be revoked (sections 130 and 131). A change in the terms of the contract between the creditor and the principal debtor, made without the surety's consent, discharges him as to later transactions (section 133). The surety is also discharged in these cases. The principal debtor is released (section 134). The creditor makes a composition with the debtor, gives him time or promises not to sue (section 135). The creditor's act or omission impairs the surety's remedy (section 139). A security is lost (section 141). Key points for the answer: each section, its words and the Act's illustration.
en.meaning:
Discharge by revocation of a continuing guarantee (sections 130 and 131)

Rule. The surety may revoke a continuing guarantee by notice to the creditor (section 130). His death also revokes it, unless the contract says otherwise (section 131). Both operate as to future transactions only. The full treatment is in the topic "Kinds of Guarantee".

Example. Anil guarantees all rice supplied to Chandu by Babu for a year. After four months Anil gives notice to Babu. Supplies after the notice are no longer covered. Supplies before the notice remain covered.

Discharge by variance in the terms of the contract (section 133)

Rule. Any variance, made without the surety's consent, in the terms of the contract between the principal debtor and the creditor, discharges the surety as to transactions subsequent to the variance.

The Act gives five illustrations. Three of them show the point clearly.

(a) A is surety for B's conduct as a manager in C's bank. B and C agree, without A's consent, to raise B's salary and to make him liable for one-fourth of overdraft losses. B allows an overdraft and the bank loses money. A is discharged and is not liable. (c) A is surety for B, a clerk paid a fixed salary. C and B agree, without A's knowledge or consent, to pay B a commission instead. A is not liable for B's later misconduct. (e) C contracts to lend B 5,000 rupees on 1 March and A guarantees repayment. C pays the money on 1 January. A is discharged, because C might sue B for the money before 1 March.

Illustration (b) covers a later Act that materially alters the office. Illustration (d) covers a continuing guarantee of 3,000 rupees for oil supplied on credit, which the debtor and creditor change, without A's knowledge, into supply for ready money. A is not liable for goods supplied after the new arrangement.

Example. Hema sells goods to Gopi on three months' credit, with Ibrahim as surety. Without telling Ibrahim, Hema and Gopi change the credit period to one month. Ibrahim is discharged as to later transactions under section 133.

Discharge by release of the principal debtor (section 134)

Rule. The surety is discharged by any contract between the creditor and the principal debtor by which the principal debtor is released. He is also discharged by any act or omission of the creditor, the legal consequence of which is the discharge of the principal debtor.

(a) B becomes embarrassed and contracts with his creditors, including C, to assign them his property in return for releasing him from their demands. B is released from his debt to C, and A, his surety, is discharged. (b) A contracts with B to grow indigo and C guarantees A's performance. B diverts the water that A needs and prevents the crop. C is no longer liable. (c) A contracts to build a house for B, who is to supply the timber. C guarantees A's performance. B omits to supply the timber. C is discharged.

Example. A co-operative society lends Rs 1 lakh to Ravi on Sita's guarantee. The society and Ravi agree that the society releases Ravi from the loan. Sita is discharged under section 134.

Discharge by composition, time or promise not to sue (section 135)

Rule. A contract between the creditor and the principal debtor, by which the creditor makes a composition with, or promises to give time to, or not to sue, the principal debtor, discharges the surety, unless the surety assents to such contract.

Example. The bank agrees with Ravi, without asking Sita, to give him one more year to repay. Sita is discharged unless she assents to the agreement.

Not discharged: time given to the debtor by a contract with a third person (section 136)

Rule. Where a contract to give time to the principal debtor is made by the creditor with a third person, and not with the principal debtor, the surety is not discharged.

The Act's illustration: C, the holder of an overdue bill of exchange drawn by A as surety for B and accepted by B, contracts with M to give time to B. A is not discharged.

Example. The bank promises Ravi's neighbour Kiran, not Ravi, that it will give Ravi time to repay. The promise is made with a third person, not with the principal debtor. Sita is not discharged.

Not discharged: forbearance and release of a co-surety (sections 137 and 138)

Rule. Mere forbearance by the creditor to sue the principal debtor, or to enforce any other remedy against him, does not discharge the surety, in the absence of any provision in the guarantee to the contrary (section 137). The Act's illustration: B owes C a debt guaranteed by A. The debt becomes payable. C does not sue B for a year. A is not discharged.

Where there are co-sureties, a release by the creditor of one does not discharge the others. It also does not free the released surety from his responsibility to the other sureties (section 138).

Discharge by the creditor's act or omission impairing the surety's eventual remedy (section 139)

Rule. If the creditor does any act which is inconsistent with the rights of the surety, or omits to do any act which his duty to the surety requires him to do, and the eventual remedy of the surety against the principal debtor is thereby impaired, the surety is discharged.

(a) B contracts to build a ship for C, payable by instalments as the work reaches certain stages. A is surety. C, without A's knowledge, prepays the last two instalments to B. A is discharged by the prepayment. (b) C lends money to B on a promissory note made by B and by A as surety, with a bill of sale of B's furniture. C sells the furniture, but through his misconduct and wilful negligence only a small price is realized. A is discharged from liability on the note. (c) A puts M as apprentice to B and guarantees M's fidelity. B promises to see M make up the cash at least once a month. B omits to do so and M embezzles. A is not liable to B on his guarantee.

Example. A builder is to be paid by instalments as work proceeds. The owner, without telling the builder's surety, pays the last two instalments in advance. The surety's remedy against the builder is impaired. The surety is discharged, as in illustration (a) to section 139.

Discharge by loss of securities (section 141)

Rule. The surety is entitled to the benefit of every security the creditor holds against the principal debtor when the guarantee is given. If the creditor loses it or parts with it without the surety's consent, the surety is discharged to the extent of its value.

(a) C lends B 2,000 rupees on A's guarantee and also holds a mortgage of B's furniture. C cancels the mortgage. A is discharged to the value of the furniture. (b) C holds a decree against B and a guarantee from A. C takes B's goods in execution and then, without A's knowledge, withdraws the execution. A is discharged. (c) A is surety for B, and C afterwards obtains from B a further security and later gives it up. A is not discharged.

Is the surety discharged? How to read this: find what happened and follow the line to the section and the result. 1. The surety revokes a continuing guarantee by notice, or the surety dies. Discharged as to future transactions (sections 130, 131). 2. The creditor and the principal debtor vary their contract without the surety's consent. Discharged as to later transactions (section 133). 3. The creditor releases the principal debtor by contract, or an act or omission of the creditor discharges him. Discharged (section 134). 4. The creditor compounds with, gives time to, or agrees not to sue the principal debtor, and the surety does not assent. Discharged (section 135). 5. The creditor's act or omission impairs the surety's eventual remedy. Discharged (section 139). 6. The creditor loses or parts with a security held when the guarantee was given. Discharged to the extent of its value (section 141).

The creditor compounds with, gives time to, or agrees not to sue the principal debtor, and the surety does not assent. Discharged (section 135). 5. The creditor's act or omission impairs the surety's eventual remedy. Discharged (section 139). 6. The creditor loses or parts with a security held when the guarantee was given. Discharged to the extent of its value (section 141).
keyPoints: Revocation of a continuing guarantee, by notice or by the surety's death, operates as to future transactions (sections 130, 131). A variance without the surety's consent discharges him as to later transactions (section 133). Release of the principal debtor discharges the surety (section 134). Composition, time or promise not to sue the principal debtor discharges the surety, unless he assents (section 135). Time given by a contract with a third person does not discharge the surety (section 136). Mere forbearance does not (section 137). Release of one co-surety does not discharge the others (section 138). Impairing the surety's eventual remedy discharges him (section 139). So does loss of a security, to the extent of its value (section 141).

law-of-contract-ii-u1-t13.subtitle: Sections 153, 159, 160, 161 and 162 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: The Act has no single section on how a bailment ends. Sections 153, 159, 160, 161 and 162 deal with these events. The bailor may avoid the contract when the bailee acts inconsistently with its conditions (section 153). A gratuitous lender may require the goods back at any time (section 159). A gratuitous bailment ends on the death of the bailor or of the bailee (section 162). On expiry of time, or accomplishment of the purpose, the bailee must return the goods (sections 160 and 161). Key points for the answer: each event with its section and the Act's illustration.
en.meaning:
Event 1: the bailee's act inconsistent with the conditions (section 153)

Rule. The bailment is avoidable at the bailor's option if the bailee does any act with regard to the goods that is inconsistent with the conditions of the bailment. The bailment is not ended automatically. It ends if the bailor chooses.

Example. Ravi hires out a horse to Sita for her own riding. Sita yokes it to her cart. This is inconsistent with the condition. At Ravi's option, the bailment is terminated. This follows the Act's illustration.

Event 2: return of a gratuitous loan on demand (section 159)

Rule. The lender of a thing for use may at any time require its return if the loan was gratuitous, even though he lent it for a specified time or purpose. If early return causes the borrower loss exceeding the benefit he derived, the lender must indemnify him for the excess.

Example. Dev lends his bicycle free of charge to Esha for a month. After a week he asks for it back. He may require its return (section 159).

Event 3: death in a gratuitous bailment (section 162)

Rule. A gratuitous bailment is terminated by the death either of the bailor or of the bailee. Section 162 speaks only of a gratuitous bailment.

Example. Farid lends his cart to Gopi free of charge for a fortnight. Farid dies in the first week. The bailment is terminated (section 162).

Event 4: expiry of time or accomplishment of purpose (sections 160 and 161)

Rule. When the time for which the goods were bailed has expired, or the purpose has been accomplished, the bailee must return them, or deliver them as the bailor directs, without demand (section 160). If, by his default, he does not return, deliver or tender them at the proper time, he is responsible for any loss, destruction or deterioration from that time (section 161).

Example. Hema gives her scooter to a garage for repair. When the repair is done, the garage must return it without waiting for Hema to ask. If the garage fails to return it at the proper time by its own default, it is responsible for any loss or damage to the scooter from that time.

How a bailment ends How to read this: find the event and follow it to the section. 1. The bailee does an act inconsistent with the conditions. Bailor may avoid the contract (section 153). 2. The loan is gratuitous and the lender asks for the thing back. He may require return at any time (section 159). 3. The bailor or the bailee of a gratuitous bailment dies. Bailment is terminated (section 162). 4. The time expires, or the purpose is accomplished. Bailee returns the goods without demand (section 160). Default makes him responsible (section 161).
keyPoints: Bailee's inconsistent act: bailment avoidable at the bailor's option (section 153). Gratuitous loan: the lender may require return at any time (section 159). Gratuitous bailment: terminated by the death of the bailor or the bailee (section 162). Expiry or accomplishment: return without demand (section 160). Default: responsible for loss from that time (section 161).

law-of-contract-ii-u1-t14.subtitle: Section 172 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: A pledge is a special kind of bailment. Section 172 says the bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt or performance of a promise is called a pledge. The bailor is the pawnor . The bailee is the pawnee . Key points for the answer: the definition word for word, the two names, and the link to bailment.
en.meaning:
The meaning of pledge (section 172)

Rule. A pledge is a bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt or performance of a promise. Take the definition in parts.

It is a bailment of goods. The goods are bailed as security. The security is for payment of a debt or performance of a promise.

Example. Anil borrows Rs 50,000 from Babu and hands his gold chain to Babu as security until he repays. This is a bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt. It is a pledge.

Pawnor and pawnee

Rule. The bailor in a pledge is the pawnor. The bailee is the pawnee.

Example. In the example above, Anil is the pawnor. Babu is the pawnee.

Pledge and bailment

Rule. Every pledge is a bailment, but not every bailment is a pledge. Section 172 calls a bailment a pledge only where the goods are bailed as security for a debt or a promise.

Example. Chandu gives his cycle to a repairer for repair. This is a bailment for repair, not a pledge, because the goods are not security for a debt or a promise.

Is it a pledge? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Are goods bailed (section 148)? 2. Are they bailed as security? 3. Is the security for payment of a debt or performance of a promise? If yes to all, it is a pledge (section 172). The bailor is the pawnor and the bailee is the pawnee.
keyPoints: Pledge is the bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt or performance of a promise (section 172). The bailor is the pawnor. The bailee is the pawnee. Every pledge is a bailment. A bailment is a pledge only where the goods are security.

Section 128 provides that, unless the contract provides otherwise, the liability of the surety is:

Explanation. Section 128 makes the surety's liability coextensive with the principal debtor's, unless the contract says otherwise. The Act's illustration holds a guarantor of a dishonoured bill liable for the amount, interest and charges.

Explanation. The Supreme Court held that the surety's liability was immediate and not deferred until the creditor exhausted his remedies against the principal debtor. It set the direction aside and ordered the surety to pay the Bank's costs.

law-of-contract-ii-u1-t16.subtitle: Sections 178, 178A and 179 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: The Act makes a pledge by a person who is not the owner valid in three cases. A mercantile agent in possession of the goods with the owner's consent may pledge them in the ordinary course of business (section 178). A person who got the goods under a voidable contract that has not been rescinded may give a good title to a pawnee (section 178A). A person with only a limited interest in the goods may pledge them to the extent of that interest (section 179). Key points for the answer: the three sections, with the conditions of each, especially good faith and no notice of the defect.
en.meaning:
Case 1: pledge by a mercantile agent (section 178)

Rule. A pledge made by a mercantile agent is as valid as if the owner had expressly authorised it, if these conditions are met.

The mercantile agent is in possession of the goods or the document of title to them, with the owner's consent. He makes the pledge when acting in the ordinary course of business of a mercantile agent. The pawnee acts in good faith. The pawnee has no notice at the time of the pledge that the pawnor has no authority to pledge.

Example. Ravi gives his cloth stock to a mercantile agent, Sita, to sell on his behalf. Sita, acting in the ordinary course of her business, pledges the cloth to a lender, Babu, who acts in good faith and has no notice that Sita lacks authority to pledge. The pledge is as valid as if Ravi had expressly authorised it. If Babu had known Sita had no authority to pledge, the pledge would not be protected.

Case 2: pledge by a person in possession under a voidable contract (section 178A)

Rule. The pawnee acquires a good title if all of these are met.

The pawnor obtained possession of the goods under a contract voidable under section 19 or section 19A. The contract has not been rescinded at the time of the pledge. The pawnee acts in good faith. The pawnee has no notice of the pawnor's defect of title.

Example. Chandu obtains goods from Dev on a contract that Dev may cancel under section 19. Dev has not cancelled it. Chandu pledges the goods to Esha, who acts in good faith and has no notice of any defect in Chandu's title. Esha acquires a good title to the goods as pawnee.

Case 3: pledge by a person with a limited interest (section 179)

Rule. Where a person pledges goods in which he has only a limited interest, the pledge is valid to the extent of that interest.

Example. Farid holds a limited interest in certain goods. He pledges the goods to Gopi. The pledge is valid only to the extent of Farid's limited interest.

When is a pledge by a non-owner valid? How to read this: find the pawnor's position and follow it to the section. 1. The pawnor is a mercantile agent in possession with the owner's consent, acting in the ordinary course of business. Valid as if authorised, if the pawnee acts in good faith without notice (section 178). 2. The pawnor got the goods under a contract voidable under section 19 or 19A that has not been rescinded. The pawnee gets a good title if he acts in good faith without notice of the defect (section 178A). 3. The pawnor has only a limited interest. Valid to the extent of that interest (section 179).
keyPoints: Section 178: pledge by a mercantile agent in possession with the owner's consent, in the ordinary course of business, valid if the pawnee acts in good faith without notice. Section 178A: pledge by a person holding under a voidable contract not rescinded, valid if the pawnee acts in good faith without notice of the defect. Section 179: pledge of a limited interest is valid to the extent of that interest. Good faith and no notice are central to sections 178 and 178A.

Section 178A: pledge by a person holding under a voidable contract not rescinded, valid if the pawnee acts in good faith without notice of the defect. Section 179: pledge of a limited interest is valid to the extent of that interest. Good faith and no notice are central to sections 178 and 178A.
