law-of-contract-ii-u1-t15.subtitle: Sections 173 to 177 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: The pawnee may retain the pledged goods for the debt, the interest and his necessary expenses (section 173). He may not retain them for any other debt unless there is a contract to that effect (section 174). If the pawnor defaults, the pawnee may sue on the debt and keep the goods as collateral security , or sell the goods after giving reasonable notice (section 176). The defaulting pawnor may redeem the goods before they are actually sold (section 177). Key points for the answer: the pawnee's right of retainer, his right on default, the duty to give notice and pay over any surplus, and the pawnor's right to redeem.
en.meaning:
Rights of the pawnee

Rule. The pawnee has these rights.

Retainer (section 173). He may retain the goods for payment of the debt or performance of the promise, for the interest of the debt, and for all necessary expenses incurred in respect of the possession or preservation of the goods. Extraordinary expenses (section 175). He is entitled to receive from the pawnor extraordinary expenses incurred for the preservation of the goods. Remedies on default (section 176). He may sue on the debt and retain the goods as collateral security. Or he may sell the goods after reasonable notice.

Example. Anil pledges his gold chain to Babu for a loan of Rs 50,000. Babu may keep the chain until Anil pays the Rs 50,000, the interest, and the necessary expenses Babu incurred in keeping it safe (section 173).

Limits and conditions on the pawnee

Rule. The Act sets these limits.

He may not retain the goods for any debt or promise other than that for which they are pledged, in the absence of a contract to that effect (section 174). Such a contract is presumed for subsequent advances he makes, in the absence of anything to the contrary. He must give the pawnor reasonable notice of a sale (section 176). He must pay over to the pawnor any surplus if the sale proceeds exceed the amount due (section 176).

Example. Babu holds Anil's chain for the Rs 50,000 loan. Anil also owes Babu Rs 10,000 on a separate old debt. Without a contract to that effect, Babu may not retain the chain for the old debt (section 174). If Babu lends Anil a further Rs 20,000 later, a contract to retain the chain for that advance is presumed, unless there is anything to the contrary.

The pawnee's remedies on default (section 176)

Rule. If the pawnor makes default in payment, or in performance of the promise at the stipulated time, the pawnee has two remedies.

He may sue the pawnor on the debt or promise, and retain the goods as collateral security. He may sell the thing pledged, on giving the pawnor reasonable notice of the sale.

After a sale, the accounts work as follows.

Proceeds less than the amount due: the pawnor is still liable to pay the balance. Proceeds more than the amount due: the pawnee must pay the surplus to the pawnor.

Example. Anil defaults on the Rs 50,000 loan. Babu gives Anil reasonable notice and sells the chain for Rs 45,000. The amount due is Rs 50,000. Anil still owes Babu the balance of Rs 5,000. Had the chain fetched Rs 55,000, Babu would have to pay Anil the surplus of Rs 5,000.

Rights and duties of the pawnor

Rule. The pawnor has the right to redeem the goods after default, at any subsequent time before the actual sale, if a time was stipulated for payment (section 177). He must then pay, in addition, any expenses that arose from his default. He must pay extraordinary expenses incurred by the pawnee for the preservation of the goods (section 175). He is liable for any balance after a sale (section 176), and entitled to any surplus.

Example. Anil defaults on the due date. Before Babu sells the chain, Anil pays the Rs 50,000 with the expenses that arose from his default. Anil may redeem the chain (section 177).

What happens when the pawnor defaults How to read this: start at the top. 1. The pawnor defaults at the stipulated time. 2. The pawnee may sue on the debt and keep the goods as collateral security, or sell the goods on reasonable notice (section 176). 3. Before the actual sale, the pawnor may redeem by paying the debt and the expenses from his default (section 177). 4. After a sale, a shortfall is still owed by the pawnor. A surplus is paid to him (section 176).
keyPoints: Retainer: for the debt or promise, the interest and necessary expenses (section 173). No retainer for another debt without a contract. Presumed for subsequent advances (section 174). Extraordinary expenses for preservation: from the pawnor (section 175). On default: sue and retain as collateral security, or sell on reasonable notice. Shortfall owed. Surplus paid over (section 176). The pawnor may redeem before the actual sale, paying the expenses of his default (section 177).

He may retain the goods for payment of the debt or performance of the promise, for the interest of the debt, and for all necessary expenses incurred in respect of the possession or preservation of the goods. Extraordinary expenses (section 175). He is entitled to receive from the pawnor extraordinary expenses incurred for the preservation of the goods. Remedies on default (section 176). He may sue on the debt and retain the goods as collateral security. Or he may sell the goods after reasonable notice. Example. Anil pledges his gold chain to Babu for a loan of Rs 50,000. Babu may keep the chain until Anil pays the Rs 50,000, the interest, and the necessary expenses Babu incurred in keeping it safe (section 173). Limits and conditions on the pawnee Rule. The Act sets these limits. He may not retain the goods for any debt or promise other than that for which they are pledged, in the absence of a contract to that effect (section 174). Such a contract is presumed for subsequent advances he makes, in the absence of anything to the contrary. He must give the pawnor reasonable notice of a sale (section 176). He must pay over to the pawnor any surplus if the sale proceeds exceed the amount due (section 176). Example. Babu holds Anil's chain for the Rs 50,000 loan. Anil also owes Babu Rs 10,000 on a separate old debt. Without a contract to that effect, Babu may not retain the chain for the old debt (section 174). If Babu lends Anil a further Rs 20,000 later, a contract to retain the chain for that advance is presumed, unless there is anything to the contrary. The pawnee's remedies on default (section 176) Rule. If the pawnor makes default in payment, or in performance of the promise at the stipulated time, the pawnee has two remedies. He may sue the pawnor on the debt or promise, and retain the goods as collateral security. He may sell the thing pledged, on giving the pawnor reasonable notice of the sale. After a sale, the accounts work as follows. Proceeds less than the amount due: the pawnor is still liable to pay the balance. Proceeds more than the amount due: the pawnee must pay the surplus to the pawnor. Example. Anil defaults on the Rs 50,000 loan. Babu gives Anil reasonable notice and sells the chain for Rs 45,000. The amount due is Rs 50,000. Anil still owes Babu the balance of Rs 5,000. Had the chain fetched Rs 55,000, Babu would have to pay Anil the surplus of Rs 5,000. Rights and duties of the pawnor Rule. The pawnor has the right to redeem the goods after default, at any subsequent time before the actual sale, if a time was stipulated for payment (section 177). He must then pay, in addition, any expenses that arose from his default. He must pay extraordinary expenses incurred by the pawnee for the preservation of the goods (section 175). He is liable for any balance after a sale (section 176), and entitled to any surplus. Example. Anil defaults on the due date. Before Babu sells the chain, Anil pays the Rs 50,000 with the expenses that arose from his default. Anil may redeem the chain (section 177). What happens when the pawnor defaults How to read this: start at the top. 1. The pawnor defaults at the stipulated time. 2. The pawnee may sue on the debt and keep the goods as collateral security, or sell the goods on reasonable notice (section 176). 3. Before the actual sale, the pawnor may redeem by paying the debt and the expenses from his default (section 177). 4. After a sale, a shortfall is still owed by the pawnor. A surplus is paid to him (section 176).
keyPoints: Retainer: for the debt or promise, the interest and necessary expenses (section 173). No retainer for another debt without a contract. Presumed for subsequent advances (section 174). Extraordinary expenses for preservation: from the pawnor (section 175). On default: sue and retain as collateral security, or sell on reasonable notice. Shortfall owed. Surplus paid over (section 176). The pawnor may redeem before the actual sale, paying the expenses of his default (section 177).

selfTest.q: 1. What must the pawnee give the pawnor before selling the pledged goods?
selfTest.a: Reasonable notice of the sale (section 176). 2. Up to when may a defaulting pawnor redeem the goods? At any subsequent time before the actual sale, paying also the expenses that arose from his default (section 177). 3. If the sale proceeds exceed the amount due, what must the pawnee do? Pay over the surplus to the pawnor (section 176).

Under section 129 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a guarantee which extends to a series of transactions is called a:

Explanation. Section 129 calls a guarantee which extends to a series of transactions a continuing guarantee.

A guarantees B, a tea-dealer, payment to the amount of £100 for any tea B may from time to time supply to C. This guarantee is:

Explanation. Illustration (b) to section 129 says this is a continuing guarantee, because it covers tea supplied from time to time.

A guarantees payment of the price of five sacks of flour to be delivered by B to C. B later delivers four more sacks which C does not pay for. A is:

Explanation. Illustration (c) to section 129 says the guarantee was not a continuing guarantee, so A is not liable for the price of the four sacks.

en.meaning:
Under section 133, a variance in the terms of the contract between the principal debtor and the creditor, made without the surety's consent, discharges the surety as to:

Explanation. Section 133 says such a variance discharges the surety as to transactions subsequent to the variance.

A contract between the creditor and the principal debtor to give time to the principal debtor discharges the surety, unless the surety assents. This is in section:

Explanation. Section 135 provides that a contract by which the creditor makes a composition with, or promises to give time to, or not to sue, the principal debtor discharges the surety unless the surety assents.

Where the creditor contracts with a third person, not the principal debtor, to give time to the principal debtor, the surety is:

Explanation. Section 136 says the surety is not discharged where the contract to give time is made with a third person and not with the principal debtor.

Mere forbearance by the creditor to sue the principal debtor, with no contrary provision in the guarantee:

Which section of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 defines bailment?

Explanation. Section 148 defines bailment, bailor and bailee. Section 149 says how delivery to the bailee is made. Section 172 defines pledge.

A bailment is the delivery of goods by one person to another:

Explanation. Section 148 defines bailment as delivery of goods for some purpose, upon a contract that they shall, when the purpose is accomplished, be returned or otherwise disposed of according to the directions of the person delivering them.

The person delivering the goods in a bailment is called the:

Explanation. Under section 148, the person delivering the goods is the bailor.

The person to whom the goods are delivered in a bailment is called the:

Under section 150 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, if the goods are bailed for hire, the bailor is responsible for damage arising directly from faults in the goods:

Explanation. The second part of section 150 says that if the goods are bailed for hire, the bailor is responsible for such damage whether he was or was not aware of the faults.

A hires a carriage from B. The carriage is unsafe, though B is not aware of it, and A is injured. Under illustration (b) to section 150:

Explanation. Illustration (b) to section 150 says B is responsible to A for the injury, because the carriage was hired.

Explanation. Section 158 applies where, by the conditions of the bailment, the goods are to be kept, carried or have work done on them and the bailee is to receive no remuneration.

en.meaning:
Under section 151 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the bailee must take as much care of the goods as:

Explanation. Section 151 sets the standard as the care a man of ordinary prudence would, under similar circumstances, take of his own goods of the same bulk, quality and value.

In the absence of any special contract, the bailee who has taken the care described in section 151 is:

Explanation. Section 152 says the bailee is not responsible for loss, destruction or deterioration if he has taken the care described in section 151.

A lends B a motor car for B's own drive. B lets his daughter C drive. The car is damaged during C's drive. Under section 154, B is:

Explanation. Section 154 makes the bailee liable for any damage arising to the goods from or during a use not according to the conditions of the bailment. Illustration (a) deals with a family member riding a horse with care.

law-of-contract-ii-u2-t1.subtitle: Sections 182 to 185 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: An agent is a person employed to do any act for another, or to represent another in dealings with third persons. The person for whom the act is done, or who is represented, is the principal (section 182). Any person of the age of majority and of sound mind may employ an agent (section 183). No consideration is needed to create an agency (section 185). Key points for the answer: the definition, who may employ an agent, who may be an agent, and no consideration.
en.meaning:
Agent and principal (section 182)

Rule. An agent is a person employed to do any act for another, or to represent another in dealings with third persons. The other person is the principal. Take the definition in two parts: employed to do an act for another, or employed to represent another with third persons.

Example. Ravi lives in Hyderabad and owns a shop in Guntur. He employs Sita to run the shop and to buy goods for it from suppliers. Sita is employed to do acts for Ravi and to represent him in dealings with suppliers. Sita is the agent and Ravi is the principal.

Who may employ an agent (section 183)

Rule. Any person who is of the age of majority according to the law to which he is subject, and who is of sound mind, may employ an agent.

Example. Anil is an adult of sound mind. He may employ an agent. A person who is not of the age of majority is outside section 183.

Who may be an agent (section 184)

Rule. As between the principal and third persons, any person may become an agent. But a person who is not of the age of majority and of sound mind cannot become an agent so as to be responsible to his principal according to the Act's provisions.

Example. Babu employs a minor, Chandu, as his agent to buy goods. As between Babu and the third persons, any person may become an agent (section 184). The section also says a person who is not of the age of majority and of sound mind cannot become an agent so as to be responsible to his principal under the Act's provisions.

No consideration (section 185)

Rule. No consideration is necessary to create an agency.

Example. Dev asks his friend Esha to collect a parcel for him, and offers her nothing in return. If Esha accepts and acts for him, an agency can still arise. Section 185 does not require consideration.

Who can be a principal and an agent How to read this: follow each line to the section. 1. The principal: of the age of majority and of sound mind (section 183). 2. The agent: employed to do an act for the principal or to represent him with third persons (section 182). As between the principal and third persons, any person may be an agent. To be responsible to his principal under the Act, he must be of the age of majority and of sound mind (section 184). 3. Consideration is not necessary (section 185).
keyPoints: Agent: a person employed to do any act for another or to represent another in dealings with third persons (section 182). Any person of the age of majority and of sound mind may employ an agent (section 183). As between the principal and third persons, any person may be an agent. To be responsible to his principal, he must be of the age of majority and of sound mind (section 184). No consideration is necessary (section 185).

law-of-contract-ii-u2-t4.subtitle: Sections 190 to 195 and 210 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: An agent cannot lawfully employ another to perform acts he has undertaken to perform personally, unless trade custom allows a sub-agent or the nature of the agency requires one (section 190). A sub-agent is a person employed by, and acting under the control of, the original agent in the business of the agency (section 191). Where an agent holds authority to name another person to act for the principal, the person named is not a sub-agent but an agent of the principal (section 194). The rules on the principal's and agent's responsibility are in sections 192, 193 and 195. Key points for the answer: the definition, the three situations, and who is responsible to whom.
en.meaning:
When an agent cannot delegate (section 190)

Rule. An agent cannot lawfully employ another to perform acts he has expressly or impliedly undertaken to perform personally. The exceptions are: the ordinary custom of trade allows a sub-agent, or the nature of the agency requires one.

Example. Ravi appoints Sita to negotiate a sale herself. Sita hands the negotiation to her cousin. She undertook to perform the acts personally, and neither custom of trade nor the nature of the agency is stated. She could not lawfully do so (section 190).

A properly appointed sub-agent (sections 191 and 192)

Rule. A sub-agent is a person employed by, and acting under the control of, the original agent in the business of the agency. Where he is properly appointed, three things follow.

The principal is represented by the sub-agent as regards third persons, and is bound by and responsible for his acts as if he were an agent originally appointed by the principal. The agent is responsible to the principal for the acts of the sub-agent. The sub-agent is responsible to the agent, but not to the principal, except in cases of fraud or wilful wrong.

Example. Anil, an agent for sale, properly appoints Babu as his sub-agent to sell goods in another town. Babu's sale binds the principal as to the buyer. Anil answers to the principal for Babu's acts. Babu answers to Anil.

A sub-agent appointed without authority (section 193)

Rule. Where an agent, without authority, appoints a person as sub-agent, the agent stands towards that person as principal to agent. He is responsible for that person's acts to the principal and to third persons. The principal is not represented by, or responsible for the acts of, that person. That person is not responsible to the principal.

Example. Chandu is an agent with no authority to delegate. He appoints Dev to act. Chandu is Dev's principal and is responsible for Dev's acts to the real principal and to third persons. The real principal is not bound by Dev's acts.

A person named under authority to name (sections 194 and 195)

Rule. Where an agent has an express or implied authority to name another person to act for the principal, the person named is not a sub-agent. He is an agent of the principal for the part of the business entrusted to him (section 194). In selecting him the agent must exercise the discretion of a man of ordinary prudence in his own case. If he does, he is not responsible to the principal for the acts or negligence of the agent so selected (section 195).

Example. Esha authorizes her solicitor Farid to sell her estate by auction and to employ an auctioneer. Farid names Gopi. Gopi is not a sub-agent but Esha's agent for the sale (illustration (a) to section 194).

Termination (section 210)

Rule. The termination of an agent's authority causes the termination, subject to the rules on termination, of the authority of all sub-agents appointed by him.

Who is the other person? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Did the agent have authority to name another person to act for the principal? Yes: the person named is the principal's agent for that part (section 194), and the agent must exercise ordinary prudence in choosing (section 195). 2. Otherwise, was a sub-agent properly appointed (custom of trade, nature of the agency, or authority)? Yes: the principal is bound by his acts. The agent answers to the principal for him (section 192). 3. Was a sub-agent appointed without authority? The agent is principal to him and responsible to the principal and third persons. The principal is not bound (section 193).
keyPoints: No delegation of acts undertaken personally, unless trade custom allows or the nature of the agency requires (section 190). Sub-agent: employed by and under the control of the agent (section 191). Properly appointed: principal bound. Agent responsible to principal. Sub-agent responsible to agent, to principal only for fraud or wilful wrong (section 192). Without authority: agent is principal to the sub-agent. The principal is not bound (section 193). Person named under authority to name: the principal's agent (section 194). Ordinary prudence in choosing (section 195). Termination of the agent's authority ends sub-agents' authority (section 210).

No. The principal is not represented by, or responsible for the acts of, such a person (section 193).

A sub-agent is a person employed by, and acting under the control of, the original agent in the business of the agency (section 191). Where an agent holds authority to name another person to act for the principal, the person named is not a sub-agent but an agent of the principal (section 194). The rules on the principal's and agent's responsibility are in sections 192, 193 and 195. Key points for the answer: the definition, the three situations, and who is responsible to whom.
te.meaning: When an agent cannot delegate (section 190) Rule. An agent cannot lawfully employ another to perform acts he has expressly or impliedly undertaken to perform personally. The exceptions are: the ordinary custom of trade allows a sub-agent, or the nature of the agency requires one. Example. Ravi appoints Sita to negotiate a sale herself. Sita hands the negotiation to her cousin. She undertook to perform the acts personally, and neither custom of trade nor the nature of the agency is stated. She could not lawfully do so (section 190). A properly appointed sub-agent (sections 191 and 192) Rule. A sub-agent is a person employed by, and acting under the control of, the original agent in the business of the agency. Where he is properly appointed, three things follow. The principal is represented by the sub-agent as regards third persons, and is bound by and responsible for his acts as if he were an agent originally appointed by the principal. The agent is responsible to the principal for the acts of the sub-agent. The sub-agent is responsible to the agent, but not to the principal, except in cases of fraud or wilful wrong. Example. Anil, an agent for sale, properly appoints Babu as his sub-agent to sell goods in another town. Babu's sale binds the principal as to the buyer. Anil answers to the principal for Babu's acts. Babu answers to Anil. A sub-agent appointed without authority (section 193) Rule. Where an agent, without authority, appoints a person as sub-agent, the agent stands towards that person as principal to agent. He is responsible for that person's acts to the principal and to third persons. The principal is not represented by, or responsible for the acts of, that person. That person is not responsible to the principal. Example. Chandu is an agent with no authority to delegate. He appoints Dev to act. Chandu is Dev's principal and is responsible for Dev's acts to the real principal and to third persons. The real principal is not bound by Dev's acts. A person named under authority to name (sections 194 and 195) Rule. Where an agent has an express or implied authority to name another person to act for the principal, the person named is not a sub-agent. He is an agent of the principal for the part of the business entrusted to him (section 194). In selecting him the agent must exercise the discretion of a man of ordinary prudence in his own case. If he does, he is not responsible to the principal for the acts or negligence of the agent so selected (section 195). Example. Esha authorizes her solicitor Farid to sell her estate by auction and to employ an auctioneer. Farid names Gopi. Gopi is not a sub-agent but Esha's agent for the sale (illustration (a) to section 194). Termination (section 210) Rule. The termination of an agent's authority causes the termination, subject to the rules on termination, of the authority of all sub-agents appointed by him. Who is the other person? Yes: the person named is the principal's agent for that part (section 194), and the agent must exercise ordinary prudence in choosing (section 195). 2. Otherwise, was a sub-agent properly appointed (custom of trade, nature of the agency, or authority)? Yes: the principal is bound by his acts. The agent answers to the principal for him (section 192). 3. Was a sub-agent appointed without authority? The agent is principal to him and responsible to the principal and third persons. The principal is not bound (section 193).

Under section 173 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the pawnee may retain the goods pledged for the debt and also for:

Explanation. Section 173 lets the pawnee retain the goods for the debt or promise, the interest of the debt, and all necessary expenses of possession or preservation.

In the absence of a contract to that effect, under section 174 the pawnee may retain the goods pledged for:

Under section 174, a contract to retain the goods for subsequent advances made by the pawnee is:

Explanation. Section 174 says such a contract shall be presumed in regard to subsequent advances made by the pawnee, in the absence of anything to the contrary.

law-of-contract-ii-u2-t5.subtitle: Sections 230, 233, 235 and 236 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: The general rule is that, in the absence of a contract to that effect, an agent cannot personally enforce contracts made for his principal, and is not personally bound by them (section 230). The Act presumes a contract to the contrary in three cases: an agent for a merchant resident abroad, an agent who does not disclose his principal's name, and a principal who, though disclosed, cannot be sued. Where the agent is personally liable, the third person may hold either him or his principal, or both, liable (section 233). A pretended agent is liable to compensate the other if the alleged employer does not ratify (section 235). Key points for the answer: the rule, the three cases, and sections 233, 235 and 236.
en.meaning:
The general rule (section 230)

Rule. Without a contract to that effect, an agent cannot personally enforce contracts he makes for his principal and is not personally bound by them.

Example. Ravi, an agent, signs a contract with Sita for the sale of Chandu's goods, naming Chandu as principal. There is no contract that Ravi is personally bound. Ravi cannot sue Sita on the contract, and Sita cannot sue Ravi personally on it.

Three cases where a contract to the contrary is presumed (section 230)

Rule. The Act presumes that the agent is personally bound and may enforce in three cases.

The agent makes the contract for the sale or purchase of goods for a merchant resident abroad. The agent does not disclose the name of his principal. The principal, though disclosed, cannot be sued.

Example. Anil buys goods from Babu for a principal and does not tell Babu the principal's name. The Act presumes a contract that Anil is personally bound (case 2).

Choice of whom to hold liable (section 233)

Rule. Where the agent is personally liable, the third person may hold either the agent or the principal, or both, liable.

Example. A contracts to sell B 100 bales of cotton, and afterwards discovers that B was acting as agent for C. A may sue B or C, or both, for the price (the Act's illustration).

Pretended agent (section 235)

Rule. A person who untruly represents himself as the authorized agent of another, and thereby induces a third person to deal with him as agent, is liable to compensate the third person for any loss or damage incurred by so dealing, if his alleged employer does not ratify his acts.

Example. Dev falsely tells Esha that he is Farid's authorized agent and sells her goods in Farid's name. Farid does not ratify. Dev must compensate Esha for her loss from dealing with him.

Person falsely contracting as agent (section 236)

Rule. A person who contracted in the character of agent cannot require performance, if he was in reality acting on his own account and not as agent.

Is the agent personally liable? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Is there a contract that the agent is personally bound? If yes, he is personally bound. 2. If not, is the contract for goods for a merchant resident abroad, or is the principal's name not disclosed, or can the disclosed principal not be sued? If yes, such a contract is presumed (section 230). 3. Where the agent is personally liable, the third person may hold him, the principal, or both liable (section 233). 4. Was he not an authorized agent at all? He must compensate the third person if the alleged employer does not ratify (section 235).
keyPoints: General rule: the agent neither enforces nor is bound by the contract, absent a contract to that effect (section 230). Presumed to the contrary: agent for a merchant abroad, undisclosed principal's name, principal who cannot be sued (section 230). Where the agent is personally liable, the third person may hold him, the principal or both liable (section 233). A pretended agent compensates the third person if the alleged employer does not ratify (section 235). A person acting on his own account as a false agent cannot require performance (section 236).

law-of-contract-ii-u2-t3.subtitle: Sections 211 to 225 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: An agent must follow his principal's directions or the custom of the place (section 211), use reasonable skill and diligence (section 212), render accounts (section 213), communicate in difficulty (section 214), and pay over what he receives for the principal (section 218). He must not deal on his own account in the agency business without the principal's consent (sections 215 and 216). The agent may retain what is due to him out of sums received (section 217), has a lien (section 221), and is entitled to be indemnified (sections 222 and 223). Key points for the answer: each duty and right with its section and the Act's illustrations.
en.meaning:
Duties of the agent

Rule. The agent has these duties.

Follow directions or custom (section 211). Loss on departure is made good, and profit is accounted for. Skill and diligence (section 212). As much skill as persons in similar business generally have, unless the principal knows of his want of skill. Reasonable diligence always. Compensation for direct, not remote, consequences of his neglect. Accounts (section 213). Proper accounts on demand. Communicate (section 214). In difficulty, use all reasonable diligence to communicate and seek instructions. Do not deal on own account (sections 215 and 216). Consent and disclosure are needed. Without them, the principal may repudiate if a material fact was dishonestly concealed or the dealing was disadvantageous (section 215). If the agent deals for himself without the principal's knowledge, the principal may claim the benefit (section 216). Pay over sums received (section 218), after the deductions in section 217.

Example. Ravi directs his agent Sita to buy a particular house for him. Sita tells Ravi it cannot be bought and buys it herself. Ravi may compel Sita to sell it to him at the price she paid (section 216, the Act's illustration).

Rights of the agent

Rule. The agent has these rights.

Retainer (section 217). He may retain, out of sums received on the principal's account, moneys due for advances, expenses properly incurred and his remuneration. Remuneration (sections 219 and 220). In the absence of a special contract it is due on completion of the act. He may detain moneys received for goods sold. An agent guilty of misconduct has no remuneration for the part misconducted. Lien (section 221). In the absence of a contract to the contrary, he may retain the principal's goods, papers and other property until the amount due for commission, disbursements and services is paid or accounted for. Indemnity (sections 222 to 225). The principal must indemnify him against the consequences of lawful acts done in exercise of his authority (section 222) and of acts done in good faith, though they injure third persons (section 223). He is not entitled to indemnity for a criminal act (section 224). The principal must compensate injury caused by his own neglect or want of skill (section 225).

Example. Anil, a broker, buys oil for Babu on Babu's orders. Babu repudiates the contract, and the seller sues Anil, who defends unsuccessfully and pays damages and costs. Babu must indemnify Anil for the damages, costs and expenses (section 222, illustration (b)).

When the agent deals on his own account How to read this: start at the top. 1. The agent deals on his own account in the business of the agency. 2. Did he first obtain the principal's consent and tell him all material circumstances? If not, the principal may repudiate if a material fact was dishonestly concealed or the dealing was disadvantageous (section 215). 3. Did he deal without the principal's knowledge, instead of on the principal's account? The principal may claim any benefit the agent gained (section 216).
keyPoints: The agent follows directions or custom (section 211) and uses skill and diligence (section 212). Accounts on demand (section 213). Communicate in difficulty (section 214). No dealing on his own account without consent and disclosure (sections 215, 216). Retainer (section 217). Remuneration (sections 219, 220). Lien (section 221). Indemnity (sections 222, 223). Not for a criminal act (section 224). Compensation for the principal's neglect (section 225).

In the absence of a contract to the contrary, until the amount due to him for commission, disbursements and services is paid or accounted for (section 221). 3. Is the employer bound to indemnify the agent for a criminal act? No (section 224).

hi.inOneMinute: An agent must follow his principal's directions or the custom of the place (section 211), use reasonable skill and diligence (section 212), render accounts (section 213), communicate in difficulty (section 214), and pay over what he receives for the principal (section 218). He must not deal on his own account in the agency business without the principal's consent (sections 215 and 216). The agent may retain what is due to him out of sums received (section 217), has a lien (section 221), and is entitled to be indemnified (sections 222 and 223). Key points for the answer: each duty and right with its section and the Act's illustrations.
hi.meaning: Duties of the agent Rule. The agent has these duties. Follow directions or custom (section 211). Loss on departure is made good, and profit is accounted for. Skill and diligence (section 212). As much skill as persons in similar business generally have, unless the principal knows of his want of skill. Reasonable diligence always. Compensation for direct, not remote, consequences of his neglect. Accounts (section 213). Proper accounts on demand. Communicate (section 214). In difficulty, use all reasonable diligence to communicate and seek instructions. Do not deal on own account (sections 215 and 216). Consent and disclosure are needed. Without them, the principal may repudiate if a material fact was dishonestly concealed or the dealing was disadvantageous (section 215). If the agent deals for himself without the principal's knowledge, the principal may claim the benefit (section 216). Pay over sums received (section 218), after the deductions in section 217. Example. Ravi directs his agent Sita to buy a particular house for him. Sita tells Ravi it cannot be bought and buys it herself. Ravi may compel Sita to sell it to him at the price she paid (section 216, the Act's illustration). Rights of the agent Rule. The agent has these rights. Retainer (section 217). He may retain, out of sums received on the principal's account, moneys due for advances, expenses properly incurred and his remuneration. Remuneration (sections 219 and 220). In the absence of a special contract it is due on completion of the act. He may detain moneys received for goods sold. An agent guilty of misconduct has no remuneration for the part misconducted. Lien (section 221). In the absence of a contract to the contrary, he may retain the principal's goods, papers and other property until the amount due for commission, disbursements and services is paid or accounted for. Indemnity (sections 222 to 225). The principal must indemnify him against the consequences of lawful acts done in exercise of his authority (section 222) and of acts done in good faith, though they injure third persons (section 223). He is not entitled to indemnity for a criminal act (section 224). The principal must compensate injury caused by his own neglect or want of skill (section 225). Example. Anil, a broker, buys oil for Babu on Babu's orders. Babu repudiates the contract, and the seller sues Anil, who defends unsuccessfully and pays damages and costs. Babu must indemnify Anil for the damages, costs and expenses (section 222, illustration (b)). When the agent deals on his own account How to read this: start at the top. 1. The agent deals on his own account in the business of the agency. 2. Did he first obtain the principal's consent and tell him all material circumstances? If not, the principal may repudiate if a material fact was dishonestly concealed or the dealing was disadvantageous (section 215). 3. Did he deal without the principal's knowledge, instead of on the principal's account? The principal may claim any benefit the agent gained (section 216).
keyPoints: The agent follows directions or custom (section 211) and uses skill and diligence (section 212). Accounts on demand (section 213). Communicate in difficulty (section 214). No dealing on his own account without consent and disclosure (sections 215, 216). Retainer (section 217). Remuneration (sections 219, 220). Lien (section 221). Indemnity (sections 222, 223). Not for a criminal act (section 224). Compensation for the principal's neglect (section 225).

law-of-contract-ii-u2-t2.subtitle: Sections 185 to 189, 196 to 200 and 237 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: An agent's authority may be express or implied (sections 186 and 187). No consideration is necessary (section 185). An agent has authority in an emergency to protect his principal from loss (section 189). A person may also ratify acts done on his behalf without his authority (sections 196 to 200). A principal who leads third persons to believe that an agent's acts were authorized is bound by them (section 237). Key points for the answer: express and implied authority, emergency, ratification with its limits, and a principal who induces belief in authority.
en.meaning:
Express and implied authority (sections 186 and 187)

Rule. An agent's authority is express when given by words spoken or written, and implied when inferred from the circumstances. The ordinary course of dealing may be a circumstance. No consideration is necessary (section 185).

Example. Ravi tells Sita in writing to buy stock for his shop. That is express authority. Sita has long ordered goods in Ravi's name for the shop, and Ravi, with knowledge, has paid for them from his own funds. Sita has implied authority to order further goods for the shop. This follows the illustration to section 187.

Extent of authority (section 188)

Rule. An agent authorized to do an act may do every lawful thing necessary to do it. An agent authorized to carry on a business may do every lawful thing necessary, or usually done in conducting that business.

Authority in an emergency (section 189)

Rule. In an emergency the agent may do all such acts to protect the principal from loss as a person of ordinary prudence would do in his own case.

Example. Kiran, agent of Lata, receives fruit to forward to another town. The fruit will spoil on the journey. Kiran may sell it where he is, as in the Act's illustration (b).

Ratification (sections 196 to 199)

Rule. Where acts are done on behalf of a person without his knowledge or authority, he may ratify or disown them. If he ratifies them, the effects are the same as if they had been done with his authority (section 196). Ratification may be express or implied in his conduct (section 197). It is not valid if his knowledge of the facts is materially defective (section 198). Ratifying one act ratifies the whole transaction of which it was a part (section 199).

Example. Dev buys goods in Esha's name without authority. Esha later sells those goods to Farid on her own account. Her conduct implies ratification of the purchase. This follows illustration (a) to section 197.

Limits on ratification (section 200)

Rule. An unauthorized act that would subject a third person to damages, or end a right or interest of a third person, cannot be given that effect by ratification.

Example. Gopi holds a lease from Hema, ending on three months' notice. Ibrahim, without Hema's authority, gives Gopi notice to end the lease. Hema cannot ratify the notice so as to bind Gopi. This is illustration (b) to section 200.

A principal who induces belief in authority (section 237)

Rule. A principal is bound by his agent's unauthorized acts if by his words or conduct he induced third persons to believe they were within the agent's authority.

Example. A consigns goods to B for sale with a private instruction not to sell below a fixed price. C, knowing nothing of the instruction, buys below that price. A is bound by the contract (illustration (a) to section 237).

Ratification: can the principal ratify? How to read this: start at the top. 1. An act was done on his behalf without his knowledge or authority. He may ratify or disown it (section 196). 2. Is his knowledge of the facts materially defective? If yes, no valid ratification (section 198). 3. Would the act subject a third person to damages or end his right or interest? If yes, ratification cannot give it that effect (section 200). 4. Otherwise he ratifies the whole transaction (section 199), with the same effect as if authorized.
keyPoints: No consideration is necessary to create an agency (section 185). Authority may be express or implied (sections 186 and 187). In an emergency the agent may act as a person of ordinary prudence would to protect the principal (section 189). Ratification: same effect as authority (section 196). Not valid on materially defective knowledge (section 198). The whole transaction (section 199). Cannot hurt a third person (section 200). Holding out binds the principal (section 237).

Otherwise he ratifies the whole transaction (section 199), with the same effect as if authorized.

law-of-contract-ii-u2-t7.subtitle: Sections 201 to 210 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: An agency is terminated by the principal revoking his authority, by the agent renouncing the business, by completion of the business, by the death or unsoundness of mind of either, or by the principal being adjudicated an insolvent (section 201). Where the agent has an interest in the subject-matter, the agency cannot be terminated to the prejudice of that interest without an express contract (section 202). Reasonable notice is needed (section 206), and the termination takes effect only when it becomes known (section 208). Key points for the answer: the ways of termination, the limits on revocation, and the effect of notice.
en.meaning:
Ways an agency ends (section 201)

Rule. An agency is terminated in these ways.

The principal revokes the authority. The agent renounces the business of the agency. The business of the agency is completed. Either the principal or the agent dies or becomes of unsound mind. The principal is adjudicated an insolvent under any Act for the relief of insolvent debtors.

Example. Ravi appoints Sita as his agent to sell his scooter. Sita sells it and hands over the price. The business of the agency is completed, and the agency ends.

Agent with an interest in the subject-matter (section 202)

Rule. Where the agent has himself an interest in the property which is the subject-matter of the agency, then, without an express contract, the agency cannot be terminated to the prejudice of that interest.

Example. Anil authorizes Babu to sell Anil's land and to pay himself out of the proceeds the debts Anil owes him. Anil cannot revoke the authority, and Anil's death or insanity does not end it (the Act's illustration (a)).

Revocation (sections 203 and 204)

Rule. Subject to section 202, the principal may revoke at any time before the authority has been exercised so as to bind him (section 203). He cannot revoke after it has been partly exercised, as regards acts and obligations arising from acts already done (section 204).

Example. Chandu authorizes Dev to buy 1,000 bales of cotton for him, to be paid for from Chandu's money in Dev's hands. Dev buys in his own name, making himself personally liable. Chandu cannot revoke Dev's authority as regards payment for that cotton (section 204, illustration (a)).

Compensation and notice (sections 205 and 206)

Rule. Where there is an express or implied contract that the agency will continue for a period, the party who revokes or renounces earlier without sufficient cause must compensate the other (section 205). Reasonable notice must be given of revocation or renunciation. Otherwise the damage must be made good by the one to the other (section 206).

Express or implied revocation (section 207)

Rule. Revocation and renunciation may be express or implied in conduct. If A empowers B to let A's house and then lets it himself, this implies revocation of B's authority.

When termination takes effect (section 208)

Rule. Termination does not take effect as regards the agent before it becomes known to him, or as regards third persons before it becomes known to them.

Example. A directs B to sell goods at five per cent commission and later revokes by letter. B sells for 100 rupees after the letter is sent but before he receives it. The sale binds A, and B is entitled to 5 rupees commission (the Act's illustration (a)).

Duty on the principal's death or insanity, and sub-agents (sections 209 and 210)

Rule. When the agency ends by the principal's death or unsoundness of mind, the agent must take all reasonable steps, on behalf of the principal's representatives, to protect and preserve the interests entrusted to him (section 209). Termination of the agent's authority terminates the authority of his sub-agents, subject to the rules in the Chapter (section 210).

Can the principal revoke? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Does the agent have an interest in the subject-matter, and is there no express contract to the contrary? Then the agency cannot be terminated to the prejudice of that interest (section 202). 2. Has the authority been partly exercised? The principal cannot revoke as regards acts and obligations arising from acts already done (section 204). 3. Otherwise he may revoke before the authority has been exercised so as to bind him (section 203), giving reasonable notice (section 206). The termination takes effect when it becomes known to the agent and to third persons (section 208).
keyPoints: Section 201: revocation, renunciation, completion, death or unsound mind of either, insolvency of the principal. An agent's interest in the subject-matter limits termination (section 202). No revocation after partial exercise, as regards acts already done (section 204). Reasonable notice (section 206). Compensation for earlier termination without sufficient cause (section 205). Termination takes effect when it becomes known (section 208). Termination ends sub-agents' authority (section 210).

Which section of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 lists the ways in which an agency is terminated?

Explanation. Section 201 lists revocation, renunciation, completion, death or unsound mind of either party, and insolvency of the principal.

Which of these does NOT terminate an agency under section 201?

Explanation. A change of the agent's residence is not among the ways listed in section 201.

Under section 202, where the agent has himself an interest in the subject-matter of the agency, the agency, in the absence of an express contract, cannot be terminated:

Explanation. Section 202 says the agency cannot, in the absence of an express contract, be terminated to the prejudice of such interest.

Subject to section 202, under section 203 the principal may revoke the authority:

Where a sub-agent is properly appointed, the principal, as regards third persons, is:

law-of-contract-ii-u2-t6.subtitle: Sections 226 to 229, 231, 232, 234, 237 and 238 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: Contracts made through an agent have the same legal consequences as if the principal had made them himself (section 226). Where an agent does more than he is authorized to do, the principal is bound only by what is within the authority if it can be separated (section 227), and not at all if it cannot (section 228). Notice given to the agent in the course of the business is notice to the principal (section 229). The Act also deals with a contract made with an agent who is supposed to be the principal (sections 231 and 232), with inducing a belief that only one of them will be held liable (section 234), with a principal who induces belief in the agent's authority (section 237), and with an agent's misrepresentation or fraud (section 238). Key points for the answer: each section with the Act's illustration.
en.meaning:
Enforcement and consequences of the agent's contracts (section 226)

Rule. Contracts entered into through an agent, and obligations from acts done by him, are enforced and have the same consequences as if the principal had done them.

Example. Ravi's agent Sita, with authority to receive money, receives Rs 10,000 due to Ravi from Chandu. Chandu is discharged of his obligation to pay it to Ravi (illustration (b)).

Agent exceeds authority (sections 227 and 228)

Rule. If the part within authority can be separated, the principal is bound by that part only (section 227). If it cannot be separated, the principal is not bound to recognize the transaction (section 228).

Example. Anil authorizes Babu to buy 500 sheep. Babu buys 500 sheep and 200 lambs for one sum. The excess cannot be separated. Anil may repudiate the whole transaction (the Act's illustration to section 228).

Notice to the agent (section 229)

Rule. Notice given to, or information obtained by, the agent in the course of the business he transacts for the principal has the same consequences as if given to or obtained by the principal.

Contract with an agent supposed to be the principal (sections 231, 232 and 234)

Rule. Where a person contracts with an agent without knowing or having reason to suspect that he is an agent, the principal may require performance (section 231). The other party has against the principal the rights he would have had against the agent. If the principal discloses himself before the contract is completed, the other party may refuse to fulfil it if he can show he would not have entered into it had he known who the principal was or that the agent was not a principal. The principal obtains performance only subject to the rights and obligations between the agent and the other party (section 232). A person who induces the agent to believe that the principal only will be held liable, or the principal to believe that the agent only will be held liable, cannot afterwards hold the other liable (section 234).

Example. A, who owes B 500 rupees, sells B rice worth 1,000 rupees as agent for C, and B does not know this. C cannot compel B to take the rice without allowing B to set off A's debt (the Act's illustration to section 232).

Principal who induces belief in authority (section 237)

Rule. The principal is bound by the agent's unauthorized acts if by his words or conduct he induced third persons to believe they were within the agent's authority.

Misrepresentation or fraud by the agent (section 238)

Rule. Misrepresentation or fraud by agents acting in the course of their business has the same effect on agreements as if by the principals. In matters that do not fall within the agents' authority, it does not affect the principals. Illustration (a): A, B's agent for sale, induces C to buy by a misrepresentation he was not authorized to make. The contract is voidable, as between B and C, at the option of C.

Is the principal bound? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Was the contract entered into through an agent? Yes: same consequences as if the principal made it (section 226). 2. Did the agent exceed his authority? Can the excess be separated? Yes: the principal is bound only by the part within authority (section 227). No: he is not bound to recognize the transaction (section 228). 3. Did the principal by words or conduct induce the third person to believe the act was authorized? Yes: he is bound (section 237).
keyPoints: An agent's contract has the same consequences as the principal's own (section 226). Excess of authority: separable, the principal is bound by the part within authority (section 227). Not separable, he is not bound (section 228). Notice to the agent in the course of the business is notice to the principal (section 229). Undisclosed principal: sections 231 and 232, with set-off. Inducing belief of exclusive liability bars a later claim against the other (section 234). The principal is bound where his words or conduct induced belief in the agent's authority (section 237). An agent's misrepresentation in the course of business binds the principal as his own (section 238).

selfTest.q: 1. What if the agent's excess of authority cannot be separated from what is within it?
selfTest.a: The principal is not bound to recognize the transaction (section 228). 2. Under section 232, on what footing may the principal obtain performance of a contract made with an agent supposed to be the principal? Subject to the rights and obligations subsisting between the agent and the other party. 3. If an agent induces a buyer by a misrepresentation he was not authorized to make, whose option is the contract? The buyer's. It is voidable at his option (section 238, illustration (a)).

hi.inOneMinute: Contracts made through an agent have the same legal consequences as if the principal had made them himself (section 226). Where an agent does more than he is authorized to do, the principal is bound only by what is within the authority if it can be separated (section 227), and not at all if it cannot (section 228). Notice given to the agent in the course of the business is notice to the principal (section 229). The Act also deals with a contract made with an agent who is supposed to be the principal (sections 231 and 232), with inducing a belief that only one of them will be held liable (section 234), with a principal who induces belief in the agent's authority (section 237), and with an agent's misrepresentation or fraud (section 238). Key points for the answer: each section with the Act's illustration.
hi.meaning: Enforcement and consequences of the agent's contracts (section 226) Rule. Contracts entered into through an agent, and obligations from acts done by him, are enforced and have the same consequences as if the principal had done them. Example. Ravi's agent Sita, with authority to receive money, receives Rs 10,000 due to Ravi from Chandu. Chandu is discharged of his obligation to pay it to Ravi (illustration (b)). Agent exceeds authority (sections 227 and 228) Rule. If the part within authority can be separated, the principal is bound by that part only (section 227). If it cannot be separated, the principal is not bound to recognize the transaction (section 228). Example. Anil authorizes Babu to buy 500 sheep. Babu buys 500 sheep and 200 lambs for one sum. The excess cannot be separated. Anil may repudiate the whole transaction (the Act's illustration to section 228). Notice to the agent (section 229) Rule. Notice given to, or information obtained by, the agent in the course of the business he transacts for the principal has the same consequences as if given to or obtained by the principal. Contract with an agent supposed to be the principal (sections 231, 232 and 234) Rule. Where a person contracts with an agent without knowing or having reason to suspect that he is an agent, the principal may require performance (section 231). The other party has against the principal the rights he would have had against the agent. If the principal discloses himself before the contract is completed, the other party may refuse to fulfil it if he can show he would not have entered into it had he known who the principal was or that the agent was not a principal. The principal obtains performance only subject to the rights and obligations between the agent and the other party (section 232). A person who induces the agent to believe that the principal only will be held liable, or the principal to believe that the agent only will be held liable, cannot afterwards hold the other liable (section 234). Example. A, who owes B 500 rupees, sells B rice worth 1,000 rupees as agent for C, and B does not know this. C cannot compel B to take the rice without allowing B to set off A's debt (the Act's illustration to section 232). Principal who induces belief in authority (section 237) Rule. The principal is bound by the agent's unauthorized acts if by his words or conduct he induced third persons to believe they were within the agent's authority. Misrepresentation or fraud by the agent (section 238) Rule. Misrepresentation or fraud by agents acting in the course of their business has the same effect on agreements as if by the principals. In matters that do not fall within the agents' authority, it does not affect the principals. Illustration (a): A, B's agent for sale, induces C to buy by a misrepresentation he was not authorized to make. The contract is voidable, as between B and C, at the option of C. Is the principal bound? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Was the contract entered into through an agent? Yes: same consequences as if the principal made it (section 226). 2. Did the agent exceed his authority? Can the excess be separated? Yes: the principal is bound only by the part within authority (section 227). No: he is not bound to recognize the transaction (section 228). 3. Did the principal by words or conduct induce the third person to believe the act was authorized? Yes: he is bound (section 237).
keyPoints: An agent's contract has the same consequences as the principal's own (section 226). Excess of authority: separable, the principal is bound by the part within authority (section 227). Not separable, he is not bound (section 228). Notice to the agent in the course of the business is notice to the principal (section 229). Undisclosed principal: sections 231 and 232, with set-off. Inducing belief of exclusive liability bars a later claim against the other (section 234). The principal is bound where his words or conduct induced belief in the agent's authority (section 237). An agent's misrepresentation in the course of business binds the principal as his own (section 238).

selfTest.q: 1. What if the agent's excess of authority cannot be separated from what is within it?
selfTest.a: The principal is not bound to recognize the transaction (section 228). 2. Under section 232, on what footing may the principal obtain performance of a contract made with an agent supposed to be the principal? Subject to the rights and obligations subsisting between the agent and the other party. 3. If an agent induces a buyer by a misrepresentation he was not authorized to make, whose option is the contract? The buyer's. It is voidable at his option (section 238, illustration (a)).

law-of-contract-ii-u3-t3.subtitle: Sections 11 to 13 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930

en.inOneMinute: A stipulation in a contract of sale may be a condition or a warranty (section 12(1)). A condition is essential to the main purpose of the contract, and its breach gives a right to treat the contract as repudiated (section 12(2)). A warranty is collateral to the main purpose, and its breach gives a claim for damages only (section 12(3)). Whether a stipulation is a condition or a warranty depends on the construction of the contract, not on the name used (section 12(4)). A buyer may waive a condition or treat its breach as a breach of warranty, and after accepting the goods in a contract that is not severable he can generally only claim for breach of warranty (section 13). Time of payment is not of the essence unless a different intention appears (section 11).
en.meaning:
Condition and warranty (section 12)

Rule. A stipulation about the goods may be a condition or a warranty.

A condition is essential to the main purpose of the contract. Its breach gives a right to treat the contract as repudiated. A warranty is collateral to the main purpose. Its breach gives a claim for damages, but no right to reject the goods and treat the contract as repudiated.

Example. Asha orders a "new" refrigerator. The refrigerator delivered is old. Being new is essential to what she bought, so this is a breach of a condition, and she may treat the contract as repudiated (section 12(2)). If instead the seller had promised a free carry-bag with it and did not give it, that stipulation is collateral to the main purpose and the claim is for damages (section 12(3)).

Name does not decide (section 12(4))

Rule. Whether a stipulation is a condition or a warranty depends in each case on the construction of the contract. A stipulation may be a condition though called a warranty in the contract.

Stipulations as to time (section 11)

Rule. Unless a different intention appears from the terms of the contract, stipulations as to time of payment are not of the essence of a contract of sale. For any other stipulation as to time, whether it is of the essence depends on the terms of the contract.

Example. A buyer agrees to pay on the 1st of the month and pays on the 5th. Unless the contract shows a different intention, the seller cannot treat the contract as repudiated only for the late payment (section 11).

When a condition is treated as a warranty (section 13)

Rule. Section 13 gives three rules.

Where the contract is subject to a condition to be fulfilled by the seller, the buyer may waive it, or elect to treat its breach as a breach of warranty (section 13(1)). Where the contract is not severable and the buyer has accepted the goods or part of them, the breach of any condition to be fulfilled by the seller can only be treated as a breach of warranty. He cannot reject the goods and treat the contract as repudiated, unless there is a term of the contract, express or implied, to that effect (section 13(2)). The section does not affect a condition or warranty whose fulfilment is excused by law by reason of impossibility or otherwise (section 13(3)).

Example. Bala buys a whole lot of 100 chairs under one contract that is not severable. He accepts the lot. Later he finds that the chairs do not match the stipulated condition. Unless the contract says otherwise, he can only treat it as a breach of warranty and claim damages. He cannot reject the chairs (section 13(2)).

Breach by the seller: reject the goods or claim damages? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Is the broken stipulation essential to the main purpose of the contract (section 12(2))? If yes, it is a condition. Go to step 2. If it is only collateral, it is a warranty: the buyer claims damages and cannot reject the goods (section 12(3)). 2. Has the buyer waived the condition or chosen to treat the breach as a breach of warranty (section 13(1))? If yes, he claims damages only. 3. Is the contract non-severable and has the buyer accepted the goods or part of them (section 13(2))? If yes, and the contract has no term to the contrary, he can treat the breach only as a breach of warranty. Otherwise he may treat the contract as repudiated.
keyPoints: Condition: essential to the main purpose. Breach gives a right to repudiate (section 12(2)). Warranty: collateral to the main purpose. Breach gives damages only (section 12(3)). The construction of the contract decides, not the name (section 12(4)). Time of payment is not of the essence unless a different intention appears (section 11). The buyer may waive a condition or treat its breach as a breach of warranty (section 13(1)). After acceptance in a non-severable contract, breach of condition is treated as breach of warranty, unless the contract says otherwise (section 13(2)).

Its breach gives a claim for damages, but no right to reject the goods and treat the contract as repudiated. Example. Asha orders a "new" refrigerator. The refrigerator delivered is old. Being new is essential to what she bought, so this is a breach of a condition, and she may treat the contract as repudiated (section 12(2)). If instead the seller had promised a free carry-bag with it and did not give it, that stipulation is collateral to the main purpose and the claim is for damages (section 12(3)). Name does not decide (section 12(4)) Rule. Whether a stipulation is a condition or a warranty depends in each case on the construction of the contract. A stipulation may be a condition though called a warranty in the contract. Stipulations as to time (section 11) Rule. Unless a different intention appears from the terms of the contract, stipulations as to time of payment are not of the essence of a contract of sale. For any other stipulation as to time, whether it is of the essence depends on the terms of the contract. Example. A buyer agrees to pay on the 1st of the month and pays on the 5th. Unless the contract shows a different intention, the seller cannot treat the contract as repudiated only for the late payment (section 11). When a condition is treated as a warranty (section 13) Rule. Section 13 gives three rules. Where the contract is subject to a condition to be fulfilled by the seller, the buyer may waive it, or elect to treat its breach as a breach of warranty (section 13(1)). Where the contract is not severable and the buyer has accepted the goods or part of them, the breach of any condition to be fulfilled by the seller can only be treated as a breach of warranty. He cannot reject the goods and treat the contract as repudiated, unless there is a term of the contract, express or implied, to that effect (section 13(2)). The section does not affect a condition or warranty whose fulfilment is excused by law by reason of impossibility or otherwise (section 13(3)). Example. Bala buys a whole lot of 100 chairs under one contract that is not severable. He accepts the lot. Later he finds that the chairs do not match the stipulated condition. Unless the contract says otherwise, he can only treat it as a breach of warranty and claim damages. He cannot reject the chairs (section 13(2)). Breach by the seller: reject the goods or claim damages? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Is the broken stipulation essential to the main purpose of the contract (section 12(2))? If yes, it is a condition. Go to step 2. If it is only collateral, it is a warranty: the buyer claims damages and cannot reject the goods (section 12(3)). 2. Has the buyer waived the condition or chosen to treat the breach as a breach of warranty (section 13(1))? If yes, he claims damages only. 3. Is the contract non-severable and has the buyer accepted the goods or part of them (section 13(2))? If yes, and the contract has no term to the contrary, he can treat the breach only as a breach of warranty. Otherwise he may treat the contract as repudiated.
keyPoints: Condition: essential to the main purpose. Breach gives a right to repudiate (section 12(2)). Warranty: collateral to the main purpose. Breach gives damages only (section 12(3)). The construction of the contract decides, not the name (section 12(4)). Time of payment is not of the essence unless a different intention appears (section 11). The buyer may waive a condition or treat its breach as a breach of warranty (section 13(1)). After acceptance in a non-severable contract, breach of condition is treated as breach of warranty, unless the contract says otherwise (section 13(2)).

selfTest.q: 1. What is a condition under section 12(2)?
selfTest.a: A stipulation essential to the main purpose of the contract, the breach of which gives rise to a right to treat the contract as repudiated. 2. What is the remedy for breach of a warranty under section 12(3)? A claim for damages. There is no right to reject the goods and treat the contract as repudiated. 3. Is a stipulation called a warranty always a warranty? No. It may be a condition, because the construction of the contract decides (section 12(4)). 4. Are stipulations as to time of payment of the essence? Not unless a different intention appears from the terms of the contract (section 11).

law-of-contract-ii-u3-t5.subtitle: Sections 9, 10, 63 and 64A of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930

en.inOneMinute: The price in a contract of sale may be fixed by the contract, left to be fixed in the manner agreed, or determined by the course of dealing between the parties (section 9(1)). If it is not determined in any of these ways, the buyer must pay a reasonable price , which is a question of fact (section 9(2)). If the price is to be fixed by a third party's valuation and he does not make it, the agreement is avoided, except that the buyer who has received and appropriated goods pays a reasonable price (section 10). A change in customs, excise or sales tax after the contract can change the price, unless the contract shows a different intention (section 64A). Key points for the answer: the three ways in section 9(1), the reasonable-price fall-back in section 9(2), and the effect of failure of valuation.
en.meaning:
How the price is ascertained (section 9)

Rule. The price may be (1) fixed by the contract, (2) left to be fixed in the manner agreed, or (3) determined by the course of dealing between the parties. If none of these applies, the buyer pays a reasonable price. What is reasonable is a question of fact in each case.

Example. Rita regularly buys milk from a dairy, and the dairy has always charged the same rate. They agree to continue. The price is determined by the course of dealing (section 9(1)). If Rita and the dairy had agreed nothing about price at all, Rita would pay a reasonable price (section 9(2)).

Agreement to sell at valuation (section 10)

Rule. If the agreement is to sell at a price fixed by a third party's valuation and the third party cannot or does not make the valuation, the agreement is avoided. But if the goods or any part have been delivered to and appropriated by the buyer, he must pay a reasonable price for them.

If the third party is prevented from making the valuation by the fault of the seller or the buyer, the party not at fault may sue the party at fault for damages (section 10(2)).

Example. Sunil agrees to sell his painting to Tara at the price a named valuer will fix. The valuer dies before valuing it. The agreement is avoided (section 10(1)). If Sunil had already delivered the painting and Tara had taken it as her own, she would have to pay a reasonable price (proviso).

Reasonable time (section 63)

Rule. Wherever the Act refers to a reasonable time, what is a reasonable time is a question of fact.

Changes in taxes after the contract (section 64A)

Rule. Unless a different intention appears from the terms of the contract, the seller and the buyer share the effect of changes in customs duty, excise duty, or a tax on the sale or purchase of goods after the contract is made.

If a tax or an increase takes effect, the seller may add to the price the amount paid or payable, and may sue to recover it (section 64A(1)(a)). If a decrease or remission takes effect, the buyer may deduct the amount of the decrease or the remitted tax from the price (section 64A(1)(b)). The taxes covered are duties of customs or excise on goods and taxes on the sale or purchase of goods (section 64A(2)).

Example. Umesh agrees to sell goods at Rs 1,000 with no mention of tax, when no tax was chargeable. A sales tax of Rs 50 is imposed afterwards and Umesh has to pay it. Unless the contract shows a different intention, he may add Rs 50 to the price and sue for it (section 64A(1)(a)).

What price must the buyer pay? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Is the price fixed by the contract, left to be fixed in the agreed manner, or determined by course of dealing (section 9(1))? That price is payable. 2. Is the price to be fixed by a third party's valuation (section 10)? If he does not make the valuation, the agreement is avoided, but a buyer who has received and appropriated goods pays a reasonable price. 3. Is the price not determined in any of these ways? The buyer pays a reasonable price, a question of fact (section 9(2)). 4. Did a customs, excise or sales tax change after the contract (section 64A)? Unless a different intention appears, the seller adds an increase and the buyer deducts a decrease.
keyPoints: Price: the money consideration (section 2(10)). Fixed by the contract, left to be fixed as agreed, or determined by course of dealing (section 9(1)). Otherwise a reasonable price, a question of fact (section 9(2)). Valuation by a third party fails: agreement avoided, but a buyer who has received and appropriated goods pays a reasonable price (section 10(1)). Party at fault for preventing valuation: suit for damages (section 10(2)). Reasonable time is a question of fact (section 63). Tax changes after the contract: seller may add, buyer may deduct (section 64A).

The price may be (1) fixed by the contract, (2) left to be fixed in the manner agreed, or (3) determined by the course of dealing between the parties. If none of these applies, the buyer pays a reasonable price. What is reasonable is a question of fact in each case. Example. Rita regularly buys milk from a dairy, and the dairy has always charged the same rate. They agree to continue. The price is determined by the course of dealing (section 9(1)). If Rita and the dairy had agreed nothing about price at all, Rita would pay a reasonable price (section 9(2)). Agreement to sell at valuation (section 10) Rule. If the agreement is to sell at a price fixed by a third party's valuation and the third party cannot or does not make the valuation, the agreement is avoided. But if the goods or any part have been delivered to and appropriated by the buyer, he must pay a reasonable price for them. If the third party is prevented from making the valuation by the fault of the seller or the buyer, the party not at fault may sue the party at fault for damages (section 10(2)). Example. Sunil agrees to sell his painting to Tara at the price a named valuer will fix. The valuer dies before valuing it. The agreement is avoided (section 10(1)). If Sunil had already delivered the painting and Tara had taken it as her own, she would have to pay a reasonable price (proviso). Reasonable time (section 63) Rule. Wherever the Act refers to a reasonable time, what is a reasonable time is a question of fact. Changes in taxes after the contract (section 64A) Rule. Unless a different intention appears from the terms of the contract, the seller and the buyer share the effect of changes in customs duty, excise duty, or a tax on the sale or purchase of goods after the contract is made. If a tax or an increase takes effect, the seller may add to the price the amount paid or payable, and may sue to recover it (section 64A(1)(a)). If a decrease or remission takes effect, the buyer may deduct the amount of the decrease or the remitted tax from the price (section 64A(1)(b)). The taxes covered are duties of customs or excise on goods and taxes on the sale or purchase of goods (section 64A(2)). Example. Umesh agrees to sell goods at Rs 1,000 with no mention of tax, when no tax was chargeable. A sales tax of Rs 50 is imposed afterwards and Umesh has to pay it. Unless the contract shows a different intention, he may add Rs 50 to the price and sue for it (section 64A(1)(a)). What price must the buyer pay? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Is the price fixed by the contract, left to be fixed in the agreed manner, or determined by course of dealing (section 9(1))? That price is payable. 2. Is the price to be fixed by a third party's valuation (section 10)? If he does not make the valuation, the agreement is avoided, but a buyer who has received and appropriated goods pays a reasonable price. 3. Is the price not determined in any of these ways? The buyer pays a reasonable price, a question of fact (section 9(2)). 4. Did a customs, excise or sales tax change after the contract (section 64A)? Unless a different intention appears, the seller adds an increase and the buyer deducts a decrease.
keyPoints: Price: the money consideration (section 2(10)). Fixed by the contract, left to be fixed as agreed, or determined by course of dealing (section 9(1)). Otherwise a reasonable price, a question of fact (section 9(2)). Valuation by a third party fails: agreement avoided, but a buyer who has received and appropriated goods pays a reasonable price (section 10(1)). Party at fault for preventing valuation: suit for damages (section 10(2)). Reasonable time is a question of fact (section 63). Tax changes after the contract: seller may add, buyer may deduct (section 64A).
