law-of-contract-ii-u3-t1.subtitle: Sections 1 to 5 and 64 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930

en.inOneMinute: A contract of sale of goods is a contract in which the seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a price (section 4(1)). It is made by an offer to buy or sell goods for a price and its acceptance (section 5(1)). If the property passes at once, the contract is a sale. If it passes at a future time or after a condition is met, it is an agreement to sell (section 4(3)). Key points for the answer: the definition, the two kinds, how the contract is made, and the rules of an auction sale (section 64).
en.meaning:
Contract of sale: the definition (section 4(1))

Rule. A contract of sale of goods is a contract whereby the seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a price.

Four things follow from the words of the section.

There are two parties, a seller and a buyer. The subject-matter is goods. Goods are moveable property other than actionable claims and money (section 2(7)). There is a transfer, or an agreement to transfer, of the property in the goods. "Property" means the general property in goods and not merely a special property (section 2(11)). The consideration is a price. "Price" means the money consideration for a sale of goods (section 2(10)).

There may be a contract of sale between one part-owner and another (section 4(1)). A contract of sale may be absolute or conditional (section 4(2)).

Example. Ravi agrees to sell his scooter to Sita for Rs 40,000. Ravi is the seller, Sita is the buyer, the scooter is the goods, and Rs 40,000 is the price. This is a contract of sale.

Sale and agreement to sell (section 4(3) and (4))

Rule. If the property in the goods is transferred from the seller to the buyer under the contract, the contract is called a sale. If the transfer is to take place at a future time, or subject to some condition to be fulfilled later, it is called an agreement to sell. An agreement to sell becomes a sale when the time elapses or the conditions are fulfilled.

Example. Anil sells a specific table to Babu and the property in it passes to Babu now. This is a sale. If Anil instead agrees that the property will pass to Babu on 1 January, this is an agreement to sell. On 1 January it becomes a sale.

How a contract of sale is made (section 5)

Rule. A contract of sale is made by an offer to buy or sell goods for a price and the acceptance of the offer.

The contract may provide for immediate delivery, immediate payment, or both. It may provide for delivery or payment by instalments. It may provide that delivery or payment, or both, are postponed. Subject to any law in force, it may be in writing, by word of mouth, partly in writing and partly by word of mouth, or implied from the conduct of the parties (section 5(2)).

Example. A customer picks up a packet of rice from a shop shelf and pays at the counter. The contract is implied from the conduct of the parties. No writing is needed unless some other law requires it.

Application of the Indian Contract Act (section 3)

Rule. The unrepealed provisions of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 continue to apply to contracts for the sale of goods, except where they are inconsistent with the express provisions of the Sale of Goods Act. Section 2(15) also gives expressions defined in the Contract Act but not here the meaning assigned in the Contract Act.

Auction sale (section 64)

Rule. Section 64 sets six rules for a sale by auction.

Goods put up in lots: each lot is prima facie a separate contract of sale. The sale is complete when the auctioneer announces it by the fall of the hammer or in another customary manner. Until then any bidder may retract his bid. The seller may reserve a right to bid, expressly. Only where it is so reserved may the seller, or one person on his behalf, bid. If the sale is not notified to be subject to a right to bid on behalf of the seller, the seller may not bid or employ anyone to bid, and the auctioneer may not knowingly take such a bid. The buyer may treat a sale in breach of this rule as fraudulent. The sale may be notified to be subject to a reserved or upset price. If the seller uses pretended bidding to raise the price, the sale is voidable at the option of the buyer.

Example. At an auction, a bidder says Rs 5,000 for a lamp. Before the auctioneer brings down the hammer, the bidder changes his mind. He may retract his bid, because the sale is not yet complete (section 64(2)).

Sale or agreement to sell? How to read this: start at the top. The property means the general property in the goods. 1. Is there a contract by which the seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a price? If yes, it is a contract of sale (section 4(1)). If not, it is not a contract of sale under this Act. 2. Is the property transferred from the seller to the buyer under the contract now? If yes, it is a sale (section 4(3)). 3. Is the transfer to take place at a future time, or after a condition is fulfilled? Then it is an agreement to sell. It becomes a sale when the time elapses or the condition is fulfilled (section 4(3) and (4)).
keyPoints: A contract of sale: seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a price (section 4(1)). Sale: property transferred now. Agreement to sell: property to pass later or on a condition (section 4(3)). An agreement to sell becomes a sale when the time elapses or the conditions are fulfilled (section 4(4)). Made by offer and acceptance. It may be in writing, by words, or implied from conduct (section 5). The Contract Act applies unless inconsistent (section 3). Auction: the sale is complete at the fall of the hammer, and a bidder may retract before it (section 64(2)). Seller bidding without a reserved right: the buyer may treat the sale as fraudulent (section 64(4)).

When the time elapses or the conditions are fulfilled subject to which the property in the goods is to be transferred (section 4(4)). 4. When is an auction sale complete? When the auctioneer announces its completion by the fall of the hammer or in other customary manner (section 64(2)).

hi.inOneMinute: A contract of sale of goods is a contract in which the seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a price (section 4(1)). It is made by an offer to buy or sell goods for a price and its acceptance (section 5(1)). If the property passes at once, the contract is a sale. If it passes at a future time or after a condition is met, it is an agreement to sell (section 4(3)). Key points for the answer: the definition, the two kinds, how the contract is made, and the rules of an auction sale (section 64).
hi.meaning: Contract of sale: the definition (section 4(1)) Rule. A contract of sale of goods is a contract whereby the seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a price. Four things follow from the words of the section. There are two parties, a seller and a buyer. The subject-matter is goods. Goods are moveable property other than actionable claims and money (section 2(7)). There is a transfer, or an agreement to transfer, of the property in the goods. "Property" means the general property in goods and not merely a special property (section 2(11)). The consideration is a price. "Price" means the money consideration for a sale of goods (section 2(10)). There may be a contract of sale between one part-owner and another (section 4(1)). A contract of sale may be absolute or conditional (section 4(2)). Example. Ravi agrees to sell his scooter to Sita for Rs 40,000. Ravi is the seller, Sita is the buyer, the scooter is the goods, and Rs 40,000 is the price. This is a contract of sale. Sale and agreement to sell (section 4(3) and (4)) Rule. If the property in the goods is transferred from the seller to the buyer under the contract, the contract is called a sale. If the transfer is to take place at a future time, or subject to some condition to be fulfilled later, it is called an agreement to sell. An agreement to sell becomes a sale when the time elapses or the conditions are fulfilled. Example. Anil sells a specific table to Babu and the property in it passes to Babu now. This is a sale. If Anil instead agrees that the property will pass to Babu on 1 January, this is an agreement to sell. On 1 January it becomes a sale. How a contract of sale is made (section 5) Rule. A contract of sale is made by an offer to buy or sell goods for a price and the acceptance of the offer. The contract may provide for immediate delivery, immediate payment, or both. It may provide for delivery or payment by instalments. It may provide that delivery or payment, or both, are postponed. Subject to any law in force, it may be in writing, by word of mouth, partly in writing and partly by word of mouth, or implied from the conduct of the parties (section 5(2)). Example. A customer picks up a packet of rice from a shop shelf and pays at the counter. The contract is implied from the conduct of the parties. No writing is needed unless some other law requires it. Application of the Indian Contract Act (section 3) Rule. The unrepealed provisions of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 continue to apply to contracts for the sale of goods, except where they are inconsistent with the express provisions of the Sale of Goods Act. Section 2(15) also gives expressions defined in the Contract Act but not here the meaning assigned in the Contract Act. Auction sale (section 64) Rule. Section 64 sets six rules for a sale by auction. Goods put up in lots: each lot is prima facie a separate contract of sale. The sale is complete when the auctioneer announces it by the fall of the hammer or in another customary manner. Until then any bidder may retract his bid. The seller may reserve a right to bid, expressly. Only where it is so reserved may the seller, or one person on his behalf, bid. If the sale is not notified to be subject to a right to bid on behalf of the seller, the seller may not bid or employ anyone to bid, and the auctioneer may not knowingly take such a bid. The buyer may treat a sale in breach of this rule as fraudulent. The sale may be notified to be subject to a reserved or upset price. If the seller uses pretended bidding to raise the price, the sale is voidable at the option of the buyer. Example. At an auction, a bidder says Rs 5,000 for a lamp. Before the auctioneer brings down the hammer, the bidder changes his mind. He may retract his bid, because the sale is not yet complete (section 64(2)). Sale or agreement to sell? How to read this: start at the top. The property means the general property in the goods. 1. Is there a contract by which the seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a price? If yes, it is a contract of sale (section 4(1)). If not, it is not a contract of sale under this Act. 2. Is the property transferred from the seller to the buyer under the contract now? If yes, it is a sale (section 4(3)). 3. Is the transfer to take place at a future time, or after a condition is fulfilled? Then it is an agreement to sell. It becomes a sale when the time elapses or the condition is fulfilled (section 4(3) and (4)).
keyPoints: A contract of sale: seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a price (section 4(1)). Sale: property transferred now. Agreement to sell: property to pass later or on a condition (section 4(3)). An agreement to sell becomes a sale when the time elapses or the conditions are fulfilled (section 4(4)). Made by offer and acceptance. It may be in writing, by words, or implied from conduct (section 5). The Contract Act applies unless inconsistent (section 3). Auction: the sale is complete at the fall of the hammer, and a bidder may retract before it (section 64(2)). Seller bidding without a reserved right: the buyer may treat the sale as fraudulent (section 64(4)).

selfTest.q: 1. What is a contract of sale of goods under section 4(1)?
selfTest.a: A contract whereby the seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a price. 2. What is the difference between a sale and an agreement to sell in section 4(3)? In a sale the property is transferred under the contract. In an agreement to sell the transfer is to take place at a future time or subject to a condition to be fulfilled. 3. When does an agreement to sell become a sale? When the time elapses or the conditions are fulfilled subject to which the property in the goods is to be transferred (section 4(4)). 4. When is an auction sale complete? When the auctioneer announces its completion by the fall of the hammer or in other customary manner (section 64(2)).

law-of-contract-ii-u3-t2.subtitle: Sections 2(6), 2(7), 2(14), 6, 7 and 8 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930

en.inOneMinute: The subject-matter of a contract of sale is goods: every kind of moveable property other than actionable claims and money (section 2(7)). Goods may be existing goods, owned or possessed by the seller, or future goods (section 6(1)). A contract for specific goods is void if, without the seller's knowledge, the goods had already perished when the contract was made (section 7). An agreement to sell specific goods is avoided if they perish later, without fault of either party, before the risk passes to the buyer (section 8). Key points for the answer: the definition of goods, the kinds of goods, and sections 7 and 8.
en.meaning:
What counts as goods (section 2(7))

Rule. Goods are every kind of moveable property other than actionable claims and money.

Included: stock and shares, growing crops, grass. Included: things attached to or forming part of the land which are agreed to be severed before sale or under the contract of sale. Excluded: actionable claims and money.

Example. A farmer sells the standing sugarcane in his field to a mill. The sugarcane is a growing crop and so falls within the definition of goods.

Existing goods and future goods (sections 2(6) and 6(1))

Rule. Goods that are the subject of a contract of sale may be existing goods, owned or possessed by the seller, or future goods. Future goods are goods to be manufactured or produced or acquired by the seller after the contract is made.

Example. A furniture maker agrees on 1 March to sell a cupboard to Rani. He will build it in April. The cupboard is future goods on 1 March.

Goods depending on a contingency (section 6(2))

Rule. There may be a contract for the sale of goods the acquisition of which by the seller depends upon a contingency which may or may not happen.

Example. A trader agrees to sell a consignment he hopes to buy at an auction next week. His acquiring it depends on whether he wins the bid. The contract is allowed by section 6(2).

Present sale of future goods (section 6(3))

Rule. Where the seller purports to effect a present sale of future goods, the contract operates as an agreement to sell the goods.

This links to the topic on sale and agreement to sell. A sale needs the property in the goods to pass under the contract (section 4(3)). Goods the seller does not yet have cannot be transferred now, so the contract is an agreement to sell.

Specific goods (section 2(14))

Rule. Specific goods are goods identified and agreed upon at the time a contract of sale is made.

Example. Karan agrees to buy "that black horse in the stable", which both have seen. The horse is identified and agreed upon when the contract is made. It is specific goods.

Goods perishing before the contract (section 7)

Rule. If a contract is for specific goods, and the goods, without the seller's knowledge, had perished or become so damaged as no longer to answer to their description in the contract when the contract was made, the contract is void.

Example. Lata agrees on Monday to sell a specific car to Mohan. Unknown to Lata, the car was burnt in a fire on Sunday night. The contract is void under section 7.

Goods perishing after the agreement, before the risk passes (section 8)

Rule. If there is an agreement to sell specific goods, and afterwards the goods perish or become so damaged as no longer to answer to their description in the agreement, without fault of the seller or the buyer, before the risk passes to the buyer, the agreement is avoided.

Example. Nisha agrees to sell a specific tractor to Om, delivery next month. Before the risk passes to Om, lightning destroys the tractor. Neither party is at fault. The agreement is avoided under section 8.

Did the goods perish? Which section applies? How to read this: start at the top. Both sections speak only of specific goods. 1. Are the goods specific, that is, identified and agreed upon when the contract was made (section 2(14))? If not, sections 7 and 8 do not apply on their words. 2. Had they perished, without the seller's knowledge, when the contract was made? The contract is void (section 7). 3. Did they perish later, without fault of seller or buyer, before the risk passed to the buyer, under an agreement to sell? The agreement is avoided (section 8).
keyPoints: Goods: all moveable property except actionable claims and money (section 2(7)). Includes stock and shares, growing crops, grass, and things agreed to be severed. Existing goods or future goods (sections 2(6), 6(1)). Contingent goods are allowed (section 6(2)). A present sale of future goods is an agreement to sell (section 6(3)). Specific goods: identified and agreed upon at the time of the contract (section 2(14)). Section 7: specific goods already perished at the contract, without the seller's knowledge, so the contract is void. Section 8: specific goods perish later, without fault, before the risk passes, so the agreement is avoided.

selfTest.q: 1. What is excluded from goods under section 2(7)?
selfTest.a: Actionable claims and money. 2. What are future goods? Goods to be manufactured or produced or acquired by the seller after the making of the contract of sale (section 2(6)). 3. What is a present sale of future goods under section 6(3)? The contract operates as an agreement to sell the goods. 4. What is the difference between sections 7 and 8? Section 7 applies where the specific goods had already perished when the contract was made, without the seller's knowledge. Section 8 applies where they perish afterwards, without fault of either party, before the risk passes to the buyer.

te.inOneMinute: The subject-matter of a contract of sale is goods: every kind of moveable property other than actionable claims and money (section 2(7)). Goods may be existing goods, owned or possessed by the seller, or future goods (section 6(1)). A contract for specific goods is void if, without the seller's knowledge, the goods had already perished when the contract was made (section 7). An agreement to sell specific goods is avoided if they perish later, without fault of either party, before the risk passes to the buyer (section 8). Key points for the answer: the definition of goods, the kinds of goods, and sections 7 and 8.
te.meaning: What counts as goods (section 2(7)) Rule. Goods are every kind of moveable property other than actionable claims and money. Included: stock and shares, growing crops, grass. Included: things attached to or forming part of the land which are agreed to be severed before sale or under the contract of sale. Excluded: actionable claims and money. Example. A farmer sells the standing sugarcane in his field to a mill. The sugarcane is a growing crop and so falls within the definition of goods. Existing goods and future goods (sections 2(6) and 6(1)) Rule. Goods that are the subject of a contract of sale may be existing goods, owned or possessed by the seller, or future goods. Future goods are goods to be manufactured or produced or acquired by the seller after the contract is made. Example. A furniture maker agrees on 1 March to sell a cupboard to Rani. He will build it in April. The cupboard is future goods on 1 March. Goods depending on a contingency (section 6(2)) Rule. There may be a contract for the sale of goods the acquisition of which by the seller depends upon a contingency which may or may not happen. Example. A trader agrees to sell a consignment he hopes to buy at an auction next week. His acquiring it depends on whether he wins the bid. The contract is allowed by section 6(2). Present sale of future goods (section 6(3)) Rule. Where the seller purports to effect a present sale of future goods, the contract operates as an agreement to sell the goods. This links to the topic on sale and agreement to sell. A sale needs the property in the goods to pass under the contract (section 4(3)). Goods the seller does not yet have cannot be transferred now, so the contract is an agreement to sell. Specific goods (section 2(14)) Rule. Specific goods are goods identified and agreed upon at the time a contract of sale is made. Example. Karan agrees to buy "that black horse in the stable", which both have seen. The horse is identified and agreed upon when the contract is made. It is specific goods. Goods perishing before the contract (section 7) Rule. If a contract is for specific goods, and the goods, without the seller's knowledge, had perished or become so damaged as no longer to answer to their description in the contract when the contract was made, the contract is void. Example. Lata agrees on Monday to sell a specific car to Mohan. Unknown to Lata, the car was burnt in a fire on Sunday night. The contract is void under section 7. Goods perishing after the agreement, before the risk passes (section 8) Rule. If there is an agreement to sell specific goods, and afterwards the goods perish or become so damaged as no longer to answer to their description in the agreement, without fault of the seller or the buyer, before the risk passes to the buyer, the agreement is avoided. Example. Nisha agrees to sell a specific tractor to Om, delivery next month. Before the risk passes to Om, lightning destroys the tractor. Neither party is at fault. The agreement is avoided under section 8. Did the goods perish? Which section applies? How to read this: start at the top. Both sections speak only of specific goods. 1. Are the goods specific, that is, identified and agreed upon when the contract was made (section 2(14))? If not, sections 7 and 8 do not apply on their words. 2. Had they perished, without the seller's knowledge, when the contract was made? The contract is void (section 7). 3. Did they perish later, without fault of seller or buyer, before the risk passed to the buyer, under an agreement to sell? The agreement is avoided (section 8).
keyPoints: Goods: all moveable property except actionable claims and money (section 2(7)). Includes stock and shares, growing crops, grass, and things agreed to be severed. Existing goods or future goods (sections 2(6), 6(1)). Contingent goods are allowed (section 6(2)). A present sale of future goods is an agreement to sell (section 6(3)). Specific goods: identified and agreed upon at the time of the contract (section 2(14)). Section 7: specific goods already perished at the contract, without the seller's knowledge, so the contract is void. Section 8: specific goods perish later, without fault, before the risk passes, so the agreement is avoided.

law-of-contract-ii-u3-t4.subtitle: Sections 14 to 17 and 62 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930

en.inOneMinute: Some terms of a contract of sale are written by the parties (express). Others are implied by the Sale of Goods Act unless the contract shows a different intention. The Act implies a condition that the seller has a right to sell, and warranties of quiet possession and freedom from encumbrance (section 14). It also implies a condition that goods sold by description correspond with it (section 15). It implies conditions of fitness and merchantable quality in the cases set out in section 16, and conditions in a sale by sample (section 17). Section 62 lets the parties negative or vary implied terms by express agreement, course of dealing or usage. Key points for the answer: each section and whether it implies a condition or a warranty.
en.meaning:
Express and implied terms

Rule. An express term is one the parties themselves state in the contract. An implied term is one the law reads in. Section 62 speaks of a right, duty or liability arising "by implication of law". Section 16(4) says an express warranty or condition does not negative an implied one unless it is inconsistent with it.

Example. A contract says "warranty: six months service". That is an express term. The law adds an implied condition that the seller has a right to sell (section 14(a)) even though the contract does not mention it.

Implied undertaking as to title (section 14)

Rule. Unless a different intention appears, three terms are implied.

Condition: in a sale, the seller has a right to sell the goods. In an agreement to sell, he will have a right to sell when the property is to pass (section 14(a)). Warranty: the buyer shall have and enjoy quiet possession of the goods (section 14(b)). Warranty: the goods shall be free from any charge or encumbrance in favour of a third party not declared or known to the buyer before or at the time of the contract (section 14(c)).

Example. Dev buys a motorcycle from Eshan. Later a bank proves that it holds an undisclosed charge on the motorcycle, which Dev did not know about. The implied warranty in section 14(c) is broken.

Sale by description (section 15)

Rule. In a sale of goods by description there is an implied condition that the goods shall correspond with the description. In a sale by sample as well as by description, it is not enough that the bulk corresponds with the sample. The goods must also correspond with the description.

Example. Farid orders "Grade A basmati rice" by description. The goods delivered are another grade. The implied condition in section 15 is broken.

Quality or fitness (section 16)

Rule. There is no implied warranty or condition as to quality or fitness for any particular purpose, except as follows.

Fitness for purpose (section 16(1)). The buyer makes known the particular purpose, expressly or by implication, so as to show he relies on the seller's skill or judgment, and the goods are of a description the seller supplies in the course of his business. There is then an implied condition that the goods are reasonably fit for that purpose. Exception: where a specified article is sold under its patent or other trade name, there is no implied condition as to fitness. Merchantable quality (section 16(2)). Goods are bought by description from a seller who deals in goods of that description. There is an implied condition that they are of merchantable quality. Exception: if the buyer has examined the goods, there is no implied condition as regards defects which the examination ought to have revealed. Usage of trade (section 16(3)). An implied warranty or condition as to quality or fitness for a particular purpose may be annexed by the usage of trade. Express terms (section 16(4)). An express warranty or condition does not negative a warranty or condition implied by the Act unless inconsistent with it.

Example. Geeta tells a chemist she needs a cream for an infant's skin rash and relies on the chemist's advice. The chemist supplies a cream of a kind he sells in his business. There is an implied condition that it is reasonably fit for that purpose (section 16(1)).

Sale by sample (section 17)

Rule. A contract is by sample where it has a term, express or implied, to that effect. law-of-contract-ii-u3-t6.subtitle: Section 16 and sections 14, 15 and 17 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930

en.inOneMinute: Caveat emptor is a Latin phrase meaning "let the buyer beware ". The Sale of Goods Act, 1930 does not use the phrase. Its rule is in the opening words of section 16: there is no implied warranty or condition as to the quality or fitness for any particular purpose of goods supplied under a contract of sale, except as the Act provides. The exceptions are the implied terms of the Act: the seller's right to sell and the other terms in section 14, correspondence with description (section 15), fitness for a known purpose and merchantable quality (section 16(1) and (2)), terms annexed by trade usage (section 16(3)), and the terms of a sale by sample (section 17). Key points for the answer: the rule, then each exception with its section.
en.meaning:
The rule (opening words of section 16)

Rule. The Act implies no warranty or condition as to quality or fitness for any particular purpose of goods supplied under a contract of sale, except as the Act provides. The buyer must therefore satisfy himself about quality and fitness, or get an express term.

Example. Rohit buys a second-hand pump from a neighbour, who is not in the business of selling pumps. Rohit did not state any particular purpose. If the pump is weak, section 16 gives no implied condition of fitness or quality, and none of the exceptions below applies on these facts.

Exceptions: terms the Act implies

Rule. The Act gives these exceptions.

Title (section 14). Implied condition of right to sell. Implied warranties of quiet possession and freedom from undisclosed encumbrance. Description (section 15). Implied condition that goods correspond with the description. Fitness for a known purpose (section 16(1)). Where the buyer makes known the purpose, relies on the seller's skill or judgment, and the goods are of a description the seller supplies in his business. Not for a specified article sold under its patent or other trade name. Merchantable quality (section 16(2)). Where goods are bought by description from a seller who deals in such goods. Not for defects which the buyer's examination ought to have revealed. Usage of trade (section 16(3)). A term as to quality or fitness annexed by trade usage. Sample (section 17). Three implied conditions in a sale by sample.

Example. Sheela tells a dealer in bicycles that she needs a bicycle for daily use on a rough village road, relying on the dealer's advice. He supplies one that breaks on the first day. The exception in section 16(1) applies: there is an implied condition of reasonable fitness for that purpose.

Express terms and exclusion (sections 16(4) and 62)

Rule. An express warranty or condition does not negative an implied one unless inconsistent with it (section 16(4)). Implied terms may also be negatived or varied by express agreement, course of dealing or usage binding both parties (section 62).

Is the buyer protected, or must he beware? How to read this: start at the top. Stop at the first step that fits. 1. Is it a question of the seller's title, possession or an undisclosed charge (section 14)? The Act implies terms. The buyer is protected. 2. Was the sale by description (section 15), or by sample (section 17)? The Act implies conditions. The buyer is protected. 3. Did the buyer make known the purpose and rely on the seller's skill, or buy by description from a dealer (section 16(1), (2)), or does trade usage supply a term (section 16(3))? The Act implies conditions, subject to the provisos. The buyer is protected. 4. None of the above? No implied warranty or condition of quality or fitness (section 16). The buyer must beware.
keyPoints: Caveat emptor: "let the buyer beware". The rule is in the opening words of section 16. No implied warranty or condition as to quality or fitness, except as the Act provides. Exceptions: section 14 (title), 15 (description), 16(1) (fitness), 16(2) (merchantable quality), 16(3) (trade usage), 17 (sample). Fitness needs the purpose made known and reliance on the seller's skill or judgment. No fitness condition for patent or trade name articles. No quality condition for defects the buyer's examination ought to have revealed. Implied terms can be negatived or varied (section 62).

selfTest.q: 1. What does caveat emptor mean?

law-of-contract-ii-u4-t2.subtitle: Sections 27 to 30 and 54(3) of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930

en.inOneMinute: Nemo dat quod non habet is a Latin maxim meaning "no one gives what he does not have". Under section 27 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, where goods are sold by a person who is not the owner and who does not sell with the owner's authority or consent, the buyer acquires no better title than the seller had. The Act itself lists exceptions where a non-owner can pass a good title: the owner is precluded by his conduct, or a mercantile agent sells in the ordinary course (section 27); a joint owner in sole possession sells (section 28); a seller who obtained possession under a voidable contract, not yet rescinded, sells (section 29); a seller or buyer in possession after sale disposes of the goods (section 30); and an unpaid seller resells (section 54(3)).
en.meaning:
The rule (section 27)

Rule. If a person who is not the owner, and who does not sell under the owner's authority or with his consent, sells goods, the buyer acquires no better title than the seller had. The exception in the same section is where the owner is by his conduct precluded from denying the seller's authority to sell.

Example. Tarun finds a camera lying in a park and sells it to Usha, who knows nothing of this. Tarun has no title, and the owner did not authorise the sale. Usha gets no better title than Tarun had, and the owner can claim the camera.

Exceptions in the Act

Rule. A buyer gets a good title in these cases.

Owner precluded by conduct (section 27). The owner by his conduct cannot deny the seller's authority to sell. Mercantile agent (proviso to section 27). A mercantile agent in possession of the goods or a document of title with the owner's consent sells in the ordinary course of business of a mercantile agent. The buyer acts in good faith and has no notice that the agent lacks authority. Joint owner (section 28). One of several joint owners has sole possession by permission of the co-owners, and sells to a buyer in good faith without notice. Voidable contract (section 29). The seller obtained possession under a contract voidable under section 19 or 19A of the Contract Act, which had not been rescinded when he sold. The buyer buys in good faith and without notice of the defect of title. Seller in possession after sale (section 30(1)). Having sold, he continues in possession of the goods or documents of title, and delivers or transfers them under a sale, pledge or other disposition to a person in good faith without notice of the previous sale. Buyer in possession after sale (section 30(2)). Having bought or agreed to buy, he obtains possession with the seller's consent and transfers under a sale, pledge or other disposition to a person in good faith without notice of any lien or other right of the original seller. Resale by an unpaid seller (section 54(3)). An unpaid seller who has exercised lien or stoppage in transit re-sells. The buyer gets a good title against the original buyer.

Example. Vimal gives his goods to a commission agent, who customarily sells goods for others, to sell. The agent sells in the ordinary course of business to Wasim, who acts in good faith and does not know of any limit on the agent's authority. Wasim gets a good title (proviso to section 27).

Does the buyer get a good title? How to read this: start at the top. Good faith and lack of notice are stated in sections 27 (proviso), 28, 29 and 30. Section 54(3) and the owner's-conduct exception do not state them. 1. Did the seller sell with the owner's authority or consent? If yes, the title passes in the ordinary way. 2. Is the owner precluded by his conduct from denying the seller's authority (section 27)? If yes, the buyer gets a good title. 3. Is the seller a mercantile agent in possession with the owner's consent (section 27 proviso), a joint owner in sole possession (section 28), a person with a voidable title not yet rescinded (section 29), or a seller or buyer in possession after sale (section 30)? If yes, and the buyer acted in good faith and without notice, he gets a good title. 4. Otherwise The buyer acquires no better title than the seller had (section 27).
keyPoints: Nemo dat: a buyer from a non-owner gets no better title than the seller had (section 27). Exceptions: owner's conduct, mercantile agent (section 27), joint owner (section 28), voidable title (section 29), seller or buyer in possession (section 30), unpaid seller's resale (section 54(3)). Good faith and no notice are stated for sections 27 (proviso), 28, 29 and 30. Section 54(3) does not state them. Mercantile agent: section 2(9). Section 27 is subject to the Act and to any other law.

selfTest.q: 1. What does section 27 say about a buyer from a non-owner?
selfTest.a: He acquires no better title than the seller had, unless the owner is by his conduct precluded from denying the seller's authority to sell. 2. Name the three kinds of seller or possessor in sections 28, 29 and 30. A joint owner in sole possession, a person who got possession under a voidable contract not yet rescinded, and a seller or buyer in possession after sale. 3. selfTest.q: 1. What does section 27 say about a buyer from a non-owner?

law-of-contract-ii-u4-t3.subtitle: Sections 2(2) and 33 to 40 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930

en.inOneMinute: "Delivery" means voluntary transfer of possession from one person to another (section 2(2)). Under section 33, delivery of goods sold may be made by doing anything which the parties agree shall be treated as delivery, or which has the effect of putting the goods in the possession of the buyer or of any person authorised to hold them on his behalf. Sections 34 to 40 give the detailed rules: part delivery, the buyer's application, place and time, delivery of the wrong quantity, instalments, delivery to a carrier or wharfinger, and risk where goods go to a distant place. Key points for the answer: the meaning of delivery, then each rule with its section.
en.meaning:
What delivery is (sections 2(2) and 33)

Rule. Delivery is the voluntary transfer of possession. It may be made by doing anything the parties agree shall be treated as delivery, or anything which has the effect of putting the goods in the possession of the buyer or of a person authorised to hold them for him. The Act does not use the words "actual", "constructive" or "symbolic" delivery.

Example. A seller hands the goods over the counter to the buyer. The goods are in the buyer's possession, so delivery is made. If the parties agree that handing over the keys of the godown shall count as delivery, that too is delivery under section 33.

Part delivery (section 34)

Rule. Delivery of part, in progress of the delivery of the whole, has the same effect for passing the property as delivery of the whole. Delivery of part with an intention of severing it from the whole does not operate as delivery of the remainder.

When the seller must deliver (sections 35 and 36)

Rule. Unless the contract says otherwise, the seller need not deliver until the buyer applies for delivery (section 35). Section 36 then gives these defaults.

Whether the buyer takes possession or the seller sends the goods depends on the contract. Apart from it, the place of delivery is where the goods are at the time of the sale or agreement, or, if not then in existence, where they are manufactured or produced (section 36(1)). If the seller must send the goods but no time is fixed, he must send them within a reasonable time (section 36(2)). If a third person holds the goods, there is no delivery until he acknowledges to the buyer that he holds them on the buyer's behalf. This does not affect the issue or transfer of a document of title (section 36(3)). Demand or tender of delivery may be treated as ineffectual unless made at a reasonable hour, a question of fact (section 36(4)). Unless otherwise agreed, the seller bears the expenses of putting the goods into a deliverable state (section 36(5)).

Wrong quantity and instalments (sections 37 and 38)

Rule. If less than the contract quantity is delivered, the buyer may reject, or accept and pay at the contract rate. If more is delivered, he may accept the contract quantity and reject the rest, reject the whole, or accept the whole and pay at the contract rate. If contract goods are mixed with goods of a different description, he may accept the contract goods and reject the rest, or reject the whole (section 37). The buyer is not bound to accept delivery by instalments unless otherwise agreed. For separately paid instalments, whether a default is a repudiation of the whole or a severable breach depends on the terms of the contract and the circumstances (section 38).

Example. Kiran contracts to buy 100 kg of sugar. The seller delivers 120 kg. Kiran may take 100 kg and reject 20 kg, or reject all 120 kg, or accept all and pay at the contract rate (section 37(2)).

Delivery to a carrier, and distant places (sections 39 and 40)

Rule. Where the seller is authorised or required to send the goods, delivery to a carrier or wharfinger is prima facie delivery to the buyer. Unless authorised otherwise, the seller must make a reasonable contract with the carrier or wharfinger on the buyer's behalf. If he omits to do so and the goods are lost or damaged in transit or custody, the buyer may decline to treat it as delivery to himself or hold the seller responsible in damages. For sea transit where it is usual to insure, the seller must give the buyer notice enabling him to insure, failing which the goods are at the seller's risk during sea transit (section 39). If the seller agrees to deliver at his own risk at a distant place, the buyer takes, unless otherwise agreed, any risk of deterioration necessarily incident to transit (section 40).

Has delivery been made? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Did the parties agree something shall count as delivery, or are the goods in the buyer's possession or that of a person authorised to hold them for him (section 33)? Delivery is made. 2. Are the goods held by a third person (section 36(3))? No delivery until he acknowledges to the buyer that he holds them on the buyer's behalf. 3. Were the goods sent to a carrier or wharfinger as the contract required (section 39)? Prima facie delivery to the buyer. 4. Does the quantity or description match the contract (section 37)? If not, the buyer may accept or reject as section 37 allows.
keyPoints: Delivery is the voluntary transfer of possession (section 2(2)). It may be made by what the parties agree, or by putting the goods in the buyer's possession (section 33). The seller need not deliver until the buyer applies (section 35). Third person holds the goods: no delivery until he acknowledges to the buyer (section 36(3)). Wrong quantity: the buyer's options are in section 37. Instalments: section 38. Delivery to a carrier is prima facie delivery to the buyer (section 39).

Where the seller is authorised or required to send the goods, it is prima facie deemed delivery to the buyer (section 39(1)).

hi.inOneMinute: "Delivery" means voluntary transfer of possession from one person to another (section 2(2)). Under section 33, delivery of goods sold may be made by doing anything which the parties agree shall be treated as delivery, or which has the effect of putting the goods in the possession of the buyer or of any person authorised to hold them on his behalf. Sections 34 to 40 give the detailed rules: part delivery, the buyer's application, place and time, delivery of the wrong quantity, instalments, delivery to a carrier or wharfinger, and risk where goods go to a distant place. Key points for the answer: the meaning of delivery, then each rule with its section.
hi.meaning: What delivery is (sections 2(2) and 33) Rule. Delivery is the voluntary transfer of possession. It may be made by doing anything the parties agree shall be treated as delivery, or anything which has the effect of putting the goods in the possession of the buyer or of a person authorised to hold them for him. The Act does not use the words "actual", "constructive" or "symbolic" delivery. Example. A seller hands the goods over the counter to the buyer. The goods are in the buyer's possession, so delivery is made. If the parties agree that handing over the keys of the godown shall count as delivery, that too is delivery under section 33. Part delivery (section 34) Rule. Delivery of part, in progress of the delivery of the whole, has the same effect for passing the property as delivery of the whole. Delivery of part with an intention of severing it from the whole does not operate as delivery of the remainder. When the seller must deliver (sections 35 and 36) Rule. Unless the contract says otherwise, the seller need not deliver until the buyer applies for delivery (section 35). Section 36 then gives these defaults. Whether the buyer takes possession or the seller sends the goods depends on the contract. Apart from it, the place of delivery is where the goods are at the time of the sale or agreement, or, if not then in existence, where they are manufactured or produced (section 36(1)). If the seller must send the goods but no time is fixed, he must send them within a reasonable time (section 36(2)). If a third person holds the goods, there is no delivery until he acknowledges to the buyer that he holds them on the buyer's behalf. This does not affect the issue or transfer of a document of title (section 36(3)). Demand or tender of delivery may be treated as ineffectual unless made at a reasonable hour, a question of fact (section 36(4)). Unless otherwise agreed, the seller bears the expenses of putting the goods into a deliverable state (section 36(5)). Wrong quantity and instalments (sections 37 and 38) Rule. If less than the contract quantity is delivered, the buyer may reject, or accept and pay at the contract rate. If more is delivered, he may accept the contract quantity and reject the rest, reject the whole, or accept the whole and pay at the contract rate. If contract goods are mixed with goods of a different description, he may accept the contract goods and reject the rest, or reject the whole (section 37). The buyer is not bound to accept delivery by instalments unless otherwise agreed. For separately paid instalments, whether a default is a repudiation of the whole or a severable breach depends on the terms of the contract and the circumstances (section 38). Example. Kiran contracts to buy 100 kg of sugar. The seller delivers 120 kg. Kiran may take 100 kg and reject 20 kg, or reject all 120 kg, or accept all and pay at the contract rate (section 37(2)). Delivery to a carrier, and distant places (sections 39 and 40) Rule. Where the seller is authorised or required to send the goods, delivery to a carrier or wharfinger is prima facie delivery to the buyer. Unless authorised otherwise, the seller must make a reasonable contract with the carrier or wharfinger on the buyer's behalf. If he omits to do so and the goods are lost or damaged in transit or custody, the buyer may decline to treat it as delivery to himself or hold the seller responsible in damages. For sea transit where it is usual to insure, the seller must give the buyer notice enabling him to insure, failing which the goods are at the seller's risk during sea transit (section 39). If the seller agrees to deliver at his own risk at a distant place, the buyer takes, unless otherwise agreed, any risk of deterioration necessarily incident to transit (section 40). Has delivery been made? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Did the parties agree something shall count as delivery, or are the goods in the buyer's possession or that of a person authorised to hold them for him (section 33)? Delivery is made. 2. Are the goods held by a third person (section 36(3))? No delivery until he acknowledges to the buyer that he holds them on the buyer's behalf. 3. Were the goods sent to a carrier or wharfinger as the contract required (section 39)? Prima facie delivery to the buyer. 4. Does the quantity or description match the contract (section 37)? If not, the buyer may accept or reject as section 37 allows.
keyPoints: Delivery is the voluntary transfer of possession (section 2(2)). It may be made by what the parties agree, or by putting the goods in the buyer's possession (section 33). The seller need not deliver until the buyer applies (section 35). Third person holds the goods: no delivery until he acknowledges to the buyer (section 36(3)). Wrong quantity: the buyer's options are in section 37. Instalments: section 38. Delivery to a carrier is prima facie delivery to the buyer (section 39).

law-of-contract-ii-u4-t6.subtitle: Sections 55 to 61 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930

en.inOneMinute: The seller may sue the buyer for the price where the property has passed and the buyer wrongfully refuses to pay, or where the price is payable on a day certain irrespective of delivery (section 55). Where the buyer wrongfully neglects or refuses to accept and pay for the goods, the seller may sue for damages for non-acceptance (section 56). Where the seller wrongfully neglects or refuses to deliver, the buyer may sue for damages for non-delivery (section 57). The Court may order specific performance in a suit for breach of a contract to deliver specific or ascertained goods (section 58). For a breach of warranty the buyer may set it up against the price or sue for damages (section 59). Section 60 deals with repudiation before the due date, and section 61 with interest and special damages.
en.meaning:
Seller's suit for the price (section 55)

Rule. The seller may sue for the price in two cases. First, the property has passed and the buyer wrongfully neglects or refuses to pay according to the contract. Second, the price is payable on a day certain irrespective of delivery and the buyer wrongfully neglects or refuses to pay; here the seller may sue although the property has not passed and the goods have not been appropriated to the contract.

Example. Anwar sells a tractor to Balaji, and the property passes to Balaji. Balaji wrongfully refuses to pay. Anwar may sue for the price (section 55(1)).

Damages for non-acceptance and non-delivery (sections 56 and 57)

Rule. If the buyer wrongfully neglects or refuses to accept and pay, the seller may sue for damages for non-acceptance (section 56). If the seller wrongfully neglects or refuses to deliver, the buyer may sue for damages for non-delivery (section 57).

Specific performance (section 58)

Rule. In a suit for breach of a contract to deliver specific or ascertained goods, the Court may, if it thinks fit, on the plaintiff's application, direct by its decree that the contract be performed specifically, without giving the defendant the option of retaining the goods on payment of damages. The section is subject to Chapter II of the Specific Relief Act, 1877. The decree may be unconditional or on terms about damages, payment of the price or otherwise. The application may be made at any time before the decree.

Breach of warranty (section 59)

Rule. The buyer cannot reject the goods only because of a breach of warranty, including where he elects or is compelled to treat a breach of condition as a breach of warranty. He may set up the breach in diminution or extinction of the price, or sue for damages. Setting it up against the price does not stop him suing for the same breach if he has suffered further damage.

Example. Chitra buys a machine with a warranty of one year's free servicing. The seller refuses to service it. Chitra may deduct a part of the price on that account or sue for damages, but she cannot reject the machine for that breach alone (section 59(1)).

Repudiation before the due date (section 60)

Rule. If either party repudiates the contract before the date of delivery, the other may treat the contract as subsisting and wait till the date of delivery, or treat it as rescinded and sue for damages for the breach.

Interest and special damages (section 61)

Rule. The Act does not affect the right to recover interest or special damages where the law allows them, or to recover money paid where the consideration has failed (section 61(1)). Absent a contrary contract, the Court may award interest on the price at a rate it thinks fit: to the seller from the date of tender of the goods or the date the price was payable, and to the buyer, in a suit for refund of the price for the seller's breach, from the date of payment (section 61(2)).

Which remedy? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Buyer will not pay. Has the property passed, or is the price payable on a day certain? Suit for the price (section 55). Otherwise damages for non-acceptance (section 56). 2. Seller will not deliver? Damages for non-delivery (section 57). For specific or ascertained goods, specific performance may be sought (section 58). 3. Breach of warranty by the seller? The buyer cannot reject for it alone. He may reduce the price or sue for damages (section 59). 4. Repudiation before the delivery date? Wait for the date, or treat the contract as rescinded and sue for damages (section 60).
keyPoints: Seller's suit for the price: property passed and wrongful refusal to pay, or price payable on a day certain (section 55). Damages for non-acceptance (section 56). Damages for non-delivery (section 57). Specific performance may be ordered for specific or ascertained goods (section 58). Breach of warranty: no right to reject for it alone. Set it against the price or sue for damages (section 59). Repudiation before the due date: wait, or rescind and sue (section 60). Interest and special damages are not affected, and money paid on failed consideration can be recovered (section 61).

selfTest.q: 1. When may the seller sue for the price?
selfTest.a: Where the property has passed and the buyer wrongfully refuses to pay, or where the price is payable on a day certain irrespective of delivery (section 55). 2. What may the buyer do if the seller wrongfully refuses to deliver? Sue for damages for non-delivery (section 57). 3. May the buyer reject the goods for a breach of warranty? Not by reason only of that breach. He may set it up against the price or sue for damages (section 59). 4. What are the options when one party repudiates before the delivery date? The other may wait till the date of delivery, or treat the contract as rescinded and sue for damages (section 60).

te.inOneMinute: The seller may sue the buyer for the price where the property has passed and the buyer wrongfully refuses to pay, or where the price is payable on a day certain irrespective of delivery (section 55). Where the buyer wrongfully neglects or refuses to accept and pay for the goods, the seller may sue for damages for non-acceptance (section 56). Where the seller wrongfully neglects or refuses to deliver, the buyer may sue for damages for non-delivery (section 57). The Court may order specific performance in a suit for breach of a contract to deliver specific or ascertained goods (section 58). For a breach of warranty the buyer may set it up against the price or sue for damages (section 59). Section 60 deals with repudiation before the due date, and section 61 with interest and special damages.
te.meaning: Seller's suit for the price (section 55) Rule. The seller may sue for the price in two cases. First, the property has passed and the buyer wrongfully neglects or refuses to pay according to the contract. Second, the price is payable on a day certain irrespective of delivery and the buyer wrongfully neglects or refuses to pay; here the seller may sue although the property has not passed and the goods have not been appropriated to the contract. Example. Anwar sells a tractor to Balaji, and the property passes to Balaji. Balaji wrongfully refuses to pay. Anwar may sue for the price (section 55(1)). Damages for non-acceptance and non-delivery (sections 56 and 57) Rule. If the buyer wrongfully neglects or refuses to accept and pay, the seller may sue for damages for non-acceptance (section 56). If the seller wrongfully neglects or refuses to deliver, the buyer may sue for damages for non-delivery (section 57). Specific performance (section 58) Rule. In a suit for breach of a contract to deliver specific or ascertained goods, the Court may, if it thinks fit, on the plaintiff's application, direct by its decree that the contract be performed specifically, without giving the defendant the option of retaining the goods on payment of damages. The section is subject to Chapter II of the Specific Relief Act, 1877. The decree may be unconditional or on terms about damages, payment of the price or otherwise. The application may be made at any time before the decree. Breach of warranty (section 59) Rule. The buyer cannot reject the goods only because of a breach of warranty, including where he elects or is compelled to treat a breach of condition as a breach of warranty. He may set up the breach in diminution or extinction of the price, or sue for damages. Setting it up against the price does not stop him suing for the same breach if he has suffered further damage. Example. Chitra buys a machine with a warranty of one year's free servicing. The seller refuses to service it. Chitra may deduct a part of the price on that account or sue for damages, but she cannot reject the machine for that breach alone (section 59(1)). Repudiation before the due date (section 60) Rule. If either party repudiates the contract before the date of delivery, the other may treat the contract as subsisting and wait till the date of delivery, or treat it as rescinded and sue for damages for the breach. Interest and special damages (section 61) Rule. The Act does not affect the right to recover interest or special damages where the law allows them, or to recover money paid where the consideration has failed (section 61(1)). Absent a contrary contract, the Court may award interest on the price at a rate it thinks fit: to the seller from the date of tender of the goods or the date the price was payable, and to the buyer, in a suit for refund of the price for the seller's breach, from the date of payment (section 61(2)). Which remedy? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Buyer will not pay. Has the property passed, or is the price payable on a day certain? Suit for the price (section 55). Otherwise damages for non-acceptance (section 56). 2. Seller will not deliver? Damages for non-delivery (section 57). For specific or ascertained goods, specific performance may be sought (section 58). 3. Breach of warranty by the seller? The buyer cannot reject for it alone. He may reduce the price or sue for damages (section 59). 4. Repudiation before the delivery date? Wait for the date, or treat the contract as rescinded and sue for damages (section 60).

Damages for non-delivery (section 57). Specific performance may be ordered for specific or ascertained goods (section 58). Breach of warranty: no right to reject for it alone. Set it against the price or sue for damages (section 59). Repudiation before the due date: wait, or rescind and sue (section 60). Interest and special damages are not affected, and money paid on failed consideration can be recovered (section 61).

law-of-contract-ii-u4-t1.subtitle: Sections 2(2), 2(11) and 18 to 26 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930

en.inOneMinute: "Property" in goods means the general property in them, not merely a special property (section 2(11)). "Delivery" means voluntary transfer of possession (section 2(2)). A seller who gives possession does not necessarily pass the property, and the Act has separate rules for when the property passes to the buyer. No property passes in unascertained goods until they are ascertained (section 18). Otherwise the property passes when the parties intend it to pass, judged from the contract, conduct and circumstances (section 19). Sections 20 to 24 give the rules for specific goods, unascertained goods and goods on approval. Section 25 allows the seller to reserve the right of disposal. Risk prima facie passes with the property (section 26).
en.meaning:
Property and possession (sections 2(2) and 2(11))

Rule. Property is the general property in the goods. Delivery is the voluntary transfer of possession. The Act treats them as different things: section 25(1) says that even after delivery to a buyer or carrier, the property does not pass until conditions imposed by the seller are fulfilled. Section 26 says the goods are at the buyer's risk once the property passes, whether delivery has been made or not.

Example. Kavya hands a laptop to Lalit to try for a week. Lalit has possession. Whether the property has passed depends on the rules in section 24 and on the intention of the parties.

Unascertained goods (sections 18 and 23)

Rule. No property passes in unascertained goods unless and until they are ascertained (section 18). Under section 23(1), in a contract for unascertained or future goods by description, the property passes when goods of that description and in a deliverable state are unconditionally appropriated to the contract, by the seller with the buyer's assent or by the buyer with the seller's assent. Under section 23(2), delivery to the buyer or to a carrier or other bailee for transmission, without reserving the right of disposal, is deemed unconditional appropriation.

Example. Manoj agrees to sell Nita 100 kg of rice out of a godown full of rice. Until the 100 kg is set apart for Nita with her assent, no property passes (section 18). When Manoj puts 100 kg in sacks marked for Nita, and she agrees, the property passes (section 23(1)).

Intention of the parties (section 19)

Rule. For specific or ascertained goods, the property passes when the parties intend. Regard is had to the contract's terms, the parties' conduct and the circumstances. Unless a different intention appears, sections 20 to 24 are the rules for finding that intention.

Specific goods (sections 20, 21 and 22)

Rule. Three rules apply to specific goods.

Unconditional contract, goods in a deliverable state: the property passes when the contract is made, even if payment or delivery is postponed (section 20). Seller bound to put the goods in a deliverable state: the property does not pass until he does so and the buyer has notice (section 21). Goods in a deliverable state, but the seller must weigh, measure, test or do some other act to ascertain the price: the property does not pass until it is done and the buyer has notice (section 22).

Example. Om buys a particular secondhand bike, in running order, under an unconditional contract. He will pay and collect it next week. The property passes to Om when the contract is made (section 20).

Goods on approval or on sale or return (section 24)

Rule. The property passes (a) when the buyer signifies approval or acceptance or does any other act adopting the transaction, or (b) if he does not, but keeps the goods without giving notice of rejection, when the fixed time for return expires, or, if no time was fixed, when a reasonable time expires.

Example. A jeweller sends a necklace to Pooja on approval with no time fixed. Pooja keeps it, gives no notice of rejection, and a reasonable time passes. The property passes to her (section 24(b)).

Reservation of the right of disposal (section 25)

Rule. The seller may reserve the right of disposal until certain conditions are fulfilled. The property then does not pass until they are fulfilled, even if the goods are delivered to the buyer or a carrier. Where goods are shipped or delivered to a railway for carriage and the bill of lading or railway receipt makes them deliverable to the order of the seller or his agent, the seller is prima facie deemed to reserve the right (section 25(2)). If the seller sends the bill of exchange with the bill of lading or railway receipt and the buyer does not honour the bill, he must return the document, and if he wrongfully retains it the property does not pass to him (section 25(3)).

Risk (section 26)

Rule. Unless otherwise agreed, the goods are at the seller's risk until the property passes, and at the buyer's risk afterwards, whether or not delivery has been made. If delivery is delayed by the fault of either party, that party bears any loss which would not have occurred but for the fault. The section does not affect the duties of either as a bailee of the other's goods.

When does the property pass? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Are the goods unascertained? No property passes until they are ascertained (section 18). Then it passes on unconditional appropriation with assent (section 23). 2. Are they specific or ascertained goods? The property passes when the parties intend (section 19). The rules in sections 20 to 22 help find that intention. 3. Sent on approval or sale or return? The property passes under section 24. 4. Has the seller reserved the right of disposal? The property does not pass until the conditions are fulfilled (section 25). 5. Who bears the risk? The owner of the property, unless otherwise agreed (section 26).
keyPoints: Unascertained goods: no property until ascertained (section 18). Passes on unconditional appropriation with assent (section 23). Specific goods: property passes when the parties intend (section 19). Section 20: unconditional contract, deliverable state, property passes when the contract is made. Sections 21 and 22: property passes after the seller's act and notice to the buyer. Section 24: approval or sale or return, property passes on adoption or on expiry of time. Section 25: the seller may reserve the right of disposal. Section 26: risk prima facie passes with the property.

selfTest.q: 1. When does property pass in unascertained goods?
selfTest.a: Not until they are ascertained (section 18). Then on unconditional appropriation with assent (section 23). 2. What is section 20? For an unconditional contract for specific goods in a deliverable state, the property passes when the contract is made, even if payment or delivery is postponed. 3. When does property pass in goods on approval? When the buyer signifies approval or acceptance or adopts the transaction, or when the fixed or a reasonable time expires without notice of rejection (section 24). 4. Who bears the risk unless otherwise agreed? The seller until the property passes, the buyer afterwards, whether delivery has been made or not (section 26).

te.inOneMinute: "Property" in goods means the general property in them, not merely a special property (section 2(11)). "Delivery" means voluntary transfer of possession (section 2(2)). A seller who gives possession does not necessarily pass the property, and the Act has separate rules for when the property passes to the buyer. No property passes in unascertained goods until they are ascertained (section 18). Otherwise the property passes when the parties intend it to pass, judged from the contract, conduct and circumstances (section 19). Sections 20 to 24 give the rules for specific goods, unascertained goods and goods on approval. Section 25 allows the seller to reserve the right of disposal. Risk prima facie passes with the property (section 26).
te.meaning: Property and possession (sections 2(2) and 2(11)) Rule. Property is the general property in the goods. Delivery is the voluntary transfer of possession. The Act treats them as different things: section 25(1) says that even after delivery to a buyer or carrier, the property does not pass until conditions imposed by the seller are fulfilled. Section 26 says the goods are at the buyer's risk once the property passes, whether delivery has been made or not. Example. Kavya hands a laptop to Lalit to try for a week. Lalit has possession. Whether the property has passed depends on the rules in section 24 and on the intention of the parties. Unascertained goods (sections 18 and 23) Rule. No property passes in unascertained goods unless and until they are ascertained (section 18). Under section 23(1), in a contract for unascertained or future goods by description, the property passes when goods of that description and in a deliverable state are unconditionally appropriated to the contract, by the seller with the buyer's assent or by the buyer with the seller's assent. Under section 23(2), delivery to the buyer or to a carrier or other bailee for transmission, without reserving the right of disposal, is deemed unconditional appropriation. Example. Manoj agrees to sell Nita 100 kg of rice out of a godown full of rice. Until the 100 kg is set apart for Nita with her assent, no property passes (section 18). When Manoj puts 100 kg in sacks marked for Nita, and she agrees, the property passes (section 23(1)). Intention of the parties (section 19) Rule. For specific or ascertained goods, the property passes when the parties intend. Regard is had to the contract's terms, the parties' conduct and the circumstances. Unless a different intention appears, sections 20 to 24 are the rules for finding that intention. Specific goods (sections 20, 21 and 22) Rule. Three rules apply to specific goods. Unconditional contract, goods in a deliverable state: the property passes when the contract is made, even if payment or delivery is postponed (section 20). Seller bound to put the goods in a deliverable state: the property does not pass until he does so and the buyer has notice (section 21). Goods in a deliverable state, but the seller must weigh, measure, test or do some other act to ascertain the price: the property does not pass until it is done and the buyer has notice (section 22). Example. Om buys a particular secondhand bike, in running order, under an unconditional contract. He will pay and collect it next week. The property passes to Om when the contract is made (section 20). Goods on approval or on sale or return (section 24) Rule. The property passes (a) when the buyer signifies approval or acceptance or does any other act adopting the transaction, or (b) if he does not, but keeps the goods without giving notice of rejection, when the fixed time for return expires, or, if no time was fixed, when a reasonable time expires. Example. A jeweller sends a necklace to Pooja on approval with no time fixed. Pooja keeps it, gives no notice of rejection, and a reasonable time passes. The property passes to her (section 24(b)). Reservation of the right of disposal (section 25) Rule. The seller may reserve the right of disposal until certain conditions are fulfilled. The property then does not pass until they are fulfilled, even if the goods are delivered to the buyer or a carrier. Where goods are shipped or delivered to a railway for carriage and the bill of lading or railway receipt makes them deliverable to the order of the seller or his agent, the seller is prima facie deemed to reserve the right (section 25(2)). If the seller sends the bill of exchange with the bill of lading or railway receipt and the buyer does not honour the bill, he must return the document, and if he wrongfully retains it the property does not pass to him (section 25(3)). Risk (section 26) Rule. Unless otherwise agreed, the goods are at the seller's risk until the property passes, and at the buyer's risk afterwards, whether or not delivery has been made. If delivery is delayed by the fault of either party, that party bears any loss which would not have occurred but for the fault. The section does not affect the duties of either as a bailee of the other's goods. When does the property pass? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Are the goods unascertained? No property passes until they are ascertained (section 18). Then it passes on unconditional appropriation with assent (section 23). 2. Are they specific or ascertained goods? The property passes when the parties intend (section 19). The rules in sections 20 to 22 help find that intention. 3. Sent on approval or sale or return? The property passes under section 24. 4. Has the seller reserved the right of disposal? The property does not pass until the conditions are fulfilled (section 25). 5. Who bears the risk? The owner of the property, unless otherwise agreed (section 26).
keyPoints: Unascertained goods: no property until ascertained (section 18). Passes on unconditional appropriation with assent (section 23). Specific goods: property passes when the parties intend (section 19). Section 20: unconditional contract, deliverable state, property passes when the contract is made. Sections 21 and 22: property passes after the seller's act and notice to the buyer. Section 24: approval or sale or return, property passes on adoption or on expiry of time. Section 25: the seller may reserve the right of disposal. Section 26: risk prima facie passes with the property.

law-of-contract-ii-u4-t4.subtitle: Sections 31, 32 and 41 to 44 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930

en.inOneMinute: It is the duty of the seller to deliver the goods and of the buyer to accept and pay for them, in accordance with the terms of the contract of sale (section 31). Unless otherwise agreed, delivery and payment are concurrent conditions (section 32). The buyer has a right to a reasonable opportunity of examining the goods (section 41). He is deemed to have accepted them in the cases listed in section 42, and is not bound to return rejected goods (section 43). If he neglects or refuses to take delivery, he is liable for loss and the cost of custody (section 44). Key points for the answer: the duties in sections 31 and 32, then each right with its section.
en.meaning:
Duties of seller and buyer (section 31)

Rule. The seller must deliver the goods and the buyer must accept and pay for them, in accordance with the terms of the contract.

Payment and delivery together (section 32)

Rule. Unless otherwise agreed, delivery and payment are concurrent conditions. The seller must be ready and willing to give possession in exchange for the price. The buyer must be ready and willing to pay the price in exchange for possession.

Example. Naveen agrees to sell a cycle to Omkar for Rs 5,000. Naveen need not hand over the cycle unless Omkar is ready and willing to pay. Omkar need not pay unless Naveen is ready and willing to give possession.

Examining the goods (section 41)

Rule. A buyer who has not previously examined the goods is not deemed to have accepted them until he has had a reasonable opportunity of examining them to see whether they conform to the contract. Unless otherwise agreed, the seller who tenders delivery must, on request, give that opportunity.

Acceptance (section 42)

Rule. The buyer is deemed to have accepted the goods in any of three cases.

He intimates to the seller that he has accepted them. The goods have been delivered to him and he does an act in relation to them that is inconsistent with the seller's ownership. After a reasonable time he retains the goods without intimating to the seller that he has rejected them.

Rejected goods (section 43)

Rule. Unless otherwise agreed, a buyer who has the right to refuse the goods and does so is not bound to return them. It is enough that he intimates to the seller that he refuses to accept them.

Buyer's neglect or refusal to take delivery (section 44)

Rule. If the seller is ready and willing to deliver and asks the buyer to take delivery, and the buyer does not do so within a reasonable time, he is liable for any loss caused by his neglect or refusal and for a reasonable charge for the care and custody of the goods. The seller's rights are not affected where the neglect or refusal amounts to repudiation of the contract.

Example. Pooja has bought 50 chairs. The seller is ready to deliver and asks her to take them. She does not collect them for two months. She is liable for the seller's loss and for a reasonable charge for keeping the chairs (section 44).

Duties, examination, acceptance How to read this: start at the top. 1. Duties (section 31) and concurrent conditions (section 32) Seller delivers, buyer accepts and pays, each ready and willing in exchange for the other, unless otherwise agreed. 2. Goods delivered but not yet examined (section 41) No acceptance until a reasonable opportunity to examine. 3. Acceptance (section 42) By intimation, by an act inconsistent with the seller's ownership, or by retaining beyond a reasonable time without intimating rejection. 4. Rejection (section 43) and neglect to take delivery (section 44) A buyer who rightly rejects need not return the goods; a buyer who neglects delivery pays for loss and custody.
keyPoints: Seller delivers, buyer accepts and pays, as the contract says (section 31). Delivery and payment are concurrent unless otherwise agreed (section 32). No acceptance without a reasonable opportunity to examine (section 41). Acceptance: intimation, an act inconsistent with the seller's ownership, or retention beyond a reasonable time (section 42). A buyer who rightly rejects need not return the goods (section 43). Neglect to take delivery: liable for loss and custody charges (section 44).
