law-of-contract-ii-u5-t9.subtitle: Sections 18 to 29 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932

en.inOneMinute: A partner is the agent of the firm for the purposes of the business of the firm (section 18). The act of a partner done to carry on, in the usual way, business of the kind carried on by the firm binds the firm. This authority is called his implied authority (section 19(1)). Section 19(2) lists acts that implied authority does not cover, unless a usage or custom of trade is to the contrary. The partners may extend or restrict implied authority by contract, but a restriction does not bind a third person who does not know of it or does not know or believe the partner to be a partner (section 20). Every partner is liable, jointly with all the others and also severally, for all acts of the firm done while he is a partner (section 25). Key points for the answer: sections 18 and 19, then 20 to 22 and 25.
en.meaning:
Partner as agent and implied authority (sections 18 and 19)

Rule. A partner is the agent of the firm for the purposes of its business. An act of a partner done to carry on, in the usual way, business of the kind carried on by the firm binds the firm. This is his implied authority. Unless a usage or custom of trade is to the contrary, implied authority does not cover eight acts: submitting a dispute to arbitration; opening a bank account in his own name for the firm; compromising or relinquishing a claim; withdrawing a suit; admitting liability in a suit against the firm; acquiring immovable property for the firm; transferring the firm's immovable property; and entering into partnership on behalf of the firm.

Example. Rakesh is a partner in a firm that sells groceries. He buys rice from a wholesaler for the shop. This is an act done to carry on the firm's business in the usual way, so it binds the firm (section 19(1)). If he sold the firm's shop building, that is a transfer of immovable property, which implied authority does not cover (section 19(2)).

Extension and restriction (section 20)

Rule. The partners may by contract extend or restrict a partner's implied authority. But an act within his implied authority still binds the firm unless the person dealing with him knows of the restriction or does not know or believe him to be a partner.

Emergency (section 21)

Rule. A partner may do, in an emergency, all such acts to protect the firm from loss as a person of ordinary prudence would do in his own case in similar circumstances, and such acts bind the firm.

Mode of binding the firm (section 22)

Rule. To bind a firm, an act or instrument must be done or executed in the firm name, or in another manner expressing or implying an intention to bind the firm.

Admissions and notice (sections 23 and 24)

Rule. A partner's admission or representation about the affairs of the firm, made in the ordinary course of business, is evidence against the firm (section 23). Notice to a partner who habitually acts in the business operates as notice to the firm, except in a fraud on the firm committed by or with the consent of that partner (section 24).

Liability for acts of the firm (sections 25 to 27)

Rule. Every partner is liable jointly with all the others and also severally for all acts of the firm done while he is a partner (section 25). The firm is liable to the same extent as the partner for a third party's loss or injury, or a penalty, caused by a partner's wrongful act or omission in the ordinary course of business or with his partners' authority (section 26). The firm must make good money or property misapplied by a partner acting within apparent authority, or misapplied by any partner while in the firm's custody (section 27).

Example. A firm owes a supplier Rs 1,00,000 for goods bought while Sana and Tariq were partners. The supplier may claim the whole amount from Sana alone, from Tariq alone, or from both together (section 25).

Holding out (section 28)

Rule. A person who by words or conduct represents himself, or knowingly permits himself to be represented, as a partner in a firm is liable as a partner to anyone who has on the faith of the representation given credit to the firm. It does not matter whether he knows that the representation has reached the person giving credit. Continued use of the old firm name after a partner's death does not itself make his legal representative or estate liable for later acts (section 28(2)).

Rights of a transferee of a partner's interest (section 29)

Rule. A transferee of a partner's interest, absolute or by mortgage or charge, cannot interfere in the business, require accounts or inspect the books while the firm continues. He is entitled only to the transferring partner's share of profits. On dissolution, or when the transferring partner ceases to be a partner, he is entitled against the remaining partners to the share of the assets to which the transferring partner is entitled, and to an account from the date of the dissolution.

Does the partner's act bind the firm? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Was the act done to carry on, in the usual way, business of the kind the firm carries on (section 19(1))? If yes, it binds the firm, if done in the firm name or in a manner implying an intention to bind it (section 22). 2. Is it one of the eight acts in section 19(2), with no usage or custom of trade to the contrary? Then implied authority does not cover it. 3. Did the partners restrict his authority (section 20)? The act still binds the firm unless the third person knows of the restriction or does not know or believe him to be a partner. 4. Was it an emergency act to protect the firm from loss (section 21)? Such acts bind the firm.
keyPoints: A partner is the agent of the firm (section 18). His acts in the usual course of business bind the firm: implied authority (section 19(1)). Eight acts are outside implied authority unless usage or custom says otherwise (section 19(2)). A restriction by the partners does not bind a third person who does not know of it or does not know or believe him to be a partner (section 20). Emergency acts bind the firm (section 21). Act must be in the firm name or imply an intention to bind (section 22). Partners are liable jointly and severally (section 25). The firm is liable for a partner's wrongful acts in the ordinary course (section 26). Holding out makes a person liable as a partner (section 28).

On dissolution, or when the transferring partner ceases to be a partner, he is entitled against the remaining partners to the share of the assets to which the transferring partner is entitled, and to an account from the date of the dissolution. Does the partner's act bind the firm? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Was the act done to carry on, in the usual way, business of the kind the firm carries on (section 19(1))? If yes, it binds the firm, if done in the firm name or in a manner implying an intention to bind it (section 22). 2. Is it one of the eight acts in section 19(2), with no usage or custom of trade to the contrary? Then implied authority does not cover it. 3. Did the partners restrict his authority (section 20)? The act still binds the firm unless the third person knows of the restriction or does not know or believe him to be a partner. 4. Was it an emergency act to protect the firm from loss (section 21)? Such acts bind the firm.
keyPoints: A partner is the agent of the firm (section 18). His acts in the usual course of business bind the firm: implied authority (section 19(1)). Eight acts are outside implied authority unless usage or custom says otherwise (section 19(2)). A restriction by the partners does not bind a third person who does not know of it or does not know or believe him to be a partner (section 20). Emergency acts bind the firm (section 21). Act must be in the firm name or imply an intention to bind (section 22). Partners are liable jointly and severally (section 25). The firm is liable for a partner's wrongful acts in the ordinary course (section 26). Holding out makes a person liable as a partner (section 28).

selfTest.q: 1. What is implied authority?
selfTest.a: The authority of a partner to bind the firm by an act done to carry on, in the usual way, business of the kind carried on by the firm (section 19(1)). 2. What is a transferee of a partner's interest entitled to while the firm continues? Only the transferring partner's share of profits (section 29(1)).

law-of-contract-ii-u5-t13.subtitle: Sections 39 to 55 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932

en.inOneMinute: The dissolution of partnership between all the partners of a firm is called the "dissolution of the firm" (section 39). A firm may be dissolved by agreement (section 40), compulsorily (section 41), on the happening of certain contingencies (section 42), by notice in a partnership at will (section 43), or by the Court (section 44). After dissolution, partners remain liable to third parties until public notice is given (section 45). Every partner is entitled to have the firm's property applied in payment of its debts and the surplus distributed (section 46). The authority of partners continues only so far as needed to wind up (section 47). Accounts are settled by the rules in section 48. Sections 49 to 55 deal with joint and separate debts, personal profits, return of premium, fraud, use of the firm name, restraint of trade and goodwill.
en.meaning:
Modes of dissolution (sections 40 to 44)

Rule. A firm may be dissolved in these five ways.

By agreement: with the consent of all the partners or in accordance with a contract between them (section 40). Compulsorily: by the adjudication of all the partners, or all but one, as insolvent; or by an event that makes the business, or carrying it on in partnership, unlawful. Illegality of one of several separate undertakings does not of itself dissolve the firm for the lawful ones (section 41). On contingencies, subject to contract: expiry of a fixed term; completion of the adventure or undertaking; death of a partner; adjudication of a partner as an insolvent (section 42). By notice in a partnership at will: any partner gives written notice to all the other partners. The firm is dissolved from the date in the notice, or if none is mentioned, from the date the notice is communicated (section 43). By the Court, at the suit of a partner, on the seven grounds in section 44(a) to (g): unsound mind of a partner; permanent incapacity of a partner other than the one suing; conduct prejudicial to the business; wilful or persistent breach of agreements or conduct making it not reasonably practicable to carry on in partnership; transfer of the whole interest to a third party or its being charged or sold; business cannot be carried on save at a loss; and any ground that makes it just and equitable.

Example. Anwar and Bhavna agree in writing to run a shop for five years. At the end of five years, the firm is dissolved by the expiry of the fixed term, subject to their contract (section 42(a)).

Liability after dissolution (section 45)

Rule. After dissolution, the partners remain liable to third parties for acts that would have been acts of the firm if done before dissolution, until public notice of the dissolution is given. The estate of a partner who dies or is adjudicated insolvent, and a partner who retired without being known to the third party to be a partner, are not liable for acts after the date they cease to be partners. Any partner may give the notice.

Winding up and continuing authority (sections 46 and 47)

Rule. Every partner or his representative is entitled to have the firm's property applied in paying its debts and liabilities, and the surplus distributed according to the partners' rights (section 46). The partners' authority to bind the firm, and their mutual rights and obligations, continue after dissolution only so far as necessary to wind up and to complete unfinished transactions. The firm is never bound by the acts of a partner adjudicated insolvent (section 47).

Settlement of accounts (sections 48 and 49)

Rule. Subject to the partners' agreement, section 48 sets the rules. Losses, including capital deficiencies, are paid first out of profits, next out of capital, and lastly by the partners individually in the profit-sharing proportions. The assets, including sums contributed by partners to make up capital deficiencies, are applied in this order: debts to third parties; each partner's advances, rateably; each partner's capital, rateably; the residue, divided in the profit-sharing proportions. Where there are joint debts of the firm and separate debts of a partner, the firm's property goes first to the firm's debts, with any surplus applied to the separate debts of each partner. A partner's separate property goes first to his separate debts and any surplus to the firm's debts (section 49).

Example. On dissolution, a firm's assets are Rs 5,00,000. It owes third parties Rs 2,00,000. Partner Asha advanced Rs 50,000 as a loan to the firm, and the capital contributed was Rs 2,00,000. In order: Rs 2,00,000 to third parties; Rs 50,000 to Asha as advances; then capital; then the residue in profit-sharing proportions (section 48(b)).

Personal profits, premium, fraud, firm name, restraint, goodwill (sections 50 to 55)

Rule. These sections do the following.

Section 50: subject to contract, a surviving partner or a deceased partner's representatives must account for personal profits (section 16(a)) from transactions after dissolution by death and before the affairs are wound up. Section 51: a partner who paid a premium for a fixed term is entitled to its repayment, or a reasonable part, if the firm is dissolved early otherwise than by a partner's death, unless the dissolution is mainly due to his misconduct or follows an agreement with no provision for return. Section 52: where a partnership contract is rescinded for fraud or misrepresentation, the party entitled to rescind has a lien on the surplus or assets for sums paid for a share and capital contributed, may rank as a creditor for payments towards the firm's debts, and is indemnified by the guilty partner or partners against all the firm's debts. Section 53: after dissolution, unless the contract says otherwise, each partner may restrain another from carrying on a similar business in the firm name, or from using the firm's property for his own benefit, until the affairs are wound up. A partner who has bought the goodwill may still use the firm name. Section 54: partners may agree that some or all will not carry on a similar business within a specified period or local limits, valid if reasonable, notwithstanding section 27 of the Contract Act. Section 55: goodwill is included in the assets and may be sold. After its sale a partner may carry on a competing business and advertise it, but, subject to agreement with the buyer, may not use the firm name, represent himself as carrying on the firm's business, or solicit its old customers. An agreement with the buyer not to carry on a similar business within specified limits is valid if reasonable.

How can a firm be dissolved? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Do all the partners consent, or does the contract provide for it? Dissolution by agreement (section 40). 2. Have all (or all but one) been adjudicated insolvent, or has the business become unlawful? Compulsory dissolution (section 41). 3. Has the term expired, the undertaking been completed, or a partner died or been adjudicated insolvent (subject to contract)? Dissolution on contingencies (section 42). 4. Is it a partnership at will? Any partner may dissolve by written notice to all (section 43). 5. Is there a ground in section 44(a) to (g)? A partner may sue and the Court may dissolve the firm.
keyPoints: Dissolution of the firm: dissolution of partnership between all the partners (section 39). Five modes: agreement (40), compulsory (41), contingencies subject to contract (42), notice if at will (43), Court (44). Partners are liable to third parties until public notice (section 45). Authority continues only for winding up (section 47). Order of payment: third-party debts, advances, capital, residue (section 48(b)). Goodwill is an asset and may be sold (section 55).

selfTest.q: 1. Name the five modes of dissolution. By agreement, compulsorily, on certain contingencies, by notice in a partnership at will, and by the Court (sections 40 to 44). 2. When can a partner dissolve a firm by notice?
selfTest.a: Where the partnership is at will, by written notice to all the other partners (section 43). 3. In what order are assets applied on dissolution? Debts to third parties, advances, capital, then the residue in profit-sharing proportions (section 48(b)). 4. Until when do partners remain liable to third parties after dissolution? Until public notice of the dissolution is given (section 45).

A partner may sue and the Court may dissolve the firm.

hi.inOneMinute: The dissolution of partnership between all the partners of a firm is called the "dissolution of the firm" (section 39). A firm may be dissolved by agreement (section 40), compulsorily (section 41), on the happening of certain contingencies (section 42), by notice in a partnership at will (section 43), or by the Court (section 44). After dissolution, partners remain liable to third parties until public notice is given (section 45). Every partner is entitled to have the firm's property applied in payment of its debts and the surplus distributed (section 46). The authority of partners continues only so far as needed to wind up (section 47). Accounts are settled by the rules in section 48. Sections 49 to 55 deal with joint and separate debts, personal profits, return of premium, fraud, use of the firm name, restraint of trade and goodwill.
hi.meaning: Modes of dissolution (sections 40 to 44) Rule. A firm may be dissolved in these five ways. By agreement: with the consent of all the partners or in accordance with a contract between them (section 40). Compulsorily: by the adjudication of all the partners, or all but one, as insolvent; or by an event that makes the business, or carrying it on in partnership, unlawful. Illegality of one of several separate undertakings does not of itself dissolve the firm for the lawful ones (section 41). On contingencies, subject to contract: expiry of a fixed term; completion of the adventure or undertaking; death of a partner; adjudication of a partner as an insolvent (section 42). By notice in a partnership at will: any partner gives written notice to all the other partners. The firm is dissolved from the date in the notice, or if none is mentioned, from the date the notice is communicated (section 43). By the Court, at the suit of a partner, on the seven grounds in section 44(a) to (g): unsound mind of a partner; permanent incapacity of a partner other than the one suing; conduct prejudicial to the business; wilful or persistent breach of agreements or conduct making it not reasonably practicable to carry on in partnership; transfer of the whole interest to a third party or its being charged or sold; business cannot be carried on save at a loss; and any ground that makes it just and equitable. Example. Anwar and Bhavna agree in writing to run a shop for five years. At the end of five years, the firm is dissolved by the expiry of the fixed term, subject to their contract (section 42(a)). Liability after dissolution (section 45) Rule. After dissolution, the partners remain liable to third parties for acts that would have been acts of the firm if done before dissolution, until public notice of the dissolution is given. The estate of a partner who dies or is adjudicated insolvent, and a partner who retired without being known to the third party to be a partner, are not liable for acts after the date they cease to be partners. Any partner may give the notice. Winding up and continuing authority (sections 46 and 47) Rule. Every partner or his representative is entitled to have the firm's property applied in paying its debts and liabilities, and the surplus distributed according to the partners' rights (section 46). The partners' authority to bind the firm, and their mutual rights and obligations, continue after dissolution only so far as necessary to wind up and to complete unfinished transactions. The firm is never bound by the acts of a partner adjudicated insolvent (section 47). Settlement of accounts (sections 48 and 49) Rule. Subject to the partners' agreement, section 48 sets the rules. Losses, including capital deficiencies, are paid first out of profits, next out of capital, and lastly by the partners individually in the profit-sharing proportions. The assets, including sums contributed by partners to make up capital deficiencies, are applied in this order: debts to third parties; each partner's advances, rateably; each partner's capital, rateably; the residue, divided in the profit-sharing proportions. law-of-contract-ii-u5-t14.subtitle: Sections 2, 3 to 8, 11, 12, 14, 23, 24, 26 to 30, 32, 33 and 42 of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008

en.inOneMinute: A limited liability partnership (LLP) is a partnership formed and registered under the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008 (section 2(1)(n)). It is a body corporate and a legal entity separate from its partners, with perpetual succession (section 3). The Indian Partnership Act, 1932 does not apply to it, save as otherwise provided (section 4). It needs at least two partners (section 6) and at least two designated partners who are individuals, at least one resident in India (section 7). It is incorporated by filing an incorporation document with the Registrar (sections 11 and 12). The obligations of the LLP are its own, and a partner is not personally liable for them solely by being a partner (sections 27 and 28), except in fraud (section 30).
en.meaning:
Nature of an LLP (sections 2, 3, 4 and 14)

Rule. An LLP is a body corporate and a legal entity separate from its partners, with perpetual succession. On registration it can sue and be sued, own property, have a common seal, and do what bodies corporate may do. The Partnership Act does not apply to it, save as otherwise provided.

Example. Three friends register an LLP to run a design studio. The studio, and not the friends personally, owns its computers and signs its contracts. If one friend leaves, the LLP continues (section 3(3)).

Partners and designated partners (sections 5 to 8)

Rule. Any individual or body corporate may be a partner, except an individual of unsound mind found by a Court, an undischarged insolvent, or one with a pending application to be adjudicated insolvent. At least two partners are required. At least two designated partners who are individuals are required, one resident in India. A designated partner is responsible for the LLP's compliance and liable to the penalties imposed on the LLP for contraventions.

Incorporation (sections 11 and 12)

Rule. Two or more persons associated for a lawful business with a view to profit subscribe their names to an incorporation document, filed with the Registrar of the State of the registered office, with a statement by an advocate, Company Secretary, Chartered Accountant or Cost Accountant, and a subscriber, that the requirements are complied with. The Registrar registers within fourteen days and gives a certificate which is conclusive evidence of incorporation.

Mutual rights and exit (sections 23 and 24)

Rule. The LLP agreement governs mutual rights and duties, and is filed with the Registrar. Without agreement on a matter, the First Schedule applies. A partner may leave by agreement or on thirty days' written notice, and a former partner is still treated as a partner towards a person who has no notice, unless notice was delivered to the Registrar.

Liability (sections 26 to 30)

Rule. A partner is the agent of the LLP and not of other partners. The LLP is bound by acts of a partner except where he has no authority and the other person knows it. The LLP's obligations are its own, met out of its property. A partner is not personally liable for them solely by being a partner, nor for another partner's wrongful act, but is liable for his own. Holding out as a partner creates liability. In fraud, the liability of the LLP and of the partners who acted is unlimited.

Example. A partner of an LLP signs a contract with a supplier without any authority, and the supplier knows he has none. The LLP is not bound (section 27(1)).

Contributions and transfer (sections 32, 33 and 42)

Rule. A contribution may be money, property, benefits or services. The obligation to contribute follows the LLP agreement, and a creditor who relied on it, without notice of a compromise between partners, may enforce the original obligation. A partner's share of profits and losses is transferable, but the transfer does not by itself end his partnership or the LLP and gives the transferee no right in management or information.

Who is liable for an LLP's debt? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Is it an obligation of the LLP, in contract or otherwise (section 27(3))? It is solely the LLP's obligation, met out of its property (section 27(4)). 2. Is a partner being sued only because he is a partner (section 28(1))? He is not personally liable. 3. Did the partner commit a wrongful act or omission himself (section 28(2))? He is liable for his own act, not for another partner's. 4. Was there intent to defraud creditors or a fraudulent purpose (section 30)? Liability of the LLP and the partners who acted is unlimited.
keyPoints: An LLP is a body corporate and a separate legal entity with perpetual succession (section 3). The Partnership Act does not apply, save as otherwise provided (section 4). At least two partners (section 6); at least two designated partners who are individuals, one resident in India (section 7). Incorporated by registration with the Registrar; the certificate is conclusive evidence (section 12). Obligations are the LLP's own; partners are not personally liable solely as partners (sections 27 and 28); unlimited liability in fraud (section 30). The LLP agreement governs, with the First Schedule as default (section 23).

hi.inOneMinute: A limited liability partnership (LLP) is a partnership formed and registered under the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008 (section 2(1)(n)). It is a body corporate and a legal entity separate from its partners, with perpetual succession (section 3). The Indian Partnership Act, 1932 does not apply to it, save as otherwise provided (section 4). It needs at least two partners (section 6) and at least two designated partners who are individuals, at least one resident in India (section 7). It is incorporated by filing an incorporation document with the Registrar (sections 11 and 12). The obligations of the LLP are its own, and a partner is not personally liable for them solely by being a partner (sections 27 and 28), except in fraud (section 30).
hi.meaning: Nature of an LLP (sections 2, 3, 4 and 14) Rule. An LLP is a body corporate and a legal entity separate from its partners, with perpetual succession. On registration it can sue and be sued, own property, have a common seal, and do what bodies corporate may do. The Partnership Act does not apply to it, save as otherwise provided. Example. Three friends register an LLP to run a design studio. The studio, and not the friends personally, owns its computers and signs its contracts. If one friend leaves, the LLP continues (section 3(3)). Partners and designated partners (sections 5 to 8) Rule. Any individual or body corporate may be a partner, except an individual of unsound mind found by a Court, an undischarged insolvent, or one with a pending application to be adjudicated insolvent. At least two partners are required. At least two designated partners who are individuals are required, one resident in India. A designated partner is responsible for the LLP's compliance and liable to the penalties imposed on the LLP for contraventions. Incorporation (sections 11 and 12) Rule. Two or more persons associated for a lawful business with a view to profit subscribe their names to an incorporation document, filed with the Registrar of the State of the registered office, with a statement by an advocate, Company Secretary, Chartered Accountant or Cost Accountant, and a subscriber, that the requirements are complied with. The Registrar registers within fourteen days and gives a certificate which is conclusive evidence of incorporation. Mutual rights and exit (sections 23 and 24) Rule. The LLP agreement governs mutual rights and duties, and is filed with the Registrar. Without agreement on a matter, the First Schedule applies. A partner may leave by agreement or on thirty days' written notice, and a former partner is still treated as a partner towards a person who has no notice, unless notice was delivered to the Registrar. Liability (sections 26 to 30) Rule. A partner is the agent of the LLP and not of other partners. The LLP is bound by acts of a partner except where he has no authority and the other person knows it. The LLP's obligations are its own, met out of its property. A partner is not personally liable for them solely by being a partner, nor for another partner's wrongful act, but is liable for his own. Holding out as a partner creates liability. In fraud, the liability of the LLP and of the partners who acted is unlimited. Example. A partner of an LLP signs a contract with a supplier without any authority, and the supplier knows he has none. The LLP is not bound (section 27(1)). Contributions and transfer (sections 32, 33 and 42) Rule. A contribution may be money, property, benefits or services. The obligation to contribute follows the LLP agreement, and a creditor who relied on it, without notice of a compromise between partners, may enforce the original obligation. A partner's share of profits and losses is transferable, but the transfer does not by itself end his partnership or the LLP and gives the transferee no right in management or information. Who is liable for an LLP's debt? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Is it an obligation of the LLP, in contract or otherwise (section 27(3))? It is solely the LLP's obligation, met out of its property (section 27(4)). 2. Is a partner being sued only because he is a partner (section 28(1))? He is not personally liable. 3. Did the partner commit a wrongful act or omission himself (section 28(2))? He is liable for his own act, not for another partner's. 4. Was there intent to defraud creditors or a fraudulent purpose (section 30)? Liability of the LLP and the partners who acted is unlimited.

Obligations are the LLP's own; partners are not personally liable solely as partners (sections 27 and 28); unlimited liability in fraud (section 30).
